title: The Pontic Alps: a wall between the coast and the plateau
summary: The Pontic mountains (Strabo's Paryadres and Skydises; today's Doğu Karadeniz Dağları) run parallel to the coast from the Halys to the Akampsis (Çoruh), rising to 3,937 m at Kaçkar. The coast strip is narrow and cut by short, steep valleys, so the sea was the easiest road between the Greek towns. A few passes link the coast to the high, dry Armenian plateau behind: Zigana (c. 2,025 m) on the Trapezous–Gümüşhane–Bayburt–Erzurum road (later the Tabriz caravan route), Soğanlı, Ovit and Kop. The Ten Thousand met this wall from the plateau side in winter 401/400.

title: The rivers: Halys, Iris, Lykos, Thermodon, Akampsis, Pyxites
summary: The Halys (Kızılırmak), Anatolia's longest river, had been the Lydian–Median frontier (Herodotus 1.72) and reaches the sea in the Bafra delta. The Iris (Yeşilırmak) flows past Komana and Amaseia, takes in the Lykos (Kelkit) from Neokaisareia's valley, and crosses the Themiskyra plain; the Thermodon (Terme) is the Amazons' river. The Akampsis (Çoruh) breaks through the mountains to the sea south of Batumi. These valleys are the only easy routes inland, and their deltas are the only wide plains of the coast. Xenophon gives widths for some of them: Thermodon and Iris 3 plethra each, Halys at least 2 stades (5.6.9).
disputed: The name Pyxites. Arrian (Periplus 7.4) places the Pyxites between the Prytanis and the Archabis, east of Rize, 90 stades from each. Pliny (NH 6.12) puts it 'in ora ante Trapezunta', on the coast 'before Trapezus', which can be read as near the city. Only Arrian clearly puts it east of Rize.

title: Climate and resources
summary: The coast is the wettest part of Anatolia (Rize gets more than 2,000 mm of rain a year), with mild winters and thick forest up to the treeline; behind the mountains the plateau has long, snowy winters. Ancient writers prized its timber, fish (the bonito, pelamys, and dolphins: Strabo 12.3.19), iron (the Chalybes; Strabo's iron mines near Pharnakeia), silver (later Gümüşhane, 'silver house'), hazelnuts and cherries (Kerasous). The rhododendrons that cover the hills make the poisonous 'mad honey' that felled the Ten Thousand (Xen. 4.8.20–21) and Pompey's soldiers (Strabo 12.3.18).

title: Before the Greeks: villages on the coast
summary: The deltas and the Sinop peninsula were settled thousands of years before any Greek came. İkiztepe near Bafra, in the Halys delta, was a large Late Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age settlement known for its arsenical-copper metalwork; there were other mounds near Samsun (Dündartepe, Tekkeköy). Survey shows dense Late Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age settlement around Sinop (Koçak 2003), and Bronze Age material lies under Sinop's fortress (Doonan et al. 2016). The coast was neither empty nor unknown when the colonists arrived.
disputed: Dates of the İkiztepe levels vary between publications (roughly 4500–2000 BC).

title: Zalpa, the Hittites' city by the sea
summary: Old Hittite texts tell of Zalpa (Zalpuwa) 'on the sea', which most scholars put on the Black Sea near the Halys mouth. In the tale of the Queen of Kanesh her thirty sons were set adrift and washed up at Zalpa; Anitta of Kanesh and the early kings of Hattusa fought the city. It is the first named place on this coast in any written record.
disputed: Zalpa's site is not known; İkiztepe and other sites in the Bafra area have been proposed.

title: The Kaska, the Hittites' northern enemy
summary: From the 15th century BC Hittite texts name the Kaska: kingless tribal groups in the hills between the Hittite heartland and the Black Sea, roughly from Kastamonu to Samsun and Tokat. The prayer of Arnuwanda I and Asmunikal mourns the northern temples lost to them, among them the holy city of Nerik; letters from Tapikka (Maşat Höyük) record their raids. In Tudhaliya III's reign Kaska forces burned Hattusa itself (KBo 6.28). Hattusili III won back Nerik in the 13th century. The Kaska were also treaty partners, labourers and soldiers; after the Hittite collapse 4,000 'Kaskaeans and Urumaeans' submitted to Tiglath-Pileser I (c. 1114 BC). Then they vanish from the record.
disputed: Dates of the first Kaska texts depend on the Middle Hittite chronology.

title: Azzi-Hayasa in the north-east
summary: North-east of the Hittite Upper Land lay Hayasa, with Azzi, on the upper Euphrates and probably in the Çoruh basin, behind the Pontic mountains. Suppiluliuma I bound its king Huqqana by treaty and gave him his sister in marriage (CTH 42); Mursili II later campaigned there against Anniya of Azzi. The name Hayasa is often linked with the Armenians' own name, Hay; that link is possible but unproven.
disputed: The location is uncertain (some have placed Azzi on the coast near Trapezous), and the link between the names Hay and Hayasa is debated.

date_text: Mythical time (the generation before Troy); texts from the 5th c. BC on
title: The Amazons of Themiskyra on the Thermodon
summary: From the 5th century BC Greek tradition placed the Amazons' home in the plain of Themiskyra at the mouth of the Thermodon. Herakles came there for Hippolyte's girdle; Theseus carried off Antiope, and the Amazons invaded Attica; after a defeat at the Thermodon, captive Amazons sailed away and became mothers of the Sauromatians (Herodotus 4.110–117). In Homer the Amazons belong to Phrygia and Lycia (Iliad 3.189, 6.186). The Pontic setting is probably a later move, made as Greeks came to know this coast. Steppe graves of armed women give the story a distant historical echo (Mayor 2014).
disputed: When the Amazons were first placed on the Thermodon, in the 6th or the 5th century BC, is uncertain, and so is whether the story has any historical kernel.

title: The Argonauts sail along the Pontic coast
summary: The voyage of the Argo was an old story. Homer speaks of 'Argo, known to all', sailing from Aietes (Odyssey 12.69–72); Hesiod tells how Jason carried off Aietes' daughter after the labours set by Pelias (Theogony 992–1002); and Pindar brings the Argonauts to the Phasis and the Colchians (Pythian 4, 462 BC). The first full account that survives is Apollonius' Argonautica, about 250 BC. In its second book the Argo follows the south coast of the Black Sea from the Bosporus to Colchis. It passes the Symplegades and Thynias, the Mariandynoi at Heraclea, Sinope, the Halys and Iris, the Thermodon and the Amazons, the iron-working Chalybes, the Tibarenoi (whose men lie in bed when their wives give birth), the Mossynoikoi in their wooden towers, and the island of Ares (Aretias, Giresun Adası), where the sons of Phrixos join the crew. Then come the Makrones, Becheires, Sapeires and Byzeres, the Phasis, and Aia. Apollonius' list of the peoples of the coast agrees closely with Xenophon's.
disputed: When Aia was first placed in Colchis, on the Phasis, is debated. Homer names Aietes but not his land; the earliest writers who may place him there are Eumelos of Corinth (in Pausanias 2.3.10) and Mimnermus (fr. 11 West).

title: Urartu reaches toward the Pontic mountains: Diauehi and Qulha
summary: The kings of Urartu, from their capital Tushpa on Lake Van, pushed north-west. Menua (c. 810–786) and Argishti I (c. 786–764) attacked Diauehi, a kingdom around the upper Araxes and the Pasin plain; Argishti captured its king Utupurshi and imposed tribute in gold, silver, copper and cattle. Sarduri II (c. 764–735) campaigned against Qulha, usually identified with Colchis. Menua's Yazılıtaş inscription near Delibaba (Horasan) marks Urartu's north-western reach; no Urartian inscription is known from the Pontic coast.
disputed: That Qulha is Colchis, and that Diauehi is the land of Xenophon's Taochoi (Tao), rests only on the likeness of the names. The Yazılıtaş inscription is cut in a rock about 3 m above the ground beside Yazılıtaş village, east of Erzurum and south of Horasan (Köroğlu 2000); Köroğlu also lists inscriptions of Menua from Pasinler, Delibaba and Pirabat near Eleşkirt.

date_text: Described c. 430 BC (Herodotus) to c. AD 20 (Strabo); placed as in 401–400 BC
title: The peoples named by the Greeks
summary: Greek writers named the mountain peoples but never learned their languages. The Chalybes: inland, between the Taochoi and the Harpasos, they were 'the bravest' (Xen. 4.7.15); on the coast near Kotyora they were iron-workers subject to the Mossynoikoi (5.5.1). The Tibarenoi lived around Kotyora; the Mossynoikoi in wooden towers between Kerasous and Kotyora; the Makrones in the hills south of Trapezous; the warlike Drilai in the mountains near it; the Kolchoi around Trapezous and on to the Phasis. The Taochoi held the Tao country (Oltu–Tortum), the Skythenoi the upper Çoruh around Bayburt, and the Phasianoi the Pasin plain. Herodotus' list (3.94) and Strabo (12.3.18–19) move some names: Strabo has the Chalybes as Chaldaioi, the Makrones as Sannoi (the later Tzanoi), and the Mossynoikoi as Heptakometai.
disputed: The names move from author to author: Xenophon's Mossynoikoi live on the coast west of Kerasous, Strabo's inland of Trapezous, and Herodotus (1.28) even puts Chalybes west of the Halys. Their languages are unknown; a link with the Kartvelian languages (the forebears of Laz and Mingrelian) in the east is a reasonable guess, not a fact.

date_text: Mythical time; texts from the 7th c. BC (Eumelos) to the 1st c. AD
title: Sinope's heroes: the nymph Sinope and the Thessalians
summary: Sinope took its name from the nymph Sinope, daughter of Asopos, whom Apollo carried off (Diodorus 4.72.2; Eumelos in the scholia to Apollonius 2.946), or from an Amazon (Ps.-Skymnos 941–942). Ps.-Skymnos (943–946) says 'Syrians' lived there first, then the Thessalians Autolykos, Deileon and Phlogios, Greeks who had crossed over against the Amazons (with Herakles, in Apollonius); in Apollonius they join the Argonauts at Sinope (2.955–961). Autolykos was worshipped as founder with an oracle; Lucullus carried off his statue by Sthennis in 70 BC (Strabo 12.3.11; Plutarch, Luc. 23).
disputed: These are the colony's own founder stories. They do not show that Greeks settled here before the 7th century.

title: Trapezous founded from Sinope: 756 BC (Eusebius)
summary: Trapezous was a colony of Sinope: Xenophon, who reached it in 400 BC, calls it 'an inhabited Greek city, a colony of the Sinopeans, in the land of the Colchians' (Anab. 4.8.22). The ancient foundation date comes from the Chronicle of Eusebius, which places it at Olympiad 6.1, 756/755 BC (Year of Abraham 1260, in the Armenian version), followed by Synkellos and Michael the Syrian. The historians of Trebizond give 756 BC: Ioannidis (1870), 'shortly before Rome', with the founder Askres, probably a Milesian; Evangelidis (1898), whose history runs from 756 BC; Samouilidis (2007). Trabzon has been lived in without a break, so its earliest levels lie under the modern city and have not been excavated.
disputed: Modern scholars differ on the date. Huxley (1993, a British scholar) argues that the entry, which is in the Armenian version of Eusebius, in Synkellos and in Michael the Syrian but not in Jerome, belongs to the same mistaken system as Eusebius' early dates for Battos of Cyrene and Thales; that Trapezous, a colony of Sinope (whose own date in Jerome is 631 BC), was not founded before the 7th century; and that the 8th century was a time of exploration rather than settlement. Drews (1976) argued for taking the early dates seriously. Eastmond (2016, British) calls the early date legend. Çilingir gives the 6th century BC, after Bilge Umar (2000). The Greek historians of Trebizond, Ioannidis (1870), Samouilidis (2007) and Chrysanthos (1933), follow Eusebius and Xenophon.

title: The Cimmerians in Anatolia, and at Sinope
summary: Cimmerians appear in Assyrian letters from 714 BC. In Anatolia they broke Phrygia, killed Gyges of Lydia (c. 652/644) and took Sardis except its citadel, until Alyattes drove them out (Herodotus 1.15–16). Herodotus says that, fleeing the Scythians, they settled 'the peninsula where now the Greek city of Sinope is' (4.12.2). In Sinope's traditions they are the break between a first and a second Milesian foundation.
disputed: Whether Cimmerians really held the Sinope peninsula is uncertain, and Gyges' death is dated either 652 or 644 BC.

title: Habrondas' first Sinope, ended by the Cimmerians
summary: Ps.-Skymnos (947–948) says that after the heroes came 'Habrondas, a Milesian by birth', who 'seems to have been killed by the Cimmerians'. If this is historical, it was a short-lived Milesian venture of about 700 BC or a little earlier (Huxley 1993). No archaeological trace of it has been found.
disputed: Drews (1976) used this first Sinope to support 8th-century dates for the colonies; most others see it as a story with no evidence behind it.

title: Sinope founded again by Milesian exiles; Eusebius' 631
summary: Ps.-Skymnos (949–952) says that after the Cimmerians, Milesian exiles refounded Sinope 'when the army of the Cimmerians overran Asia'. The founders are 'Koos and Kretines', or, as Phlegon has it (in Stephanus), 'Kretines of Kos'. Jerome's version of Eusebius puts Sinope at Olympiad 37.2 = 631/630 BC (the Armenian version has 37.3, with the name corrupted to 'Sidon'). Xenophon (6.1.15), Strabo (12.3.11) and Arrian (Periplus 14.5) all call the Sinopeans Milesian colonists. The date fits the earliest Greek finds.
disputed: Was 'Koos' a second founder or the ethnic 'the Coan'? The year 631 is a chronographer's date: it fits the archaeology, but it is not confirmed by it.

title: The earliest Greek finds at Sinope
summary: Akurgal and Budde's excavations of 1951–53 found graves with Greek pottery of the late 7th century, Corinthian and East Greek, and nothing Greek earlier. The 2015 excavations in Sinop's fortress (Doonan et al.) found Archaic Ionian pottery of the 6th century with a rectangular stone house, and local handmade wares in use beside it. Sunken houses there are linked to a first phase c. 650–630. The Sinop Regional Archaeological Project (survey from 1996) found native sites inland, such as Kocagöz Höyük, and no Greek-style settlement of the hinterland before the Hellenistic period. In short: Greek material from c. 630–600 BC, nothing from the 8th century, and a colony that lived alongside natives.
disputed: Whether the sunken houses come before 630 (Doonan's c. 650–630) is not settled. Boardman (1991) warned that some supposed 'early' Black Sea finds elsewhere are unreliable.

title: Sinope's colonies on the east coast: Kotyora, Kerasous, Trapezous
summary: By 400 BC Sinope had three colonies east of Amisos. Kotyora lay in the land of the Tibarenoi (Xen. 5.5.3); Kerasous, in Colchian land three days west of Trapezous (5.3.2); and Trapezous, also in Colchian land (4.8.22). Kotyora paid tribute to Sinope and had a Sinopean governor (harmost) (5.5.7–10, 5.5.19), and the Sinopean envoy Hekatonymos says that Kerasous and Trapezous also paid Sinope a fixed tribute (5.5.10): this was a small maritime empire. None of the three has a foundation date we can trust, or an excavated level earlier than the Hellenistic period; c. 600–450 BC is a guess on general grounds. Hermonassa, a small settlement near Trapezous (Strabo 12.3.17), is undated.
disputed: Where these places were is uncertain. Xenophon's Kerasous is usually put east of Vakfıkebir, not at Giresun, which is Pharnakeia (Arrian 16.4 says it was 'formerly Kerasous'). Kotyora is probably Ordu. Hermonassa's site is unknown.

title: Amisos founded
summary: Theopompus (in Strabo 12.3.14) says Milesians founded Amisos first. Ps.-Skymnos (917–920, preserved through the Anonymous Periplus) calls it 'a colony of the Phocaeans' in the land of the Leukosyroi, 'founded four years before Heraclea', which 'received an Ionian foundation': i.e. c. 564 BC. Excavations in Samsun put the earliest Greek settlement, at the Çakalca-Karadoğan mound in Atakum, in the mid-6th century (Şirin 2026). The ancient city stood on the Kara Samsun promontory, west of the modern centre.
disputed: Whether the founders were Milesians (Theopompus) or Phocaeans (Ps.-Skymnos) is uncertain.

title: Heraclea Pontica founded among the Mariandynoi
summary: Megarians, with Boeotians from Tanagra, founded Heraclea among the Mariandynoi, whom they reduced to a dependent serf-like status. It became the strongest Greek city of the western Pontic coast. The Ten Thousand were supplied there in 400 (Xen. 6.2.1–3).
disputed: The date is given as about 560 or about 554 BC.

title: Akalan: a native stronghold behind Amisos
summary: At Akalan, inland of Samsun, Theodor Macridy excavated for the Imperial Ottoman Museum (published 1907) a walled hilltop settlement with painted architectural terracottas of East Greek and Phrygian style of the 6th century BC. It is usually read as the seat of a local, perhaps Persian-era, ruler who hired Greek craftsmen. It shows how colonists and natives lived side by side in Amisos' hinterland. New excavations (2022–23) found more decorated terracottas and showed that the site was inhabited from the Early Bronze Age (Yılmaz 2024).
disputed: Who lived there, a local dynast or a Persian official, and the exact dates are uncertain.

title: Persia takes over: the end of the Halys frontier
summary: The Halys had been the Lydian–Median border since the battle of the eclipse (585 BC; Herodotus 1.74). Croesus crossed it and fought Cyrus at Pteria, 'in line with Sinope' (1.76), and then lost Sardis. The whole south coast of the Black Sea passed under Persian overlordship: Cappadocia (Old Persian Katpatuka), Paphlagonia, and the peoples of the east. How far Persian control reached into the Greek coastal cities is unknown.
disputed: The year of the fall of Sardis (547 or a little later) and the identification of Kerkenes Dağ with Pteria are debated.

title: Darius' tribute districts
summary: Herodotus' list of tribute districts (3.89–97) puts the Moschoi, Tibarenoi, Makrones, Mossynoikoi and Mares together in the 19th district (300 talents). The 13th took in Armenia 'as far as the Euxine' (400 talents); the 3rd included the Paphlagonians, Mariandynoi and 'Syrians', i.e. Cappadocians (360 talents). The Colchians and their neighbours up to the Caucasus sent 'gifts' every four years: 100 boys and 100 girls (3.97).
disputed: Whether Herodotus' list copies a Persian document or is a Greek construction is debated.

title: Sinope strikes coins
summary: From the early 5th century Sinope struck silver drachms with the head of a sea-eagle; later types show the eagle on a dolphin. This is the earliest coinage of the south Black Sea coast, and the sign of a rich, self-governing city.
sources_modern: Price 1993, SNG British Museum IX: The Black Sea | Kraay 1976, Archaic and Classical Greek Coins

title: Pontic peoples in Xerxes' army
summary: In Xerxes' army of 480 (Herodotus 7.78–79), the Moschoi and Tibarenoi, with wooden helmets, small shields and long-pointed spears, served under Ariomardos son of Darius. The Makrones and Mossynoikoi served under Artayktes, later governor of Sestos; the Mares and Kolchoi, with wooden helmets, rawhide shields and daggers, under Pharandates son of Teaspis.
disputed: Whether the catalogue reflects a real muster list or is a literary composition is debated.
sources_primary: Herodotus 7.78–79
sources_modern: Briant 2002

title: Pericles' Pontic expedition: Athenians at Sinope
summary: Pericles sailed into the Pontus with a large and splendid fleet, helped the Greek cities, and showed Athenian power to the native peoples and their kings (Plutarch, Per. 20). He left Lamachus with 13 ships at Sinope against the tyrant Timesileos. When the tyrant's party was expelled, Athens voted to send 600 volunteers to live there and share the houses and land of the tyrant's party. Plutarch gives no date; c. 437/436 BC is the usual estimate.
disputed: Date: most say c. 437/436; others suggest the 440s or c. 435.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Pericles 20.1–2

title: Amisos refounded by Athens as 'Peiraieus'
summary: Theopompus (in Strabo 12.3.14) says that after the Milesians (and, in a gap in the text, a Cappadocian ruler), Athenocles and Athenians settled Amisos and renamed it Peiraieus. Plutarch says Athens settled it at the height of its sea power (Luc. 19.7), and Appian calls it an Athenian colony (Mith. 83). Silver coins of Amisos with an owl and the legend ΠΕΙΡΑ confirm the name. The refoundation is usually tied to Pericles' expedition; Şirin (2026) places the new centre at Toraman Tepe.
disputed: The date, the 'Cappadocian' second founder in a gap of Strabo's text, and the date of the ΠΕΙΡΑ coins (late 5th or 4th century) are uncertain.

title: Lamachus loses his ships at Heraclea
summary: In summer 424 the Athenian general Lamachus, sent to collect money in the Pontus with ten ships, anchored in the river Kalex in Heracleot territory. A sudden flood wrecked the ships, and he marched overland through Bithynia to Chalcedon (Thuc. 4.75.1–2). This shows Athens claiming tribute from Pontic cities during the Archidamian War.
disputed: Which Pontic cities, if any, were assessed in 425/4 is uncertain because the stone is restored.

title: Satraps and free peoples c. 400 BC
summary: In 401–400 the Persian King ruled the plateau through satraps: Orontas held Armenia, and Tiribazos, the King's 'friend', Western Armenia, the Phasianoi and the Hesperitai. Korylas ruled Paphlagonia, and Pharnabazos Bithynia and Hellespontine Phrygia. Other peoples were independent of the King: the Kardouchoi, Chalybes, Chaldaioi, Makrones, Kolchoi, Mossynoikoi, Koitoi and Tibarenoi (the list at Anab. 7.8.25, probably a later addition). The Greek cities of the coast acted on their own. Sinope dealt with Korylas as an equal and ruled colonies of its own.
disputed: Anab. 7.8.25 (the list of governors and free peoples) is generally thought to be an interpolation.

title: Datames and Sinope
summary: In the 370s–360s Datames, satrap of Cappadocia, tried to take Sinope; ancient handbooks of stratagems record his siege (Aeneas Tacticus 40.4; Polyaenus 7.21.2, 5). Later the Persians split Cappadocia into a southern satrapy and 'Cappadocia by the Pontus' (Strabo 12.1.4), the seed of the kingdom of Pontus (chapter 3).
disputed: The siege is dated only roughly, to the 370s or 360s BC.

title: Arcadians from Trapezous join their Pontic namesake
summary: Pausanias (8.27.6) says that when the Arcadians founded Megalopolis, the people of Arcadian Trapezous refused to move there. Those who escaped being killed sailed to the Pontus, where the Trapezountines received them as people of their mother city with the same name. This is a late tradition. The name ('table') suits the flat-topped rock of the Pontic city and need not mean an Arcadian origin.
disputed: Whether the kinship was real or a later claim is uncertain; Pausanias calls the Pontic city the 'mother city', a reversal that may be rhetoric.

title: Diogenes of Sinope, son of the banker Hikesias, exiled over the coinage
summary: Diogenes the Cynic was a citizen of Sinope, 'son of Hikesias, a banker' (Diogenes Laertius 6.20). His exile is tied to a scandal over Sinope's coinage, told in several versions that Diogenes Laertius sets side by side (6.20–21): Diocles says his father, who ran the public bank, debased the currency and Diogenes went into exile; Eubulides says Diogenes did it himself and left with his father; Diogenes himself was said to admit it in his Pordalos; others add that an oracle told him to 'alter the currency' and that his father died in prison. Asked about the Sinopeans' sentence of exile, he is said to have answered that he sentenced them to stay at home (6.49). He lived at Athens and Corinth, where he died, nearly ninety, in 323 BC (6.76–79). The best-known son of Sinope, he shows the city's mint and bank at work in the 4th century.
disputed: Who debased the coinage (the father, according to Diocles; Diogenes himself, according to Eubulides and the Pordalos; or both), whether he was banished or left of his own accord, and when. The ancient lives are full of anecdote; the exile itself is not doubted.

title: The route of the Ten Thousand, Cunaxa to Byzantium
summary: The route of the retreat in 39 stages, as drawn on the map; for each, Xenophon's stages (stathmoi) and parasangs from the one before, how sure its location is, and whether it was reached by land or by sea. From the Kentrites to Trapezous Xenophon's stages add up to 49 stages and 257 parasangs (255 on the Loeb's reading of 4.5.3), with 8 days that he does not measure. The total at 5.5.4, generally regarded as a later addition, gives 122 stages, 620 parasangs, 18,600 stadia and eight months from the battlefield to Kotyora. Only the ends are secure. Most points between the Kentrites and Trapezous are conjectural; for Theches the map follows Mitford (2000), the leading proposal.

The parasang is nominally 30 stadia (c. 5.5–6 km), but Xenophon's figures shrink in the mountains (3.4 parasangs a day from Theches to Trapezous).

title: Cunaxa: Cyrus is killed
summary: At Cunaxa on the Euphrates, about 500 stadia above Babylon, Cyrus the Younger met his brother Artaxerxes II. The Greek mercenaries (10,400 hoplites and 2,500 peltasts, 1.7.10) routed the wing facing them, but Cyrus was killed charging the King. The Greeks were left victorious on their own wing, stranded in the heart of the empire, more than 1,500 km from the sea.
disputed: The day is often given as 3 September 401, a modern reckoning. The battlefield has not been found (Tell Kuneise has been proposed).

title: The generals seized; Xenophon elected
summary: The Greeks marched north with Tissaphernes, crossing the Tigris at Sittake on a bridge of 37 boats and passing Opis and Kainai. At the Great Zab (Zapatas) Tissaphernes invited Klearchos and four other generals to a parley and had them arrested and later executed. That night the young Athenian Xenophon roused the officers. New generals were elected, among them Xenophon and the Spartan Cheirisophos, and the army chose to fight its way north (3.1–3.2).
disputed: The sites of Sittake, Opis and Kainai are uncertain.

title: Up the Tigris: Larisa and Mespila
summary: Harried by Persian cavalry and slingers, the Greeks marched up the east bank of the Tigris. They passed two deserted cities that Xenophon calls Larisa and Mespila, once held by the Medes: in fact the Assyrian capitals of Nimrud and Nineveh, ruined two centuries earlier. Where the Kardouchian mountains came down to the river they turned north into the mountains.
disputed: Where exactly the army left the Tigris is uncertain.

title: Seven days through the Kardouchoi
summary: The Kardouchoi (in the mountains of today's Hakkari and Şırnak) were independent of the King, and Xenophon says they had once destroyed a royal army of 120,000. For seven days they fought the Greeks in narrow defiles, rolling stones and shooting arrows from bows nearly three cubits long. The Greeks 'suffered more than from the King and Tissaphernes together' (4.3.2).
disputed: The exact route through the mountains is unknown.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.1–4.3.2

title: Crossing the Kentrites into Armenia
summary: At the Kentrites (Bohtan Su), about 2 plethra wide, the boundary between the Kardouchoi and Armenia, the satrap Orontas and Artouchas held the far bank with Armenians, Mardoi and Chaldaioi mercenaries, while the Kardouchoi pressed from behind. Two young soldiers found a ford, and the army crossed in a deceptive double movement (4.3.8–34).
disputed: The crossing point on the Bohtan is not known.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.3
sources_modern: Lendle 1995

title: Western Armenia: the Teleboas and the truce with Tiribazos
summary: Beyond the Kentrites they marched 1 stage of 5 parasangs to a village with a satrap's palace, 2 stages of 10 parasangs past 'the sources of the Tigris', and 3 stages of 15 parasangs to the Teleboas, 'a beautiful river, though not a large one' (4.4.1–3). This was Western Armenia, under Tiribazos, the King's 'friend', who alone was allowed to help him mount his horse. He made a truce: the Greeks could take supplies if they burned nothing (4.4.4–6).
disputed: The Teleboas is usually taken as the Kara Su of the Muş plain; some take it as a stretch of the Murat.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.4.1–6

title: Snow, and Tiribazos' camp taken
summary: After 3 more stages (15 parasangs) to a palace among villages, heavy snow fell at night. A captured scout revealed that Tiribazos meant to ambush the Greeks in a pass. They struck first, took his camp with his silver-footed couch and his cup-bearers, and crossed the pass (4.4.7–22).

title: Crossing the Euphrates near its sources
summary: After three stages (15 parasangs) 'through desert country' the army waded the Euphrates, wetted to the navel, and was told its sources were not far away (4.5.2). This was probably the Murat, the eastern Euphrates.
disputed: Which branch of the Euphrates was crossed, and where, is uncertain.

title: The snow march
summary: Then came three stages through deep snow (15 parasangs in Marchant's OCT; 13 in Brownson's Loeb). On the third a north wind blew in their faces and froze the army; the seers sacrificed to the wind, and it seemed to drop. The snow lay a fathom deep (c. 1.8 m); many pack animals and slaves died, and about 30 soldiers. Men went snow-blind and lost toes to frostbite, and Xenophon drove stragglers on in the rearguard (4.5.3–22).
disputed: The parasangs of this leg are 15 in Marchant's Oxford text and 13 in Brownson's Loeb, a difference between the manuscripts.

title: The underground villages of Armenia
summary: The army rested about a week in villages where the houses were dug into the ground, with entrances like wells, and men and animals lived together. They drank barley wine through reeds from great bowls. Xenophon lodged with the village chief (komarch), whose daughter had been married nine days before, and who was rearing colts as tribute for the King. Taken as a guide, the chief led them for three days, until Cheirisophos struck him for not finding villages; he slipped away in the night (4.5.23–4.6.3).
disputed: Where the villages were is unknown; the Hınıs–Karaçoban region is a guess.

title: Seven stages to the Phasis
summary: Then came 7 stages at 5 parasangs a day to the river Phasis, a plethron wide (4.6.4). This was not the Phasis of Colchis but, almost certainly, the upper Araxes (Aras) in the Pasin plain, whose people Xenophon calls Phasianoi.
disputed: Older scholars took it for the Phasis of Colchis; the upper Araxes is now the accepted identification.

title: Forcing the pass of the Chalybes, Taochoi and Phasianoi
summary: Two stages (10 parasangs) on, the Chalybes, Taochoi and Phasianoi held the pass down to the next plain. Xenophon and Cheirisophos joked about whether Spartans or Athenians were better thieves. Then a night detachment seized a height on the flank, the defenders fled, and the Greeks came down to well-stocked villages (4.6.5–27).
disputed: The pass lay north of the Pasin plain; its exact place is unknown.

places: Pass held by Chalybes, Taochoi and Phasianoi (40.17, 41.88)

title: The Taochoi stronghold
summary: After 5 stages (30 parasangs) into the land of the Taochoi, food ran out. The Taochoi had gathered their families and herds in a stronghold on a cliff. When the Greeks broke in, women threw their children and then themselves over the edge, and Aeneas of Stymphalus, grabbing a man who was about to jump, was dragged over with him (4.7.1–14).
disputed: The stronghold lay in the Tao country (Oltu–Tortum); its exact site is unknown.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.1–14
sources_modern: Lendle 1995 | Lane Fox (ed.) 2004

title: Through the Chalybes
summary: Seven stages (50 parasangs) led through the Chalybes, 'the bravest of all the peoples they passed'. They wore linen corselets, greaves and helmets, and carried a curved knife like the Spartan's and a spear 15 cubits long. They cut off the heads of the dead and lived in strongholds, from which they harassed the column (4.7.15–17).
disputed: Fifty parasangs is a long way for seven stages, which suggests a detour or a fault in the text.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.15–17
sources_modern: Lendle 1995

title: The Harpasos and the Skythenoi
summary: They reached the river Harpasos, 4 plethra wide, and then marched 4 stages (20 parasangs) through the level land of the Skythenoi to villages, where they rested three days (4.7.18).
disputed: The Harpasos is usually taken as the upper Çoruh (Akampsis); others suggest a tributary.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.18
sources_modern: Lendle 1995 | Manfredi 1986
places: Harpasos (Çoruh) crossing (40.6, 41.2) | Villages of the Skythenoi (40.42, 40.75)

title: Gymnias
summary: Four more stages (20 parasangs) brought them to 'a large, prosperous, inhabited city called Gymnias'. Its ruler sent a guide to lead them through the land of his enemies. The guide promised that within five days he would bring them to a place from which they could see the sea, or they could put him to death (4.7.19–20).
disputed: Gymnias is usually placed at Bayburt, or near Gümüşhane; Paradeisopoulos (2013, Greek) argues from Diodorus' '15 days' for a site far to the east, in Armenia. The guide led the army through the land of his own enemies, so that the Greeks served as his weapon.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.19–20 | Diodorus 14.29.3
sources_modern: Brennan & Tuplin 2023 ('the normal view' is the Gümüşhane–Bayburt region) | Lendle 1995 | Mitford 2000 | Paradeisopoulos 2013, 2014 (Gymnias far to the east, in Armenia)
places: Gymnias, candidate: Bayburt (40.258, 40.227) | Gymnias, candidate: Gümüşhane area (40.46, 39.481)

date_text: Late winter or spring 400 BC (estimates run from February to May)
title: Mount Theches: 'Thalatta, thalatta!'
summary: On the fifth day they reached a mountain called Theches. The vanguard shouted, the shout spread, and Xenophon rode up expecting an attack, then heard 'The sea! The sea!'. Men embraced their generals and captains in tears. They built a great cairn of stones and laid on it raw ox-hides, sticks and captured wicker shields. They gave the guide a horse, a silver bowl, a Persian robe and ten darics; he asked above all for rings and got many, showed them a village to camp in, and left at night (4.7.21–27). The place has never been identified with certainty.
disputed: Brennan & Tuplin (2023) count about twenty proposals since 1818 and call Mitford's site 'the current leading contender'; their own 'viable hypothesis' is the north-west spur of Polut Dağı, but they conclude that the spot 'must remain a matter for conjecture'. Diodorus' 'Chenion' and '15 days' are usually treated as copying errors. Arrian says that he looked at the sea at Trapezous 'from the same spot' as Xenophon, but this is not taken as evidence for the site.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.21–27 | Diodorus 14.29.3–4 (mountain 'Chenion', 15 days from Gymnias) | Arrian, Periplus 1.1–4 (Arrian views the sea at Trapezous 'from the same spot' as Xenophon)
sources_modern: Brennan & Tuplin 2023, 'Theches: an elusive mountain', Anatolian Studies 73: 129–149 | Mitford 2000, 'Thalatta, thalatta: Xenophon's view of the Black Sea', Anatolian Studies 50: 127–131 | Mitford 2018, East of Asia Minor (OUP) | Manfredi 1986, La strada dei Diecimila, pp. 223–228 | Manfredi 2004, 'The identification of Mount Thekes...', in Tuplin (ed.), Xenophon and his World, pp. 319–324 | Lendle 1995, pp. 272–280 | Rood 2004, The Sea! The Sea! | Waterfield 2006 | Lane Fox (ed.) 2004, The Long March
places: Theches, candidate: Mitford's site (Kolat area, c. 20 km SSW of Maçka) (40.645, 39.54) | Theches, candidate: east of the Zigana pass (40.63, 39.45) | Theches, candidate: south of Toplukdüzü Tepe, NW of Torul (40.62, 39.21) | Theches, candidate: İskobel (40.685, 39.691) | Theches, candidate: Polut Dağı north-west spur (2,315 m) (40.673, 39.963) | Theches, candidate: Madur Dağı (2,742 m) (40.652, 40.041) | Theches, candidate: Vavuk pass (old proposal) (40.32, 39.93) | Theches, candidate: Kop Dağı (old proposal) (40.03, 40.49)

title: Theches: the alternative routes from Gymnias to Trapezous
summary: The map shows a route from Gymnias (Bayburt) to Trapezous for each of the three main proposals for Theches: by Mitford's site south-south-west of Maçka (the route shown by default), by the Zigana pass (Lendle), and by the north-west spur of Polut Dağı (Brennan & Tuplin).
disputed: The routes are reconstructions. Mitford (2000) traces his from Bayburt by Maden Hanları and Kolat Hanları, where the sea is first seen from a plateau on the Roman road, down to Maçka, but gives no coordinates for his viewpoint or for Deveboynu Tepe, so those points are approximate. The descent of the eastern route by the Karadere valley to Araklı is inferred.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.7.19–4.8.22
sources_modern: Mitford, T. 2000, 'Thalatta, thalatta: Xenophon's view of the Black Sea', Anatolian Studies 50: 127–132 (route Bayburt – Kale (Kovans) – Son Kale – Maden Hanları – Anzarya Hanları – Kolat Hanları; the sea first seen from a plateau about a mile north-west of Kolat on the Roman road, c. 8,250 ft; Theches 'presumably' Deveboynu Tepe, c. 10,100 ft, 'the highest summit between Bayburt and Trabzon'; descent by Turnagöl, Karakaban and Meşecik han to Maçka) | Lendle 1995, pp. 272–280 and map 49 | Tuplin, C. & Brennan, S. 2023, 'Theches: an elusive mountain', Anatolian Studies 73: 129–149, doi 10.1017/S0066154623000054
