title: Through the Makrones
summary: The march through the Makrones took 3 stages (10 parasangs); on the first day the army came to the river between the Makrones and the Skythenoi, where the Makrones blocked the crossing. A peltast who had been a slave at Athens recognised their language and could talk to them. Spears were exchanged as pledges, the Makrones helped cut a road, and they brought the Greeks in three days to the Colchian border (4.8.1–8).
disputed: The river depends on the route: on Mitford's it is at the junction of the Değirmendere and the Sumela stream near Maçka, on Lendle's a stream north-north-east of Hamsiköy, on the Polut route the Karadere confluence.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.8.1–8
sources_modern: Brennan & Tuplin 2023 (the river's candidates by variant) | Lendle 1995 (stream near Hamsiköy)
places: River between the Makrones and the Skythenoi (40.81, 39.61)

title: Battle on the Colchian mountain
summary: The Colchians held a high mountain on the way down to the sea. Xenophon formed the hoplites into companies in column (orthioi lochoi), about eighty of them, each of about 100 men (4.8.15), with gaps between them, so that the line could cross broken ground without breaking up. The Greeks overlapped the Colchian line at both ends, and the defenders fled (4.8.9–19).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.8.9–19
sources_modern: Lee 2007 | Lendle 1995

title: The mad honey
summary: In the Colchian villages beyond the mountain there were many beehives. Every soldier who ate the honey lost his senses, vomited and had diarrhoea, and none could stand. Those who ate a little were like drunk men; those who ate much were like madmen, and some like dying men. They lay about as if after a defeat. No one died, and about the same hour next day they came round; on the third and fourth days they got up as if after a drugging (4.8.20–21). The cause is grayanotoxin in honey from rhododendrons (Rhododendron ponticum and luteum), still known locally as deli bal.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.8.20–21 | Diodorus 14.30.1–2 | Strabo 12.3.18 (the Heptakometai use honey against Pompey's men) | Stephanus of Byzantium s.v. Τραπεζοῦς (citing Aristotle on maddening boxwood honey at Trapezous) | Pliny, NH 21.77 (the Sanni's 'maenomenon' honey, from rhododendron flowers)
sources_modern: Mayor 2003, Greek Fire, Poison Arrows and Scorpion Bombs | Jansen et al. 2012, Cardiovascular Toxicology 12: 208–215

title: Trapezous: a month among the Colchian villages
summary: Two stages (7 parasangs) later they reached the sea at Trapezous, 'an inhabited Greek city (πόλιν Ἑλληνίδα οἰκουμένην) on the Euxine Sea, a colony of the Sinopeans in the land of the Colchians' (4.8.22). This is the first certain record of the city. The army camped for about 30 days in Colchian villages and plundered Colchian land from there. The Trapezountines provided a market and gave gifts of oxen, barley meal and wine, and spoke for their Colchian neighbours in the plain, who also sent oxen (4.8.22–24).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.8.22–24 | Diodorus 14.30.3
sources_modern: Avram, Hind & Tsetskhladze 2004, no. 734 | Bryer & Winfield 1985, pp. 178–250 (Trebizond) | Mitford 2018, vol. 1, pp. 385–425

title: The games at Trapezous
summary: The army sacrificed the oxen it had been given to Zeus the Saviour and to Herakles the Guide, as it had vowed, and held games on the hill where it camped. The organiser was Drakontios, a Spartan exiled as a boy for accidentally killing another boy with a dagger. The events were a stadion race (mostly captive boys), a long race with more than 60 Cretans, wrestling, boxing and the pankration, and a horse race down the steep slope into the sea and back up to the altar, amid much shouting and laughter (4.8.25–28).
disputed: Which hill is not known; Boztepe above the city is the usual guess.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 4.8.25–28
sources_modern: Lee 2007 | Lane Fox (ed.) 2004

title: Waiting for ships
summary: Leon of Thurii spoke for the army: he was tired of packing, marching, running, carrying arms, keeping in line, standing guard and fighting, and wanted to finish the journey stretched out asleep, like Odysseus. Cheirisophos sailed to the Spartan admiral Anaxibios at Byzantium for ships. Xenophon borrowed a penteconter from Trapezous for the Laconian Dexippos, who deserted with it, and a triaconter for the Athenian Polykrates, who brought in passing merchant ships (5.1).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.1
sources_modern: Lee 2007

title: The raid on the Drilai
summary: The Trapezountines led half the army against the Drilai, the most warlike people of the Pontus, rather than against the Colchians, who were their friends. The Drilai burned their lowland villages and withdrew to a fortified 'metropolis' with a ditch, palisade and wooden towers. The Greeks broke in, plundered, and fought their way out under cover of fire (5.2). Arrian later thought the Drilai were the Sannoi (Periplus 11).
disputed: Where the Drilai lived is uncertain; south-east of Trapezous is likely if they were the Sannoi.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.2 | Arrian, Periplus 11 (Roos)
sources_modern: Lendle 1995

title: Kerasous: review of the army and the tithe
summary: The sick, those over forty, the women and children and the spare baggage went by ship with the oldest generals, Philesios and Sophainetos; the rest marched by a well-made road and reached Kerasous on the third day. Kerasous was a Greek city by the sea, a colony of Sinope in Colchian land (5.3.2). They stayed ten days. A review under arms counted 8,600 men, and the rest had died by enemies, snow or sickness. The proceeds from the sale of captives were divided, and a tenth set aside for Apollo and for Artemis of Ephesus. Xenophon later used his share for Artemis to buy an estate and shrine at Skillous near Olympia (5.3.4–13).
disputed: Xenophon's Kerasous was not Giresun, which became Pharnakeia, but a harbour three days west of Trapezous; its exact site is unknown.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.3.1–13 | Diodorus 14.30.5
sources_modern: Erciyas 2007
places: Kerasous (Xenophon's, east of Vakfıkebir) (41.05, 39.33) | Ephesus (37.94, 27.34) | Delphi (38.482, 22.501) | Skillous (37.64, 21.69)

title: Among the Mossynoikoi
summary: The Trapezountine Timesitheos, proxenos of the Mossynoikoi, interpreted. The Greeks allied with one faction of the Mossynoikoi, who came in 300 dugout canoes, against the other, and captured their 'metropolis'. The king, who lived in a wooden tower (mossyn), refused to come out and was burned in it. The children of the rich were fattened on boiled chestnuts until they were nearly as broad as tall, and tattooed with flowers. Xenophon calls the Mossynoikoi the most barbarous people they passed, doing in public what others do in private (5.4).
disputed: Location: Xenophon's Mossynoikoi lived on the coast west of his Kerasous; Strabo places them inland near Trapezous.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.4 | Apollonius, Arg. 2.1015–1029 | Diodorus 14.30.6–7
sources_modern: Lendle 1995 | Lane Fox (ed.) 2004 (on Xenophon's ethnography)

title: Chalybes and Tibarenoi to Kotyora: the end of the land march
summary: After 8 stages through the Mossynoikoi came the Chalybes, few, subject to the Mossynoikoi, and living mostly by iron-working. Then the Tibarenoi, whose land was flatter and their coastal forts weaker; the generals wanted to plunder them, but the omens forbade it, and the Tibarenoi sent gifts. After 2 stages through Tibarenian land they reached Kotyora, a colony of Sinope (5.5.1–3). A summary at 5.5.4, generally regarded as an interpolation, gives from the battlefield to Kotyora 122 stages, 620 parasangs, 18,600 stadia and 8 months.
disputed: Kotyora is probably Ordu.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.5.1–4
sources_modern: Erciyas 2007 | Lendle 1995

title: Forty-five days at Kotyora; Sinope's envoys; Xenophon's colony plan
summary: Kotyora would not open a market or take the sick inside its walls. The army took supplies from Kotyorite and Paphlagonian land and stayed 45 days, with sacrifices and games. Sinope, which drew tribute from Kotyora and had a governor (harmost) there (and, Hekatonymos says, tribute from Kerasous and Trapezous too, 5.5.10), sent envoys led by Hekatonymos, who threatened an alliance with Korylas of Paphlagonia. He then advised going by sea, describing Paphlagonia's cavalry and its rivers: Thermodon, Iris, Halys, Parthenios. Xenophon thought of founding a city on the Pontus with the army. The seer Silanos betrayed the plan, Timasion and Thorax stirred opposition, and the generals were tried in an assembly (5.5.5–5.8).
disputed: Xenophon says only that he meant to found his city on the Pontus (5.6.15–16).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 5.5.5–5.8
sources_modern: Lane Fox (ed.) 2004 (on the colony plan) | Lee 2007

title: By sea to Sinope; Cheirisophos made sole commander
summary: Envoys from Korylas were feasted with armed dances: the Thracian sword dance, the Karpaia of the Ainianes and Magnetes, a Mysian shield dance, the Mantineans' war dance, and a girl dancing the pyrrhic (6.1.1–13). Ships came, and the army sailed a day and a night with a fair wind and anchored next day at Harmene, the harbour of Sinope. The Sinopeans, 'Milesian colonists in Paphlagonia', sent 3,000 medimnoi of barley meal and 1,500 jars of wine. Cheirisophos returned, bringing only praise from Anaxibios. After five days the army chose a single commander: Xenophon declined after the omens, and Cheirisophos was elected (6.1.14–33).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 6.1
sources_modern: Lee 2007

title: Heraclea: the army splits in three
summary: From Harmene the army sailed two days with a fair wind, past the mouth of the Parthenios, to Heraclea, a Megarian colony in Mariandynian land (6.2.1). The text then lists sights of the voyage (Jason's Cape, where the Argo was said to have anchored, and the mouths of the Thermodon, Iris, Halys and Parthenios), a list Brownson brackets as an interpolation. They anchored by the Acherousian Chersonese, where Herakles went down for Kerberos (6.2.1–2). The Heracleots gave 3,000 medimnoi of barley meal, 2,000 jars of wine, 20 oxen and 100 sheep. When the army tried to extort money from Heraclea, it split: the Arcadians and Achaeans (more than 4,000 hoplites) went their own way; Cheirisophos kept 1,400 hoplites and 700 peltasts, and Xenophon 1,700 hoplites, 300 peltasts and 40 horsemen (6.2.3–16).
disputed: Brownson (Loeb) brackets the list of sights at 6.2.1 as an interpolation, geographically impossible on a voyage starting at Sinope (Jason's Cape and the Thermodon, Iris and Halys lie east of it); Marchant prints it.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 6.2
sources_modern: Burstein 1976 | Lee 2007
places: Heraclea Pontica (41.283, 31.418) | Acherousian Chersonese (Baba Burnu) (41.3, 31.39) | Jason's Cape (Yason Burnu) (41.11, 37.68)

title: Kalpe Harbour
summary: The Arcadians sailed to Kalpe Harbour, halfway between Heraclea and Byzantium, and were mauled by the Bithynian Thracians. Cheirisophos marched by land; Xenophon landed at the Heracleot–Thracian border and marched inland (6.2.17–19). Reunited at Kalpe, the army lost Cheirisophos to a fever and a drug (6.4.11), beat Pharnabazos' cavalry and the Bithynians (6.5), and quarrelled with Kleandros, the Spartan governor of Byzantium (6.6).
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 6.2.17–6.6
sources_modern: Lee 2007

title: Chrysopolis and Byzantium
summary: The army marched through Bithynia to Chrysopolis, where it spent seven days selling its booty (6.6.37–38). Anaxibios then ferried it across to Byzantium, where the soldiers, cheated of pay, nearly sacked the city (7.1). The retreat from Cunaxa was over. The later summary at 7.8.26 gives the whole journey up and down as 215 stages, 1,150 parasangs, 34,255 stadia and 1 year 3 months (probably interpolated: Brownson's 'a late editor').
disputed: The totals at 7.8.26 do not agree with each other or with the time actually taken; they are usually thought to be a later addition.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 6.6.37–38, 7.1 | Anab. 7.8.26
sources_modern: Lee 2007 | Stronk 1995, The Ten Thousand in Thrace

title: Service with Seuthes; handed to Thibron
summary: The rest of the army, about 6,000 men (Xenophon's own round figure, 7.7.23), wintered in Thrace in the pay of the Odrysian prince Seuthes. In spring 399 it crossed back to Asia and was taken into Spartan service under Thibron against the Persians (7.2–7.8). This lies outside the atlas, but it closes the story.
disputed: About 6,000 is Xenophon's own round figure ('to be well spoken of by six thousand men', 7.7.23), not a muster count.
sources_primary: Xenophon, Anab. 7.2–7.8 (7.7.23: about 6,000)
sources_modern: Stronk 1995

title: Mithridates (later 'Ktistes') escapes Antigonus and seizes Kimiata
summary: After Antigonus the One-Eyed had Mithridates of Kios killed (302), the younger Mithridates, a companion of Demetrius, fled east with six horsemen when Antigonus, warned by a dream, planned to arrest him. He fortified a stronghold, Kimiata at the foot of the Olgassys range, gathered followers and made himself lord of Cappadocia-by-the-Sea (Pontus). This is the foundation story of the Mithridatid dynasty, which later bore the epithet Ktistes, 'the Founder', for him.
disputed: Diodorus makes him the successor of Mithridates of Kios (ruling 36 years, i.e. to 266); Plutarch calls him son of Ariobarzanes. The exact family tree and whether Ktistes was son or nephew of the Kian dynast are reconstructed differently (Bosworth & Wheatley 1998). The dream and the 'Flee, Mithridates' written in the sand by Demetrius are court legend.
sources_primary: Diodorus 20.111.4 | Plutarch, Demetrius 4 | Appian, Mith. 9 | Strabo 12.3.41
sources_modern: Bosworth & Wheatley 1998 (JHS 118) | McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Erciyas 2006

title: Epoch of the Pontic royal era
summary: The later coins of Mithridates VI are dated by a royal era whose year 1 began in autumn 297 BC. The same epoch is used by the Bithynian kings, so the era may mark a claim to independence from the successors of Alexander rather than a Pontic event. It gives a second possible start for the kingdom, between the flight of 302 and the royal title of 281.
disputed: Whether the era is genuinely Pontic or borrowed from Bithynia is debated; it does not by itself prove a royal title in 297.
sources_primary: Dated tetradrachms of Mithridates VI (e.g. year 202 = 96/95 BC)
sources_modern: de Callatay 1997 (L'histoire des guerres mithridatiques vue par les monnaies) | McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Mithridates I takes the royal title
summary: After Seleucus' victory at Corupedium and his murder (281), Mithridates styled himself king (basileus). The chronographer Syncellus gives the Pontic kings 218 years, i.e. 281-63 BC, which is the conventional span of the kingdom. Amaseia in the Iris gorge became the royal city.
disputed: The kingdom's beginning is dated to 302 (the flight), 297/6 (the era) or 281 (the royal title).
sources_primary: George Syncellus, Chronographia (218 years of the Pontic kings) | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 9-11 | Strabo 12.3.39
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Hojte 2009 (ed.)

title: Borders c. 281 BC: the first kingdom
summary: The early kingdom held the interior between the Halys and the Iris: Kimiatene at the foot of the Olgassys, the Phazemonitis, the Amaseia gorge and the middle Iris valley around Gaziura and Komana. It had no Greek city of its own on the coast until Amastris was handed over about 279; Sinope, Amisos, Kotyora, Kerasous and Trapezous were still independent Greek cities.
disputed: The early extent is inferred; no ancient source draws it. When Amisos came under the kings, in the 3rd or early 2nd century, is unknown.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.39-41 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 9
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Erciyas 2006, ch. 2

title: Amastris handed to Ariobarzanes
summary: Eumenes, who held Amastris, handed the city to Ariobarzanes son of Mithridates rather than to Heraclea, which wanted it. It was the dynasty's first Greek port on the Black Sea, west of Sinope.
disputed: The identity of this Eumenes and the exact year are uncertain.
sources_primary: Memnon, FGrH 434 F 9.4
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Saprykin 1997

title: Ariobarzanes king (c. 266-c. 250)
summary: Ariobarzanes succeeded his father. Memnon records trouble with the Galatians, the Celtic invaders settled in central Anatolia from 278/7, during his reign and that of his young son.
disputed: His reign is dated only approximately, from about 266 to about 255 or 250.
sources_primary: Memnon, FGrH 434 F 16
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Mithridates II king (c. 250-c. 220); Seleucid marriages
summary: Mithridates II married a Seleucid princess, Laodice, and married his daughters to Antiochus III and to the usurper Achaeus. Polybius reports that the house claimed descent from one of the seven Persians who made Darius king. With Galatian allies he helped Antiochus Hierax defeat Seleucus II at Ankyra (c. 240/239).
disputed: The date of the battle of Ankyra (about 240–235) and Mithridates' part in it are debated.
sources_primary: Polybius 5.43.1-4 | Polybius 8.20.11 | Justin 27.2.10-12 | Eusebius, Chronicle
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Mithridates II besieges Sinope; Rhodes helps the city
summary: Mithridates II attacked Sinope, the leading Greek city of the coast. The Rhodians sent money (140,000 drachmas) and war material, and the city held out. The episode shows the kings' long ambition for the great harbour.
sources_primary: Polybius 4.56
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Mithridates III (c. 220-c. 185)
summary: A king Mithridates between Mithridates II and Pharnaces I is known mainly from portrait coins. Most modern king lists count him as Mithridates III.
disputed: His existence and dates rest on coins; some scholars merge him with Mithridates II. The modern numbering of the kings depends on it.
sources_primary: Royal tetradrachms with the portrait of a king Mithridates
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | de Callatay 2009 (in Hojte ed.)

title: Pharnaces I king (c. 189/185-c. 160/155)
summary: Pharnaces I was the most aggressive of the early kings: he took Sinope and fought a four-year war against Pergamon, Bithynia and Cappadocia. He married the Seleucid princess Nysa.
disputed: His accession is dated about 189 or 185, his death between about 170 and 155 (see the Athenian decree, H2-017).
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Pharnakeia founded: the end of Kotyora
summary: After seizing Sinope in 183 BC, Pharnaces I of Pontus founded Pharnakeia by moving in the people of Kotyora (Strabo 12.3.17). Arrian says Pharnakeia was 'formerly called Kerasous' and was itself a Sinopean colony (Periplus 16.4). Pharnakeia is generally placed at Giresun. Kotyora shrank to a village (Arrian), and Sinope's old colonial chain passed to the kings of Pontus.
disputed: The new city is said to have taken in the people of Kotyora (Strabo) or of Kerasous (Arrian, the Anonymous Periplus), or both. Pharnakeia is usually placed at Giresun. Strabo (12.3.17) also lists a separate Kerasous, in a bay with Hermonassa east of Pharnakeia, which supports keeping the two names apart; whether Xenophon's Kerasous lay at Giresun or further west is debated, and Bryer & Winfield discuss the options. The foundation date is inferred from Pharnaces' reign.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.17 | Arrian, Periplus 16.3–4 | Anonymous Periplus Ponti Euxini 34–35 | Arrian, Periplus 16.4 | Pliny, NH 6.11
sources_modern: Olshausen & Biller 1984, Historisch-geographische Aspekte der Geschichte des Pontischen und Armenischen Reiches | Tabula Peutingeriana database (tp-online, no. 1539) | Bryer & Winfield 1985 (on Kerasous and Pharnakeia) | McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Pharnaces I takes Sinope
summary: Pharnaces took Sinope in 183: Strabo says the city 'was taken by siege and was subject first to Pharnaces' (12.3.11), and Rhodian envoys complained about it at Rome in the winter of 183/2 (Polybius 23.9.2). Sinope later became the royal city: Mithridates VI Eupator was born and raised there and, in Strabo's words, 'treated it as the metropolis of the kingdom'. That the court moved there already in 183 is a modern inference. The capture made Pontus a sea power with the best harbour of the southern coast.
disputed: Strabo credits Eupator, not Pharnaces, with making Sinope the 'metropolis' (12.3.11).
sources_primary: Polybius 23.9.2 | Strabo 12.3.11 | Livy 40.2.6-8
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Magie 1950, vol. 1

title: The Pontic War of Pharnaces
summary: Pharnaces, allied with Mithridates, ruler of Lesser Armenia, invaded Galatia and Paphlagonia and took Tios on the Bithynian border. Eumenes II of Pergamon, Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and later Prusias II fought him, while Roman embassies came and went. Polybius is the near-contemporary source.
disputed: The course of the war is known only in fragments.
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Hansen 1971 (The Attalids)

title: Peace of 179: Pharnaces keeps Sinope
summary: Under the treaty quoted by Polybius, Pharnaces evacuated Galatia and Paphlagonia, gave back Tios, and paid 900 talents to Ariarathes and 300 to Eumenes; Mithridates of Armenia paid 300. Sinope stayed Pontic. The treaty names as parties or adherents Artaxias of Armenia, Sarmatian chiefs, and the free cities of Heraclea, Mesembria, Chersonesos and Cyzicus, which shows how far Pontic diplomacy reached.
sources_primary: Polybius 25.2
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Borders 179 BC: Pontus as a coastal power
summary: After the Pontic War the kingdom held interior Pontus (Amaseia, Gaziura, Komana, Zela, the Iris and Lykos valleys) and the coast from Amastris through Sinope and Amisos to Kotyora and Pharnakeia. Trapezous may have come under Pontic control in this period, perhaps through the ally in Lesser Armenia, but there is no direct evidence. Lesser Armenia and Colchis were outside the kingdom.
disputed: The status of Amisos and Trapezous in 179 is uncertain.
sources_primary: Polybius 25.2 | Strabo 12.3.11, 12.3.17
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Treaty of Pharnaces with Chersonesos
summary: An inscription from Chersonesos in the Crimea records an oath of alliance in which Pharnaces promised to protect the city's democracy and freedom against the Scythians. It is the first sign of the Pontic kings' role north of the sea that Mithridates VI later turned into an empire.
disputed: The date depends on which era the inscription's 'year 157' counts from: 179 BC or 155 BC are both defended.
sources_primary: IOSPE I(2) 402
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Saprykin 1997

title: Athens honours Pharnaces and Nysa
summary: An Athenian decree found on Delos honours King Pharnaces and Queen Nysa for gifts to Athens. It is early evidence of the dynasty's courting of Greek opinion, which Mithridates VI pursued on a much larger scale.
disputed: The archon Tychandros is dated to 160/59 by most epigraphists; an earlier date (196/5) was once argued.
sources_primary: OGIS 771 (Inscr. Delos 1497bis)
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1 | Tracy (on the archon date)

title: Mithridates IV Philopator Philadelphos and Laodice
summary: Pharnaces' brother Mithridates IV ruled with his sister-wife Laodice. In 154 he sent help to Attalus II of Pergamon against Prusias II of Bithynia, keeping Pontus on Rome's side.
disputed: His reign is dated only approximately.
sources_primary: Polybius 33.12.1 | Royal coins and dedications
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 1

title: Mithridates V Euergetes, friend of Rome
summary: Mithridates V sent ships to Rome in the Third Punic War (149-146) and fought for Rome against Aristonicus in the war over the Pergamene inheritance (133-129). In reward Manius Aquillius gave him Phrygia Major (129), which the Senate revoked after his death. He married his daughter Laodice to Ariarathes VI of Cappadocia and extended Pontic influence into Paphlagonia and Galatia.
disputed: The Phrygian grant was later called a bribe by Roman sources; its exact extent is unclear.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 10, 12, 57 | Strabo 14.1.38 | Justin 37.1.2; 38.5.3 | Eutropius 4.20
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 2 | Sherwin-White 1984

title: Mithridates V murdered at Sinope; accession of Mithridates VI
summary: Mithridates V was assassinated by members of his court at Sinope. His son Mithridates VI Eupator, born at Sinope c. 134/132, was still a boy; his mother Laodice ruled as regent with his younger brother. Justin's story of Eupator's years in hiding, hunting in the wild and taking antidotes, is legend built on his later fame; the comets said to mark his birth and accession may match comets recorded in Chinese annals for 135 and 119 BC.
disputed: He was born in 134 or 132 (Appian 112 gives his age at death as 68 or 69). The years in hiding are romance.
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 2 | Mayor 2010, chs. 3-5 | Ramsey 1999 (HSCP 99)

title: Borders c. 120 BC: the inheritance of Eupator
summary: At Eupator's accession the kingdom held Pontus proper from Amastris to Pharnakeia and inland to Zela and the Lykos, plus influence (not rule) in Paphlagonia, Galatia and Cappadocia. Phrygia Major, granted in 129, was taken back by the Senate c. 116. Lesser Armenia (under Antipater son of Sisis), Colchis and the Bosporus were independent.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.1 | Justin 38.5.3
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 2

title: Eupator takes sole power
summary: Returning to Sinope, the young king imprisoned his mother and later had her and his brother killed, then married his sister Laodice. From this point he ruled alone and began a programme of expansion around the Black Sea.
disputed: The exact year is unknown (about 116–113).
sources_primary: Memnon, FGrH 434 F 22.2 | Appian, Mith. 112 | Sallust, Histories fr. (Mithridates' letter)
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 2 | Mayor 2010

title: Lesser Armenia ceded to Mithridates; 75 treasure-forts
summary: Antipater son of Sisis, ruler of Lesser Armenia, handed his country to Mithridates. Strabo says the king built 75 fortresses there, in which he kept most of his treasure; Pompey later destroyed many of them. Lesser Armenia linked Pontus to the upper Euphrates and to Armenia proper.
disputed: The date of the cession is not given; most place it before 106.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.28
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 3
places: Lesser Armenia (later Nicopolis) (40.19, 38.12) | Upper Lykos / Satala area (40.03, 39.6)

title: Colchis annexed
summary: Mithridates took Colchis, the rich coastland of the Phasis with its timber, flax, pitch and wax for shipbuilding, and ruled it through governors; Moaphernes, Strabo's great-uncle, held the post late in the reign. The Colchian coast connected Pontus by sea to the Bosporus.
disputed: The date is unknown; it is sometimes put after the Crimean campaigns.
sources_primary: Strabo 11.2.18; 12.3.33 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 22.4
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 3 | Braund 1994 (Georgia in Antiquity)

title: Diophantus' campaigns in the Crimea; the Bosporus becomes Pontic
summary: Chersonesos asked Mithridates for help against the Scythians of Palakos. His general Diophantus of Sinope fought three campaigns, defeated the Scythians, put down the revolt of Saumakos, who had killed King Paerisades V at Pantikapaion, and secured the Bosporan kingdom for Mithridates. A long decree of Chersonesos honouring Diophantus is the contemporary record.
disputed: Absolute dates of the three campaigns (c. 110-107 or 112-109) and of Saumakos' revolt are debated.
sources_primary: IOSPE I(2) 352 (Diophantus decree) | Strabo 7.4.3, 7.4.4, 7.4.7
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 3 | Saprykin 1997 | Mayor 2010
places: Chersonesos (44.611, 33.493) | Neapolis Scythica (Simferopol) (44.95, 34.13) | Theodosia (45.03, 35.38) | Pantikapaion (Kerch) (45.35, 36.47) | Sinope (42.026, 35.153)

title: Paphlagonia and Galatia partitioned with Nicomedes III
summary: Mithridates and Nicomedes III of Bithynia shared out Paphlagonia, and Mithridates also occupied part of Galatia. When Roman envoys ordered them out, Mithridates answered that the land was his father's inheritance.
disputed: The date is approximate.
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 3

title: Borders c. 107 BC: the Black Sea empire
summary: Before he moved against Rome, Mithridates' 'Pontic empire' comprised Pontus from Amastris to Trapezous, Lesser Armenia, Colchis to Dioskourias, the Bosporan kingdom on both sides of the Kerch strait, a protectorate over Chersonesos, and shares of Paphlagonia and Galatia. Alliances with Olbia, Tyras and the Scythians, Sarmatians and Bastarnae extended his reach round the north and west coasts.
disputed: The 'alliances' on the north and west coasts are loosely attested, and the borders in the steppe are notional.
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 3 | Hojte 2009 (ed.)
places: Amastris (41.747, 32.386) | Sinope (42.026, 35.153) | Trapezous (41.005, 39.727) | Lesser Armenia (40.19, 38.12) | Colchis (Phasis) (42.15, 41.67) | Dioskourias (42.995, 41.01) | Pantikapaion (45.35, 36.47) | Phanagoria (45.28, 36.97) | Chersonesos (44.611, 33.493) | Olbia (46.69, 31.9) | Paphlagonia (40.6, 33.615)

title: The monument of Helianax on Delos
summary: Helianax, priest of Poseidon and of the Kabeiroi, built on Delos a shrine for Mithridates VI and his court, with portrait medallions of the king's Greek courtiers (among them Dorylaus, his foster-brother, and Papias of Amisos, his chief physician) and of fellow kings. It shows a Pontic court presented to the Greek world as Greek.
disputed: The inscriptions of the monument are published in the Inscriptions de Délos, in a series that runs at least to no. 1581. I.Délos 1560, a dedication of statues of Mithridates and his brother by Dionysios son of Neon (about 115/4 BC), is a separate monument.
sources_primary: I.Délos 1572 = OGIS 372: statue of Dorylaos of Amisos, son of Philetairos, foster-brother of the king and commander of the bodyguard, dedicated by Helianax son of Asklepiodoros, priest, 102/1 BC (attalus.org/docs/ogis/s372.html) | I.Délos 1581 = OGIS 430: statue of a 'first friend' of Arsakes (Mithridates II of Parthia), dedicated by Helianax, c. 102/1 BC (attalus.org/docs/ogis/s430.html)
sources_modern: Erciyas 2006 | McGing 1986, ch. 4 | Kreuz 2009 (in Hojte ed.)

title: Cappadocia: Ariarathes IX and the Roman veto
summary: Mithridates had his brother-in-law Ariarathes VI murdered (c. 116), killed Ariarathes VII at a parley (c. 100) and set his own eight-year-old son on the throne as Ariarathes IX. The Senate ordered him out of Cappadocia and Paphlagonia; the Cappadocians chose Ariobarzanes I, whom Sulla installed (in 96 or 92).
disputed: Sulla's mission to Cappadocia is dated 96 or 92 BC.
sources_primary: Justin 38.1-2 | Plutarch, Sulla 5 | Appian, Mith. 10 | Strabo 12.2.11
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 4 | Sherwin-White 1984

title: Alliance with Tigranes II of Armenia
summary: Mithridates married his daughter Cleopatra to Tigranes II, the new king of Armenia, and the two agreed that Mithridates would take cities and land and Tigranes the people and movable goods. The alliance made Armenia the refuge to which Mithridates fled in 71.
sources_primary: Justin 38.3.1-5 | Plutarch, Lucullus 22
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 4

title: Nicomedes IV raids Pontus; war begins
summary: Pressed by the Roman legate Manius Aquillius, Nicomedes IV of Bithynia raided Pontic territory as far as Amastris. Mithridates' protests went unanswered and he went to war.
disputed: Responsibility for the war: Appian blames Roman greed; modern views range from Roman provocation (Sherwin-White) to Mithridates' long preparation (McGing).
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 11-17 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 22.3-5
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 4 | Sherwin-White 1984

title: Battle of the Amnias
summary: Mithridates' generals Archelaus and Neoptolemus destroyed the army of Nicomedes IV on the plain of the Amnias river in Paphlagonia, near later Pompeiopolis. Appian gives the Pontic army as 250,000 foot, 40,000 horse, 300 decked ships and 100 two-banked ships (figures certainly inflated).
disputed: Appian's figures for the armies are not credible as given.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 17-18 | Strabo 12.3.40 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 22.6
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 4

title: Roman armies collapse; Aquillius executed at Pergamon
summary: After a Pontic victory near Protopachium (Mount Scorobas) the Roman commanders scattered. Mithridates overran Bithynia, Phrygia, Mysia and the province of Asia, where many cities welcomed him. Manius Aquillius was captured, paraded on an ass, and killed at Pergamon by molten gold poured down his throat, a punishment for Roman greed.
disputed: Protopachium and Mount Scorobas have not been located.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 19-21 | Athenaeus 5.213b (Posidonius) | Velleius 2.18
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 4 | Mayor 2010
places: Protopachium / Mt Scorobas (location unknown, approximate) (41.2, 31.9) | Pergamon (39.132, 27.184)

title: The Asian Vespers
summary: Mithridates sent secret letters to his satraps and to the cities of Asia ordering that on the thirtieth day all Romans and Italians, with their wives, children and Italian freedmen, be killed and left unburied; slaves who betrayed masters were freed, and debtors who killed creditors had half their debts cancelled. Appian describes killings at Ephesus, Pergamon, Adramyttion, Kaunos and Tralles, often in sanctuaries. Ancient totals run from 80,000 to 150,000.
disputed: The numbers run from 80,000 (Memnon, Valerius Maximus) to 150,000 (Plutarch); many modern scholars, such as Brunt, think the true number far lower. Whether the local Greeks took part willingly, as Appian implies, or under orders is also debated.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 22-23 | Plutarch, Sulla 24.4 (150,000) | Valerius Maximus 9.2.ext.3 (80,000: 'una epistola LXXX civium Romanorum … interemit') | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 1, 22.9 (80,000 'on that one day') | Cicero, De imperio Cn. Pompei 7
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5 | Sherwin-White 1984 | Kallet-Marx 1995 | Mayor 2010, ch. 8

title: Siege of Rhodes fails
summary: Rhodes, the main Greek holdout, beat off Mithridates' fleet and his siege engine (the sambuca). Magnesia by Sipylos and Stratonikeia also resisted.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 24-27
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5

title: Sack of Delos; Athens goes over to Mithridates
summary: A Pontic fleet under Menophanes and Archelaus sacked Delos, the great Italian trading centre; Appian says 20,000 people, mostly Italians, were killed on Delos and the islands. Athens, led by Athenion and then Aristion, joined Mithridates, who presented himself as liberator of the Greeks.
disputed: The figure of 20,000 is Appian's alone.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 28 | Pausanias 3.23.3-5 | Athenaeus 5.211d-215b (Posidonius)
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5 | Habicht 1997 (Athens from Alexander to Antony)

title: Borders 88 BC: the greatest extent
summary: At the height of his power, besides the Black Sea empire of c. 107, Mithridates held Bithynia, Paphlagonia, Cappadocia, Galatia, Phrygia, the Roman province of Asia (except Rhodes, Magnesia by Sipylos, Stratonikeia and some Lycian cities), many Aegean islands, and through Archelaus Athens, Boeotia and Euboea (87-86). The king moved his court to Pergamon.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 20-29 | Plutarch, Sulla 11
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5

title: Sulla besieges Athens and Piraeus
summary: Sulla landed in Greece in 87 and besieged Athens and Archelaus in Piraeus. Athens fell on the Kalends of March 86 after famine; Piraeus was taken and burned.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 30-41 | Plutarch, Sulla 12-14
sources_modern: Keaveney 1982/2005 (Sulla) | Habicht 1997

title: Battle of Chaeronea
summary: Sulla routed the Pontic army of Archelaus and Taxiles in Boeotia. The Pontic army is given as 110,000–120,000: Plutarch has Taxiles bring 100,000 foot, 10,000 horse and 90 scythed chariots (Sulla 15.1) but speaks of 120,000 later (22.4), and Appian gives 120,000 (Mith. 41); the Romans were fewer than 17,000. Sulla's memoirs claimed only 14 men missing, of whom two came back (Plutarch, Sulla 19.4); Appian has 15, two of whom returned (45). Only about 10,000 of the Pontic army escaped (Plutarch; Appian).
disputed: All the figures come from the winners' side, through Sulla's memoirs; the Pontic army is best given as a range, 110,000–120,000.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 41–45 | Plutarch, Sulla 15–19 (15.1, 19.4), 22.4
sources_modern: Keaveney 2005 | McGing 1986, ch. 5

title: Battle of Orchomenos
summary: A second Pontic army under Dorylaus and Archelaus was destroyed by Sulla in the marshes at Orchomenos. Pontic power in Greece ended.
disputed: The battle is dated late 86 or early 85.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 49-50 | Plutarch, Sulla 20-21
sources_modern: Keaveney 2005

title: Fimbria's campaign in Asia
summary: Fimbria murdered the consul Flaccus at Nicomedia, took his army, defeated the king's son at the Rhyndakos, nearly trapped Mithridates at Pitane (Lucullus' fleet refused to help) and sacked Ilion.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 51-53 | Plutarch, Lucullus 3 | Plutarch, Sulla 23 | Orosius 6.2.11
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5

title: Peace of Dardanus
summary: Sulla and Mithridates met at Dardanos in the Troad. Mithridates gave up all his conquests (Asia, Bithynia, Paphlagonia, Cappadocia) and paid an indemnity of 2,000 talents and 70 bronze-armoured ships with their equipment (Plutarch, Sulla 22.5; 70 ships and 500 archers at the handover, 24.3); Memnon gives 80 triremes and 3,000 talents, paid to Sulla personally (F 1, 25.2). He kept his kingdom and was recognised as a friend of Rome.
disputed: The indemnity and fleet are given as 2,000 talents and 70 ships (Plutarch) or 3,000 talents and 80 triremes (Memnon).
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 54-58 | Plutarch, Sulla 22-24 (22.5, 24.3) | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 1, 25.2
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 5 | Keaveney 2005

title: Borders 85 BC: back to the Black Sea
summary: After Dardanus Mithridates kept Pontus, Lesser Armenia and Colchis. The Bosporan cities and Colchis rose against him in the following years; he recovered Colchis, and the Bosporus was retaken c. 80 under his son Machares.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 58, 64, 67
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 6

title: Second Mithridatic War: Murena invades
summary: Sulla's legate Lucius Licinius Murena, on a pretext, invaded Pontic territory, attacked the rich temple-village of Komana and raided some 400 villages.
disputed: Which Komana Appian means is not certain.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 64-65 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 26
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 6

title: Murena defeated on the Halys
summary: Mithridates beat Murena in a battle near the Halys. Sulla sent Aulus Gabinius to stop the war; Mithridates betrothed a daughter to Ariobarzanes and kept a slice of Cappadocia for a time (81).
disputed: The site of the battle is unknown.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 65-66
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 6

title: Machares king of the Bosporus; disaster among the Achaeans
summary: Mithridates retook the Bosporus and made his son Machares king there. A campaign against the 'Achaeans', a people of the Caucasus coast north of Colchis, cost him two thirds of his army.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 67, 102
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 6

title: Bithynia bequeathed to Rome; alliance with Sertorius
summary: Nicomedes IV died and left Bithynia to Rome, which put Roman power on Pontus' western border. Mithridates had already made an alliance with the Roman rebel Sertorius in Spain (c. 75), who sent him officers.
disputed: The date of Nicomedes' death, 75 or 74, is tied to the debate over when the Third War began.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 68-71 | Plutarch, Sertorius 23-24 | Livy, Per. 93 | Eutropius 6.6
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 7 | Sherwin-White 1984

title: Third Mithridatic War: invasion of Bithynia; Cotta beaten at Chalcedon
summary: Mithridates invaded Bithynia with a great army and fleet and defeated the consul Marcus Aurelius Cotta by land and sea at Chalcedon.
disputed: The war is dated to 74 (the older view) or 73 (McGing, Sherwin-White).
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 69-71 | Plutarch, Lucullus 7-8 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 27
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 7 | Keaveney 1992 (Lucullus)

title: Siege of Cyzicus
summary: Mithridates besieged Cyzicus by land and sea while Lucullus cut his supply lines. Hunger and plague broke the besiegers; Lucullus destroyed the retreating army at the Rhyndakos and at the Aisepos and Granikos.
disputed: Plutarch's 300,000 for the Pontic army is an ancient figure, not a count.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 72-76 | Plutarch, Lucullus 9-11 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 28 | Strabo 12.8.11
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992 | McGing 1986, ch. 7

title: Lucullus invades Pontus: Amisos, Eupatoria and Themiskyra besieged
summary: Lucullus marched through Galatia into Pontus and besieged Amisos, the neighbouring royal foundation Eupatoria, and Themiskyra on the Thermodon, whose defenders, Appian says, sent bears and swarms of bees into the Roman tunnels.
disputed: Appian places Eupatoria next to Amisos; Strabo (12.3.30) places a half-built Eupatoria where the Lykos joins the Iris, later Pompey's Magnopolis. Whether these are two places or one is debated.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 78 | Plutarch, Lucullus 14
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992 | McGing 1986, ch. 7

title: Battle of Kabeira; Mithridates flees to Armenia
summary: Mithridates wintered at Kabeira, his favourite residence. After cavalry battles and a failed supply war, panic broke out in his camp as he began to withdraw; the army dissolved and the king escaped by way of Komana to Tigranes in Armenia, who kept him waiting twenty months.
disputed: Winter 72/71 is the usual date; some put the battle in 72.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 79-82 | Plutarch, Lucullus 15-19, 22 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 29
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992 | McGing 1986, ch. 7
places: Kabeira (Niksar) (40.592, 36.955) | Komana Pontica (40.355, 36.635) | Lesser Armenia (40.19, 38.12) | Armenia (Artaxata) (39.88, 44.58)

title: The royal women killed at Pharnakeia
summary: Fearing they would fall into Roman hands, Mithridates sent the eunuch Bacchides to kill his sisters Roxane and Statira and his wives Berenice of Chios and Monime of Miletus, who were kept at Pharnakeia. Plutarch's account of Monime's death became famous; it also shows how many of the king's wives were Greeks of the Aegean cities.
disputed: Plutarch is the only source.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 18
sources_modern: Mayor 2010, ch. 13 | McGing 1986

title: Fall of Amisos
summary: Amisos was taken after a long siege; its commander, the engineer Callimachus, set fire to the city as he escaped by sea. Lucullus, recalling Sulla at Athens, wept, rebuilt the city, freed it and resettled its people; among the captives was the grammarian Tyrannion of Amisos, later Strabo's teacher in Rome.
disputed: Dated 71, by some 70.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 19 | Appian, Mith. 83 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 30 | Strabo 12.3.16
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992

title: Fall of Sinope
summary: Sinope, held by a Cilician garrison under Leonippus and Cleochares (Strabo names Bacchides, who oppressed the citizens), was stormed by Lucullus; the garrison burned the heavier ships and fled. Lucullus freed the city but took away the statue of its founder Autolykos and the sphere of Billaros.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 23 | Strabo 12.3.11 | Appian, Mith. 83 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 37 | Orosius 6.3.2
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992

title: Amaseia surrenders; Strabo's family changes sides
summary: Amaseia and the remaining Pontic fortresses surrendered. Strabo records that his mother's father, angered by the king's execution of his cousin Tibius and Tibius' son Theophilus, made terms with Lucullus and brought fifteen garrisons over to him. Machares in the Bosporus also made peace with Lucullus.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 83 | Strabo 12.3.33; 10.4.10 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 37
sources_modern: Dueck 2000, ch. 1 | Keaveney 1992

title: Borders 70 BC: Pontus under Lucullus
summary: Under the Roman occupation, Roman forces held the Pontic coast (Amastris, Sinope, Amisos, Pharnakeia) and the interior (Amaseia, Kabeira, Komana); Mithridates held nothing in Pontus, and the Bosporus under Machares was allied to Rome.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 19-23 | Appian, Mith. 82-83
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992

title: Battle of Tigranocerta
summary: Lucullus invaded Armenia and defeated Tigranes' great army before his new capital, Tigranocerta, on the day before the Nones of October; Plutarch says Tigranes had over 250,000 men and Lucullus about 11,000, and that only five Romans died. The city, peopled by Greeks and others deported from Cappadocia and Cilicia, fell and Lucullus sent the deportees home.
disputed: The site of Tigranocerta is unresolved (Silvan, Arzan, or the Garzan valley proposed by Sinclair). Plutarch's numbers are Roman propaganda.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 24-29 | Appian, Mith. 84-86 | Memnon, FGrH 434 F 38 | Strabo 11.14.15; 12.2.9
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992 | Sinclair 1994-1997 (on the site)
places: Melitene (38.42, 38.36) | Tigranocerta (proposed: near Silvan; alternatives Arzan, Garzan valley) (38.14, 41.0)

title: Artaxata and Nisibis; Lucullus' army balks
summary: Lucullus beat the allied kings again near Artaxata, but his troops refused to go on into the Armenian highlands; he turned south and took Nisibis in winter 68/67. Mutiny, stirred up by Publius Clodius, ended his offensive.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Lucullus 31-34 | Cassius Dio 36.6-7, 36.14-17
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992

title: Mithridates returns: the Roman disaster at Zela
summary: Mithridates came back into Pontus, defeated the legate Fabius and then Triarius at Zela, where 7,000 Romans fell, among them 24 tribunes and 150 centurions. He regained most of his kingdom.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 88-89 | Plutarch, Lucullus 35 | Cassius Dio 36.12-13
sources_modern: Keaveney 1992 | McGing 1986, ch. 7

title: Pompey's night victory near Nicopolis
summary: Given the command by the lex Manilia, Pompey trapped Mithridates in Lesser Armenia and attacked his camp at night by the light of a low moon, which threw the Romans' shadows far ahead of them. Plutarch says 'many more than ten thousand' Pontic soldiers fell (Pomp. 32.7), Orosius 40,000 killed or captured (6.4.5); Mithridates broke out with 800 horsemen and fled with three companions (Pomp. 32.8), among them his concubine Hypsikrateia, who rode and fought dressed as a man. Pompey founded Nicopolis, 'Victory City', on the site.
disputed: Pontic losses run from 'many more than ten thousand slain' (Plutarch) to 40,000 killed or captured (Orosius, who gives the Roman losses as 1,000 wounded and scarcely 40 killed). The site of the battle (Dasteira?) is debated. An epitaph found at Phanagoria in 2004 naming 'Hypsikrates, wife of King Mithridates Eupator Dionysos' (Bernard 2006; Heinen 2012; Gabelko 2013) appears to confirm Hypsikrateia.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 97-101 | Plutarch, Pompey 32 (32.7–8) | Cassius Dio 36.45-50 | Strabo 12.3.28 | Livy, Per. 101 | Orosius 6.4.3-5 (6.4.5: 'XL milia caesa uel capta')
sources_modern: Seager 2002 (Pompey) | McGing 1986, ch. 7 | Mayor 2010, ch. 15 | Bernard 2006, CRAI, pp. 280–288 (the Phanagoria epitaph) | Gabelko 2013 (on the epitaph)

title: Mithridates' flight round the Caucasus to the Bosporus
summary: Mithridates wintered at Dioskourias in Colchis, then marched along the Caucasus coast through the lands of the Heniochoi, Zygoi and Achaeans to the Bosporus, where his son Machares killed himself (or was killed). He planned, according to Appian, to march round the Black Sea and up the Danube to invade Italy.
disputed: The route over the coastal mountains is not recorded; only the peoples along the coast are named.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 101-102, 109 | Cassius Dio 36.50; 37.3 | Plutarch, Pompey 32.9-11
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 7 | Mayor 2010

title: Pompey in the Caucasus
summary: Pompey followed into Iberia and Albania (eastern Georgia and Azerbaijan), fought the Albanians near the Kyros (Kura) and reached the Phasis, where his fleet under Servilius blockaded the Pontic coast. He then turned back, judging Mithridates out of reach.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Pompey 34-36 | Appian, Mith. 103 | Cassius Dio 37.1-5
sources_modern: Seager 2002 | Braund 1994
places: Iberia (Mtskheta-Tbilisi area) (41.7, 44.8) | Albania (Kura valley, approximate) (41.2, 46.9) | Phasis (42.15, 41.67)

title: The Heptakometai's mad honey
summary: Strabo tells that the Heptakometai, a mountain people between Trapezous and Pharnakeia (the Mossynoikoi of Xenophon), destroyed three of Pompey's maniples by setting out bowls of the 'maddening' rhododendron honey along the road and attacking the stupefied soldiers. It echoes Xenophon's account of the mad honey near Trapezous.
disputed: Strabo gives no date; it is inferred from Pompey's movements.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.18 | cf. Xenophon, Anabasis 4.8.20-21
sources_modern: Mayor 2003 (Greek Fire, Poison Arrows and Scorpion Bombs) | Bryer & Winfield 1985
places: Heptakometai country (mountains south of the coast between Pharnakeia and Trapezous, approximate) (40.85, 38.9)

title: Pompey's settlement: Pontus et Bithynia and the new cities
summary: Pompey joined the western half of Pontus to Bithynia as a single province and divided it into eleven city territories (politeiai). He founded or refounded Nicopolis, Magnopolis (Eupatoria), Diospolis (Kabeira), Neapolis (Phazemon), Megalopolis (later Sebasteia), Pompeiopolis and Zela as cities. The east, with Lesser Armenia and the coast towards Colchis, went to allied kings (Deiotarus); the priesthood of Komana to Archelaus; inner Paphlagonia to the house of Pylaemenes.
disputed: Which eleven cities formed the city territories is reconstructed differently (Marek; Madsen), and so is the eastern border of the province (Amisos, or the Iris).
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.1, 12.3.28, 12.3.30-31, 12.3.37-38, 12.3.40 | Appian, Mith. 114-115 | Cassius Dio 37.20.2 | Pliny, Ep. 10.79 (lex Pompeia) | Plutarch, Pompey 38
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Madsen 2009 (Eager to be Roman) | Mitchell 1993, vol. 1 | Magie 1950

title: Revolt of Phanagoria; death of Mithridates at Pantikapaion
summary: Exhausted by levies, Phanagoria revolted; Mithridates' son Pharnaces won over the army, which proclaimed him king. Mithridates, immune to the poison he took, had his Gallic officer Bituitus kill him in the citadel of Pantikapaion. He was 68 or 69 and had reigned 57 years. Pompey heard the news near Jericho.
disputed: The season, spring or summer 63, is uncertain. The poison story is ancient tradition.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 107-112 | Cassius Dio 37.10-14 | Plutarch, Pompey 41-42 | Orosius 6.5
sources_modern: McGing 1986, ch. 7 | Mayor 2010, ch. 16

title: Mithridates buried at Sinope among the kings
summary: Pharnaces sent the embalmed body to Pompey, who gave it a royal funeral and had it buried in the tombs of the kings at Sinope. Pharnaces received the Bosporan kingdom, except Phanagoria, which was declared free.
disputed: The Sinope tombs have not been found.
sources_primary: Appian, Mith. 113 | Plutarch, Pompey 42.4 | Cassius Dio 37.14
sources_modern: McGing 1986

title: Borders 63 BC: Pompey's Pontus
summary: Pompey's settlement. The province of Pontus et Bithynia: Bithynia plus coastal and inner Pontus from Heraclea and Amastris through Sinope and Amisos, with interior cities such as Pompeiopolis, Neapolis, Amaseia, Diospolis, Magnopolis, Zela and Megalopolis. Client rulers: Deiotarus (Lesser Armenia, Gazelonitis and the coast east towards Trapezous), Archelaus (Komana), Attalus and the Pylaemenids (inner Paphlagonia), Aristarchus (Colchis), Pharnaces II (Bosporus, minus free Phanagoria).
disputed: The eastern boundary of the province and the attribution of Amaseia, Trapezous and Pharnakeia are uncertain.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.1, 12.3.13, 12.3.38-39 | Appian, Mith. 114 | Cassius Dio 37.20
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Sullivan 1980 (ANRW II.7.2) | Mitchell 1993

title: Pompey's triumph over Mithridates
summary: Pompey's two-day triumph in Rome displayed the conquered peoples (Pontus, Armenia, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia, Media, Colchis, Iberia, Albania, the Heniochoi, Achaeans and others), Mithridates' treasures and his children. Pompey's dedication in the temple of Minerva, quoted by Pliny (NH 7.97), claimed 12,183,000 people 'routed, put to flight, killed or received in surrender', 846 ships sunk or taken and 1,538 towns and forts taken under Roman protection; his inscriptions also claimed 39 cities founded (Plutarch, Pomp. 45.2).
disputed: The figures are Pompey's own propaganda. Pliny's 12,183,000 counts people routed, killed or taken in surrender, not a population 'subdued'.
sources_primary: Plutarch, Pompey 45 (45.2: 39 cities) | Appian, Mith. 116-117 | Pliny, NH 7.97 (the dedication: 12,183,000 people), 7.98 (the triumph, a.d. III Kal. Oct.); 37.12-16
sources_modern: Beard 2007 (The Roman Triumph) | Seager 2002

title: Pharnaces II invades Pontus; victory at Nicopolis
summary: During Rome's civil war Pharnaces crossed from the Bosporus to recover his father's kingdom, overran Lesser Armenia, Cappadocia and Pontus, and defeated Caesar's legate Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus near Nicopolis.
sources_primary: Bellum Alexandrinum 34-40 | Cassius Dio 42.45-46 | Appian, Mith. 120
sources_modern: Sullivan 1990 (Near Eastern Royalty and Rome)

title: Pharnaces takes Sinope and sacks Amisos
summary: Pharnaces captured Sinope and stormed Amisos, which had held to Rome; he killed or sold the citizens and castrated the boys.
sources_primary: Bellum Alexandrinum 41 | Cassius Dio 42.46.3-4 | Appian, Mith. 120
sources_modern: Sullivan 1990

title: Battle of Zela: 'veni, vidi, vici'
summary: Caesar, arriving from Egypt and Syria, met Pharnaces at Zela, where Pharnaces camped on the hill of his father's victory over Triarius. Pharnaces attacked uphill and was routed within about four hours. Caesar summed it up as 'I came, I saw, I conquered', in a letter (Plutarch) or on a placard in his Pontic triumph of 46 (Suetonius).
disputed: The date is in the pre-Julian calendar: 2 August 47 is about 21 May 47 BC in the Julian calendar (J. Lendering, livius.org); Lord (1938) gives 2 August from the Roman calendars.
sources_primary: Bellum Alexandrinum 72-76 | Plutarch, Caesar 50 | Suetonius, Divus Julius 35.2, 37.2 | Appian, Civil Wars 2.91 | Cassius Dio 42.47-48 | Fasti Amiternini (date)
sources_modern: Gelzer 1968 (Caesar) | Sullivan 1990 | Lord, L. E. 1938, 'The date of Julius Caesar's departure from Alexandria', JRS 28: 19–40 (Pharnaces 'defeated at Zela, in Pontus, on August 2nd', after the Roman calendars, CIL I, pp. 304 and 324)

title: Caesar's settlement; Pharnaces killed
summary: Pharnaces fled to the Bosporus and was killed by his governor Asander. Caesar gave the Bosporus to Mithridates of Pergamon, freed Amisos, and adjusted the client states, reducing Deiotarus.
sources_primary: Bellum Alexandrinum 77-78 | Appian, Mith. 120-121 | Cassius Dio 42.47.5-48.4 | Strabo 13.4.3
sources_modern: Sullivan 1990

title: Colonia Iulia Felix Sinope
summary: Caesar settled Roman colonists at Sinope, which became Colonia Iulia Felix Sinope; the colony's coins count an era from 45 BC. Strabo notes the Roman colony beside the Greek city.
disputed: Founded between 47 and 45; the colony's coins count an era from 45 BC.
sources_primary: Strabo 12.3.11 | Colonial coins of Sinope
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Mitchell 1993

title: Antony gives Pontus to Darius son of Pharnaces
summary: Mark Antony, reorganising the east, gave Pontus to Darius, a son of Pharnaces II and grandson of Mithridates VI. The Mithridatid line thus briefly returned.
disputed: The extent of Darius' kingdom is uncertain.
sources_primary: Appian, Civil Wars 5.75
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980 (ANRW II.7.2)

title: Polemon I king of Pontus
summary: Antony made Polemon, son of the orator Zeno of Laodiceia, king of Pontus east of the Halys and later added Lesser Armenia. Polemon survived Antony's fall and was confirmed by Augustus as a friend and ally of the Roman people; the Polemonid kingdom held the eastern coast, including Trapezous and Pharnakeia, until AD 64.
disputed: When Polemonion, the older Side, took its name is not known.
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980 | Mitchell 1993
places: Kabeira region (40.592, 36.955) | Trapezous (41.005, 39.727) | Pharnakeia (40.917, 38.388) | Polemonion (Bolaman near Fatsa, approximate) (41.05, 37.52)

title: Borders 36 BC: Antony's client kingdoms
summary: Under Antony: Polemon I held Pontus east of the Halys and Iris (Kabeira, Pharnakeia, Trapezous) with Lesser Armenia. Inner Pontus around Amaseia and Gaziura under local dynasts ('given to kings' in Strabo's words). The coastal west (Sinope, Amisos, Amastris) remained in the province of Bithynia et Pontus, with Amisos briefly under a tyrant.
disputed: Internal boundaries are uncertain.
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980 | Marek 1993

title: Polemon I given the Bosporus
summary: Agrippa gave Polemon the Bosporan kingdom; he married its queen Dynamis, granddaughter of Mithridates VI. For a few years one king ruled both Pontus and the Kerch strait again.
sources_primary: Cassius Dio 54.24.4-6
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980

title: Polemon killed; Pythodoris queen of Pontus
summary: Polemon died fighting the Aspurgians near Sindike. His widow Pythodoris, daughter of Pythodoros of Tralles and through her mother a granddaughter of Mark Antony, ruled Pontus. She later married Archelaus of Cappadocia; Strabo, writing in her lifetime, calls her wise and able and lists her lands: Pharnakeia and Trapezous, the Tibarenoi and Chaldaioi up to Colchis, and the Kabeira district, which she made her residence under the name Sebaste.
disputed: The end of her reign is unknown (after AD 21; some lists run it to 38).
sources_primary: Strabo 11.2.11; 12.3.29; 12.3.31 | Inscriptions naming Pythodoris and her Antonian descent
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980 | Dueck 2000
places: Aspurgian country (Kuban, approximate) (45.1, 37.8) | Sebaste (Kabeira) (40.592, 36.955) | Pharnakeia (40.917, 38.388) | Trapezous (41.005, 39.727)

title: Borders c. 8 BC-AD 20: Pythodoris' Pontus
summary: From Strabo (12.3.29–31): Queen Pythodoris held the Kabeira-Sebaste district, Phanaroia, Pharnakeia, Trapezous, the Tibarenoi and Chaldaioi as far as Colchis, and Polemonion. Inner Pontus (Amaseia, Sebastopolis, Megalopolis-Sebasteia) passed to Rome in 3/2 BC; Komana stayed a temple-state until 34/35.
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980 | Marek 1993

title: Pontus Galaticus annexed to Galatia
summary: Inner Pontus around Amaseia, with Sebastopolis and Megalopolis-Sebasteia, was annexed and attached to the province of Galatia; the cities' coins count their era from 3/2 BC. The area came to be called Pontus Galaticus.
disputed: Which cities joined in 3/2 BC and which later is debated; Zela's status is unclear.
sources_primary: City coin eras | Ptolemy, Geography 5.6.3-4 (Pontus Galaticus)
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Mitchell 1993, vol. 1

title: Death of Archelaus; Cappadocia a province
summary: Archelaus of Cappadocia, Pythodoris' second husband, died in Rome and Tiberius annexed Cappadocia. Pythodoris kept her Pontic kingdom.
sources_primary: Tacitus, Annals 2.42 | Strabo 12.1.4
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993

title: Strabo of Amaseia describes his homeland (Geography book 12)
summary: Strabo, born at Amaseia c. 64 BC into a Greek family of the Mithridatic court, wrote the Pontic part of his Geography under Tiberius. He describes 'our city' in the Iris gorge with the palaces and 'memorials of the kings', the iron mines of the Chaldaioi, Kabeira's palace, water-mill and game parks, the temple-states of Komana ('not fewer than 6,000' temple servants, 12.3.34) and Zela, the plain of Themiskyra, and the 'maddening honey'. It is the only eyewitness description of Pontus from antiquity.
disputed: Most of it was written about AD 18–24: it mentions Zeno-Artaxias' accession (18) and Archelaus' death (17).
sources_modern: Dueck 2000 | Roller 2018 (Commentary)

title: Komana Pontica annexed
summary: The temple-state of Komana Pontica, ruled by its priest-dynasts since Pompey, was absorbed into the province; its coins count an era from 34/35.
sources_primary: City coin era
sources_modern: Marek 1993

title: Polemon II king of Pontus
summary: Caligula made Polemon II, son of Polemon I and Pythodoris, king of Pontus; in 41 Claudius gave the Bosporus to another dynast and compensated Polemon with land in Cilicia.
sources_primary: Cassius Dio 59.12.2; 60.8.2
sources_modern: Sullivan 1980

title: Jews and the first Christians of Pontus
summary: Jews 'from Pontus' are among the crowd at Pentecost in Acts, and Aquila, the companion of Paul, was a Jew born in Pontus. The First Letter of Peter is addressed to the 'exiles of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia'. These are the earliest references to Christianity reaching the region, probably through the Jewish communities of the coastal cities.
disputed: The date and authorship of 1 Peter are debated (about 65–95).
sources_primary: Acts 2:9; 18:2 | 1 Peter 1:1 | Philo, Legatio 281 (Jews in Pontus)
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993, vol. 2 | Elliott 2000 (1 Peter)

date_text: 1st century AD (church tradition; no date given)
title: The Apostle Andrew at Trapezous: the founding tradition
summary: Chrysanthos puts the Apostle Andrew at the head of his list of the bishops of Trapezous. Following Symeon Metaphrastes and the Menaion (30 November), he has Andrew come to Trapezous twice from Amisos and preach also at Sousourmaina, Apsaros, Phasis and Sebastopolis. A cave of St Andrew below the later metropolitan church of St Gregory of Nyssa was still used for the liturgy on 30 November. He quotes Joseph Lazaropoulos (14th c.) that 'our whole people never received any other belief about the faith' ('μὴ ἄλλην δόξαν δεδέχθαι ποτὲ περὶ πίστεως ὅλον τὸ φῦλον ἡμῶν').
disputed: This is tradition only: Chrysanthos' sources are medieval hagiography and liturgy. Andrew is a founder figure, not a resident bishop.
sources_primary: Symeon Metaphrastes, Life of St Andrew (as cited by Chrysanthos) | Menaion, 30 November | Joseph Lazaropoulos, on the miracles of St Eugenios (14th c.)

title: Trapezous supplies Corbulo's Armenian war
summary: In Corbulo's war with Parthia over Armenia, supplies came by the Black Sea through Trapezous and up over the Pontic mountains. This is the first clear sign of Trapezous' role as the sea gate of the Armenian frontier, which defined it for the next six centuries.
sources_primary: Tacitus, Annals 13.39.1
sources_modern: Mitford 2018 | Bryer & Winfield 1985

title: Nero annexes Pontus Polemoniacus
summary: Polemon II gave up his kingdom and Nero made it a province; the coins of Neocaesarea, Trapezous and other cities count a new era from 64. The kingdom was attached to Galatia as Pontus Polemoniacus, and the royal fleet became the Roman Pontic fleet. With this, all of Pontus was under direct Roman rule.
disputed: Some king lists end Polemon's reign in 62/63; the city eras support 64.
sources_primary: Suetonius, Nero 18 | Eutropius 7.14.1 | Aurelius Victor, De Caesaribus 5.2 | Tacitus, Histories 3.47 | City coin eras
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Mitchell 1993, vol. 1 | Magie 1950

title: Borders AD 64: the provinces of Pontus
summary: After 64, western Pontus (Amastris, Sinope, Amisos, Pompeiopolis, Neapolis) lay in the province of Bithynia et Pontus; Pontus Galaticus (Amaseia, Zela, Sebastopolis, Sebasteia, Komana) and the new Pontus Polemoniacus (Neocaesarea, Polemonion, Kerasous, Trapezous) were both attached to Galatia; Cappadocia lay to the south, and Lesser Armenia stayed under client kings until 72.
disputed: The exact line between Bithynia et Pontus and Pontus Galaticus west of Amisos is uncertain.
sources_primary: Ptolemy, Geography 5.6 | Coin eras
sources_modern: Marek 1993 | Mitchell 1993

title: Forty warships keep the Black Sea
summary: In the speech Josephus gives Agrippa II, the peoples round the Black Sea and the Maeotis (Heniochoi, Colchians, Taurians, Bosporans) are kept in order by 3,000 soldiers and 40 warships, which have made a once unnavigable sea safe. It is the earliest description of the classis Pontica, based at Trapezous.
disputed: The speech is rhetorical, and the figures may be Josephus' own.
sources_primary: Josephus, Jewish War 2.366-367
sources_modern: Mitford 2018 | Starr 1960 (The Roman Imperial Navy)

title: Anicetus' revolt at Trapezous
summary: Anicetus, a freedman of Polemon II and former commander of the royal fleet, rose for Vitellius against Vespasian. He seized Trapezous, 'a city of ancient fame founded by Greeks at the far end of the Pontic coast', killed the cohort there (former royal auxiliaries given Roman citizenship) and burned the fleet. Vespasian's officer Virdius Geminus caught him at the mouth of the Chobos in Colchis, where the king of the Sedochezi handed him over.
sources_primary: Tacitus, Histories 3.47-48
sources_modern: Mitford 2018 | Braund 1994

title: Vespasian builds the eastern frontier
summary: Vespasian joined Galatia and Cappadocia (with the Pontic districts and annexed Lesser Armenia) under a consular legate with legions. Legio XII Fulminata was posted to Melitene and Legio XVI Flavia Firma to Satala on the upper Lykos, and roads were built linking Satala to Trapezous. From now on Pontus was the rear and supply base of the Armenian frontier.
disputed: The date of the garrison at Satala (about 72–76) is approximate.
sources_primary: Josephus, Jewish War 7.18 | Suetonius, Vespasian 8.4 | Milestones of the Flavian road programme
sources_modern: Mitford 2018 | Mitchell 1993, vol. 1 | Speidel 2009 (Heer und Herrschaft)

title: Pliny the Younger governs Bithynia et Pontus
summary: Trajan's special legate Pliny wrote to the emperor from the Pontic part of his province about Sinope's need for an aqueduct and Amisos' status as a free and federate city with its own laws. His famous letter on the Christians, the first pagan account of Christian worship, was probably written in the eastern (Pontic) part of the province, perhaps at Amastris or Amisos.
disputed: The exact years (109–111 or 110–112) and the place where the letter on the Christians (10.96) was written are debated.
sources_primary: Pliny, Letters 10.90-93, 10.96-97
sources_modern: Sherwin-White 1966 (Letters of Pliny) | Mitchell 1993, vol. 2

title: Cappadocia separated from Galatia
summary: Under Trajan the great Galatian-Cappadocian command was split. Pontus Galaticus and Pontus Polemoniacus, with Trapezous and the coast to Dioskourias, went with Cappadocia, whose governor commanded the two legions; Arrian later held this post.
disputed: The year of the division (107–113) is debated.
sources_primary: Ptolemy, Geography 5.6 | Arrian, Periplus 1-11
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993 | Mitford 2018

title: Trajan at Satala and Elegeia
summary: Starting his Parthian war, Trajan came to Satala, where he received client kings of the Caucasus and gave gifts to Anchialus, king of the Heniochoi and Machelones; he then annexed Armenia.
sources_primary: Cassius Dio 68.18-19 | Eutropius 8.3.1
sources_modern: Bennett 1997 (Trajan) | Mitford 2018

title: Legio XV Apollinaris at Satala
summary: Legio XV Apollinaris replaced XVI Flavia Firma at Satala around the end of Trajan's reign and stayed there into the 5th century. With XII Fulminata at Melitene it formed the garrison of Cappadocia.
disputed: The date of the change (about 114–120) is approximate.
sources_primary: Arrian, Ektaxis kata Alanon 5-6, 15 | Notitia Dignitatum, Oriens 38.13-14 | Inscriptions from Satala
sources_modern: Mitford 2018 | Speidel 2009 | Bryer & Winfield 1978, 'Cities of Heraclius', BMGS 4 (repr. Bryer 1980, I), p. 26 (the Trapezous–Satala axis of the old Legio XV Apollinaris; Satala still a station of the Notitia Dignitatum)

title: Aquila of Sinope translates the Bible
summary: Aquila, a convert to Judaism from Sinope (in Epiphanius' story a relative of Hadrian), made a strictly literal Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible used by Greek-speaking Jews for centuries.
disputed: The link to Hadrian is late legend.
sources_primary: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.21.1 | Epiphanius, On Weights and Measures 14-15
sources_modern: Fernandez Marcos 2000 (The Septuagint in Context)

title: Arrian's Periplus: the governor sails from Trapezous to Sebastopolis
summary: Arrian of Nicomedia, governor of Cappadocia, inspected the forts of the eastern Black Sea and sent Hadrian a Greek report. From Trapezous he sailed to Hyssou Limen (180 stades; a cohort and 20 horse), Athenai, Apsaros (five cohorts), Phasis (a fort with 400 picked men) and Sebastopolis-Dioskourias, the last Roman post, about 2,260 stades in all. He lists the client peoples and kings on the way, including the first mention of the Lazoi (king Malassas) and the Sannoi; the death of King Kotys II of the Bosporus (17.3) dates the work to 131/132.
disputed: Arrian's stage figures do not add up exactly to his total of 2,260 stades, and some identifications (Hyssou Limen, the Prytanis, the Pyxites) are disputed. Whether the Greek Periplus is a literary companion to a lost Latin report is debated. Bryer & Winfield (1978, British) place Hyssou Limen at the rectangular Roman camp (200 × 300 m) near Canayer, inland of the coastal fort of Sourmaina, 1 km from Araklı, the natural port for the direct route up the Kara Dere valley to Satala.
sources_primary: Arrian, Periplus Ponti Euxini 1-11 (voyage), 11.1-3 (peoples), 12-25 (coastal list), 17.3 (death of Kotys)
