title: Trapezous in Arrian's report: Hadrian's harbour
summary: At Trapezous Arrian saw the temple of Hermes and new altars, criticised the inscriptions and the statue of Hadrian pointing out to sea, and asked for better ones. Hadrian, who had looked out over the sea from the same spot as Xenophon, was building the city's first proper harbour, where before ships could ride at anchor only in summer.
disputed: When Hadrian visited Trapezous, in 129 or 131, is not certain.
sources_primary: Arrian, Periplus 1.1-4, 16.6
sources_modern: Liddle 2003 | Bryer & Winfield 1985

title: Arrian turns back the Alans
summary: When the Alans raided from the Caucasus into Armenia and Cappadocia, Arrian led legions XV Apollinaris and XII Fulminata with auxiliaries against them; his 'Order of battle against the Alans' survives. The Alans withdrew.
disputed: Where the armies met is not known.
sources_primary: Arrian, Ektaxis kata Alanon | Cassius Dio 69.15.1
sources_modern: Bosworth 1977 (HSCP 81) | Mitford 2018

title: Marcion of Sinope
summary: Marcion, a wealthy shipowner of Sinope and, according to Epiphanius, son of the city's bishop, went to Rome, where his break with the church is dated to 144. The story is the earliest evidence for a bishop at Sinope.
disputed: The detail of the bishop father is late (Epiphanius) and may be polemic.
sources_primary: Tertullian, Against Marcion 1.1, 1.19 | Epiphanius, Panarion 42.1-2 | Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.27.2 | Eusebius, HE 5.13.3
sources_modern: Lieu 2015 (Marcion and the Making of a Heretic)

title: 'Pontus is full of atheists and Christians'
summary: Lucian's satire on the oracle-founder Alexander of Abonoteichos has Alexander complain that Pontus is 'full of atheists and Christians', and exclude them from his mysteries. It shows Christians as a visible group in the Pontic cities by the later 2nd century.
disputed: It is satire, but the remark had to be believable.
sources_primary: Lucian, Alexander 25, 38
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993, vol. 2

title: Gregory (Theodore) born at Neocaesarea; studies with Origen
summary: Theodore, later called Gregory, was born to a wealthy pagan family of Neocaesarea. With his brother Athenodorus he studied with Origen at Caesarea in Palestine (c. 233-238) and became a Christian; his speech of thanks to Origen survives.
disputed: He was born about 210–215; a few scholars doubt that the Address is his.
sources_primary: Eusebius, HE 6.30 | Gregory Thaumaturgus, Address of Thanksgiving to Origen | Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Gregory the Wonderworker
sources_modern: Slusser 1998 (Fathers of the Church 98) | Mitchell 1999 (in Portraits of Spiritual Authority)

title: Gregory bishop of Neocaesarea
summary: Phaidimos, bishop of Amaseia, consecrated Gregory bishop of his home city. Gregory of Nyssa's Life says he found seventeen Christians there and left only seventeen pagans at his death; it tells of his miracles (moving a rock, drying a lake, stopping the flooding Lykos with his staff), which gave him the name Thaumaturgos, 'Wonderworker'.
disputed: The seventeen Christians and seventeen pagans, and the miracles, are hagiography, written about 380 from family and local tradition.
sources_primary: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Gregory the Wonderworker | Basil, On the Holy Spirit 29.74 | Basil, Letters 28, 204, 207
sources_modern: Slusser 1998 | Mitchell 1999

title: Decian persecution in Pontus
summary: During the persecution under Decius Gregory withdrew with his flock into the mountains around Neocaesarea; later tradition lists Pontic martyrs of these years.
sources_primary: Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Gregory the Wonderworker
sources_modern: Slusser 1998

title: First Gothic raids: Pityous holds, then falls
summary: The Borani, carried across the sea in ships of the weakened Bosporan kingdom, attacked Pityous, but the commander Successianus drove them off. In a second expedition they took Pityous, raided towards the Phasis, but failed to take the temple there.
disputed: Zosimus gives no year; dates between 253 and 257 are proposed.
sources_primary: Zosimus 1.31-33
sources_modern: Kulikowski 2007 (Rome's Gothic Wars) | Paschoud 2000 (Zosime I, notes)

title: The Goths sack Trapezous
summary: After a summer of good weather the raiders' fleet came to Trapezous, a large and populous city with a double wall and, Zosimus says, ten thousand more soldiers than usual. Seeing the garrison idle and drunk, they climbed the walls at night on ladders made from tree trunks, took the city, killed or captured those who did not escape, and destroyed temples, houses and public buildings before sailing home with great booty and many captives. Chrysanthos (1933) takes the 'most holy pappas' addressed in Gregory's Canonical Epistle to be the bishop of Trapezous, the first known by his office; that is his inference.
disputed: The sack is usually dated about 256–257; Zosimus gives no year, and Chrysanthos gives both 257 and 253/4. The 10,000 is Zosimus' figure, probably taken from Dexippus.
sources_primary: Zosimus 1.33 | Gregory Thaumaturgus, Canonical Epistle
sources_modern: Kulikowski 2007 | Paschoud 2000 | Bryer & Winfield 1985 | Chrysanthos 1933 (Chrysanthos Philippides, Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Τραπεζοῦντος, Ἀρχεῖον Πόντου 4–5, Athens 1933), p. 50; pp. 128–131/4; p. 216

title: Gregory's Canonical Epistle: Christians and the raiders
summary: In a letter to a fellow bishop, Gregory set penances for Christians of Pontus who during the raids of the 'Boradoi and Goths' had eaten food offered to idols, looted their neighbours' houses, kept captives who had escaped, or even joined the raiders and killed. It is the only contemporary local witness to the raids and shows the breakdown of order in Pontus.
disputed: Whether it refers to the raid of 254 or the sack of Trapezous (c. 257) is debated.
sources_primary: Gregory Thaumaturgus, Canonical Epistle, canons 1-11
sources_modern: Heather & Matthews 1991 (The Goths in the Fourth Century, ch. 1) | Slusser 1998 | Chrysanthos 1933 (Chrysanthos Philippides, Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Τραπεζοῦντος, Ἀρχεῖον Πόντου 4–5, Athens 1933), p. 50; pp. 128–131/4; p. 216

title: Third raid: Bithynia burned
summary: Encouraged by the booty of Trapezous, other Gothic groups came by land and sea to the Bosporus, took Chalcedon and burned Nicomedia and Nicaea, and plundered Kios, Apameia and Prusa; a flooded river saved Cyzicus.
sources_primary: Zosimus 1.34-35
sources_modern: Kulikowski 2007

title: Gregory at the synod of Antioch
summary: Gregory and his brother Athenodorus attended the first synod at Antioch against Paul of Samosata, a sign of the Pontic church's standing in the wider church.
sources_primary: Eusebius, HE 7.28.1
sources_modern: Slusser 1998

title: Death of Gregory the Wonderworker
summary: Gregory died at Neocaesarea. His cult made Neocaesarea the spiritual centre of Christian Pontus; Basil's grandmother Macrina the Elder had learned the faith from his disciples.
disputed: The year is uncertain; 270 is traditional.
sources_primary: Suda s.v. Gregorios | Basil, Letter 204.6 | Gregory of Nyssa, Life of Gregory the Wonderworker
sources_modern: Slusser 1998

title: Goths from the Maeotis raid Pontus and Cappadocia
summary: Goths from the Sea of Azov landed and raided through Pontus into Cappadocia, Galatia and Cilicia; the emperor Tacitus and his prefect Florian drove them out.
sources_primary: Zosimus 1.63 | Historia Augusta, Tacitus 13.2-3 | Zonaras 12.28
sources_modern: Kulikowski 2007

title: Diocletian's provinces: Diospontus and Pontus Polemoniacus
summary: Diocletian divided the Pontic lands into smaller provinces within the diocese of Pontica: Diospontus, with its capital at Amaseia (Amisos and Sinope also belonged to it in later lists), and Pontus Polemoniacus, with its capital at Neocaesarea (Komana, Polemonion, Kerasous, Trapezous). A new legion, I Pontica, was stationed at Trapezous under the dux of Armenia.
disputed: The exact date of the division (about 293–305) is not known, and the city lists come from later sources.
sources_primary: Laterculus Veronensis (c. 314) | Notitia Dignitatum, Oriens 38.13-16 | Hierokles, Synekdemos 701-703 (6th c.)
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993, vol. 2 | Barnes 1982 (The New Empire) | Mitford 2018

title: Martyrdom of Eugenios and his companions at Trapezous
summary: According to his passion, Eugenios, a Christian of Trapezous, threw down the statue of Mithras on the hill above the city (the Minthrion, today Boztepe), and with Valerian, Kanidios and Akylas was tortured and beheaded in the persecution of Diocletian. He became the patron saint of Trapezous and, from 1204, of the Empire of Trebizond; his feast is 21 January. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 135-142) tells it from the 14th-century encomium of Constantine Loukites and the texts of Joseph Lazaropoulos: under the dux Lysias, sent by Diocletian and Maximian; the heads and relics were kept in the church of St Eugenios. The cult itself is attested early: Procopius (Buildings 3.7.1) names an aqueduct of the martyr Eugenios at Trapezous under Justinian, and c. 600 the Armenian Anania of Shirak found his teacher Tychikos at the martyr’s shrine (Rosenqvist 1996, pp. 65–66). Loukites’ encomium says a church of St John the Baptist was later built on the spot on Mt Mithrion where the temple of Mithras had stood (Rosenqvist 1996, p. 72).
disputed: The texts are late, the earliest surviving passion centuries after the event, and the date is traditional; a cult of Mithras at Trapezous is supported by 3rd-century city coins showing a Mithraic horseman. The name of the persecuting official varies between versions. On the passion itself: Martin-Hisard (French) sees the anonymous Greek passion as a reworking, after about 800, of a shorter 6th–7th-century text preserved in an Armenian version; Lampsides (Greek) dates it after Symeon Metaphrastes; Rosenqvist (1996, Swedish) thinks a late antique or early medieval date likely for both versions; Bryer & Winfield (1978, British) argue that Eugenios, the most junior of the Five Saints of Arauraka, was 'promoted' between 407 and about 550 to lead the Four Saints of Trapezous, a case of 'hagiological kidnapping'. All agree that the passion tells little about events in 303, and that the martyrs appear as Pontic rather than specifically Trapezuntine heroes (Rosenqvist).

title: Phokas the gardener, martyr of Sinope
summary: Asterius, bishop of Amaseia, preached c. 400 about Phokas, a gardener of Sinope who gave lodging to the soldiers sent to kill him, dug his own grave in his garden and was beheaded. Phokas became the patron saint of sailors on the Black Sea and beyond, and his tomb-church at Sinope a place of pilgrimage.
disputed: The date is unknown; tradition sometimes merges him with a bishop Phokas of Sinope said to have been martyred under Trajan.
sources_primary: Asterius of Amaseia, Homily 9 (On St Phokas) | John Chrysostom, Homily on St Phokas

title: Theodore 'Tiron' martyred at Amaseia
summary: Theodore, a recruit, burned the temple of the Mother of the Gods at Amaseia and was burned alive; his relics were taken to Euchaita, which became one of the great pilgrimage centres of Asia Minor. Gregory of Nyssa preached his panegyric at the shrine.
disputed: The date, under Galerius or Maximinus about 306, is traditional.
sources_primary: Gregory of Nyssa, Encomium of St Theodore | Passion of Theodore (BHG 1760)
sources_modern: Haldon 2016 (A Tale of Two Saints) | Mitchell 1993, vol. 2

title: Borders c. AD 314: the late Roman provinces
summary: From the Verona List and later lists: Diospontus (later Helenopontus): Amaseia, Amisos, Sinope, Zela, Ibora, Andrapa, Zaliches. Pontus Polemoniacus: Neocaesarea, Komana, Polemonion, Kerasous, Trapezous. Paphlagonia to the west (Gangra, Pompeiopolis), Armenia Minor to the south-east (Satala, Nicopolis, Sebasteia, Melitene), Cappadocia to the south.
disputed: Some cities moved between provinces in the 4th century.
sources_primary: Laterculus Veronensis | Hierokles, Synekdemos | Justinian, Novel 28 (preface)
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993 | Barnes 1982

title: Council of Neocaesarea
summary: Bishops met at Neocaesarea shortly after the council of Ancyra (314) and issued fifteen canons on clerical marriage, penance and church order, which entered the canon law of the Eastern church.
disputed: Dated between 314 and 325.
sources_primary: Canons of Neocaesarea (Joannou, Discipline generale antique, vol. 1.2)
sources_modern: Hefele-Leclercq, Histoire des conciles 1.1

title: Licinius' persecution at Amaseia; Basil of Amaseia
summary: Eusebius records that under Licinius churches at Amaseia and other cities of Pontus were pulled down or closed. Basil, bishop of Amaseia, was martyred; his passion says his body was thrown into the sea and recovered at Sinope.
disputed: The passion of Basil is late; Eusebius is contemporary.
sources_primary: Eusebius, HE 10.8.15 | Eusebius, Life of Constantine 2.1-2 | Passion of Basil of Amaseia (BHG 239)

title: Pontic bishops at Nicaea
summary: Bishops from Pontus took part in the council of Nicaea. In Gelzer's edition of the subscription lists (1898), Pontus Polemoniacus is represented by Longinus of Neocaesarea, Domnus of Trapezous and Stratophilus of Pityous; Eutychianus of Amaseia, Elpidius of Komana, Heraclius of Zela and Acrites of Diospontus appear together in another group. No bishop of Sinope, Amisos or Kerasous appears, and the bishop 'of Koloneia' in the Cappadocian group is of Koloneia-Archelais in Cappadocia, not of Pontic Koloneia. Chrysanthos (1933), following Gelzer, adds a bishop of Kerasous, Akouarios.
disputed: The lists survive in several versions that do not agree in every name; Chrysanthos' Akouarios of Kerasous is not in Gelzer's list.

title: Diospontus renamed Helenopontus
summary: Constantine renamed Diospontus after his mother Helena; the name Helenopontus is used from then until the 7th century. Justinian's Novel 28 later recalled the name's origin.
disputed: The exact date of the renaming is unknown.
sources_primary: Justinian, Novel 28 (preface)
sources_modern: Mitchell 1993, vol. 2

title: Basil at Annesi on the Iris
summary: Basil of Caesarea, back from his studies, withdrew to his family's estate at Annesi on the Iris near Ibora, where his mother Emmelia and sister Macrina had turned the household into a community. In a letter to Gregory of Nazianzus he describes the place: a high wooded mountain, a plain enclosed by ravines, and in front the river, 'the most rapid stream I know', falling over a precipice. The retreat was the cradle of Basil's monastic rules.
disputed: Where Annesi lay is uncertain: Silvas places it at Uluköy (Sonusa), near where the Lykos joins the Iris; older works put it near Turhal, taken for Ibora (Turhal is more likely the ancient Gaziura).

sources_modern: Silvas 2005 (The Asketikon of St Basil the Great), pp. 43-45 | Rousseau 1994 (Basil of Caesarea)
places: Annesi (Annisa), probably at Ulukoy (former Sonusa), Tasova (40.786, 36.418) | Neocaesarea (40.592, 36.955)

title: Constantinople dedicated: Pontus is ruled from the Bosporus
summary: Constantine dedicates his new capital on the Bosporus. For the next 874 years the Pontic coast is governed from a city that lies at the far end of its own sea route: Constantinople, Sinope, Amisos, Trapezous. That sea lane, not the mountain roads, ties the Greeks of Pontus to the centre of the empire throughout this chapter.
sources_primary: Chronicon Paschale, s.a. 330
sources_modern: Dagron 1974, Naissance d'une capitale | Bryer & Winfield 1985, p. 18 (the sea "has always been" the main means of communication along the Pontic coast; Constantinople to Erzurum overland about 25 days, by sea to Trebizond and over the mountains about a third of that)

title: The Soumela tradition: Barnabas and Sophronios
summary: Monastic tradition holds that two monks of Athens, Barnabas (born Basil) and his nephew Sophronios, guided by a vision of the Virgin, brought an icon ascribed to St Luke to a cave on Mt Mela above the Pyxites valley and founded Soumela in 386, under Theodosius I; both are said to have died in 412. A farmer-monk Christopher is said to have restored the house after a 7th-century sack. No contemporary text, inscription or building of the 4th–7th centuries supports this; the monastery's documented history begins with the Grand Komnenoi, above all the chrysobull of Alexios III (December 1364). The earliest surviving written forms of the legend are 18th-century: a history and office by Dionysios, archbishop of Chaldia (c. 1760, printed at Bucharest 1769), and the office with a 'sacred history' composed by Neophytos Kausokalyvites from older manuscripts sent to him from Soumela and since lost (Leipzig 1775) (Kyriakidis 1898). Chrysanthos (1933, p. 470) repeats the tradition that the church was consecrated 'in 386' by the bishop of Trapezous, and has the house refounded by Christophoros of Gozara.
disputed: The date 386 is tradition only. Bryer & Winfield (1985) treat the foundation story as tradition, but hold that 'the tradition, and hence the existence of Soumela, seems to have been established by the tenth century', without giving a source for that date. The first firm evidence is of the 13th–14th centuries, above all the chrysobull of Alexios III of December 1364, which Bryer uses without reservation (he doubts the authenticity of the chrysobulls for Vazelon, 1386, and Choutoura, 1365). Earlier, lost versions of the legend were named by Metaxopoulos (Akakios the Sabaite, whom he placed about 680, Nikodemos of Phasis, and an anonymous author), but Kyriakidis knew nothing of them beyond that statement.

title: Armenia partitioned; Theodosiopolis founded as the Roman bulwark
summary: Rome and Persia divided the kingdom of Armenia c. 387; Rome received the smaller western part (Armenia Interior), which brought the frontier to the upper Euphrates and the Araxes, three to four days south and east of Trapezous. Under Theodosius II the fortress-city of Theodosiopolis (Karin, modern Erzurum) was built as the Roman anchor of the new frontier. From now on the Pontic hinterland is a military rear for the Persian front.
disputed: The partition is dated between 384 and 390, most often about 387. Procopius credits Theodosius II with founding Theodosiopolis, Armenian tradition the general Anatolius; the dates range from about 415 to 421.

title: The Pontic provinces c. 400: Helenopontus, Pontus Polemoniacus, Armenia I and II
summary: In the late Roman diocese of Pontica the old kingdom of Pontus was split into small provinces. Helenopontus (earlier Diospontus, renamed after Constantine's mother Helena) had its metropolis at Amaseia and included Amisos, Sinope, Zela, Ibora and Andrapa. Pontus Polemoniacus had its metropolis at Neocaesarea and included Komana, Polemonion, Kerasous and Trapezous. Inland, Armenia Minor was divided under Theodosius I (c. 386) into Armenia I (Sebasteia, Nikopolis, Satala, Koloneia, Sebastopolis) and Armenia II (Melitene).
disputed: The renaming of Diospontus as Helenopontus (under Constantine, before the 330s) and the division of Armenia Minor (usually about 386) are not exactly dated.

title: John Chrysostom dies at Komana on the road to Pityous
summary: The deposed bishop of Constantinople, exiled first to Kokousos in Armenia II (404), was being marched to Pityous at the far eastern end of the Black Sea when he died at Komana in Pontus, at the shrine of the martyr Basiliskos. The route shows how the Pontic road system linked the capital with the Caucasian coast, and that Pityous, not Trapezous, marked the empire's edge on the sea.

title: Atarbios of Trapezous at Chalcedon
summary: At the Council of Chalcedon Atarbios, 'bishop of the city of Trapezous' ('Ἀτάρβιος ἐπίσκοπος τῆς πόλεως Τραπεζοῦντος'), signed also for his metropolitan Dorotheos of Neocaesarea, whose deacon Photeinos sat as his representative. Trapezous was then a suffragan see of Neocaesarea in Pontus Polemoniacus.

title: Antipatros of Trapezous at the synod of Constantinople
summary: At the 'resident synod' of Constantinople in 518 against the Monophysites, bishop Antipatros of Trapezous signed the report against Severus of Antioch submitted to Patriarch John ('Ἀντίπατρος ἐπίσκοπος Τραπεζοῦντος ὑπέγραψα'). Chrysanthos takes him to be the next bishop after Atarbios.
sources_primary: Acts of the synod of Constantinople 518 (in the acts of 536, ACO III)
sources_modern: Chrysanthos 1933 (Chrysanthos Philippides, Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Τραπεζοῦντος, Ἀρχεῖον Πόντου 4–5, Athens 1933), p. 189

title: Lazica turns to Rome: King Tzath I baptised in Constantinople
summary: Tzath I, king of the Lazi in old Colchis, broke with Persia, came to Constantinople, was baptised and crowned with Justin I as godfather. Persia saw the loss of its client as a casus belli, and Lazica's control of the passes and the eastern Black Sea coast became a cause of the wars of 526–562. For Pontus it meant that the Roman sphere now ran unbroken along the coast from Trapezous to the Caucasus.
sources_primary: Malalas 17.9 | Chronicon Paschale, s.a. 522 | Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6015 | Procopius, Wars 2.15.2
sources_modern: Braund 1994, Georgia in Antiquity | Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II

title: The Tzanoi subdued and baptised; an army command for Armenia
summary: The Tzanoi, highlanders of the Pontic Alps between Trapezous and Armenia who lived by raiding the coast and the Armenian plains, were defeated by Sittas and persuaded to accept Christianity and serve in the army. Justinian cut roads through their forests, built forts (Horonon, Barchon, Sisilisson, Bourgousnoes, Schamalinichon, Tzanzakon) and a church at Schamalinichon. In the same years he created a separate field command for Armenia (magister militum per Armeniam), with Sittas as its first holder.
disputed: None of Procopius' forts among the Tzanoi is securely located. Bryer & Winfield (1985) offer tentative sites: Horonon near Gelengeç (Lori), on the borders of Erzurum, Gümüşhane and Erzincan; Bourgousnoes at Zindanlar Arazi, Murathanoğulları; Tzanzakon at Tzanicha (Canca); and Schamalinichon somewhere in the Leri valley. None is secured by an inscription. The Tzanoi are often equated with Strabo's Sannoi and with the later 'Chan', a Georgian name for the Laz; the continuity is debated (Bryer).

title: Anthimos of Trapezous becomes patriarch and is deposed
summary: Anthimos, bishop of Trapezous (probably a Syrian, in Chrysanthos's view), took part in the conference of 532 with the anti-Chalcedonians, became patriarch of Constantinople in June 535, was deposed before 13 March 536 under pressure from Pope Agapetus and condemned in May–June 536. The church of Trapezous was left 'widowed and without a husband' ('χήραν καὶ ἄνανδρον').
sources_primary: Acts of the synod of Constantinople 536 (ACO III) | Justinian, Novel 42
sources_modern: Chrysanthos 1933 (Chrysanthos Philippides, Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Τραπεζοῦντος, Ἀρχεῖον Πόντου 4–5, Athens 1933), pp. 190–200

title: Justinian redraws the map: Trapezous goes to Armenia I
summary: Justinian abolished Pontus Polemoniacus. Neocaesarea and Polemonion were joined to Helenopontus under a moderator at Amaseia, while Trapezous and Kerasous were placed in a new Armenia I (Magna) with Theodosiopolis, Satala, Nikopolis and Koloneia, under a proconsul at Justinianopolis (Bazanis or Leontopolis). The old Armenia I around Sebasteia became Armenia II, with Sebastopolis, Brisa, Komana (taken from Pontus Polemoniacus) and Zela (taken from Helenopontus); the old Armenia II around Melitene became Armenia III, and the southern satrapies Armenia IV. The coast from Trapezous east was thus administered with the Armenian frontier, not with the rest of Pontus.
disputed: Trapezous was in Armenia I but was not its capital: the provincial capital was Justinianopolis (Bazanis or Leontopolis), whose site is uncertain, though some modern summaries call Trapezous the capital. Novel 31, as quoted by Harutyunyan (2023), puts Komana and Zela in the new Armenia II; Harutyunyan identifies Justinianopolis with Tzoumina.
sources_primary: Justinian, Novel 28 (De moderatore Helenoponti) | Justinian, Novel 31 (De quattuor Armeniis) | Procopius, Buildings 3.1.16–29

title: Justinian's works at Trapezous and on the coast
summary: Procopius records that Justinian gave Trapezous, which lacked water, an aqueduct called after the martyr Eugenios, and restored most of the churches of Trapezous and Amaseia. He also built 'a novel system of defences' at Rhizaion and new walls at Satala, Koloneia and Theodosiopolis. Procopius says nothing about walls at Trapezous. The gate inscription reported by Miller, once taken as evidence for Justinianic walls, records a renewal of the city's buildings: so Eastmond (2016, p. 11), following Bryer & Winfield (1985, p. 182). Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 216-217) reads the inscription: Justinian 'renewed with munificence the public buildings of the city' ('ἀνενέωσε ἐν φιλοτιμίᾳ τὰ δημόσια κτίσματα τῆς πόλεως') through the zeal of the most God-loving Eirenaios, dated indiction 5, year 480 (ΥΠ) of the Trapezuntine era, i.e. 542; he makes Eirenaios bishop. The text speaks of public buildings, not walls.
disputed: The aqueduct is secure (Procopius). Walls built by Justinian at Trapezous are not attested: the one inscription, recorded by Tournefort in 1701 and since lost (CIG 8636), speaks of renewed public buildings. Bryer & Winfield (1985) and Chrysanthos read the bishop's name as Eirenaios and the date as indiction 5, year 480 of the city's era, that is AD 542.

title: Petra betrayed to Chosroes: the Lazic War begins
summary: The Lazi resented the Roman garrison and the trade monopoly that the general John Tzibus ran from his new fortress of Petra (built c. 535). King Gubazes II invited Chosroes I, who marched into Lazica and took Petra; John Tzibus was killed. Persia now held a port on the Black Sea about 150 km east of Trapezous.
sources_primary: Procopius, Wars 2.15.1–35 | Procopius, Wars 2.17.1–28
sources_modern: Braund 1994, Georgia in Antiquity | Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II

title: Persian aims at the Black Sea; the first Roman siege of Petra
summary: Procopius says that Chosroes meant to remove the Lazi and settle Persians in their land, gaining a base from which a fleet could reach Constantinople and the Huns of the steppe; he sent ship timber to Lazica, which was destroyed by lightning. Gubazes changed sides again in 548, and Dagisthaios besieged Petra with 7,000 Romans and 1,000 Tzanoi but failed to take it before Mermeroes relieved it.
disputed: Whether Chosroes really planned a fleet on the Black Sea, or Procopius gave voice to Roman fears, is debated; most modern scholars take the threat as real but exaggerated.

sources_modern: Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II | Braund 1994, Georgia in Antiquity

title: Petra stormed and razed; Archaeopolis holds
summary: After a Persian defeat on the river Hippis (550), the Roman general Bessas stormed Petra in spring 551 and razed it so that it could not be used again. Mermeroes then attacked Archaeopolis, the chief Lazic fortress, and was beaten off, but occupied Kotais, Uthimereos and the lands of eastern Lazica.
sources_primary: Procopius, Wars 8.8 (Hippis) | Procopius, Wars 8.11–12 (Petra) | Procopius, Wars 8.13–14 (Archaeopolis) | Procopius, Buildings 3.7.7
sources_modern: Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II | Braund 1994, Georgia in Antiquity

title: Defeat at Telephis and the murder of King Gubazes
summary: Mermeroes routed a larger Roman–Lazic army at Telephis by a feigned retreat (554). The Roman commanders Martin and Rusticus, quarrelling with Gubazes, had him murdered (555); the Lazi nearly went over to Persia, and Justinian put the murderers on trial (Agathias reports the trial at length). Tzath II was installed as the new king.
sources_primary: Agathias, Histories 2.19–22 | Agathias, Histories 3.2–4 and 4.1–11
sources_modern: Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II | Braund 1994, Georgia in Antiquity

title: Persian siege of Phasis fails
summary: The Persian commander Nachoragan attacked the Roman port of Phasis and was routed, which ended Persian hopes of taking the Lazic coast. A truce followed in 557.
sources_primary: Agathias, Histories 3.19–28
sources_modern: Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II

title: The Tzanoi rise again
summary: The Tzanoi, Christian and enrolled in the army for a generation, rose and plundered the roads around Trapezous and Rhizaion. Theodore, himself a Tzan by birth, defeated them, and a tribute was imposed. The episode shows that the highlands behind Trapezous were still only loosely held.
disputed: Dated 557 or 558.
sources_primary: Agathias, Histories 5.1–2
sources_modern: Bryer 1966–67, 'Some notes on the Laz and Tzan'

title: The Fifty Years' Peace: Lazica stays Roman
summary: Peter the Patrician and the Persian envoy Yazdgushnasp agreed a peace near Dara. Persia withdrew from Lazica; Rome paid 30,000 nomismata (about 400 lb of gold) a year, with the first seven years in advance. The whole eastern Black Sea coast was now Roman or Roman-client, so the Pontus faced no sea-borne threat from the east.
disputed: Date: late 561 or early 562.
sources_primary: Menander Protector, fr. 6.1 (Blockley)
sources_modern: Blockley 1985, The History of Menander the Guardsman | Greatrex & Lieu 2002, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II

title: The Persian war reaches the edge of Pontus
summary: In the war of 602–628 the Persians took Theodosiopolis (c. 610), occupied Caesarea in Cappadocia (611–612), and burned Euchaita in the Armeniakon (615). The Pontic coast itself is not reported as attacked, but its hinterland was exposed for the first time since the 3rd century.
sources_primary: Sebeos, History ch. 34 | Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6103 | Miracles of St Theodore of Euchaita (for 615)
sources_modern: Kaegi 2003, Heraclius | Trombley 1985, 'The decline of the seventh-century town: the exception of Euchaita' | Haldon ed. 2018, The Archaeology of Medieval Avkat

title: Herakleios' first campaign: the army winters in Pontus
summary: Herakleios left Constantinople on 4 April 622, sailed to Pylai, drilled his army through the summer, and in autumn marched into Cappadocia, where he defeated Shahrbaraz. He went back to the capital and left the army to winter 'in Pontus'. No source names the winter quarters; Trapezous is not mentioned.
disputed: The sites of the battle of 622 and of the winter quarters are unknown.
sources_primary: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6113 | George of Pisidia, Expeditio Persica
sources_modern: Kaegi 2003, Heraclius, pp. 112–116 | Howard-Johnston 1999, 'Heraclius' Persian campaigns', War in History 6, pp. 1–44

title: Herakleios' great campaigns: Armenia, Lazica and the Turkish alliance
summary: In 624 Herakleios marched east by Caesarea and the upper Euphrates (by Satala and Theodosiopolis, according to some reconstructions) to Dvin and Ganzak. After the battle on the Saros (625), Theophanes has him winter at Sebasteia. In 626 he moved to Lazica, and in 627 he joined the Turks (the 'Khazars' of the Greek sources) before Tiflis, then struck south to Nineveh (12 December 627). Trapezous was the natural port for the Lazic phase, but no primary source names it; the claim that the army wintered at Trebizond in 625/6 (Norwich, often repeated) conflicts with Theophanes. Bryer and Winfield (1978) argue that he wintered in 625 in the valleys around Bathys Rhyax, west of Sebasteia, and that in 626 he used the old Roman camp at Sourmaina, renamed Herakleia (Araklı, 27 km east of Trapezous), as his base for contact with Constantinople and the Khazars and as his port for Lazica; they suggest the name commemorates the birth there of his son Heraklonas.
disputed: The routes are reconstructions, argued over by Howard-Johnston, Zuckerman and Kaegi. On the Pontic port of 626: Vasiliev (1935, Russian-American), followed by Stratos (1968, Greek) and Baynes (1913, British), names Trebizond, after an interpolated Georgian chronicle and Eutychios of Alexandria (died 940), the only sources that name it; Bryer & Winfield (1978, British) propose Herakleia-Sourmaina (Araklı), from the stations of the Notitia, the route up the Hyssos to Satala and the place-name Herakleia, and call it a proposal, not proof.

title: Anania of Shirak studies mathematics at Trapezous
summary: The Armenian scholar Anania of Shirak, after failing to find a teacher in Armenia, went to Trapezous and studied for eight years with Tychikos, a teacher who had learned in Constantinople, Alexandria and Rome and drew pupils from the capital. Anania's autobiography is the best evidence for Trapezous as a centre of Greek learning in the 7th century, and for Armenians coming to the Pontic coast to study. He found Tychikos ‘at the shrine of Saint Eugenia’ (an error for Eugenios), which makes the passage one of the earliest witnesses to the martyr’s shrine at Trapezous (Rosenqvist 1996, pp. 65–66).
disputed: The dates of Anania's stay are uncertain, between the 620s and the 640s; Rosenqvist (1996) puts it 'apparently c. AD 600', without arguing the point.

title: Arab raids reach Euchaita
summary: The first Arab raids into the Armeniakon hit Euchaita, the shrine town of St Theodore: an attack under Mu'awiya c. 640, then a capture in 663/4 when the raiders plundered the town, burned the saint's church and wintered there. Over the next two centuries the Arab raids struck the inland towns of Pontus (Euchaita, Amaseia, the plains of Dazimon) but are not recorded as crossing the Pontic Alps to Trapezous.
disputed: The dates (640 or 644; 663 or 664) are argued from hagiography and chronicles, and Trombley's reading is the standard one. The Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire dates the winter raids of 'Abd al-Rahman b. Khalid to 663/4–666/7 from Theophanes, Tabari and Elias of Nisibis; Theophanes does not name Euchaita, so the town's capture rests on the Miracles of St Theodore.

Khalid invades Roman territory and winters there (Euchaita not named); Elias of Nisibis: wintering in AH 44 = 663/4 (both as summarised by PBE, 'Abd ar-Rahman 9', pbe.kcl.ac.uk/data/D00/F16.htm)

title: The Paulicians begin at Kibossos (Kibossa) near Koloneia
summary: According to Peter of Sicily, Constantine (called Silvanus), born at Mananalis near Samosata of Armenia under Constans II, founded the dualist Paulician community at the fort of Kibossos near Koloneia and lived there for twenty-seven years. An imperial official, Symeon, sent by an emperor whom Peter does not name (probably Constantine IV or Justinian II), had him stoned by his own adopted son Justus; three years later Symeon returned secretly to Kibossos and led the community himself as 'Titus'. The Pontic interior thus saw the birth of the sect that later built a state at Tephrike and fought the emperors.
disputed: The chronology rests on hostile Greek sources; Garsoïan sees the Paulicians' roots in Armenian adoptionism, while Lemerle reads the Greek sources more literally. Kibossa has not been located, and the map shows Koloneia. Bryer & Winfield (1985) date the foundation at Kibossa to the 670s and Constantine-Silvanus' death to about 683, later than the usual start about 655, and suggest Sisorta Kale, 33 km west-north-west of Şebinkarahisar, for Kibossa, 'but there are no grounds, other than those of geographical likelihood'. Bryer (1977) places Mananalis, the founder's home district, in the southern Tuzlasuyu plain around Tercan.

title: Saborios' revolt: first clear record of the Armeniakon theme
summary: Saborios (Shapur), strategos of the Armeniakoi, rebelled against Constans II and offered, through his envoy Sergios, to subject the empire to the caliph Mu'awiya in return for help; an Arab force under Fadala was sent, and Constans's son Constantine sent an army under Nikephoros against him. Saborios died in a riding accident at a place called Adrianoupolis before the revolt spread. This is the first unambiguous literary record of the Armeniakon, the army corps settled in the old Pontus and Armenia Minor, with its headquarters at Amaseia.
disputed: A 'tourmarches of the Armeniakoi' appears in 629, so the corps may be older; whether it was already a territorial theme in the 660s is debated. Where Saborios died is disputed.

title: Theodoros of Trapezous at the Sixth Ecumenical Council
summary: Theodoros, 'bishop of the city of the Trapezuntines' ('ἐπίσκοπος τῆς Τραπεζουντίων πόλεως'), signed the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council at Constantinople.
sources_primary: Acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Mansi XI)
sources_modern: Chrysanthos 1933 (Chrysanthos Philippides, Ἡ Ἐκκλησία Τραπεζοῦντος, Ἀρχεῖον Πόντου 4–5, Athens 1933), pp. 200–201

title: Maslama takes Amaseia
summary: The Umayyad prince Maslama raided the Armeniakon and took Amaseia, its headquarters, and other forts. It is the deepest recorded Arab success in Pontus proper; the city was soon back in Roman hands.
disputed: Theophanes gives no detail on how long Amaseia was held.
sources_primary: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6204
sources_modern: Lilie 1976, Die byzantinische Reaktion auf die Ausbreitung der Araber | Treadgold 1997, A History of the Byzantine State and Society

title: Christophoros 'of Phasis, that is of Trapezous', at the Second Council of Nicaea
summary: At Nicaea II, Christophoros signed as 'unworthy bishop of Phasis, that is of Trapezous' ('Χριστοφόρος ἀνάξιος ἐπίσκοπος τοῦ Φάσιδος, ἤτοι Τραπεζοῦντος'). From this Chrysanthos argues that Trapezous had already taken over the metropolitan rank of Phasis by 787, earlier than the mid-9th-century date (raising by Patriarch Methodios) given by Papadopoulos-Kerameus. Later lists call it 'metropolis of Trapezous of the eparchy of Lazike'.
disputed: Trapezous became a metropolis either by 787 (Chrysanthos, from this signature) or about 843–847 (the Synaxarion of Athanasios; Papadopoulos-Kerameus).
sources_primary: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (Mansi XIII)

title: Armenians found Hamamashen (Hemşin)
summary: The Armenian historian Ghewond records that the prince Shapuh Amatuni and his son Hamam, fleeing Arab rule, crossed into Roman territory with about 12,000 people and were received by the emperor. Armenian tradition says Hamam rebuilt the ruined town of Tambur in the hills east of Rhizaion and called it Hamamashen, the origin of the Hemşin district and its Armenian-speaking people.
disputed: The figure of 12,000 is Ghewond's. The link between his migrants and Hamamashen comes from later Armenian tradition (Vardan, 13th century), and the date varies between 789 and 791.
sources_primary: Ghewond, History ch. 42 (tr. Arzoumanian 1982)
sources_modern: Simonian ed. 2007, The Hemshin (esp. Hachikian, pp. 146–147) | Vaux 2001, Hemshinli

title: Arabs seize the Armeniakon's pay near Euchaita
summary: In early 811, while Leo, strategos of the Armeniakoi (the future emperor Leo V), and a large force were escorting the pay of his troops, Arab raiders attacked them near Euchaita and captured all the money, thirteen hundred pounds of gold, and many of his men. Nikephoros I had Leo beaten and exiled for negligence. The loss shows how exposed the interior of Pontus still was in the early 9th century.
disputed: Theophanes dates it to February 811; the Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire to 1 March 811, the first Saturday of Lent.
sources_primary: Theophanes, Chronographia AM 6303 | Theophanes Continuatus I 4 (Bonn p. 11): Leo beaten and exiled | Scriptor Incertus 336 (Leo also tonsured)
sources_modern: Treadgold 1988, The Byzantine Revival 780–842 | PBE, 'Leon 15' (Leo V) (pbe.kcl.ac.uk/data/D48/F30.htm)

title: Chaldia becomes a theme, with Trapezous as its capital
summary: Chaldia began as a tourma (division) of the Armeniakon, became a semi-separate doukaton or archontate, and was a full theme by c. 840 (Taktikon Uspensky, 842/3), perhaps from c. 819–824. Its strategos sat at Trapezous. In the 10th century he drew 20 lb of gold a year, half from the treasury and half from local revenue, mainly the kommerkion (customs) on the trade through Trapezous. Muslim writers give it 6 forts (Ibn Khurradadhbih) and 4,000 troops (Qudama); Ibn al-Faqih's 10,000 is exaggerated. Keltzene was detached in the early 10th century to the new theme of Mesopotamia. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 51-52) describes the core of Chaldia as three banda, of Trapezous, Gemora and Matzouka ('τὸ βάνδον Τραπεζοῦντος, τὸ βάνδον Γημωρᾶς καὶ τὸ βάνδον Ματσουκάων'), matching the Ottoman districts of Trabzon, Yomra and Maçka. Bryer (1975, p. 117) counts seven valley banda round Trebizond, west to east: Philabonites (Harşit), Trikomia (Akçaabat), Trebizond, Matzouka (Maçka), Gemora (Yomra), Sourmaina (Sürmene) and Rhizaion (Rize); all but the Philabonites kept their military structure until 1461.
disputed: Full theme status is dated about 819, 824 or 840. Chrysanthos describes the core of Chaldia as three banda, Bryer (1975) as probably seven; both rest on evidence of the 13th–15th centuries, so the division may be later than the theme.

title: Defeat at Anzen near Dazimon
summary: The emperor Theophilos was defeated by the Abbasid general Afshin at Anzen, a hill in the plain of Dazimon between Amaseia and Tokat. The Roman army broke on a rumour of the emperor's death, and the Abbasids went on to sack Ankyra and Amorion. It is the largest battle fought on Pontic soil in this chapter.
disputed: The army sizes are modern estimates (Romans 25,000–40,000, Abbasids 20,000–30,000). The year 838 is secure; the day, 22 July, rests on Vasiliev and Treadgold. Bar Hebraeus reports a loss of 3,000 men for Afshin in an encounter with Theophilos.

title: The Khurramite Persians proclaim Theophobos emperor at Sinope
summary: Theophilos had settled Khurramite Persian refugees in the themes (fourteen thousand soldiers, in the Symeon Logothete chronicles) under a Persian commander, Theophobos. The Persians carried him off to Sinope and proclaimed him emperor against his will. They were then moved to Amastris and dispersed through the themes in regiments of two thousand, and Theophobos submitted, on promises of safety, to a fleet sent under Ooryphas. A reminder that 'Romans' in 9th-century Pontus included settled foreigners.
disputed: The number of the Khurramites (14,000 to 30,000 in the sources) and Theophobos' fate are disputed; he was later held in the Boukoleon palace and killed in 842. Bryer & Winfield (1985) date the proclamation at Sinope to 834, with Theophobos taking refuge in Constantinople in 838.

title: Koloneia becomes a theme
summary: Koloneia, on the upper Lykos, was split off from the Armeniakon, first under a doux (Theophilos appointed Kallistos, c. 842) and by 863 under a full strategos. Its 10th-century extent ran from Koloneia to Neocaesarea, Nikopolis and Tephrike, with sixteen forts. Kallistos is remembered as having been handed over by the Paulicians of Koloneia to their co-religionists under Arab rule (Karbeas's following) and executed with the 42 Martyrs of Amorion on 6 March 845.
disputed: Whether Koloneia was a frontier district (kleisoura) before it became a doukaton is debated (Oikonomides, reading al-Mas'udi).
sources_primary: Constantine VII, De thematibus (ed. Pertusi 1952), pp. 141–142 commentary | Acts of the 42 Martyrs of Amorion, BHG 1209–1214, ed. title: The Paulician state at Tephrike
summary: After the persecution under the regent Theodora (843), the Paulician officer Karbeas fled to the emir of Melitene and built a fortified Paulician principality at Tephrike, on the southern edge of the theme of Koloneia. With Arab allies the Paulicians raided deep into Asia Minor; under Chrysocheir they reached Ankyra and Nicaea and sacked Ephesos (869/70).
disputed: The figure of 100,000 Paulicians killed in 843 (Theophanes Continuatus) is not credible as a count. According to the Prosopography of the Byzantine Empire, Karbeas, an officer of the strategos of the Anatolikoi, deserted with 5,000 Paulicians after his father was killed in the persecution, went over to Amr of Melitene, and founded Argaoun and Amara before Tephrike.
sources_primary: Theophanes Continuatus IV 16 (Bonn pp. 165–167) and IV 23 (pp. 176–177) | Peter of Sicily, Historia 184–186
sources_modern: Lemerle 1973, Travaux et Mémoires 5 | Garsoïan 1967, The Paulician Heresy | PBE, 'Karbeas 1' (pbe.kcl.ac.uk/data/D42/F45.htm)

date_text: Consecrated 843–847; archiepiscopate into the reign of Basil I (867–886)
title: Athanasios the Exorcist, metropolitan in the Chrysokephalos
summary: Athanasios 'Daimonokatalytes', a Trapezuntine, monk of St Phokas at Kymina and disciple of the metropolitan Nikephoros, was raised 'from bishopric to metropolis' ('ἐξ ἐπισκοπῆς εἰς μητρόπολιν') by Patriarch Methodios and went to the 'metropolitan church of the Chrysokephalos'. Under Basil I he first celebrated the feast of the birthday of St Eugenios (24 June). Chrysanthos rejects the 1600s dating of older lists.
disputed: That the Chrysokephalos was already the metropolitan church rests on the hagiography. Rosenqvist (1996) tells the story of the first birthday festival differently: the abbot Anthony of St Eugenios paid for it with money from his relatives in Paipert, and Athanasios calmed the townspeople who had been left out; he doubts the story as a whole (C2a-01). Bryer & Winfield (1985) date Athanasios' time as metropolitan to 867–886, the reign of Basil I, rather than from 843–847.
sources_primary: Synaxarion of the Church of Constantinople (Athanasios) | Life of Athanasios the Exorcist

title: Umar of Melitene sacks Amisos; he is killed at Lalakaon
summary: Umar al-Aqta, emir of Melitene, crossed the Armeniakon and sacked Amisos on the coast. Roman chroniclers say that, angry at the sea for stopping him, he had it lashed (a story borrowed from Xerxes). Petronas then trapped his army by the river Lalakaon (Poson) and killed him on 3 September 863, the turning point of the Arab wars in Asia Minor.
disputed: Umar's army is given as 8,000 (al-Ya'qubi) or 40,000 (Genesios, Theophanes Continuatus); Haldon estimates 15,000–20,000. The battlefield has not been identified.
sources_primary: Theophanes Continuatus IV 25 (Bonn p. 179) | Genesios IV 15 | Acta Davidis, Symeonis et Georgii 31 (p. 252): the defeat near Poson on 3 September 863 | Pseudo-Symeon 665–666; Leo Grammaticus 238–239; Georgius Monachus Continuatus 825 | al-Tabari, History (vol. 35) | al-Ya'qubi, History

date_text: Reign of Basil I (867–886), by the account of Lazaropoulos; forgotten after the Seljuk invasions, late 11th c.
title: The festival of St Eugenios on 24 June and the fair of Trebizond
summary: According to John Lazaropoulos (14th c.), under Basil I the martyr revealed in visions that his birthday, 24 June (the feast of John the Baptist), should be kept besides his death-day of 21 January. The abbot Anthony of St Eugenios paid for the first celebration with help from his rich relatives in Paipert, a largely Armenian town, and Archbishop Athanasios calmed the townspeople who had been left out. The midsummer date suited the caravans that brought the monastery’s rents from Paipert over the Pontic passes, closed in January, and competed with the feast of St Orentios at Rhizaion on the same day. The festival became the city’s great fair; government officials attended it until the Seljuk invasions of the late 11th century ended the celebration, which Lazaropoulos says was revived only by Alexios II (1297–1330).
disputed: Rosenqvist (1996, Swedish) holds that the story as a whole is suspect, above all its revival by Alexios II, of which the monastery's typikon of 1346 says nothing; he accepts as genuine the break caused by the Seljuk invasion and the strong Armenian (Chalcedonian) presence at the monastery. Bryer & Winfield (1978, British), Vryonis (1971, Greek-American) and Sheard (2021, British) accept the institution under Basil I and the end of official observance about 1100. The story overlaps with C2-011, which credits Athanasios with the first celebration.

title: Bathys Ryax: the end of the Paulician state
summary: Returning from a raid, Chrysocheir was caught by the strategoi of the Armeniakon and Charsianon at the pass of Bathys Ryax west of Sebasteia; his army was routed and he was killed. Tephrike was taken and razed (878), and many Paulicians were moved to the Balkans and Italy. The frontier of the Pontic themes was secure from the south.
disputed: The battle is dated 872 (Vasiliev, Lemerle, Treadgold) or 878 (Garsoïan, Haldon). Bryer & Winfield (1978) date it 872 and place Bathys Rhyax at the Kalınırmak gorge near Menteşe station.

title: St Anne’s, the oldest standing church of Trebizond
summary: The small church of St Anne (Küçük Ayvasıl) is the only church built before 1204 that still stands in Trebizond; it was restored, or rebuilt, under Basil I in 884/5 (Eastmond 2004). All the others were rebuilt on a larger scale under the Grand Komnenoi. Over its south door is a reused classical relief: Eastmond takes it for part of a sarcophagus, Bryer & Winfield (1985) describe an armed warrior and a flying angel. In the late 14th and early 15th centuries it served as a burial chapel, with portraits and epitaphs of officials, especially churchmen (Bryer & Winfield).
disputed: Eastmond (2004) describes the work of 884/5 both as a restoration and as a rebuilding.

date_text: Notitiae of Leo VI (c. 901–907) and of the late 10th century
title: The metropolis of Trapezous and its inland bishoprics
summary: In the Notitia of Leo VI, the metropolis of Trapezous, 'of the eparchy of Lazike', has seven suffragan sees: Cheriana, Chamatzour, Chaliou, Paiper, Kerameos, Leriou and Bizanon. A list of the time of Tzimiskes has eighteen entries, seventeen sees in Chrysanthos' count, since Chachaion appears twice; it adds Mananaleos, Zarinakon, Andakou, Mesoune, Chachaion, Sakamou, Chabtzitzin, Chantierz, Olnoute, Phasiane and Sermantzou. A list of about 980 has fifteen. A letter of Patriarch Methodios III of 1670, quoted by Chrysanthos, places Chachaion at Kelkit, Bizana at Tercan, Chantierz at Erzincan, Phasiane at Pasin, Paiper at Bayburt and Leriou at 'Kouazi'. Lazaropoulos calls Cheriana (Şiran), 'between Chaldia and Koloneia', 'the first of the bishoprics of Trapezous'.
disputed: Most of the sees cannot be located with certainty, and several (Chamatzour, Kerameos, Mesoune) not at all. Bryer (1977, British) prefers Chrysanthos' identifications to those of Bees, but places Chantierz south of the 'Mountains of the Devil' (Şeytan Dağları), far south-east of Erzincan, and calls its identification with Erzincan in a Soumela manuscript of 1737 misleading; he locates Mananalis in the southern Tuzlasuyu plain around Tercan. Bryer & Winfield (1985) do not accept Kelkit for Chachaion, suggesting the region of Kalur and Aşağı Hayduruk, and place Leriou at Kabaköy in the Leri valley in Chaldia, where they describe 'probably the oldest surviving church in the Pontos'. The names in Leo VI's list are Χεριάνων, Χαμάτζουρ, Χαλίου, Παΐπερ, Κεραμέως, Λερίου and Βιζάνων; the list of Tzimiskes adds Μανανάλεως, Ζαρινάκων, Ἀνδάκου, Μεσουνῆ, Χαχαίου, Σακάμου, Χαβτζίτζιν, Χαντίερζ, Ὀλνούτην, Φασιανῆς and Σερμάντζου.

title: Metropolitan Basil renews the throne of the Chrysokephalos
summary: An inscription in the Chrysokephalos records that 'the precious and holy throne was renewed' ('Ἀνεκαινίσθη ὁ τίμιος καὶ ἅγιος θρόνος') under metropolitan Basil in AM 6422 (913/914). Chrysanthos uses it to show that the Chrysokephalos was the metropolitan church by 914. Basil's feast is 7 October.

title: Bardas Boilas, strategos of Chaldia, rebels
summary: Bardas Boilas, strategos of Chaldia, rebelled against Romanos I with local magnates; John Kourkouas suppressed the revolt. It is the first of several attempts by the governors of Trapezous to act on their own, which culminate in the Gabras family's rule after 1075.
disputed: Bryer & Winfield (1985) date the revolt to 923 and add that Boilas, with Adrian the Chaldian and Tatzakes, seized Bayburt; John Kourkouas then installed his brother Theophilos as strategos (923/4–940).

title: The frontier moves east; Pontus becomes an interior province
summary: John Kourkouas took Melitene (934) and the Romans took Theodosiopolis (949). Sayf al-Dawla's raid of 939/40, which reached the theme of Koloneia, was the last great Muslim raid on the region. From the mid-10th century until the 1050s the Pontic themes lay well behind the frontier, which favoured the growth of trade at Trapezous and of large estates inland.

title: The Muslim geographers on the fairs of Trebizond
summary: Al-Mas'udi (about 943–947) describes Trebizond as a market town on the Black Sea where, in Sheard's English after Pellat's translation, 'there is a fair once a year at which merchants assemble from all nations: Muslims, Rūm, Armenians and others from the country of Kashak'; the Kashak, probably Qipchaqs, sailed constantly to the city. Al-Istakhri (about 950) wrote that 'all the textiles of Greek manufacture, all the brocades imported into Muslim territory are carried through Trebizond'; al-Muqaddasi (late 10th century) called it the most important Muslim trade colony in the empire; al-Idrisi (12th century) still knew it as a trading town. Lazaropoulos, in the 14th century, ties the chief fair to the feast of St Eugenios (C2a-01). Sheard (2021) argues that the Seljuk wars only interrupted this trade about 1100, and that it had recovered by 1205, when Ibn al-Athir describes merchants from Syria, Iraq, Mosul, Rus' and the Qipchaqs cut off by the Seljuk siege.
disputed: Whether there was one fair a year or several is uncertain: 'a fair once a year' in al-Mas'udi as quoted by Sheard (2021) from Pellat's translation, 'several market fairs held each year' in Vryonis (1971), citing the Barbier de Meynard edition. Sheard dates Ibn Hawqal's figure of 10 quintals of gold a year to the early 13th century, which cannot be right for a 10th-century author; it is not used. On the trade of Trebizond in the 11th and 12th centuries: Jacoby (Israeli) sees a long decline from the late 10th century, as the eastern trade moved to Fatimid Egypt; Sheard (2021, British) a temporary interruption by the Seljuk wars about 1100, then recovery; Vryonis (1971, Greek-American) a break in the peace and prosperity of the emporium, shown by the interruption of the festival; and Bryer (1980, British) holds that commerce counted for less in Pontic life than farming and herding.

date_text: 988–989 (Sheard: 987–988), during the revolt of Bardas Phokas
title: Trebizond’s grain ships feed Constantinople; an Iberian army marches on the city
summary: During the revolt of Bardas Phokas, Basil II ordered the towns of the Black Sea coast ‘as far as Trebizond’ to ship grain to the capital, and many ships came from Trebizond and the places round it. Phokas’s commander Delphinas, who guarded the Bosporus, could not stop them and urged Phokas to ravage Trebizond. Two generals ‘of Persarmenia’, Pankratios and Tzourbaneles, marched on the city through Paipert and camped by the ‘Narrow Pass’ while the Trapezuntines fortified their villages; in the story St Eugenios appeared to Pankratios with news of Phokas’s death (at Abydos, 989), and the army turned back.
disputed: The story is told only by a 14th-century hagiographer, who inserted it into his summary of Zonaras (Rosenqvist). Rosenqvist suggests that the generals may not be real persons, or may be Chordvaneli II, a commander captured in 988/9, and the patrikios Bagrat II; Iberian troops of David of Tao had supported Phokas. Sheard (2021) uses the grain order as evidence for grain shipments from Trebizond and dates it 987–988. The 'Narrow Pass' has not been located.

title: David of Tao's inheritance: Rome annexes Tao
summary: The Georgian Bagratid kouropalates David III of Tao helped Basil II against the rebel Bardas Skleros (979) and was granted lands round Theodosiopolis for life; after he backed Bardas Phokas (987) he made Basil his heir. On his death in early 1001 Basil annexed Tao and the lands to Lake Van as the theme of Iberia, bringing the Roman border to the Georgian kingdom of Bagrat III just south-east of Chaldia.
disputed: Some date the annexation 1000, others 1001.

title: Basil II winters at Trapezous during his Georgian war
summary: Basil II invaded Georgia, won a costly battle at Shirimni by Lake Palakatsio (11 September 1021) and wintered at Trapezous. There, in December 1021, Senekerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan ceded his kingdom; Armenian sources say the will of John-Smbat of Ani leaving Ani to the empire was also handed to Basil at Trapezous. After a victory at Svindax in 1022, George I ceded Tao, Kola, Artaan and Javakheti and gave his son Bagrat as a hostage. For one winter Trapezous was the seat of the emperor. The 14th-c. Lazaropoulos makes St Eugenios help Basil in this Iberian campaign and Basil a benefactor of the martyr’s monastery (Rosenqvist 1996, pp. 49, 409).
disputed: The link with St Eugenios is in Lazaropoulos (14th century), not in Xiphilinos. Rosenqvist (1996) places the battle at Lake Palakatsio in March 1021, and the stay at Trebizond after it; others give 11 September 1021.

title: Armenian kings and their people resettled in Sebasteia and Cappadocia
summary: As the empire annexed the Armenian kingdoms, their rulers received lands inside it: Senekerim of Vaspurakan got Sebasteia, Larissa and Abara (1021/2) and came with a large following; Gagik II of Ani got estates in Cappadocia (1045); Gagik-Abas of Kars got Tzamandos, Larissa, Amaseia and Komana (1064/5). Armenian soldiers, nobles and peasants spread through Sebasteia, Cappadocia and the southern edge of Pontus, strengthening an Armenian presence that already went back to the 7th–10th centuries.
disputed: The numbers who moved are unknown. The 14,000 retainers of Senekerim are given by Garsoïan (1997) and by Vryonis (1971), whose notes cite Honigmann, Grousset, Michael the Syrian and Aristakes. Armenian chroniclers blame Roman policy for stripping the frontier of its defenders, and Greek writers of the 1070s blame Armenian disloyalty; Garsoïan and Dédéyan discuss both. Bryer (1970, British) holds that inner Pontus, the Lykos valley, received so many Armenian refugees in the 11th century that it had a higher proportion of Armenians than of Greeks 'until this century'; this is his judgement, not a count.

summary: Konstantinos of Trapezous sat in the patriarchal synods of November 1027 and January 1028 (AM 6536), and Leon in the synod of June 1054, the year of the break with Rome. Chrysanthos uses the signatures to fix these two metropolitans.

title: Turkish raids before Manzikert
summary: Turkmen raiders sacked Sebasteia (1059), Caesarea with the shrine of St Basil (1067) and Neocaesarea (1068). Romanos IV, marching from Sebasteia, pursued the raiders of Neocaesarea and recovered prisoners and booty. The interior of Pontus was again a war zone, a decade before Manzikert. The Pontic valleys had been hit earlier still: Paipert was raided in 1054 and Koloneia in 1057 (Vryonis 1971, p. 162), and the caravan towns that fed Trebizond’s trade fell one by one: Artze sacked in 1049, Theodosiopolis occupied c. 1071, Ardanoutzin burned in 1080 (Sheard 2021, pp. 210–211).

title: John Xiphilinos of Trebizond, patriarch of Constantinople
summary: John Xiphilinos, born at Trebizond c. 1010–1013, wrote as a young man, before leaving for Constantinople, a collection of ten miracles of St Eugenios and a new Passion of the martyr; they record events in the city in his own and his family’s lifetime. He rose to be patriarch of Constantinople (John VIII, 1064–1075), as Anthimos of Trapezous had been in 535 (C2-007).
disputed: He was born about 1010–1013 or somewhat earlier (Bones, as cited by Rosenqvist).

title: Manzikert
summary: Alp Arslan defeated and captured Romanos IV at Manzikert. The battle itself cost relatively few lives, but the civil wars that followed left the eastern themes without defence, and within fifteen years Turkish emirs held most of the Pontic interior.
disputed: Older views made the battle a single catastrophe; Cahen, Vryonis and Beihammer stress the civil wars after it.

title: Roussel de Bailleul at Amaseia; the young Alexios Komnenos takes him
summary: The Norman mercenary leader Roussel de Bailleul broke with the emperor and seized the Armeniakon, ruling from round Amaseia, where the people welcomed his protection against the Turks. Before him, in 1069, the Frankish captain Crispin had made himself master of the fortress of Koloneia, which controlled the Pontic alum mines, and Roussel succeeded him on his death in 1073 (Bryer 1970). Vryonis (1971) adds that Roussel raided Amaseia, Neocaesarea and other towns and forced them to pay their taxes to him. The young general Alexios Komnenos paid the Turkish emir Tutach to hand Roussel over, then calmed the Amaseians, who wanted him freed, by pretending to blind him. Alexios restored imperial authority for a moment (1075), but the Turks soon overran the region.

title: Theodore Gabras takes Trapezous and rules it as his own
summary: Theodore Gabras, a Chaldian officer (in 1067 already patrikios and topoteretes, as a gospel book he commissioned records), recovered Trapezous from the Turks and, in Anna Komnene's words, held it 'as a prize that had fallen to his own lot'. Alexios I recognised him as doux of Chaldia. His seals call him doux and sebastos and invoke St Theodore, and a local coinage of Trapezous of c. 1080–1110 with St Theodore is linked to his rule. He held the coast from round Kerasous to Rhizaion, the inland passes, and at times Paipert. Chrysanthos (1933, p. 53) dates the Seljuk capture of Trapezous that Gabras undid to c. 1074, noting Fallmerayer's view (after Hayton, c. 1300) that only the suburbs fell, and takes the city to be free again by 1075, since Psellos's encomium of Patriarch John Xiphilinos (died 2 August 1075) speaks of it as free. Bryer (1970, p. 175) separates two steps: Gabras retook Trebizond from the Turks in 1075, with local Chaldian troops, after an occupation of no more than three years; he then retired to Constantinople, and Alexios I (emperor from 1081) made him duke of Chaldia to get him out of the capital. As duke he defended Koloneia and Neocaesarea against the emir Danishmend and Trebizond against the Georgians, and retook Paipert.
disputed: His rule is dated from about 1075 (Bryer) or from the 1080s (Treadgold, who also dates his death to 1099). The two dates refer to different steps: the recapture of the city (1075) and his appointment as duke by Alexios I (1081 or later). How independent he was is debated: Bryer speaks of a 'personal fiefdom', others of a loyal but distant governor. Whether the Turks took the city about 1074, or only its suburbs, is also uncertain: Chrysanthos says the city, Fallmerayer, after Hayton, the suburbs.

title: Danishmend Gazi takes Sebasteia, Neocaesarea, Tokat and Amaseia
summary: A Turkish commander known as Danishmend took the inland cities of Pontus and Armenia Minor (Sebasteia, Neocaesarea, Dokeia (Tokat), Komana, Amaseia, Euchaita) and founded the Danishmendid emirate, which held them until 1174–78. The Greek-speaking Christians of these towns stayed, now under Muslim rule, while the coast stayed Roman. The dates are uncertain; Michael the Syrian has him ruling 'Cappadocia' in 1085. Their coins bore Greek legends, with the title ‘Grand Melik of All Romania and the East’ (Bryer 1970, p. 170). By the crusade of 1101 they also held Paipert and Koloneia, which Theodore Gabras retook for a time (Vryonis 1971, p. 162).
disputed: Danishmend's origin (a Turkmen; of Armenian descent, as Matthew of Edessa says; or 'Arsacid', as Choniates has it) and the order and dates of his conquests are unknown. The Turkish epic of his deeds, the Danishmendname, was written down in the 14th century. On the conquest and settlement of inner Pontus: Bryer (1970, 1975, British) holds that north-east Anatolia was not conquered by one army, but contested piecemeal between about 1072 and after 1106 by Turkmen groups and local Christian lords, castle by castle and pasture by pasture, and that the Gabras family and the Danishmendids had more in common with each other than with Constantinople or Konya; Vryonis (1971, Greek-American) holds that the sacks, flight and breakdown of the church in the interior began a long decline of Greek Christianity there, with conversion gradual and largely later; Cahen (1968, French) calls the Danishmendname 'an intricate blend of genuine memories and legendary versions' (see also C2a-06).

title: Sinope recovered from the emir Karatekin
summary: A Turkish emir, Karatekin, had seized Sinope. In Anna Komnene's account the sultan's envoy Siaous, sent to remove Turkish governors from the coastal cities, handed Sinope over to Alexios instead and became a Christian, and Alexios' general Constantine Dalassenos took over the city. The episode shows how close the Turks came to holding the whole Pontic coast.

Bryer & Winfield (1985) date Karatekin's seizure of Sinope to 1081, citing Anna Komnene; Vryonis (1971) has Sinope back in imperial hands 'by 1085'; Anna places the handover after the death of the sultan Sulayman (1086).

title: Gabras and his son Gregory: a hostage in Constantinople
summary: Alexios kept Theodore Gabras' son Gregory at court as a hostage and betrothed him to a daughter of Isaac Komnenos. When the betrothal was broken off, Theodore tried to take Gregory home by sea, but imperial ships overtook him and he gave the boy up. Gregory later tried to escape to his father and was imprisoned at Philippopolis. About the same time Theodore married a princess 'from Alania', identified by Toumanoff as the Georgian Bagratid Mariam. He had put the boy on a merchant ship at the Bosporus; the imperial ships caught them beyond Aiginos, near Karambis (Alexiad, as quoted by Sheard 2021, p. 152), evidence of ordinary shipping between the capital and Trebizond.
disputed: The identity of Theodore's Alan wife with a Georgian princess is Toumanoff's hypothesis.

title: Theodore Gabras killed by the Turks; venerated as a martyr
summary: While the crusaders besieged Antioch, Theodore Gabras was fighting the Turks in the east. He was captured on a campaign towards Theodosiopolis and put to death, according to his cult for refusing to give up his faith. The Church commemorates him as a martyr on 2 October. His family kept Chaldia as a quasi-hereditary command for two generations. Vryonis (1971, p. 360) names his captor as the emir Ali (Amirales), in the region of Paipert and Erzurum; his skull, made into a drinking cup, was brought back secretly to Trebizond by Constantine Gabras between 1115 and 1140 and became the centre of his cult. His monastery stood in the eastern suburb of Trebizond until Alexios III gave it to the Venetians in 1364 (Bryer 1970, p. 170).
disputed: Most works date his death to 1098 (Bryer 1970; Vryonis 1971; Dunn, Bryer & Nesbitt); Treadgold (1997) has 1099. Vryonis, after the synaxarion, names his captor as the emir Ali rather than the Danishmendids. The story of his torture comes from the martyr's cult texts.

title: Bohemond of Antioch a prisoner at Neocaesarea
summary: Danishmend Gazi Gümüshtigin captured Bohemond, prince of Antioch and a leader of the First Crusade, near Melitene in August 1100 and held him at Neocaesarea (Niksar) until he was ransomed in 1103. Alexios I offered 260,000 dinars to have him handed over; the ransom finally paid is given as 100,000–130,000 dinars, raised with help from the Armenian lord Kogh Vasil (Matthew of Edessa, as cited by MacEvitt 2010 and Morton 2020). The captive drew the crusade of 1101 into Pontus.
disputed: The figures are taken from modern historians (MacEvitt 2010; Morton 2020), after Matthew of Edessa.

title: The crusade of 1101 destroyed at Mersivan
summary: A large Lombard-led army, with Raymond of Toulouse and a Roman escort of Pechenegs under Tzitas, took Ankyra (23 June 1101) and returned it to Alexios, failed before Gangra, took Kastamon, and then, against Raymond's advice, marched east across the Halys to free Bohemond at Neocaesarea. Kilij Arslan and the Danishmendids surrounded it near Mersivan (Merzifon) in August 1101 and destroyed it after about five days of fighting. On the way the crusaders sacked a Greek village beyond the Halys. This is the First Crusade's one direct echo in Pontus. The survivors escaped to the coast through Paurai (Bafra) (Bryer 1970, p. 176).
disputed: The chronicles give 50,000 or more; modern estimates for the Lombard contingent start at about 10,000 (Bouchard 1998: 'the exaggerated figure of 50,000 … at least 10,000').

title: Gregory Taronites rebels at Trapezous
summary: Gregory Taronites, a relative of the emperor of Armenian (Taron) descent, had campaigned in Pontus c. 1101–1103. Appointed doux of Chaldia, he rebelled on arrival at Trapezous (1103/4), imprisoning his predecessor Dabatenos and local notables. Alexios sent his cousin John Taronites; Gregory marched inland to Koloneia to seek Danishmendid help from Sebasteia, but John's Frankish mercenaries caught him first. He was imprisoned in the Anemas tower and later pardoned.
disputed: Whether Gregory Taronites is the same man as Gregory Gabras, Theodore's son, is debated: Hopf, Vasiliev and Cahen say yes, Skoulatos and most others no.

title: Constantine Gabras allied with the Mengujekids, defeated by Gazi
summary: Constantine Gabras, doux of Chaldia, allied himself with the Mengujekid emir of Erzincan, Ibn Mangujak, against the Danishmendid Gümüshtigin Gazi; in 1119 the allies were defeated and men of Gabras's army were taken prisoner (Bryer 1970). The episode shows the duke of Trapezous acting as one more player among the Anatolian emirs.
disputed: Bryer (1970, p. 181) dates the defeat and the capture of Gabras's men to 1119, and (p. 170) names Ibn Mangujak as his ally. Whether Gabras himself was captured and ransomed, as later accounts say, is not confirmed in the sources used here.

title: Constantine Gabras, 'tyrant of Trebizond'
summary: Constantine Gabras, doux of Chaldia since shortly before 1118, ruled Trapezous practically independently from 1126 and struck his own low-value coinage; Niketas Choniates calls him the 'tyrant of Trebizond'. His exact relation to Theodore is unknown. His rule ended when John II came east with the field army in 1139–40. The metropolitan Stephen Skylitzes, elected about 1126, could not reach his see for fourteen years because of Gabras's rule and arrived only in 1140 (Theodore Prodromos's monody, as used by Chrysanthos 1933, pp. 55-56, 222-230).
disputed: Whether Constantine was Theodore's son (Feldman 2018) or of unknown relation (Bryer) is debated. A 'Song of Gabras' is a modern composition, not a medieval source.

title: John II takes Kastamon and Gangra from the Danishmendids
summary: John II campaigned in Paphlagonia against the Danishmendid Gümüshtigin, taking Kastamon (1132/3), which was lost again, and then Gangra and Kastamon (1134/5). The campaigns reopened the land route along the north of Asia Minor towards Pontus.
disputed: Vryonis gives 1130–1135 for the series of campaigns.

title: John II in Pontus: Gabras submits, Neocaesarea holds out
summary: John II marched along the Black Sea coast into Pontus against the Danishmendid emir Muhammad; the show of force ended Constantine Gabras' independence and Chaldia returned to direct rule. In 1140 John besieged Neocaesarea, but lost many horses in the winter and his nephew John went over to the Turks; he withdrew. Neocaesarea and Amaseia stayed Turkish. Around the winter solstice his cavalry grazed at Kinte in the Iris delta, which places the army on the coast. Michael the Syrian says that while John besieged Neocaesarea the Turks killed Christians in their lands who so much as named the emperor (Vryonis 1971, p. 119).
disputed: The route along the coast and the year of Gabras' submission (1139 or 1140) are uncertain. Bryer & Winfield (1985) date the wintering at Kinte to the winter of 1139/40 (21 December 1139 to February 1140), a year earlier than Bryer (1975); the siege of Neocaesarea then fell in 1140, and the army was back in Constantinople on 15 January 1141.

title: A Danishmendid madrasa at Niksar
summary: After the Danishmendid lands were divided (1142), the emir Yağıbasan, based at Sebasteia, built a madrasa at Niksar, dated 1157/8 in Turkey's entry for Niksar on the UNESCO tentative list; it is among the oldest Turkish-Islamic buildings in Anatolia. Former Roman cities of Pontus were becoming Muslim urban centres, while keeping Christian populations.

title: Andronikos Komnenos raids Chaldia from Koloneia
summary: The exiled Andronikos Komnenos, after years at the Georgian court of George III, held a castle near Koloneia, on the border of Chaldia, as a freebooter in the service of the Saltukid emir Mehmed of Erzurum (1173–1176/7), and raided Roman lands from it. Nikephoros Palaiologos, duke of Chaldia at Trapezous, captured his companion Theodora Komnene, the former queen of Jerusalem, and their children; Andronikos then submitted to Manuel I in 1180 (Bryer 1970, p. 180 n. 56). (Continued in C2a-05.)
disputed: Bryer & Winfield (1985, p. 148) suggest, as a question, that Andronikos' castle near Koloneia was Sisorta Kale (33 km WNW of Şebinkarahisar) or Kibossa; no source names it.

title: The Seljuk sultan absorbs the Danishmendids
summary: Kilij Arslan II of Rum took over the Danishmendid lands, Sebasteia (1174) and finally Melitene (1178). Two years after his victory over Manuel I at Myriokephalon (1176), one Seljuk power ruled the whole Pontic interior from Amaseia to Sebasteia, while the coast from Sinope to Trapezous stayed Roman. In 1175 Manuel sent Michael Gabras with the troops of Trebizond and Oinaion into the Pontic interior, but he abandoned Amaseia to the sultan and was later arrested for it (Bryer 1970, p. 180).
disputed: The fall of Sebasteia and Neocaesarea is dated 1174 (Melikoff, Cahen) or 1175 (Vryonis 1971; Bryer 1970; Bryer & Winfield 1985, who date the end of the Danishmendids to 1178).

title: Andronikos Komnenos rules the Pontos from Oinaion
summary: After submitting to Manuel I in 1180, Andronikos Komnenos was given the Roman Pontos to hold, with Oinaion (Ünye) as his seat; the castle there has been linked with him. In 1182 he set out from Oinaion to seize the throne in Constantinople, and he reigned 1183–1185. His grandsons Alexios and David were the founders of the Empire of Trebizond in 1204, so this brief Pontic lordship is the family’s first tie to the region.
disputed: Bryer & Winfield (1985) are cautious about the castle: its surviving sea wall is comparable to 14th-century imperial work 'but could be earlier', so a 12th-century origin is possible, not proved.

title: The metropolitan of Neocaesarea lives at Oinaion
summary: The canonist Theodore Balsamon records that the metropolitan of Neocaesarea, unable to reside in his see because it was in Turkish hands, had been allowed by imperial order and synodal decision to take as his seat his suffragan bishopric of Oinaion, on the coast and still under the emperor. Balsamon adds that many other clergy had fled from towns held by the Turks to bishoprics across the border. The case shows the church of inner Pontus being run from the coast, a century after the Danishmendid conquest.
disputed: Balsamon's remark can be dated only within his working life (about 1170–1195). Bryer & Winfield (1985) suggest that the see was probably moved to the coast during John II's expedition of 1139/40, so that Balsamon describes an arrangement already some decades old.

title: Tamar's Georgia: the new power on Chaldia's eastern border
summary: Under Queen Tamar (sole ruler from 1184), Georgia became the strongest Christian state of the region; her army defeated the Seljuk sultan Rukn al-Din at Basiani (1202). Her court sheltered Alexios and David Komnenos, grandsons of Andronikos I through his son Manuel and the Georgian princess Rusudan. Georgia, not Constantinople, would be the base for the Komnenoi's seizure of Trapezous in 1204.
disputed: The exact kinship of Tamar and the Komnenoi is debated (Panaretos calls her their relative; see chapter 6). Eastmond (2016) dates Basiani to 1203.

title: A Jewish community at Trebizond
summary: The colophon of a Bible scroll records its purchase in 1188 from ‘the community of our brethren the kahal of Tirapzin’, the first record of Jews at Trebizond; it is published in Ankori’s study of the Karaites. The city already drew Muslim, Armenian, Georgian and northern merchants; Jewish traders are now attested among them.

title: The Seljuks reach the Black Sea at Amisos
summary: After absorbing the Danishmendids, the Seljuks of Konya pushed down the Halys and Iris to the coast and took Amisos (Samsun) before the end of the 12th century, their first port on the Black Sea. Sinope and the coast east of the Iris stayed Roman. In 1200 Alexios III sent Constantine Frangopoulos into the Black Sea, nominally to look into a ship wrecked near Kerasous, in fact to plunder the merchantmen sailing to and from Amisos; among his victims were merchants from Ikonion (Konya), and the sultan obtained 50 minae of silver in compensation, on top of the 300 minae a year that the emperor already paid him.
disputed: Sheard suspects that Choniates wrote 'Phasis' for another port in describing the wrecked ship's route.

title: The fall of Andronikos I; his grandsons taken to Georgia
summary: The emperor Andronikos I Komnenos was overthrown and killed in Constantinople in September 1185; his son Manuel was blinded and soon died. Manuel's small sons Alexios (born 1182) and David were taken, by routes the sources do not describe, to Georgia, where they grew up at the court of Queen Tamar. This Georgian upbringing is the root of the Empire of Trebizond.
disputed: How the boys reached Georgia, and how exactly they were related to Tamar, are unknown. Panaretos calls Tamar Alexios' 'paternal aunt', which Bryer (1980) counts among Panaretos' loose terms of kinship, 'for what is actually first cousin once removed on the father's side'. Fallmerayer, followed by Ioannidis (1870), wrongly made Tamar a daughter of Andronikos I; Toumanoff (1940) argued that the boys' mother was the Georgian princess Rusudan, which would make Tamar their aunt on the mother's side.

title: The seven banda of the Pontos
summary: The empire's heartland was organised in seven valley districts, the banda or 'military parishes' inherited from the theme of Chaldia. From west to east they were (probably) the Philabonites (Harsit valley), Trikomia (round Platana, Akçaabat), Trebizond itself, Matzouka-Palaiomatzouka (Maçka), Gemora (Yomra), Sourmaina (Sürmene) and Rhizaion (Rize). Only the Philabonites was lost entirely to the Turkmen; the other six kept their military structure until 1461 and later became, in turn, Ottoman kazas and modern districts. Their village communities, smallholders and local defence, rather than the trade of the capital, were the strength of the empire: Bryer puts the capital at about 4,000 people after the Black Death, in a 'pocket empire' of 200,000-250,000.
disputed: Bryer gives the list as 'probably' right; the boundaries are those of the later Ottoman districts, which he argues geography made identical. The population figures are Bryer's estimates (the capital's 4,000 after Tafur), not a medieval count.
