title: Alexios and David Komnenos take Trebizond
summary: With Georgian backing from Queen Tamar, their kinswoman (Panaretos: Alexios 'set out from Iberia with the zeal and labour of his paternal aunt Tamar'), the brothers Alexios and David Komnenos came along the coast from Georgia and took Trebizond in April 1204 (indiction 7, AM 6712); Alexios, aged 22, was proclaimed emperor. This happened in the same weeks as the crusaders' capture of Constantinople (12-13 April 1204), and probably before news of it reached the Pontus. How large the Georgian share was, and what Tamar intended, are debated. The state they founded lasted until 1461 and was ruled by their descendants, the Grand Komnenoi, throughout.
disputed: Georgian help as such is attested by the Georgian royal chronicle, by Panaretos (Tamar's 'zeal and labour') and indirectly by Choniates (hired Iberians); no source known to us denies it. Its scale and purpose are disputed: a Georgian conquest handed to a client, the new state a Georgian tributary or buffer (the Georgian chronicle; Vasiliev 1936; Sheard 2021, after the Georgian historian Metreveli); a Georgian reprisal raid that became an empire only because Constantinople fell (Eastmond 2004, 2016); Tamar backing a bid for the throne of Constantinople itself (Kuršanskis 1977); or help with mercenaries or money only (Lampsides, as cited by Samouilidis). Chrysanthos (1933) does not mention Tamar and credits the refugee scholarioi and the native military families of the Doranites and Tzanichites, who are attested only from the 14th century; that is his emphasis, not evidence. The date is also disputed: Vasiliev has the brothers move before the fall of Constantinople was known; Karpov (2012), from a seal, suggests about 23 April, St George's day.

title: Sultan Kaykaus I takes Sinope; Alexios I captured
summary: The Seljuk sultan Izz al-Din Kaykaus I besieged Sinope. Alexios I, caught outside the city, was taken prisoner and shown, after torture, to the defenders, who surrendered on terms on 1 November 1214. Alexios was released as a tributary vassal of the sultan, and the Seljuks gained their first port on the Black Sea; their building inscriptions of 1215 still stand on the walls of Sinop. The price of release was tribute and vassalage; the yearly tribute is given as 10,000 dinars, 500 horses, 200 cows, 10,000 sheep and 50 loads of gifts (Ibn Bibi, as given by Eastmond) or as 12,000 gold pieces, 500 horses, 2,000 cattle, 10,000 sheep and 50 bales (Ibn Bibi, as given by Bryer & Winfield). A bilingual Arabic and Greek inscription on the walls records the Seljuk rebuilding of 1215.
disputed: The day is Ibn Bibi's. Some scholars think Sinope was held by a local lord allied to Alexios rather than by Trebizond itself. The inscription names Bedreddin son of Abu Bakir and the architect Sebastos (Bryer; Bryer & Winfield 1985); Kuruoğlu, cited by Bryer, gives the builder as Abu Ali ibn Abi'r-Rakka of Aleppo.

title: Seljuk siege of Trebizond and the 'miracle of St Eugenios'
summary: Andronikos I Gidos succeeded his father-in-law Alexios I, who died on 20 February 1222, the Sunday of Orthodoxy (Panaretos). In AM 6731 (September 1222 - August 1223), the second year of his reign, a treaty with the 'sultan Melik' was broken when the Melik's vassal Etoumes (Het'um), rais of Sinope, seized a ship that had run ashore there with the yearly revenue of Cherson and Gothia; after a Trapezuntine raid on the Sinope coast the Melik marched by Erzurum, Keltzene and Paipert and besieged Trebizond. The siege failed, the Melik was captured and released, and the city credited its patron saint, the martyr Eugenios. John Zanzes, who fell in a sortie, was buried in a monastery to which his widow gave an estate at Ammodion: St Eugenios in Lazaropoulos's text (as Rosenqvist reads it), the Chrysokephalos in Chrysanthos (p. 393). Chrysanthos adds that the empire then reached only from Soteriopolis (Sukhumi) to Oinaion.
disputed: Both medieval sources give AM 6731, September 1222 to August 1223; 1223 is the more likely calendar year if Gidos' regnal years are counted from 20 February 1222, but that cannot be proved. Chrysanthos, Kunik, Samouilidis and Eastmond (2016) write 1223; Rosenqvist and Eastmond (2004) 1222/23. The 'Melik' is a title, not a name, and has been identified as Kayqubad I (Fallmerayer; Savvides; Chrysanthos), as Mughith al-Din Tughrilshah of Erzurum (Cahen; Bryer) or as a son of Kayqubad (Janssens). Cahen and Kuršanskis tied the ship from Cherson to refugees from the Mongol raid on the Crimea of 1223. Lazaropoulos wrote more than a century later, as hagiography; only the date has an independent witness (Panaretos). Bryer & Winfield (1985) read Lazaropoulos as Rosenqvist does, with Zanzes buried at St Eugenios, and tentatively place Ammodion at Bulancak.

title: Hagia Sophia of Trebizond built under Manuel I
summary: Manuel I, 'the most fortunate', built the monastery church of Hagia Sophia on a headland west of the walled city. Its sculpted Genesis frieze, single-headed Komnenian eagle and star-shaped (muqarnas) niches mix Constantinopolitan, Georgian, Armenian and Seljuk art, and its frescoes, probably painted by one workshop in under three years, are among the finest of the 13th century. Building and decoration were probably finished in the mid-1250s. Manuel's donor portrait, still seen in the 19th century, called him 'faithful emperor and autocrat of the Romans'. It was partly a mosque by 1701, was restored as a mosque in the 1880s (when the paintings were plastered over), was conserved by David Winfield's team for the Russell Trust in 1957-1962 and then opened as a museum, and became a mosque again in 2013. Chrysanthos (1933, p. 426 ff.) cites the founder's inscription copied by Finlay in 1850 ('κτήτωρ τῆς ἁγίας μονῆς ταύτης Μανουὴλ ὁ Κομνηνός'), calls the church the monastery of Christ (feast 6 August), and dates its conversion to a mosque between 1578 and 1609.
disputed: The building was probably finished in the mid-1250s (Eastmond 2004), the paintings in the early 1250s (Winfield); Eastmond (2016) allows 'possibly up to twenty years earlier', and rejects a longer painting campaign of over a decade (Talbot Rice, Restle). The conversion to a mosque is put soon after 1461, in 1584, or, by Chrysanthos, between 1578 and 1609; graffiti on the dome recording restorations of the church in August 1486 and October 1547 (Bryer & Winfield 1985) tell against a conversion soon after 1461, and Tournefort found it partly a mosque in 1701. On what the mixed decoration means: Tamara Talbot Rice (1963, British) saw Seljuk-style panels made by Seljuk refugee craftsmen after Köse Dağ, an image of Komnenian triumph over the Turks; Bryer (1975, British) found the refugee thesis 'hardly convincing' and the interchange Armenian-Seljuk rather than Greek; Eastmond (2004, British) reads it as a Roman imperial church that adapted Constantinople to local audiences, in which 'Anatolian motifs only decorated a Byzantine body' (see also H4-041).

title: The Mongols overrun the Crimea: the Perateia lost in practice
summary: The Mongol campaigns in the western steppe (1238-1242) brought the Crimea under the Golden Horde. Trebizond's revenue from the Perateia did not survive this for long, though the claim stayed in the imperial title until 1461 and the Crimean principality of Theodoro (Gothia) kept close ties with Trebizond.
disputed: When tribute from Cherson and Gothia actually stopped is unknown.

title: Kose Dag: Trebizond passes under Mongol overlordship
summary: The Mongols under Baiju crushed the Seljuk army at Kose Dag. Trebizond, a Seljuk tributary, then accepted the overlordship of the Mongols (from 1256 the Ilkhans of Persia), which lasted until the Ilkhanate broke up in 1335. William of Rubruck, crossing the Black Sea in 1253, noted that Trebizond 'has its own prince, named Guido, who, although of the imperial race of Constantinople, is under the Tartar dominion' (Kerr's English version).
disputed: Whether a Trapezuntine contingent fought at Kose Dag on the Seljuk side is reported in some sources and doubted by others.

title: Manuel I at the Mongol kuriltai at Karakorum
summary: After Kose Dag the Mongols left Manuel I's land untouched in return for tribute. In 1246 he travelled to the kuriltai that enthroned the Great Khan Güyük at Karakorum, as the equal of the sultan of Rum, the two kings of Georgia, the sultan of Erzurum and the emir of Aleppo, and received a yarligh (decree) confirming his rule. The new Mongol order also moved the caravan trade north, away from Baghdad and Syria, towards Tabriz and Trebizond.

title: Manuel I recovers Sinope; lost again in 1265
summary: Exploiting Seljuk weakness under the Mongols, Manuel I took Sinope back in the 1250s and installed a governor of the Gabras family; the Seljuk regent, the Pervane Mu'in al-Din Suleyman, retook it in 1265, this time for good. Manuel's reign also saw the first Trapezuntine silver aspers, coins with the emperor and St Eugenios that were copied in Georgia as the standard currency (the 'kyrmanueli').
disputed: The date, and even the fact, of the recovery are questioned: Bryer & Winfield (1985) give 1254, 1258 or 1259, and the loss as summer 1265, 1267 or 1268, reading the Pervane's inscription at Sinope as 1267/8. They also record a last, unsuccessful Trapezuntine attempt on Sinope about 1280.

title: Tabriz becomes the Mongol capital: the caravan route to Trebizond
summary: After Hulegu sacked Baghdad (February 1258), Tabriz became the commercial capital of Mongol Iran, and its silk, spices and dyes came to Europe by caravan over Erzurum and the Zigana pass to Trebizond. Trebizond's customs duties made it rich, and Italian merchants settled there from the 1280s. Pegolotti's merchant manual (c. 1340) notes that the weights and measures of Tabriz were the same as Trebizond's; its list of toll stations is for the road from Ayas (Laiazzo) in Cilicia to Tabriz, not from Trebizond.
disputed: On the weight of the Tabriz trade: Heyd (1886, German) and Bratianu (1929, Romanian), from the Italian commercial records, held that the transit trade far outweighed local products, making Trebizond the 'vestibule of Central Asia'; Bryer (1967–1979, British), from Venetian and Genoese notarial records, monastic charters and Ottoman registers, holds that the Central Asian traffic was slight beside the local Black Sea trade, that the emperors lived from land rather than commerce, and that the route's real heyday was 1829–1869; Eastmond (2004, British) and Karpov (1986, Russian) see the Mongol shift of the caravan routes to Tabriz as the source of Trebizond's prosperity, with its silver mines. Pegolotti's list of toll stations is for the road from Ayas to Tabriz, not from Trebizond; Clavijo (1404) travelled the road from Trebizond by Erzurum to Tabriz.

title: Patriarchal act: the metropolitan of Trebizond to be elected at home
summary: At the request of Manuel I, a synod of 26 bishops under Patriarch Nikephoros II at Kallipolis issued an act allowing the metropolitan of Trebizond to be elected and consecrated in Trebizond in the presence of a patriarchal envoy. The patriarchate agreed, Chrysanthos quotes, looking to 'the gain from it, that is, the union of the Romans' ('τὴν τῶν Ῥωμαίων δηλονότι ἕνωσιν'), i.e. good relations with Nicaea. The church of Trebizond never became independent ('autocephalous').

title: The Chepni Turkmen appear near Sinope
summary: The Chepni, a Turkmen tribe found over much of central Anatolia, were 'causing trouble at Samsun in 1277', in the year the Pervane, the Seljuk regent who had held Sinope, was put to death by the Ilkhan; groups of them had been working east along the summer pastures from Sinope since the early 13th century. In the 14th century they took over the Philabonites (Harsit) valley, the only one of the central Trapezuntine valleys to lose its Greek settlement almost entirely.

The first mention is Ibn Bibi's, as cited by Bryer, whose guide to the Turkish sources is Faruk Sümer's Oğuzlar.

title: Emperor George betrayed; John II takes the throne
summary: George, a son of Manuel I, 'was betrayed through a plot by the archontes at the mountain of Taurezion and captured in June' 1280 (Panaretos); his brother John II then received the insignia. Bryer identifies Taurezion with Tabriz: after the Mongol defeat at Elbistan (1277) the archons escorted George to submit to the Ilkhan Abaga and abandoned him near the Ilkhan's capital. The episode shows how the archons of the Pontus, and the Mongol overlord, could make and unmake emperors.
disputed: Where 'Taurezion' was is debated: the Tauros (Lampsides and older historians), which would imply a much larger empire; a place nearer Trebizond, on an expedition against the Turkmen (Chrysanthos; Ioannidis, a mountain near Soumela); or Tabriz, whose medieval forms fit the name (Bryer 1973, followed by Asp-Talwar 2016). Bryer's reading makes George a victim of the Ilkhan's vengeance after Elbistan, like the Pervane in the same years.

title: John II marries Eudokia Palaiologina; the new imperial title
summary: John II went to Constantinople and married Eudokia, daughter of Michael VIII Palaiologos, while Michael was still alive (Panaretos); according to Pachymeres he agreed to take only the lesser title of despot and to exchange the emperor's red shoes for black ones. Manuel I had styled himself 'faithful emperor and autocrat of the Romans' in his donor portrait at Hagia Sophia; from John II the Grand Komnenoi styled themselves 'faithful emperor and autocrat of all the East, the Iberians and the Perateia', a formula seen in the signature of Alexios III's chrysobull for Dionysiou (1374). In April 1283, in John's absence, King David VI Narin of Imereti besieged Trebizond without taking it; John came back with the pregnant Eudokia on 25 April 1283. Chrysanthos (1933, p. 56) likewise has the rulers styled 'emperor and autocrat of the Romans' until the end of the 13th century, and 'of all the East, of the Iberians and of Perateia' from John II; their eagle was single-headed.
disputed: When the new title was first used is debated, and so is what 'the Iberians' meant: the Georgian and Laz subjects, or a claim on Georgia. The 'Perateia', the Crimean lands across the sea, was by then mostly a claim. Eastmond (2004) notes 'some doubt about Pachymeres' account', since the 14th-century rulers still called themselves emperor. Panaretos' date for the Georgian siege, 'after the year 6790 (1282), in April', is read as April 1283 (Asp-Talwar).

title: Theodora, daughter of Manuel I, seizes the throne
summary: After John II's return in 1283 came 'the attack and occupation by kyr George Komnenos', called 'the wanderer', and with it the usurpation, rule and sudden flight of Theodora, eldest daughter of Manuel I by the Georgian Rusudan (Panaretos). She held Trebizond in 1284-1285 before John II recovered it. She is the first of three women who held the throne.
disputed: Georgian backing is inferred, not stated; her mother Rusudan was Georgian, which makes it plausible but unproven. Panaretos links her rule with the return of 'George Komnenos the wanderer', usually taken to be the deposed emperor George, though possibly another member of the family (Asp-Talwar).

title: Edward I's embassy to the Ilkhan passes through Trebizond
summary: An English embassy sent by Edward I to the Ilkhan Arghun bought its supplies at Trebizond in June 1292 and camped on Mount Kampana, on the road south, on 22 July 1292; its accounts list bread, wine, fish, rice, olive oil, fruit, nuts and meat on the coast, against little but meat and bread beyond the mountains. Returning in 1293 it dragged a caged leopard, a present from the Ilkhan, from Tabriz to Dover; a new lock was made for the cage in Trebizond.

title: Gregory Chioniades brings Persian astronomy to Trebizond
summary: Gregory Chioniades, a physician and scholar educated in Constantinople, went by way of Trebizond to Tabriz, studied astronomy there and translated Persian astronomical works into Greek. About 1300 he told his patron Alexios II that he was going to take up the bishopric of Tabriz ('Taurez'); after leaving it he lived the rest of his life as a monk in Trebizond. Through him and his successors at Trebizond (the priest Manuel, George Chrysokokkes) the Persian tables of the Maragha school reached Greek science; by 1336 the Zij-i Ilkhani was in use at Trebizond (see C2b-04).
disputed: Pingree and later scholars differ on the dates of his journeys and on his role as a teacher at Trebizond. Mercier (1994) does not know when he died and ends his activity in the first decade of the century; Eastmond (2016) gives about 1320.

summary: Alexios II succeeded his father John II at about 14 and reigned for almost 33 years, the empire's richest period. date_text: June AM 6812 = June 1304 (Panaretos: the year after the fire of Friday 30 November 6811 = 1302); older works say 1306
title: Quarrel with the Genoese; the suburbs burned
summary: After a great fire inside the walls on Friday 30 November 1302, 'the following year' (in June, by Samouilidis' quotation of the manuscript) the Latins burned the exartesis, the shipyard or the still unwalled Lower City, 'when there was a severe conflict' (Panaretos). Pachymeres describes the quarrel in more detail: Alexios II refused the Genoese further privileges and fighting broke out. The emperor wanted the customs revenue; the Genoese, who also held Caffa in the Crimea, wanted exemptions.
disputed: Panaretos dates the fire to Friday 30 November AM 6811, which was 1302 (in 1305 that day was a Tuesday), and the Latin burning to the following year, June 1304. The year 1306 in older works (Miller 1926; Samouilidis, with a Genoese embassy of June 1306) comes from reckoning AM 6811 as 1305, which the weekday does not support; Rosenqvist has 1303. What burned is uncertain: the shipyard (Lampsides), the Lower City (Asp-Talwar), or an arsenal, probably the imperial one on the Daphnous shore (Bryer & Winfield 1985, who date the events 1303 and 1305).

title: Metropolitan Barnabas
summary: A manuscript note of May 1311 names 'the metropolitan of Trapezous and hypertimos kyr Barnabas' ('μητροπολίτου Τραπεζοῦντος καὶ ὑπερτίμου κυροῦ Βαρνάβα'). His tomb in the Chrysokephalos ('τάφος τοῦ Βαρνάβα') later received metropolitan Niphon (1364).

title: Treaties with Genoa; the Genoese at Leontokastron
summary: Peace with Genoa was confirmed by a treaty of 26 October 1314, in which the emperor also promised Genoese traders an escort as far as Mount Kampana on the road south; a further treaty is dated 1316. The Genoese held the Leontokastron, the rocky headland east of the walled city above the Daphnous landing, as their base from the first years of the 14th century until 1316, when they were moved to the arsenal of Daphnous; it was formally ceded to them on 15 June 1349, after the war of 1348–1349 (Panaretos), and they held it until 1461 (Bryer & Winfield 1985). It was a lasting source of friction. A Venetian castle later stood a few hundred metres to the west.
disputed: The treaty of 1316 is known from Bryer & Winfield (1985): in 1314 and again in 1316 the Genoese forced terms on Alexios II, including their own base in Trebizond and a large indemnity.

title: Venetian privileges; Sinopean raiders burn Trebizond
summary: Alexios II granted the Venetians a chrysobull and treaty, the first of five Venetian treaties with Trebizond (1319–1396), giving them the same terms as the Genoese; Venice then looked for a better site for its commercial base, in the end on the cape of the Holy Cross (Tzavara 2011). In the same year Turkish raiders from Sinope set fire to the city, and in 1324 Alexios II completed the walls of the Lower City, which more than doubled the walled area (Bryer & Winfield 1985).

title: Death of Alexios II and dynastic murders
summary: Alexios II died on 3 May 1330. His son Andronikos III had two of his brothers killed on his accession and died in January 1332; the boy Manuel II was deposed in September 1332 by his uncle Basil, who had him killed with a sword on 21 February 1333, the Sunday of Orthodoxy. A long run of instability began.

date_text: 30 November 1335 (13 Rabi' II 736: death of Abu Sa'id)
title: The Ilkhanate breaks up: end of Mongol overlordship
summary: The death of the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id ended the unity of Mongol Iran. Trebizond was freed of its overlord, but the Tabriz trade became less safe and Turkmen confederations, above all the Aq Qoyunlu of Diyarbakir, began to press on the Pontic frontier.

date_text: Almanac for 12 March 1336 - 12 March 1337; eclipse and riot on Monday 3 March 1337
title: An almanac for Trebizond, and the eclipse riot of 1337
summary: A Greek almanac drawn up at Trebizond for 12 March 1336 to 12 March 1337, with astrological predictions addressed to the protonotarios and protovestiarios Constantine Loukites, computed the positions of sun, moon and planets from the Persian Zij-i Ilkhani of the Maragha observatory. It survives in a manuscript copied by Andreas Libadenos, prototaboullarios and chartophylax of Trebizond; its editor ascribes it to the priest Manuel of Trebizond, the teacher of George Chrysokokkes. Persian tables are not known in Constantinople before about 1346. On Monday 3 March 1337, the first Monday of Lent, an annular eclipse, seen at Trebizond as partial, darkened the city from the fourth to the seventh hour, and 'the people rose in turmoil against the emperor' Basil and stoned the citadel (Panaretos).
disputed: The author was the priest Manuel of Trebizond (Mercier 1994), not Libadenos, who only copied it (Lambros), nor Chrysokokkes (Bryer 1986), nor Manuel Bryennios. Panaretos does not say why the people rose in 1337; Bryer (1986, as cited by Mercier) sees a protest at the emperor's immoral life, his bigamy with Irene of Trebizond. A 'school' or 'academy' of astronomy with an observatory in the tower of Hagia Sophia (Papadopoulos 1919, 1927) is rejected: the tower was built about 1426/7 (Mercier; Rosenqvist).

title: Basil dies; Irene Palaiologina seizes power; the Scholarioi and the Amytzantarioi
summary: Basil died on Thursday 6 April 1340 and his widow Irene Palaiologina, an illegitimate daughter of the emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos, took power; Basil's other wife, Irene of Trebizond, was sent to Constantinople with her sons. The archons split: the megas stratopedarches Tzanichites with the Scholarioi, the Meizomatai, Constantine Doranites, the Kabazitai and Kamachenos, part of the people and some imperial units seized the monastery of St Eugenios, while the Amytzantarioi (the holders of court titles) held the citadel with the empress. On 2 July 1340 the megas doux John the Eunuch came from Limnia, stormed the monastery with siege engines and burned it; Tzanichites and the other archons were imprisoned at Limnia and executed there in June 1341. Nine years of civil war followed.
disputed: Panaretos does not say what the factions stood for. Older accounts (Miller 1926, British) saw a court party looking to Constantinople against local landed families, with the Laz as a third force; Bryer (1979, British) sees a struggle over land, since so much crown land had gone out in grants that the emperors could no longer buy loyalty, the coastal Scholarioi and the inland Mesochaldaioi holding different kinds of estates; he also notes (1975) that the factions had nothing to do with the Turkmen and mirrored the disturbances in Constantinople. Rosenqvist (1996, Swedish), after Kislinger and Bryer, stresses Basil's bigamy with a local woman, Irene of Trebizond, which humiliated the princess from Constantinople and angered Constantinople and 'wide circles in Trebizond'; a patriarchal letter of 1340 backed Irene Palaiologina.

title: Aq Qoyunlu raid; Anna Anachoutlou takes the throne with the Laz
summary: On Wednesday 4 July 1341 the Amitiotai Turkmen (the early Aq Qoyunlu) returned; the Romans fell back without a fight, many Christians were killed and all of Trebizond, inside and outside the walls, was burned, followed by a sudden pestilence from the stench of the dead. Anna Anachoutlou, a daughter of Alexios II, escaped from her convent, was proclaimed among the Laz, and entered Trebizond on 17 July 1341. When Michael Komnenos arrived from Constantinople with three warships on 30 July to take power, the Laz and Anna's noble allies routed his men the next morning and imprisoned him at Oinaion, then Limnia. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 75-76, 231-246) adds the church side: St Eugenios burned in 1340 and the whole city in July 1341 ('Ἐκαύθη ἡ Τραπεζοῦς ὅλη'); Metropolitan Akakios received Michael on 30 July 1341 'with the Gospel', crowned John III in the Chrysokephalos at the ambo on 9 September 1342, rebuilt the Chrysokephalos 'from the ash-heaps' and crowned Alexios III in the rebuilt St Eugenios on 21 January 1350.
disputed: Panaretos dates the burning precisely to Wednesday 4 July 1341. The Amitiotai are generally identified as the early Aq Qoyunlu (Asp-Talwar). Bryer once derived their name from 'Omidia' west of Kerasous rather than from Amida, but later withdrew the proposal (Bryer & Winfield 1985, who place Omidie at Bulancak).

date_text: Sailed from Constantinople 17 August; arrived Wednesday 4 September; crowned 9 September 1342
title: John III arrives with Genoese galleys; Anna strangled
summary: The Scholarioi leaders who had fled to Constantinople on 10 September 1341 returned with Michael's son John, two galleys of their own and three hired Genoese galleys; they left on 17 August and reached Trebizond on Wednesday 4 September 1342. John III was crowned on 9 September at the ambo of the Chrysokephalos; the Amytzantarian archons were killed, and Anna Anachoutlou was strangled together with Sargale, after a reign Panaretos gives as one year, one month and eight days. The Genoese role shows the Italians as actors in Trapezuntine politics.
disputed: The day of Anna's death is not given; her 'one year, one month and eight days' from 17 July 1341 would end before the arrival, so the count is inexact.

title: Michael crowned; the Scholarioi oligarchy
summary: After the megas doux John the Eunuch, who held Michael prisoner at Limnia, was killed there in March 1344, Niketas Scholares fetched Michael, who took power on Monday 3 May and was crowned on 21 May 1344; his son John III was shut up in the cave of St Sabbas. The new court was shared out among the archons: Niketas Scholares megas doux, Gregory Meizomates megas stratopedarches, Leo Kabazites megas domestikos, Constantine Doranites protovestiarios, John Kabazites megas logariastes. In November 1345 Michael had Niketas Scholares and others of his party arrested. The western districts were meanwhile left to the Turkmen.

title: Turkmen take Oinaion: the western frontier gives way
summary: In AM 6855 (1346/47) the Turkmen of Chalybia took Hagios Andreas, probably on Cape Jason, and Oinaion with its mountain road to Neokaisareia. On 29 June 1348 a coalition attacked Trebizond itself: Ahi Ayna Beg of Erzincan, Muhammad the Rikabdar of Bayburt, Turali Beg of the Amitiotai (Aq Qoyunlu), and Boz Doğan with the Chepni; they fought for three days and left in flight. The coast west of Kerasous, the old banda of Oinaion and Limnia, was slipping into the hands of Turkmen emirs.
disputed: AM 6855 runs from September 1346 to August 1347; Bryer and Asp-Talwar write 1347, older accounts 1346. Hagios Andreas was 'probably on Cape Jason' (Bryer); it is not shown on the map.

title: The Black Death reaches Trebizond
summary: The plague, carried by ship from Caffa, struck Trebizond in September 1347 and lasted about seven months. Panaretos says only that it took 'many children and wives, brothers, mothers and relatives'; other contemporaries say nothing of it, so its scale is unknown. It came back in 1362 and 1382.

title: War with Genoa: Kerasous seized; the fleet destroyed
summary: After a massacre of Genoese in the capital, the Genoese attacked Kerasous, the empire's second city, in January 1348, and ransacked and burned the town. In May 1349 a Genoese fleet from Caffa destroyed the Trapezuntine fleet under the megas doux John Kabazites, and townspeople killed westerners in revenge. The peace left the Genoese in possession of the Leontokastron.

title: Alexios III arrives and takes the throne
summary: On 13 December 1349 Niketas Scholares and his allies deposed Michael in favour of John, a son of Basil, who had been sent from Constantinople with the support of John VI Kantakouzenos. He arrived on 22 December, took the name Alexios III and was crowned on 21 January 1350. His forty-year reign (1349-1390) ended the civil war.

title: The empire about 1350
summary: After the losses of 1346-1348 the empire runs from Kerasous (contested 1348-1355) to Makriali, with Chaldia under its own dukes of the Kabazites family. Oinaion and the coast west of Kerasous are Turkmen; Limnia is a doubtful outpost.
disputed: How far Chaldia obeyed Trebizond, and when Limnia passed to the Taceddinoğulları (before 1379), are uncertain.

title: First Turkmen marriage: Maria to Qutlugh Beg of the Aq Qoyunlu
summary: In August 1352 Alexios III married his eldest sister Maria to Fahreddin Kutlug Beg, son of Turali, emir of the Amitiotai (the early Aq Qoyunlu), whose raids had burned the city in 1341. It was the first time a princess of the Roman tradition had been given to a Turkmen, and it began a policy of marrying Komnenian princesses to Turkmen rulers to turn raiders into in-laws and allies: state visits followed (Maria in 1358, Kutlug Beg in 1365, the emperor in 1367). The marriage left a trace in Ballad 6 of the Book of Dede Korkut, where Kan Turali wins the princess of Trebizond in the Meydan.
disputed: On how 'Greek' the empire was, the question this marriage policy raises: the Genoese Belban, reported by the Egyptian compiler al-Umari (1342–1348), found it in every respect like the Turkish principalities round it; Angold (1999, British) calls it a 'Greek emirate'; Bryer (1975, British) holds that in the west the Grand Komnenos was at once emperor and 'melik of Canik', the lord of small Turkmen emirates he helped create, yet that Turkish and Laz influence on society and government was 'unexpectedly superficial' and the Trapezuntines 'even more Roman than the Romaioi' (of 192 known office-holders all but two had Pontic or Roman names); Laonikos Chalkokondyles (15th century) says the rulers kept 'Hellenic manners and the Hellenic speech' and married barbarians only to protect their lands; Eastmond (2004, British) sees a Roman empire in its own right that adapted to local audiences; and Bessarion's Encomium (about 1436) makes Trebizond the image of ancient Athens, its people of pure Hellenic stock.

title: Alexios III retakes Kerasous; defeat by the Turkmen
summary: Niketas Scholares fled to Kerasous in June 1354 and on 25 March 1355 attacked the capital with one galley and eleven small boats before withdrawing. In May 1355 Alexios III sailed against Kerasous with his mother, his empress and the metropolitan, and after a battle the city submitted; Kechrina, where Niketas held out, surrendered soon after, and in October 1355 Niketas was seized and a settlement made. On 27 November 1355 an expedition against Cheriana ended in a rout: about 50 Christians died, John Kabazites, duke of Chaldia, was captured, and Panaretos escaped only because his horse was strong. Niketas, by then reconciled, died on 30 July 1361; the emperor mourned him in white.
disputed: The weekday Panaretos gives (Wednesday) does not fit 30 July 1361 (a Friday) as printed, so the day may be corrupt; the month and year stand.

title: Cheriana won and lost
summary: In August 1355 John Kabazites, duke of Chaldia, took Cheriana (Şiran) and brought Sorogaina under imperial rule. On Friday 27 November an expedition led by Alexios III against Cheriana ravaged and besieged, then broke in panic when a few Turks gave chase: about 50 Christians and many horses were lost, the duke was captured, and Panaretos, who rode with the emperor, escaped to Trebizond in three days. Cheriana, the only rural district south of the mountains that the emperors normally could not protect, was raided again in 1373, when 140 men died in the snow.

title: Theodora married to Hacı Emir of Chalybia
summary: On 29 August 1358 Alexios III sent his sister Theodora, escorted by Basil Choupakas Scholarios, to marry Hacı Emir Ibrahim, son of Bayram, the Turkmen lord of Chalybia, the hill country behind Oinaion and Kotyora, whose raiders had broken into Matzouka on 13 November 1357. Oinaion seems to have come back to the empire with the alliance, and in December 1361 the emperor paid a state visit to the emir's 'home castle'. The Hacıemiroğulları held the coast between Oinaion and Kerasous and were the empire's nearest western neighbour; a daughter of Alexios III later married Hacı Emir's son Suleyman.

title: The Matzoukans destroy Hodja Latif's raid
summary: Hodja Latif, ruler of Bayburt, against whom Alexios III had gone into Chaldia in April 1360 to build the fortress of 'the Cuckoo', crossed into Matzouka with about 400 picked men by Lacharane (Larhan yayla, Akarsu) and Chasdenicha. The Matzoukans, who had prepared the passes, killed about 200 of them, took many animals and weapons and beheaded Hodja Latif; next day the heads were paraded through Trebizond. It shows the valley bandon defending itself, and Lazaropoulos' tale of Alexios II killing a dragon on Mount Minthrion may echo such victories.

title: Soumela refounded by Alexios III; Venetian depot
summary: Alexios III restored the monastery of the Virgin at Soumela in the Matzouka valley; a chrysobull (dated 1364 or 1365) confirms its lands and tax exemptions and names its dependent peasants. In the same year the Venetians had their privileges confirmed and received a depot in the city. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 468-476) adds an inscription of AM 6868 (1360) calling Alexios III 'new founder' ('Κτίτωρ... νέος'), the gifts of John II, Alexios II and Basil (40 paroikoi, 24 estates), and Manuel III's relic of the Cross (AM 6898, 1390). The chrysobull is dated December, indiction 3, AM 6873, i.e. December 1364 (Kyriakidis 1898, whose own text says 1365).
disputed: The founding of Soumela in 386 by the Athenian monks Barnabas and Sophronios is monastic tradition. Bryer doubts the authenticity of the chrysobulls for Vazelon and Choutoura, but uses this one without reservation.

title: Joseph Lazaropoulos, metropolitan and hagiographer
summary: Joseph Lazaropoulos (as a layman John), author of the miracles of St Eugenios, had escorted the young Alexios III to Trebizond in 1349. He was elected metropolitan in 1364, was consecrated in Constantinople, returned to the city on Easter Sunday, 13 April 1365, and left the throne in November 1367 for the Eleousa monastery by the Daphnous harbour; he died before December 1369. Chrysanthos shows that the 'John' of 1166 in older lists is his lay name.

date_text: Epiphany (6 January) 1369; Golacha retaken briefly 16 April 1374
title: Golacha falls and Chaldia is laid waste
summary: On Epiphany 1369 the Turks took the fortress of Golacha in Chaldia by a ruse, and 'Chaldia was obliterated': some died fighting, others in 'the treacherous cave there'. Golacha had survived a sixteen-day siege with a siege engine by Ahi Ayna Beg of Erzincan in October 1361, and in March 1368 the emir Kilij Arslan had blockaded Trapezuntine Chaldia; the Chaldians retook it on Sunday 16 April 1374, but it soon fell again. The losses south of the mountains, against the Turks of Erzincan and Bayburt rather than the Turkmen of the coast, were the empire's main frontier problem in Alexios III's later reign.
disputed: Bryer & Winfield (1985) identify Golacha, with a reservation ('If we are also correct'), with the castle at Colosana, now Bahçelik (Torul), about 10 km west of Gümüşhane, high above the İkisu Dere on the road from Cheriana into Chaldia; they take it for Clavijo's 'Dorileh' of 1404, the seat of the Kabazites dukes, and a large cave on the Cheriana road just south of it for Panaretos' 'treacherous cave'. They attribute the siege of 1361 once to the emir of Bayburt and once to the ahi of Erzincan, and add that after 1374 the Turks retook it almost at once and it was recovered again at some date before 1404.

title: The Theoskepastos convent
summary: The convent of the Theoskepastos ('protected by God'), built into a cave on Mount Minthrion (Boztepe) east of the city, was founded or refounded by Irene, mother of Alexios III, who was painted there as founder with her son and his empress Theodora Kantakouzene; Alexios himself probably endowed it in 1376. That year his illegitimate son, the despot Andronikos, who died after a fall from the palace on 14 March 1376, was buried there, and in 1843 an abbess had Irene's portrait repainted as Andronikos. Manuel III was buried there in 1417. It remained a Greek convent until 1923.
disputed: Bryer's date of 1376, given as 'probably', seems tied to the burial of Andronikos that year; the founder was Irene, mother of Alexios III (Eastmond 2016; Chrysanthos), and Bryer & Winfield (1985) date her founding, refounding or endowment to the 1340s. They add that Alexios IV (died 1429) was buried there before his remains were moved to a tomb outside the Chrysokephalos, and that the visible paintings appear to be of the 14th century.

title: Eudokia married to Taceddin, emir of Limnia
summary: Taceddin Çelebi, the Turkmen who was taking over Limnia and the Iris delta, had asked for a Komnenian bride in June 1362 and been refused. After years of embassies Alexios III married his daughter Eudokia to him at Oinaion on 8 October 1379; 'at that time the emperor gained control over Limnia', probably as her dowry, though in fact it was lost. Other daughters went to Mutahharten, emir of Erzincan, to Osman Kara Yülük of the Aq Qoyunlu and to Suleyman of Chalybia, and one, Anna, to King Bagrat V of Georgia (1367). The princesses ringed the shrinking empire with in-laws.
disputed: The dates of the other marriages are not all recorded. Whether Limnia was a dowry ceded in 1379 or a district the emperor really recovered ('gained control', Panaretos) is debated; Bryer argues that it was already lost to Taceddin. Mutahharten's wife was a daughter of Alexios III or, less likely, of Manuel III (Bryer).

title: Alexios III's campaign against the Chepni
summary: At the end of the winter grazing season Alexios III attacked the Chepni Turkmen by land and sea. On Sunday 4 March 1380 his army split: 600 foot went in from Petroma and raided Kotzauta, while the emperor with the cavalry went up the Philabonites (Harsit) river to the Chepni winter quarters, burned their tents and freed many of 'our captured simylika' (captives or loot: the word is disputed). Over 100 Turkish men, women and children and about 42 Romans died. The Chepni stayed; the Philabonites valley became the Chepni nahiye after 1461.
disputed: Whether the army 'spurred' along the river or 'crossed' it, and what the freed 'simylika' were, captives, loot or a place, are disputed readings (Lampsides; Bryer & Winfield; Asp-Talwar). Bryer & Winfield (1985) translate 'crossed', take 'simylika' for the Sümüklü pastures, and put the Chepni winter camps on the upper Philabonites 'though not south of Torul'; they place Petroma at the castle above the Harşit near Tirebolu, and propose the valleys round Kürtün for Kotzauta and Vakfıkebir for Sthlabopiastes, where the foot were to meet the emperor.

title: Two Turkmen sons-in-law at war; Timur takes Tbilisi
summary: On 24 October 1386 Alexios III's son-in-law Taceddin of Limnia invaded Chalybia with 12,000 men against his other son-in-law, Suleyman Beg, son of Hacı Emir; Taceddin was killed and cut to pieces, about 3,000 of his men died and 7,000 horses were abandoned. A month later, on 21 November 1386, Timur sacked Tbilisi and captured King Bagrat V with his wife, Alexios' daughter Anna, and their son David. The emperor's in-laws now fought over coastal castles and lands rather than the summer pastures, while a new power appeared in the east.

title: Death of Alexios III; Panaretos' chronicle
summary: Alexios III died after a reign of forty years and was succeeded by Manuel III. His secretary Michael Panaretos (c. 1320-after 1390) wrote the short chronicle 'On the Grand Komnenoi', which covers 1204-1390 (with notes added to 1426) and is first-hand from 1340. Almost every date in this chapter's narrative comes from it.

title: Peristera (St George Peristereota) refounded
summary: From the notes of Elias Konstantinides, Chrysanthos dates the monastery of St George Peristereota: founded 752, deserted in 1203 because of raids, refounded in 1393 by Theophanes, a native of Lazike and former hegumen of Soumela, who rebuilt the cells and church. Later, through the mediation of Bessarion, then staying in Trebizond, he obtained a chrysobull of Alexios IV; it was lost in the fire of 1495.

title: George of Trebizond born in Crete to a Trapezuntine family
summary: The humanist George of Trebizond (George Trapezountios) was born at Candia in Venetian Crete on 3 April 1395; his father told him that his great-great-grandfather had emigrated to Crete 'from Trebizond, some city of Pontus'. He signed himself 'Georgius Trapezuntius Cretensis' all his life. Invited by the Venetian Francesco Barbaro, he came to Italy about April 1416, became a leading teacher of rhetoric, a translator and a papal secretary, and a fierce opponent of Plethon and, in the end, of Bessarion. His name shows how far the memory of Trebizond reached in the Greek world of the 15th century.
disputed: Monfasani (1976) dates his birth to 3 April 1395 from George's own horoscope note; older works (Gauricus, Garcaeus) give 4 April 1395 or 1396, and Bryer 1396. He came to Italy about April 1416 (Monfasani; two other dates in George's own notes are less likely).

title: Bessarion born at Trebizond
summary: Bessarion, baptised Basil, was born at Trebizond to parents of modest means, Theodore and Theodula; his mother had fifteen children, of whom only he lived to adulthood. Entrusted as a boy to Metropolitan Dositheos, who adopted him, he went with him to Constantinople at about thirteen, became a monk in 1423, studied with Plethon at Mistra, was made metropolitan of Nicaea (1437) and, after the Council of Florence, a cardinal of the Roman Church. His lifelong friend George Amiroutzes was born at Trebizond about the same time. Bessarion never forgot his city: he wrote its encomium (H4-056), had Dositheos prayed for to the end of his life, and after 1461 was asked by Amiroutzes to help ransom his son (H5-001).
disputed: His birth is dated 2 January 1403 (Vast; Chrysanthos; Kennedy 2018; Malone-Lee 2023; from his death notice and Capranica's oration), 2 January 1408 (Monfasani 1986; Cattaneo 2020, 'more probably', because Traversari calls him tricenarius in 1438), 1401 (Joannou 1947, from the canonical ages for his ordinations in 1426 and 1431) or 1399. His baptismal name was Basil (Barbazza; Malone-Lee; Cattaneo) or John (an autograph receipt; Chrysanthos); Mioni and Bianca take 'John' for a scribal error. His family was humble (Apostolis), or a branch of the imperial house (Braccini 2006, after a 17th-century source, 'to be treated with reserve', Malone-Lee).

title: Clavijo's embassy passes through Trebizond
summary: Ruy Gonzalez de Clavijo, ambassador of Henry III of Castile to Timur, left Constantinople on 20 March 1404, landed at Trebizond on 11 April and went on over the mountains to Erzincan, Erzurum, Tabriz and Samarkand, which he reached on 4 September 1404. title: Alexios IV and the Turkmen marriages of the 15th century
summary: Alexios IV, co-emperor since 1395, succeeded on 5 March 1417. One daughter married Jihan Shah of the Qara Qoyunlu, and his daughter Maria became the third wife of John VIII Palaiologos in Constantinople (1427), a match negotiated by an embassy from Constantinople in which the young Bessarion took part (1425-1427). A marriage of another daughter to Ali Beg of the Aq Qoyunlu is often repeated but doubtful. Marriage was now the empire's main defence.

title: The tower of Hagia Sophia and its frescoes
summary: A tall free-standing tower was built west of Hagia Sophia in the last decades of the empire, probably as a belfry or lighthouse; Millet read the date AM 6935 (1426/7) on its east face, and portraits of Alexios IV and John IV were painted on that face, towards the church. Its upper chapel was painted in 1443-1444, with a dated inscription of 1443 and commemorative portraits of two turbaned officials dated 1 January, seventh indiction (1444): the last great work of art of the empire, from a time of stability and of Armenian traders passing through the city.
disputed: The tower is dated 1426/7 from Millet's reading of its inscription (followed by Mercier 1994 and Eastmond 2016), or between 1429 and 1444, the limits set by the other inscriptions (Rapti 2016). It was probably a belfry or a lighthouse; the idea that it housed the observatory of a Trapezuntine 'academy' (Papadopoulos) is rejected.

title: Bessarion's Encomium of Trebizond
summary: Bessarion, born at Trebizond (see C2b-10) and later a cardinal, wrote a long encomium of his home city, describing its walls, palace, harbours, trade, churches and the surrounding valleys. It is rhetoric, but it is also the fullest picture of the city before its fall. Chrysanthos (1933), after Vast, dates Bessarion's birth to 2 January 1403 and has him baptised John, taken to Constantinople by Metropolitan Dositheos in 1415/16, made a monk in 1423, taught by Plethon at Mistra, and sent by John VIII to Trebizond to negotiate his marriage with Maria Komnene.

summary: The Castilian traveller Pero Tafur came to Trebizond from Constantinople and met John IV; he repeated the story that John had killed his father. His account adds colour on the court and the city's dealings with the Turks.

title: Trapezuntines at the Council of Ferrara-Florence
summary: At the council that tried to unite the Churches, Bessarion (by then metropolitan of Nicaea) led the unionists; Dorotheos, metropolitan of Trebizond, and George Amiroutzes, John IV's envoy, also took part. George of Trebizond, born at Candia in Crete in 1395 to a family whose ancestor had come from Trebizond (see C2b-11), was by then among the leading Greek scholars in Italy. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 174, 212-216), after Syropoulos, has Metropolitan Dorotheos 'holding the place of Caesarea', first among the metropolitans, and makes him an opponent of the union who refused the patriarchate ('οὔτε καλή μοι φαίνεται ἡ ἕνωσις αὕτη').
disputed: Dorotheos is an opponent of the union in Chrysanthos (after Syropoulos), but some lists count him among the signers. Amiroutzes is an ally of Bessarion and the unionists in Malone-Lee (2023), a supporter of their opponents in Cattaneo (2020).

title: Sheikh Cüneyd of Ardabil attacks Trebizond
summary: In the 1450s Sheikh Cüneyd (Junayd) of Ardabil, head of the Safavid order, attacked Trebizond. John IV found his capital almost empty: by Chalkokondyles' account some 4,000 citizens had 'simply melted away' into the valleys, leaving about fifty men, whom he called 'women, cowards and traitors'. Cüneyd's son Haydar later married Martha, daughter of Uzun Hasan and Theodora of Trebizond; their son Ismail founded Safavid Iran (H4-061).

title: Constantinople falls; Trebizond the last Roman throne
summary: Mehmed II took Constantinople. Trebizond, with the despots of the Morea, was now the last Greek state of the Roman tradition, and John IV began to pay tribute to the Ottomans.

title: Ottoman raid and tribute
summary: Hizir Pasha, the Ottoman governor of Amasya, raided the countryside of Trebizond in 1456 and carried off about 2,000 people; John IV submitted and agreed to pay 2,000 gold pieces a year. In 1458 the tribute was raised to 3,000. These figures are Chalkokondyles'.

title: Theodora (Despina Khatun) marries Uzun Hasan
summary: John IV betrothed his daughter Theodora to Uzun Hasan, ruler of the Aq Qoyunlu, in 1457 and married her to him in 1458, perhaps at Diyarbakir, with David (her uncle; Bryer writes 'brother') as her escort. The terms are known: a dowry of crown and monastic land in the villages of Halanik and Sesera in the banda of Matzouka and Sourmaina (not 'Cappadocia', as was claimed to Mehmed II); Uzun Hasan's undertaking to protect Trebizond, which he did not keep in 1461; and her right to remain Orthodox with her own chaplain and household. Known as Despina Khatun, she held court at Harput, was buried in the church of St George at Diyarbakir, and through her daughter Martha became the grandmother of Shah Ismail I, founder of Safavid Iran; two of her daughters still spoke Trebizond Greek in Damascus in 1512.
disputed: Dated 1458, with the betrothal in 1457 (Bryer; Babinger 1978); other accounts range from 1456 to 1460.

title: John IV dies; David seizes the throne
summary: John IV died in April 1460, before 22 April (Ganchou 2000), and his brother David pushed aside the young heir Alexios V with the backing of the archons. David sent envoys west for a crusade; the friar Ludovico da Bologna toured European courts in 1460-1461 with envoys claiming to speak for Trebizond, Georgia and Persia. Ludovico had left the Caucasus about January 1460 with two Georgian envoys; in Florence on 15 December 1460 the merchant Michael Alighieri, a descendant of Dante acting for David, signed a treaty granting Florence a consulate, warehouse and the Genoese and Venetian trading terms in Trebizond.
disputed: John IV's death is dated 1458, 1459 or 1460 in different works. Ganchou (2000) fixes it in April 1460, before 22 April, from a Genoese memorandum of 19 April with a postscript of 5 May reporting his death; the year 1459 in a letter of Ludovico da Bologna is a copying error. Bryer suspects that a letter in David's name dated 22 April 1459 was composed by Alighieri himself.

title: Mehmed II's land campaign to Trebizond
summary: Mehmed II crossed to Bursa, gathered the armies of Europe and Asia and marched by Ankara and Sivas, taking Koyulhisar from the Aq Qoyunlu. Near Erzincan he met Uzun Hasan's mother Sara Khatun and made peace with Uzun Hasan, but refused to include Trebizond in it; the army then crossed the Pontic Alps in hard summer rain. The size of the army is unknown: the '80,000 foot and 60,000 horse' often quoted is a modern figure (Freely 2009, p. 67), not a chronicle one.

They call this a proposal from Tursun Beg's eyewitness account and the terrain. They give the fleet 100 to 300 ships with cannon, and doubt that the armies had 'the 140,000 cavalry and infantry claimed for them'.

title: Trebizond surrenders to Mehmed II
summary: David Komnenos surrendered the city on terms: his family, household and wealth were to be spared and he was to receive estates in Thrace. Mehmed entered Trebizond, and the Empire of Trebizond, the last state of the Roman emperors' tradition, came to an end after 257 years. The city became the seat of an Ottoman sanjak under Kasim Pasha, with a garrison of 400 janissaries in the citadel (Kritoboulos IV.50). Kritoboulos says Mehmed entered and toured the city and citadel, shipped David with his family and the leading men to Constantinople by sea, and himself went home by land 'after spending not many days there'.
disputed: No document gives the day. 15 August 1461, the Dormition, is 'the date... of local tradition' (Bryer 1980), used by most modern writers; Bryer & Winfield (1985) give it without reservation, and Mehmed's dated movements (at Niksar from 28 August) fit a fall in mid-August. The documents set only limits: the Venetian Niccolò Sagundino, an eyewitness of the fall, wrote to the Senate from Asia Minor on 21 September 1461 (Lambros 1905, cited by Bryer and Chrysanthos), and the news was in Venice before 20 October and in Rome by 26 October (Bryer, after Pastor). Chrysanthos gives the range 'between 2 March and 21 September 1461'. A colophon in a Petrarch manuscript at Harvard reports the fleet, about 150 ships, home by October (Bryer & Winfield). Fallmerayer's summer 1462 was refuted by Miller from a Venetian document of 26 October 1461. A Turkish tradition, following Parmaksızoğlu, dated the conquest to 21 Muharram 866, 26 October 1461, and Trabzon celebrated it on that day from 1960; in 2017 the city moved the celebration to 15 August (BirGün, 26 October 2017). Sagundino's letter excludes the October date.

title: David Komnenos and his sons executed
summary: David was settled with estates in Thrace, but in 1463 letters from his niece Theodora (Despina Khatun) asking that a son or nephew be sent to her at Uzun Hasan's court reached the sultan, it is said through George Amiroutzes. title: Mehmed II dismantles the Empire of Trebizond
summary: After the surrender, Mehmed II shipped David Komnenos, his court and leading families to Constantinople, put a Janissary garrison of 400 in the citadel and named Kasım Pasha governor. Kritoboulos says 1,500 children of both sexes were taken as the sultan's slaves; the continuator of Chalkokondyles says the townspeople were split into three groups (resettled in Constantinople, enslaved, or expelled to the countryside) and 800 boys were taken for the Janissaries. Bryer found signs that rural groups resisted for up to ten years. The deportations explain why the first Ottoman registers show a small city. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 516-519) follows the continuator of Chalkokondyles and Doukas: the three-way division, 800 boys for the janissaries, and the remaining third settled outside the walls in the parishes of St Sophia and St Philip. Lowry, reading the first register (ca. 1486), argues against the picture, from Fallmerayer and Finlay, of a city emptied of Greeks and closed to Christians: in ca. 1486 Greek households still lived inside the walls (the Meso Kastro quarter), and the early Muslims were mostly deportees from central Anatolia, 202 households from nineteen towns (Niksar, Amasya, Tokat, Samsun, Bafra and others), 78.3% of the permanent Muslim population.
disputed: The numbers are chroniclers' and differ: Kritoboulos, who wrote for Mehmed and plays the violence down, has 1,500 children taken and only the leading men deported; the continuator of Chalkokondyles a third of the population deported and 800 boys taken. Neither is a count. Lowry's registers show the city still mostly Christian about 1486, so the deportation took the elite rather than the whole population.

title: Matsouka's Christian sipahis and the monasteries' privileges
summary: In Matsouka (Maçka), the valley of Soumela, Vazelon and Peristera, the Ottomans kept Christian timar-holders (sipahis) from the old Trapezuntine landholders for decades. They also confirmed monastic property by firman. The three monasteries held land and villages and kept them through the Ottoman centuries. They later ranked as patriarchal exarchates; an archbishopric of Rhodopolis replaced them in 1863-1867 (H5-038), and they lasted until the metropolis of Rhodopolis was created in October 1902 (C3-030).

date_text: From the conquest to the end of the community
title: Two bishoprics and an ethnarchy: the Church after 1461
summary: Chrysanthos writes that after 1461 'ἐσβέσθησαν αἱ πρότερον ἀκμάζουσαι 11 ἐπισκοπαί' (the eleven formerly flourishing bishoprics died out), and that only two were formed from their remnants: Of, and Kanis (Chaldia and Cheriana). The metropolitan was recognised as millet başı, with autonomous church courts and a prison, 'κράτος ἐν κράτει' (a state within the state). Muslims and Armenians often took disputes with Orthodox to the metropolis, and during the Russian occupation of 1916–18 Muslims took even disputes among themselves there. Villages were run by an elected muhtar and azades; the community of Trebizond had nine parishes, a demogerontia and later an elected assembly.
disputed: 'A state within the state' describes the late Ottoman millet; the use of the metropolis' court by Muslims in 1916–18 rests on Chrysanthos' word.

title: Metropolitan Pankratios removed by order of Mehmed II
summary: Pankratios, ordained in 1472 by Patriarch Symeon I (himself a Trapezuntine), was in the same year 'ἐξηλάθη ἀπὸ τοῦ θρόνου' (driven from his throne) 'διὰ θέλησιν καὶ βούλησιν αὐθεντικήν' (by the sovereign's will and pleasure) and made to resign in writing. A sultanic order demanded a quick successor, and Dorotheos of Athens was transferred with the title 'ἔξαρχος πάσης Λαζικῆς' (exarch of all Lazike). Chrysanthos links the expulsion 'πιθανῶς' (probably) to Uzun Hasan's campaign of 1472 to restore Trebizond, which David's nephew Alexios joined. He dates to 1472–73 the folk traditions of castles holding out in the hills (the Helios castle at the sources of the Sera, 'τῆς Ὡριᾶς τὸ κάστρον', Petroma, the Palaiokastron of Palaiomatsouka), to which Trapezuntines had fled from the city. Chrysanthos also says that after 1461 the seat had moved to the church of St Philip, that two bishoprics (Ophis; Kanis, i.e. Chaldia and Cheriana) remained, and that Pankratios, who had succeeded 'probably the metropolitan Dorotheos', was followed in the same year by Dorotheos II from Athens.
disputed: The link with Uzun Hasan's 1472 campaign, and the dating of the castle traditions to 1472–73 rather than 1461, are Chrysanthos' inferences.

title: Prince Selim governor of Trabzon
summary: Bayezid II sent his son Selim to govern the sancak of Trabzon, a frontier province facing the Georgians and, after 1501, the Safavids. From Trabzon Selim built a reputation as a fighting prince. That reputation carried him to the throne in 1512 as Selim I.

title: Süleyman born at Trabzon

title: Selim's wars from Trabzon against the Safavids and Georgia
summary: In 1505 Selim drove a Safavid raid under Ebrahim Mirza back from Trabzon to Erzincan. In 1507 he attacked Safavid-held Erzincan and Bayburt. In 1508 he invaded western Georgia (May–June 1508 in Kemalpaşazade; the Georgian tradition gives 1509, 1510 or 1512); a figure of more than 10,000 captives appears in modern accounts but has not been traced to a source. In 1510 he beat another Safavid force sent against Trabzon. These campaigns tied the Pontic hinterland (Chaldia, Bayburt) firmly to the Ottomans.
disputed: The figure of over 10,000 captives comes from a single modern summary.

title: Monastic privileges and the exarchates of Soumela, Vazelon and Peristereota
summary: Chrysanthos writes that sultans and Moldo-Wallachian princes endowed Soumela by firmans and chrysobulls, and patriarchs by sigillia, and that by monastic tradition Selim I confirmed by hatt-ı şerif the privileges granted by the emperors of Trebizond. The three monasteries were allowed 'τὴν ἄμεσον ἐκκλησιαστικὴν ἐπίβλεψιν' (direct church supervision) of the 'eleftheric' villages around them. He dates the firm shape of this system to 'the last two centuries', through patriarchal sigillia, and rejects its derivation from the imperial chrysobulls, which in his view granted only the emperors' own villages and paroikoi (whose remnants are the mortitai and imiseiastai on monastery land). In 1564 the metropolitan still acted as bishop of the villages around Vazelon; on 8 November 1707 Metropolitan Paisios ceded to Vazelon the Matsouka villages Chortokopin, Chavas and Spelia 'καὶ ὅσα ρωμόχωρα εἶναι ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ ἄνω' (and all Rum villages from there upwards).
disputed: Selim I's confirmation rests on monastic tradition. Chrysanthos' late dating of the exarchates is set against the view that they descend from imperial grants.

summary: Chrysanthos writes that local lords ('Τερὲ-βέηδες'), especially in the 17th century, held Gonia near Batum, Rize, Of, Sourmena, Matsouka, Platana, Koralla (Görele), Tripolis and Kerasous. The city of Trebizond was split into three timars of three derebeys, with night watches and loopholes in the dividing walls. In civil strife between the janissaries of the Orta-hisar and the gunners of the Kule, the old palace on the acropolis burned and the Theoskepastos convent was used as a fort.

Bryer doubted that the see ever really functioned and called it a 'phantom bishopric'. The lack of a local church structure may have made conversion easier.

title: Evliya Çelebi at the Gümüşhane mines
summary: Evliya Çelebi counted 70 mines, working and idle, at Gümüşhane and said the inhabitants were exempt from all taxes. The miners and the villages that supplied them held privileges: exemption from extraordinary levies and freedom from the interference of local governors. These privileges drew Greek miners to Chaldia and later shaped the crypto-Christian question.

Bryer 1983 (p. 32) has the mines first recorded as an Ottoman mint in the 16th century and revived on a large scale only in the second half of the 17th, by Greek concessionaires (archimetallourgoi), whose miners and charcoal-burners were excused harac in return for mining or charcoal service; he makes that status the origin of most Pontic crypto-Christians (pp. 32-33).

title: The main wave of conversion in Of and Tonya
summary: Most historians place the decisive Islamization of the Of valley and of Tonya in the second half of the 17th century. That was a time of banditry, tax abuse and the rise of local ağas and derebeys. Local tradition blames a Bishop Alexandros of Of, who is said to have converted as Iskender after a quarrel with the metropolitan of Trebizond. Other stories tell of three Greek-speaking dervishes from Maraş, and of the priest Pavlos of Okena, forced to convert after his children were killed. Christians who refused are said to have fled over the hills to Sourmena. By the 18th century the valley was a centre of Sunni learning, with many medreses and hocas. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 530, 688-689, 707-710) places the mass conversion of Rize, Of, Sourmena and Gimora under Mehmed IV and the Köprülü viziers, with the mixed Greek and Armenian population of Hemşin and, about the same time, Tonya; he gives the Bishop Alexandros/Iskender tradition and says the converts of Sourmena and Gimora lost their Greek, while the Ophites and the people of Tonya kept it. His view that the Muslims of the diocese descend almost entirely from converts is his own opinion; Lowry's registers contradict it, showing Muslims settled in the city by the state.
disputed: The timing and the mechanism are debated. Greek tradition speaks of a forced, sudden mass conversion under the derebeys; Bryer & Winfield see no single mass conversion, only a gradual overtaking of the Christians by the Muslims; Meeker sees Christians withdrawing upstream while a Muslim elite tied to the Ottoman state and its learned men grew; Parcharides (1879) puts the beginnings earlier than the late 17th century; Mackridge shows that the Greek of Of keeps archaic features, so that its speakers descend from local Greek-speakers, not newcomers. Chrysanthos says that the converts of Sourmena and Gimora lost their Greek. Ioannidis (1870) tells of a council of notables and clergy who chose Islam under pressure from earlier converts and the Laz, part of the people emigrating to the Crimea and Moldavia; he dates Bishop Alexander's apostasy to 1685. Bryer finds no bishopric of Of and no Iskender Pasha recorded, and says that the origins of the people of Of 'need further investigation'. Agtzidis (2005) repeats the story of the missionaries from Maraş without a source, and Çilingir gives an undocumented decree of 'religion or language'.

title: Dositheos of Jerusalem describes a Pontus nearly empty of Christians

title: Sevastos Kyminitis heads the Phrontisterion of Trapezous (1683-1689)
summary: Sevastos Kyminitis, born at Kymina (Kotsi, Hotz) near Trebizond, taught at the Patriarchal School in Constantinople from 1671 and headed Manolakis Manos' school in the Phanar from 1676 until 1682, when a students' revolt made him resign. Invited home by the Trapezuntines (he turned down a call to Moscow), and partly to counter Catholic monks who had begun teaching young Trapezuntines free of charge about 1682, he took over the direction of the Phrontisterion in 1683 and was its scholarch until 1689; a letter addressed to him at Trebizond in February 1683 shows he had arrived by then. Chrysanthos stresses that teaching had gone on there before 1683: Kyminitis organised and systematised the school rather than founding it. Merchant families such as the Velissarides and Kallivazis are said to have supported it (Salvanou). He went to Bucharest about 1689/90, headed the Princely Academy under Constantin Brâncoveanu, and died there on 6 September 1702. The school ran until November 1921 and trained the region's teachers and clergy.
disputed: Both 1682 and 1683 are right, for different things: in 1682 he resigned in Constantinople and came home, and in 1683, the year Chrysanthos gives, he took over the school; a letter of February 1683 already finds him at Trebizond. 'Founded in 1682' (Bryer, after Kyriakides and Oikonomides; Agtzidis; Salvanou) runs the two together and makes him the founder of a school that Chrysanthos and Ioannidis (who says it was called the Phrontisterion 'from time immemorial') say existed before him. Some accounts have the school first sit at Soumela; Kyriakidis (1898) says that its first house was the monastery's metochion in the city, and Bryer that it was long run by the monastery of Peristereota.

date_text: Annexed in 1698 at Nektarios' request; fully united by a sigillion of July 1774
title: Kerasous exarchate annexed to the metropolis of Trebizond
summary: Chrysanthos writes that the exarchate of Kerasous, once a bishopric of Neocaesarea, raised to a metropolis in the second half of the 11th century and reduced to an exarchate in the mid-17th, was annexed to Trebizond in 1698 at Metropolitan Nektarios' request, in return for an annual payment. A sigillion of Patriarch Samuel Hantzeris of July 1774 united Kerasous, Tripolis and Koralla fully with Trebizond.

date_text: Nektarios at Argyroupolis 1706; Paisios' quarrel 1709–1717; settlement of 21 June 1767
title: The mines and the miners' clergy: disputes between Trebizond and Chaldia
summary: In 1706 Nektarios visited Argyroupolis 'ἐπὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς τῶν μεταλλείων' (at the height of the mines) to collect alms. Paisios quarrelled with Archbishop Philotheos of Chaldia, who relied on 'τοὺς προκρίτους ἀρχιμεταλλουργοὺς τῆς Ἀργυροπόλεως' (the leading mine-masters of Argyroupolis); in 1711 Paisios collected alms from the rich miners, and on 1 July 1717 he came with a royal order, exiled Philotheos and ran Chaldia until a successor was elected. On 21 June 1767, before Patriarch Samuel Hantzeris, Trebizond and Chaldia settled their dispute over Kerasous, Tripolis and Koralla 'μετὰ τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς μαδενίων' (with their mines): Trebizond kept the parish rights in the mines and the appointment of their priests, while Chaldia could collect dues from its own diocesans working there. Chrysanthos calls the arrangement uncanonical, imposed by the Chaldian mine-masters, 'powerful at the Porte'.
disputed: Bryer 1983 (p. 33 n. 43) adds that the archbishops of Chaldia, often of the Phytianos family which also supplied the archimetallourgoi of Argyroupolis, extended their exarchate to 'All Metal-Bearing Lands', including the alum mines around Tzanchraki, and that Chaldia claimed a 'corridor' to the sea at Bulancak just before the First World War.

title: Of villages deported to 'Anakra' in Georgia

title: The Porte tells officials to stop oppressing the Gümüşhane miners

title: Santa's tradition of a conversion to save a pasture

The usual figure, 800 households, goes back to a Greek church article of 1910. They founded the oldest Pontic communities of the southern Caucasus, and the Fytiana metropolitans later held Akhtala as a Georgian see. In the same year the Ottomans themselves called for miners from Gümüşhane for Ergani and Keban.

title: Kerasous taken and its derebey drowned
summary: From a note in a manuscript nomokanon of the Kerasous community, Chrysanthos records that on 6 August 1764 Kerasous 'ἠχμαλωτίσθη … ὑπὸ τοῦ Χατζίπεγιν' (was taken by Hacı Bey) after a war of 74 days ('ἡμέρας οδ´'); its derebey Tistaroglou was drowned and the town and its church were ravaged.

title: The Caniklizade derebeys of Samsun
summary: The Caniklizade family ruled Canik (Samsun) as quasi-independent ayan. Its leaders were Hacı Ali Pasha (born 1720/21, died 1785 at Erzurum), Battal Hüseyin Pasha, defeated and taken prisoner by the Russians near Anapa in 1790, and Tayyar Mahmud Pasha, executed in 1808 under Mahmud II. In the eastern Pontus, where Bryer counts fourteen derebey families, each largely confined to one valley, the Tuzcuoğulları of Rize and Of played the same game; the Hazinedarzade, originally from Adjara, held the pashalik of Trebizond (with one break) from 1811 to 1844 and put down the derebeys in 1812–1840. Their feuds made the countryside insecure and pushed highland Christians to seek protection, convert or move.
disputed: The dates come from a Turkish reference work and from Bryer.

summary: Russia annexed Kartli-Kakheti, bringing the Akhtala Greeks under the tsar and opening a Russian door for later Pontic emigrants. The same year an Ottoman document lists Koronixa and others among the idle mines of Gümüşhane.

title: Derebey coalition holds the coast; Koralla razed
summary: Chrysanthos writes that in 1811, while the vali Hazinedarzade Süleyman Pasha was away at Poti, the derebeys of Gonia, Rize, Of and Sourmena joined those of Trebizond, Koralla, Tripolis and Kerasous and held the whole coast. The pasha returned by sea and razed Koralla, destroying its Greek community. Famine and plague followed in 1811–12, and many fled Trebizond for Vazelon.

title: Tuzcuoğlu Memiş Ağa's rising
summary: Memiş Ağa of the Tuzcuoğulları, bey of Gönye and warden of Batum, was condemned at the request of the governor of Trabzon, Hazinedarzade Süleyman Pasha, and rose in revolt. In summer 1816 his men held the coast from Hopa to Giresun, and on 18 August 1816 they took the port and then the fortress of Trabzon; Tirebolu, Tonya and the road to Gümüşhane followed. Government forces of about 30,000 pushed back. Of was besieged from May 1817, and Memiş was captured and executed on 26 October 1817.

title: Savvas Triantafyllidis heads the Phrontisterion
summary: Under Savvas Triantafyllidis, director from 1817, the Phrontisterion raised its standards. After 1839, and especially after 1856, teachers trained in Athens were allowed to teach there, among them Periklis Triantafyllidis, who taught philosophy and recorded the Pontic dialect.

He treats the protection given by the Satiroglou derebeys as a timariot's protection of his serfs.

date_text: 1826–1844; act of the administrators dated 1 December 1830
title: The community's 'political fund' of Trebizond
summary: Chrysanthos describes the 'πολιτικὴ κάσσα' (political fund) of the Trebizond community, founded in 1826 as a graded tax on members under threat of excommunication. It was run by the political elder, secretaries, cashiers and key-holders (act of 1 December 1830), lasted until 1844, and its surplus went to build the Phrontisterion.

date_text: 1828-1830 (Erzurum taken 27 June 1829 Old Style; Treaty of Adrianople 14 September 1829; withdrawal 1830)
title: Paskevich takes Erzurum; Christians of the Erzurum region leave with the Russians
summary: In the war of 1828-29 Paskevich's army took Kars (1828), then Erzurum, and fought at Bayburt on the edge of Chaldia. When it withdrew in 1830 after the Treaty of Adrianople, Greeks of the Erzurum region who had sided with the Russians, or feared reprisals, left with it. Hassiotis puts the number at 42,000, under the label 'Eastern Anatolia (Erzerum)'; the Gümüşhane district was probably part of that movement but is not named in the table. They were settled in Tsalka and Trialeti, emptied districts of southern Georgia, where many of their descendants were Turkish-speaking 'Urum'. Bryer dates the failure of the Gümüşhane mines to these same years.
disputed: Hassiotis' 42,000 covers 'Eastern Anatolia (Erzerum)', not the Pontus or Gümüşhane as such, and mixes Greek-speakers and Turkish-speaking Orthodox; some summaries give only '20% of the Greek population of the eastern Pontus'. Bryer (1983) says that the Russians briefly occupied Argyroupolis (Gümüşhane) in 1829 and that Christian families left with Paskevich's army to found Pontic villages in the Caucasus; since then, he writes, 'some thousands (some estimate 90.000)' Kromlides had gone to the Russian Caucasus, without saying who made the estimate.
sources_primary: Russian military reports; Treaty of Adrianople, art. 13 (right to emigrate)

title: The Trebizond-Erzurum-Tabriz transit trade
summary: After the Treaty of Adrianople (1829), and the Anglo-Persian trade agreement of 1842, the Trebizond–Erzurum–Tabriz route reopened to Western trade: British manufactures for Persia came by steamer to Trebizond and went on by caravan to Tabriz, and Persian goods came back the same way. James Brant became the first British vice-consul at Trebizond in 1830, the Foreign Office aiming at 'the making of Trebizond a depot for the Persian trade'; steamships appeared on the south Black Sea coast from 1836, and Trebizond came to have regular lines to Feodosiya, Trieste and Southampton and up to a dozen consuls. The peak came in 1860, and by 1869 Trebizond carried about 40% of Persia's trade (Bryer). From 1869 the Suez Canal offered another route, and by 1872 Poti, with favourable Russian tariffs, had taken more than half of Trebizond's declining trade, though there were revivals, especially after 1883. A handful of Greek families with foreign connections became very rich, but the trade itself stayed largely in European hands (Bryer).
disputed: The consulate (Brant, from 1830) and the first steamers on the southern coast (1836) are attested; which line first served Trebizond is not known.
sources_primary: British consular trade reports, Trebizond (Parliamentary Papers)

title: Eyüpoğlu timariots expelled from Matsouka
summary: Chrysanthos writes that from 1831 to 1836 the churches of Trebizond and Chaldia, the three monasteries and the rayah of Matsouka fought together against the Eyüpoğlu Muslim timariots and finally, through the Patriarchate, had them expelled from Matsouka (letter of 4 January 1836).
sources_primary: Patriarchal letter of 4 January 1836, as cited by Chrysanthos
sources_modern: Chrysanthos 1933, Η Εκκλησία Τραπεζούντος (Αρχείον Πόντου 4–5), p.618

title: The last Tuzcuoğlu rising and the end of the Pontic derebeys
summary: Abdülkadir and Tahir Tuzcuoğlu rose again, seizing Gönye in September 1832 and raising about 10,000 men. Governor Hazinedarzade Osman Pasha sent 8,000 men by land and 6,000 by sea, and in spring 1834 he besieged Of with 15,000. Abdülkadir was executed at Erzurum; his brothers were exiled to Ruse and Varna in December 1834. Osman Pasha governed Trabzon until his death in 1841-42, the last great figure of the derebey era, as Mahmud II's state took direct control.
disputed: Osman Pasha's governorship is dated from 1827 or from 13 July 1831 to his death in 1841 or 1842.
sources_primary: Ottoman archival orders; Cevdet Pasha, Tarih
sources_modern: Bryer 1969 | BlackSea port-cities project, 'Hazinedarzade'

title: The Gülhane edict opens the Tanzimat
summary: The Hatt-ı Şerif of Gülhane promised all subjects security of life, honour and property, regular taxation and conscription. For the Pontic Greeks it opened the way to public churches, schools and confraternities. A penal code of 1843 declared Muslims and non-Muslims equal.
sources_primary: Hatt-ı Şerif of Gülhane
sources_modern: Zürcher 2004 | Kuş 2018 (Belleten 82/294)

title: Church of Christ and community school demolished at Easter; new Phrontisterion built
summary: Chrysanthos writes that on Easter Day 1843 a Turkish crowd demolished the church of Christ in Trebizond and on Easter Monday the newly built community school, which 'ἐξελήφθη ὡς φρούριον' (was taken for a fortress) because it was higher than the firman allowed. Metropolitan Konstantios built the Phrontisterion anew on a conspicuous site by the shore; it was finished in 1845 and he paid most of its cost himself.
sources_modern: Chrysanthos 1933, Η Εκκλησία Τραπεζούντος (Αρχείον Πόντου 4–5), p.622; pp.715–716

title: Execution for apostasy abandoned
summary: Under pressure from the British ambassador Stratford Canning, the Porte undertook to stop executing converts from Islam who returned to Christianity. It was the precondition for crypto-Christians to declare themselves without risking death.
disputed: Bryer (1983) says that a return to Christianity was punished with death 'until the Tanzimat of 1839', and names no such martyrs after 1839 (the last he names are Athanasios of Smyrna, 1819, and George of Ioannina, 1838); Canning's circular with the Porte's formal undertaking was acknowledged at the consulate at Trebizond on 13 April 1844.

Stevens, Acting Consul at Trebizond, 13 April 1844, acknowledging Stratford Canning's circular 'of the 26th Ultimo' on the Porte's engagement; PRO FO 195/225, no. 27)

title: The Crimean War on the Caucasus front
summary: The war brought fighting to the Batum-Kars front and Russian naval threats to the Pontic coast; Kars fell to the Russians in November 1855. The Kromni mines worked until 1854-55 and then failed for good. With them went the miners' privileges, which left the Kromlides facing conscription and taxes: the background to their declaration of 1857.
disputed: Bryer (1983) dates the end differently: the silver mines of Argyroupolis were 'in their last gasp' by 1829 and closed soon after, by stages; the miners 'certainly became crypto-Christians about 1829', and those of 1857 inherited that status 'a generation or more after the mines had failed'. Tzedopoulos has the Kromni mines working until 1854–55; the two may speak of different mines, and the link from the failure of the mines to the declaration of 1857 is Tzedopoulos', not Bryer's.
sources_primary: British and Russian military accounts
sources_modern: Tzedopoulos 2009, p. 173 n. 31 | Bryer 1983, Δελτίο ΚΜΣ 4, pp. 32-33

title: Pontic emigration to the Russian Caucasus after the Crimean War
summary: Hassiotis counts about 53,000 Pontic Greeks leaving for the Caucasus between 1856 and 1882. They went by sea to Sukhum, Batum (after 1878), Novorossiysk and the Kuban, and overland to Georgia. Russian consuls encouraged them, and the Russian consulate promised help to Santa. Crypto-Christian and highland villages of Chaldia sent many.
disputed: The figure is a compiled estimate, and the numbers by destination are not given. A British consular despatch of 10 November 1857 reports that some 600 Greek families of Santa, mostly stonemasons and builders, were about to leave for Poti, where the Russian consul had promised work on the new harbour and land; their grievance was the seizure of their pasture by Muslim neighbours (Bryer 1983). Bryer warns that the Kromlides' list of 1857 counts only 615 houses at Santa, so the 600 'should be treated with caution'; he lists further consular reports: about 200 Russian passports in two or three months of 1858, 200 families tempted to the Crimea in 1861, and 50–200 families leaving Gümüşhane in 1864.
sources_primary: Russian resettlement records; consular reports
