title: The Islahat Fermanı (Hatt-ı Hümayun)
summary: The reform edict, issued just before the Treaty of Paris, confirmed equality and freedom of worship and allowed churches and schools to be built and repaired. A military-exemption tax (bedel-i askeri) for non-Muslims replaced the cizye. To the crypto-Christians of Chaldia it seemed to promise that they could declare their faith openly.
sources_primary: Islahat Fermanı, 18 February 1856
sources_modern: Tzedopoulos 2009, p. 172 n. 26, p. 178 | Kuş 2018 | Bryer 1983, Δελτίο ΚΜΣ 4, p. 15 (18 February 1856, ahead of the Treaty of Paris of 30 March) and p. 56 n. 78

title: The first Kromniot declares himself Orthodox
summary: Petros Sideropoulos, a crypto-Christian of Kromni, publicly declared himself Orthodox at Trebizond, the first such declaration after the edict. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 716-717, after Ioannidis 1870, p. 144) gives the same date and calls him Petros Sava Sideropoulos of Kromni, a kavass of the Italian consulate known as Pehlil, who declared himself before the vali Hayreddin Pasha and the council, confessed three times, and was left free.
sources_primary: Greek community records as reported by Andreades

title: The Ottoman reaction: the 'tenassur' category, conscription and harassment
summary: The Porte refused to treat the declarers simply as Christians. In the registers they were 'tenassur' (those who had become Christian), held liable for military service as former Muslims and also asked for Christian taxes. There were arrests and pressure in the villages: on 16/28 March 1859 about a hundred Kromlides, young and old, were jailed on the pretext of conscription and eleven were shipped to Constantinople; at a village near Gümüşhane men were jailed over Easter 1859, made to pay 2,000 piastres and then bastinadoed; a Kromli of Kerasous holding a Russian certificate was reportedly beaten and tortured in prison (British consular despatches, the Kromlides' petition to the consuls and the Russian consul's protest, printed by Bryer 1983, Documents 7-8a, pp. 52-58). Palgrave reported in 1867 that Constantinople, with the European ambassadors' agreement, had ruled that the Kromlides should serve but be exempt from the Imdadeeyah, the Christians' 20-piastre exemption tax; since each man had signed the village registers under a double name, Christian and Muslim, some were made to do both (Document 9, pp. 63, 65-66). The conscription law of 1871, which made service a Muslim duty, clashed with the tenassur status. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 666, 670-671, 719-720) says the government treated them as 'Muslim apostates, Turks by nationality' and kept them liable for service; Metropolitan Konstantios II pressed for their exemption in 1898; Interior Ministry order no. 63 of 24 March 1326 (1910) let them register under Greek names only, and the metropolis issued a circular on 30 December 1910.
disputed: Greek scholarship stresses persecution; Tzedopoulos stresses the double burden and the politics of sovereignty. Bryer (1983) prints the consular evidence of persecution in 1859, but stresses the Kromlides' own aim: after 1856 they still claimed to carry arms, to do no military service and to pay no poll tax, wanting 'obligation to neither'. A Turkish reading, of foreign instigation and the search for privileges, is given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H5-T02). Chrysanthos dates the order of registration to 1910 but says elsewhere that the burden lasted 'until 1911'. Bryer (after Janin 1912 and Hasluck 1921) has the governor of Trebizond ask for a ruling on 24 February 1909 and convey the assurance that all Kromlides could declare their faith only on 29 December 1910, a day before the circular dated by Chrysanthos.

date_text: 15 July 1857 (the appeal sealed by 44 leaders); the list of villages is dated 30 August 1857
title: The Kromni petition: an estimated 17,260 crypto-Christians ask to be registered as Christians
summary: The Kromlides petitioned the Porte and the ambassadors of the five major Christian Powers: on 15 July 1857 forty-four of their leaders sealed the appeal (Bryer 1983, p. 16), and their delegate, Mustafa son of Tursun, the Yazıcı (clerk), took four copies to Constantinople, for the British, Austrian, French and Russian representatives; the British acting consul, G. A. Stevens, says he had advised them to petition (Document 1, p. 35). When the embassy asked for details, Stevens sent a translation of the Kromlides' own list of villages, dated Trebizond, 30 August 1857, with his despatch of 31 October (pp. 35-41). Its totals line gives 11,151 houses: 1,907 Muslim, 3,452 Kromlides (crypto-Christian) and 5,792 Greek (open Christian). Its soul figures (Muslims 9,535; Kromlides 17,260; Greeks 28,960) are the houses ('families' in the totals lines) multiplied by five, an estimate, not a count; together they make an estimated 55,755 people (52% open Christians, 31% crypto-Christians, 17% Muslims). Stevens thought the list too low, as its compilers admitted (p. 36). Bryer's note speaks of 59 villages (55 rows, four of them pairs). Kromni, Santa and Stavri held more than 22% of the crypto-Christians (771 of the list's 3,452 Kromli houses). The Russian consulate's secretary helped draft the petitions (Ioannidis 1870), and a joint commission of embassy and Ottoman officials visited Trebizond. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 717-719) prints the sealed letter of attorney of 16 July 1857 (fig. 110): representatives of crypto-Christian villages of the Trebizond and Chaldia dioceses (Kromni, Santa, Kovasa, Stavri, Mouzena, Galiana and others, with about 50 seals) met at Trebizond and appointed three attorneys to the Patriarchate and the ambassadors of England, France, Austria, Russia and Greece.
disputed: Some 17,000 (Tzedopoulos) or about 17,260 (Bryer 1983) is the list's 3,452 Kromli houses multiplied by five; Bryer prints no grand total, and 55,755 is the sum of the three estimated figures. Bryer warns that the list follows no Ottoman boundaries, covers only villages where crypto-Christians lived, probably undercounts the crypto-Christians, the open Christians more and the Muslims most, and leaves out wholly Muslim villages; but for the heartland 'almost every village seems to be included'. On motive, Bryer argues that the Chaldian miners' special status outlived the mines, which failed about 1829, leaving them neither officially Christian nor Muslim and wishing to owe 'obligation to neither'; Tzedopoulos sees several identities and the act of 1857 as a modern political choice backed by Russia. Chrysanthos' 'about 20,000' revealed and recognised is a round figure without basis or date. Ioannidis (1870) describes a meeting of 150 at the Theoskepastos in March 1857, with an oath, a collection of 18,700 piastres and reports drafted by Joseph Ricard of the Russian consulate; Chrysanthos dates the representatives' meeting in Trebizond to 15 July 1857. Ioannidis' delegate Nikolaos Tavropoulos of Poulantzaki and Chrysanthos' 'Tosunoğlu Mustafa Yazıcı, later Tavropoulos' are probably the same man under his Christian and Muslim names; that is an inference.

title: About 8,000 Kromlides recognised as Orthodox
summary: According to Kallifron, about 8,000 of the declarers were recognised as Christians in 1859; the rest remained in limbo for decades. Kromni's population fell to about half its pre-collapse level by 1870 as families emigrated to Russia or moved to the coast.
disputed: Kallifron is the only source for the 8,000. Chrysanthos' 'about 20,000' follows Ioannidis (1870), for whom it is the number who came forward and whom the government then recognised; Agtzidis (2005) gives 24,000 recognised after the Crimean War, after the British consul. Bryer (1983) has no recognition in 1859: the Kromlides' petition to the consuls of March–April 1859 still asks for their admission among the Christian subjects, Palgrave in 1867 describes a compromise ruling (military service, but no exemption tax), and Bryer puts the recognition of '12–30,000' in 1910. No British consular figure of 24,000 appears in the despatches Bryer prints, which give about 17,260 Kromlides (the list of 1857) and about 10,000 souls at Kromni (Palgrave 1867).
sources_primary: Kallifron (19th-c. Greek account)

date_text: May 1863 (patriarchal tomos creating the archbishopric) - 7 September 1867 (abolished; exarchates restored)
title: Rhodopolis: an archbishopric made from the three monastic exarchates (1863-1867)
summary: A patriarchal tomos of May 1863 created the archbishopric (not yet a metropolis) of Rhodopolis from the villages that the monasteries of Soumela, Vazelon and Peristera had governed as exarchates, 'more than forty' villages between the dioceses of Trebizond and Chaldia; its archbishop was Gennadios. The monasteries and many villagers, Santa among them, refused it: in June 1865 the monasteries' supervision was moved to the metropolitan of Trebizond, patriarchal exarchs reported against the see, and it was abolished on 7 September 1867, the exarchates being restored. After a new inquiry (1874) the Patriarchate decided again in 1876 to keep the exarchates; Rhodopolis became a metropolis only in October 1902 (C3-030), one of the six Pontic metropolises of 1920. For the three exarchates without Santa, the Matzouka district, Bryer (1983) gives for 1857 ten villages with 11,160 open and crypto-Christians and 1,450 Muslims, from the Kromlides' list of 1857. The figures often quoted for 'Rhodopolis' (14,525 people: 53 percent open Christians, 37 percent crypto-Christians, 10 percent Muslims; Topalidis) are not printed by Bryer, but they are exactly what the same list gives for Santa and the three exarchates together: 2,905 houses at five a house.
disputed: Bryer (1983) gives further counts for the district: 12,066 Christians and 18,460 Muslims in 1868 (Palgrave, the Muslims 'wildly overestimated') and 16,525 Christians and 5,335 Muslims in 1920 (Zerzelides). His own figures for 1857 cannot be rebuilt exactly from the village rows of the list, which give 2,000 Christian houses and 2,290 houses in all; the reason for the difference is not known.

title: Circassian and Ubykh refugees die in thousands at Trabzon and Samsun
summary: After Russia's final conquest of the western Caucasus, Circassians, Ubykhs and Abkhaz were shipped across the Black Sea. On 12 April 1864 about 25,000 were already at Trebizond, and by mid-1864 some 40,000 were in two camps there. Vice-Consul Stevens reported about 300 deaths a day at the Saradere and Akçakale camps in June and put mortality at 50% in September. Dr Barozzi found 70,000-80,000 at Samsun in May; a private letter spoke of 500-700 deaths a day. Survivors were settled inland, many in the Samsun, Amasya, Tokat and Sivas hinterlands, which changed the ethnic map of the western Pontus.
disputed: Fauvel's figure of over 300,000 arrivals in the empire between November 1863 and August 1864, two-thirds of them dead, may be inflated, and the daily death rates are snapshots. Whether to call the expulsion a genocide is disputed: Richmond and Circassian organisations use the word, the Russian state rejects it, and Georgia recognised it in 2011.

title: Consul Palgrave reports on the crypto-Christians
summary: William Gifford Palgrave, British consul at Trebizond (1867-73), reported on the Kromlides in a confidential report of 17 April 1867, one of many answers to a French, Russian and British circular of that year on the status of Christians. He counted at 'Kroom' 'about two thousand hearths, or ten thousand souls', long publicly Muslim and privately Christian, who after the Crimean War had declared themselves Christian, many taking Russian papers, and then refused both military service and the Imdadeeyah, the Christians' exemption tax; Constantinople ruled that they should serve but be exempt from the tax. Bryer notes that Palgrave saw three anomalies: they carried arms like Muslims, did no military service like Christians, but unlike Christians paid no poll tax in lieu of it. The explanation from the miners' old status (harac excused for mining or charcoal service) is Bryer's, not Palgrave's (pp. 32-33). The phrase 'neither Mussulmans nor Christians' is G. A. Stevens's, in 1857 (Document 1, p. 35). Bryer's 1983 study prints the report as Document 9, with the Stevens brothers' despatches of 1857-59 (Documents 1-8).
disputed: Tzedopoulos doubts that the miners were exempt from the poll tax. Bryer treats Palgrave as a biased witness, a 'mishellene' who despised Greeks and regarded the Kromlides as apostates, 'a demonstrably careless witness' who in his parliamentary report derived them from Xenophon's Ten Thousand; he also shows that Palgrave had himself lived as the Jesuit Père Michel Sohail and changed his religion up to six times.

title: The Gümüşhane mines almost all abandoned
summary: The Trabzon provincial yearbook of 1870 describes nearly all the Gümüşhane mines as abandoned and flooded, too deep to be measured. A kaymakam reported that a third of the people left their lands soon after the mines closed. The end of mining pushed Chaldiots to Russia, to the coast and to the plains of Samsun.
disputed: Bryer (1983) has the mines closed 'soon after' 1829, by stages, and the miners moving to Russia, to new mines at Ak Dag (1832) and to the alum mines north of Şebinkarahisar, taking their special status with them; the yearbook of 1870 describes the end.

title: Violence against Christians in Sourmena and Chaldia
summary: Chrysanthos records crimes in 1870 'ἰδίᾳ ἐν τῇ περιφερείᾳ Σουρμένων' (especially in the Sourmena district): seizure of property, robbery of churches and abduction of girls, against which Konstantios obtained two high orders. In 1874 he obtained the expulsion of two Ottomans, Kadir and Ahmed, from Ulu-Cheriana in Chaldia, and there was a chapel dispute at Agridi.

summary: Chrysanthos writes that in 1872 a rupture between Greeks and Armenians followed the abduction of an Orthodox girl by Armenians, and remarks that the Armenians 'συχνὰ ἐχρησιμοποιοῦντο ὑπὸ τῶν Τούρκων ὡς ὄργανα κατὰ τῶν ὀρθοδόξων' (were often used by the Turks as tools against the Orthodox).

date_text: 1877-1878 (Kars taken 18 November 1877; Treaty of Berlin 13 July 1878)
title: Russia takes Kars, Ardahan and Batum
summary: Russia annexed Kars, Ardahan and Batum. Many Muslims left Kars oblast in 1879-82, and Christians took their place: Armenians, Russians and Greeks. Greeks from Gümüşhane, Trebizond and the older Georgian colonies founded Greek villages and towns in Kars oblast (77 Greek villages of Kars and Ardahan, according to Agtzidis). Muslim Laz, Ajarians and Georgians from the ceded lands moved the other way into Ottoman territory, many settling around Ordu, Samsun and Sinop.
disputed: The numbers of Greek settlers from the Ottoman Pontus and from Georgia are not separated. The 77 villages are Agtzidis' figure.

date_text: Soumela plundered 1877–78 (arrests 5 May 1878); patriarchal letters of 3 May, 9 May and 3 June 1880
title: After the war of 1877–78: Soumela plundered, Laz and Circassian immigrants, Christian emigration from Kerasous
summary: Chrysanthos records that fourteen Turks who had sacked Soumela were arrested on 5 May 1878 after the Patriarchate intervened. With Batum annexed by Russia, 'οἱ ἐν τῇ περιφερείᾳ Βατοὺμ κατοικοῦντες Λαζοὶ καὶ Κιρκάσιοι Μουσουλμάνοι μετηνάστευσαν εἰς τὰς παραλίους ἐπαρχίας τοῦ Πόντου, συχνὰ ἐπιτιθέμενοι … κατὰ τῶν ἐκεῖ χριστιανῶν' (the Laz and Circassian Muslims of the Batum region moved to the Pontic coastal districts, often attacking the Christians there), especially around Kerasous and Kotyora. Many Christians of the Kerasous district were forced to emigrate. In 1879–80 the Russian Church detached Batum 'αὐθαιρέτως καὶ ἀντικανονικῶς' (arbitrarily and uncanonically) from the diocese.
disputed: No figures for immigrants or emigrants are given.

title: Parcharides counts the Greek-speaking Muslims of Of
summary: Ioannis Parcharides' statistics of Of give 10,000-12,000 families, of whom 8,000-10,000 spoke Greek, but only 192 families were Christian. It is the best 19th-century measure of the Greek-speaking Muslim population. Parcharides also argued that conversion began well before the late 17th century, under pressure from bandits and Anatolian settlers.
disputed: A Greek contemporary estimate, not a census.

title: Tobacco and hazelnuts: the boom of the western Pontic plains
summary: Samsun's rise began before the Régie: the chaussée to Amasya and the spread of Bafra tobacco made it, by the 1860s, the port of the Constantinople–Baghdad route with international tobacco markets; it overtook Trebizond in population in the 1870s; Bryer puts its first peak at about 70,000 in 1900 (Bryer 1980), Bryer and Winfield at over 40,000 by 1910 (1985, p. 94). After the Ottoman Public Debt handed the tobacco monopoly to the Régie (1883), Samsun-Bafra tobacco remained a major export. Greeks rose to as much as 40% of Samsun's people, and Greek and Armenian control of local business and of the tobacco market became 'almost exclusive', though this growth owed more to immigration from Ionia and Constantinople than to Pontic Hellenism (Bryer). Hazelnuts did the same for Kerasous, Ordu and Tirebolu. The two trades drew highland Greeks from Chaldia, Kromni, Santa and the Trebizond hinterland down to the Samsun, Bafra and Çarşamba plains and the Ordu-Fatsa-Ünye coast.

title: Anatolia College at Merzifon
summary: The American Board moved its seminary from Bebek to Merzifon (Marsovan) in 1862 and opened Anatolia College there in 1886, with Charles Tracy as president. Its students were mostly Greek and Armenian, with Greek, Armenian and American teachers, and a girls' school was added in 1893. It became a meeting point of the two Christian communities, and a target in 1893, 1895, 1915 and 1921.
sources_primary: Annual reports of the American Board (ABCFM)

title: Cuinet's statistics of the vilayet of Trebizond
summary: Vital Cuinet's survey gives the vilayet's population by kaza and religion, from 'les dernières données' of the early 1890s. Cuinet prints a total of 1,047,700 inhabitants (including Şiran and Kelkit) and 806,700 Muslims (691,700, plus 55,000 Laz and 60,000 Circassians). A sandjak column reading 91,000 / 77,000 / 16,000 / 9,000 sums to 193,000; Beylerian, reading Cuinet (I, pp. 10–11), gives the vilayet's Greeks as 193,000 and its Armenians as 47,200. It is the most detailed pre-1914 breakdown by kaza.
disputed: Cuinet relied on Ottoman figures, which undercounted Christians.

date_text: 8 October 1895 (Trebizond); late October (Gümüşhane, Bayburt); 15 November (Merzifon, Amasya)
title: The Hamidian massacres reach Trebizond
summary: On 2 October 1895 two Armenians wounded Bahri Pasha, a former governor, and Hamdi Pasha at Trebizond. On 8 October a massacre of Armenians followed in the streets and houses of the city, and Laz bands then plundered Armenian villages nearby. Contemporary reports put the dead in the city at several hundred: 'four hundred' in a period narrative, 'over five hundred killed' in the American minister's telegram of 16 October, and 'nine hundred … said to have been massacred' in a press cable. Estimates for the vilayet run to 1,000-2,000. Massacres followed at Gümüşhane, Bayburt, Merzifon and Amasya. Western accounts say the Greeks were not targeted.
disputed: The '8,000' in a modern notice of the French consul Cillière's report is almost certainly an error, since the same notice gives 8,000 as the Armenian population.

summary: The first Russian census counted 290,654 people in Kars oblast, of whom 32,593 (11.2%) were Greeks by native language (the census counted by native language). Turkish-speaking Orthodox (Urum) were probably counted as Turkish speakers, so the Greek total is a minimum.

title: Pressure on the Stavriotes of Akdağ Madeni
summary: From 1899 the Stavriote crypto-Christians, Chaldiot miners settled around Akdağ Madeni who had not joined the 1857 movement, came under growing pressure. Their leaders were exiled in 1905, some dying in exile, and in 1906 they appealed to Greece and the Patriarch. Ottoman documents name leaders such as Küpcüoğlu of 'the Istavri movement'.

title: The new building of the Phrontisterion
summary: The Phrontisterion moved into a new three-storey building with 36 classrooms above the seafront, near the church of St Gregory of Nyssa and the Armenian cathedral. It was the most imposing Greek monument of late Ottoman Trebizond and became a symbol of Pontic Greek education, with about 1,047 Greek schools in the region by about 1910. It closed in November 1921, and today the building houses the Kanuni Anadolu Lisesi. Chrysanthos (1933, pp. 663-665) records the community schism of 1893-1897, the decision to rebuild after the reconciliation of 1897, funds collected in Russia, the firman of 2 March 1899, and the consecration on 14 and 16 September 1902 before the vali Kadri Bey and the Muslim, Armenian and Persian representatives.

Its first metropolitan, Gervasios Sarasitis, 'δεινῶς ἐπολεμεῖτο' (was fiercely opposed) by the monasteries and by villagers they incited. In 1895 Santa still belonged to the exarchate of Soumela.

title: The Young Turk revolution reaches Pontus
summary: Sultan Abdülhamid II restores the 1876 constitution under pressure from the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP). Greeks, Armenians and Muslims celebrate together in Trebizond and Samsun, and Pontic Greeks vote in the parliamentary elections of late 1908: Matthaios Kofidis was elected for Trebizond, and again in 1912 and 1914, while at Amisos (Samsun) the Greek candidate was not elected (Boura 1983). Optimism fades quickly: the CUP's Ottomanism soon turns into a nationalist economic and military programme that the Greeks of Pontus see as aimed at them.

Kofidis' time as deputy is also stated by the Black Book and the Martyre.

title: The constitutional era: Kromlides and Stavriotes registered under Christian names
summary: After the 1908 revolution the Kromlides petitioned the deputy Bousios in the Ottoman parliament (1909). The Patriarchate published documents blaming Abdülhamid's regime. In 1910 both Kromlides and Stavriotes were allowed to register under Christian names only, although during the First World War the Stavriotes were refused recognition and drafted into Muslim units.

Chrysanthos dates the Interior Ministry order 24 March 1326 (1910) and the metropolis' circular 30 December 1910. Bryer does not deal with the Stavriotes.

title: Boycotts of Greek businesses
summary: A Muslim boycott of Greek merchants begins after the Cretan crisis of 1909–10 and is revived, now organised by the CUP, after the Balkan Wars. Its aim was a 'national economy' in Muslim hands. It hit the Aegean and Constantinople hardest; in Pontus it was weaker but present in the ports. At Trebizond, Chrysanthos says, the CUP ordered a boycott of the Pontic Greeks in early 1914, but the Turkish merchants themselves foiled it for fear of reprisals (Chrysanthos 1933, pp. 744-745). On 5 July 1914, with war with Greece feared, a circular to the provinces, Trebizond and Canik among them, ordered the boycott against the Greeks lifted while negotiations went on, and those who kept it up punished; Akçam reads this as a show for foreign opinion by a government that had organised the boycott (Akçam 2012, pp. 83-86). In wartime, a Greek report from Kerasous of 1917 says that delegates of the Committee told the Muslim villages that the Sultan had freed them from their debts to Christians and forbade paying them, or paying rent to Christian landowners; since the war began, it says, hardly any Turk had paid (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 17).
disputed: Chrysanthos, a party to events, is the only source for the failure of the boycott of 1914 at Trebizond.

date_text: July 1909 (service made compulsory for all Ottoman subjects); October 1909 (first call-up irrespective of religion)
title: Non-Muslims made liable for military service
summary: In July 1909 military service was made compulsory for all Ottoman subjects, ending the practice by which Christians paid the bedel instead of serving; in October 1909 conscripts were called up irrespective of religion for the first time (Zürcher). Many young Christian men, especially Greeks, chose to leave the country or to acquire a foreign passport; from the Pontus they left for Russia, the Caucasus and the United States, along the routes of the 19th-century emigration, in numbers not yet known. The law is the legal root of the 1914 labour battalions.
disputed: Zürcher gives no numbers for the emigration, and its scale and destinations from the Pontus are not known.
sources_primary: Ottoman military service law of 1909 (Düstur)

title: Greek counts of the Orthodox of Pontus: the 1910-12 census, and Soteriades 1918
summary: The Greek (Patriarchal-consular) census of 1910-12 counted 400,586 Orthodox in the six Pontic metropolises (Kitromilides & Alexandris). By vilayet the same series gives 298,183 for Trabzon with Canik and 74,632 for Sivas. A different set of figures, 353,533 for the vilayet of Trebizond and 99,376 for Sivas, comes from Soteriades (1918), a work of advocacy published for the peace conference that claims a Patriarchal basis; the same table quotes an 'Ottoman official' figure of 351,104 for Trebizond in 1910. The Greek counts covered every Rum Orthodox, Greek- or Turkish-speaking.
disputed: For the province of Trebizond with Canik the comparable range is 260,313 (Ottoman census of 1914) to 298,183 (Greek census of 1910–12), with 353,533 as an advocacy figure. Soteriades' 'Ottoman 1910' figure does not match the census of 1914.

title: The Balkan Wars
summary: The Ottomans lose almost all their European lands; Greece takes Macedonia, Epirus and the north Aegean islands. Some 350,000–400,000 Balkan Muslims flee to Anatolia (Pezo 2017), and CUP hostility to the empire's Christians hardens; the CUP seizes power in the coup of 23 January 1913. Pontic Greek men are conscripted for the first time in large numbers.
disputed: Muslim refugee numbers vary widely: 350,000–400,000 (Pezo) against much higher figures in some Turkish and advocacy works (e.g. 900,000 'expelled or killed' in Hofmann's essay).

The city of Trebizond had 6,720 families: 3,500 Muslim, 2,500 Greek, 600 Armenian, 60 Persian and 60 foreign; the Greeks were in nine parishes with 13 churches and 12 schools. A footnote adds 4,640 souls abroad, for 50,405.

title: Joint Greek, Turkish, Armenian and Persian water committee of Trebizond
summary: Chrysanthos says that in 1913 a committee for the water supply of Trebizond, of Greeks, Turks, Armenians and Persians and chaired alternately by the metropolitan and the mufti, raised 'ἱκαναὶ δεκάδες χιλιάδων χρυσῶν λιρῶν' (many tens of thousands of gold pounds) from an import surtax and in 1914 signed a contract with a Belgian company; the war stopped the work.

title: Kerasous detached from Trebizond and given to Chaldia; the diocese's limits
summary: Chrysanthos writes that on 12 October 1913 Kerasous was detached from Trebizond and attached to Chaldia, so that the diocese's western limit became Tripolis. 'In our days' the diocese ran along the coast from Tripolis to Batum (detached by the Russian Church in 1879–80) and inland to Kiourtouni, Dikaisimon (Tzevizlik), Olassa, Santa and Baiburt; in the northeast it had absorbed the sees of Rizaion, Ischopolis and Lazia, extinguished in the mid-17th century.

title: The Ottoman census of 1914
summary: The Ottoman census gives the vilayet of Trebizond, with Canik, 1,516,249 people. Of these, 1,187,078 were Muslims, 260,313 Greek Orthodox and 66,218 Armenians. By sancak the Greek Orthodox were 116,357 in Trabzon, 98,739 in Canik, 43,495 in Gümüşhane and 1,722 in Lazistan. Sivas vilayet, which includes Amasya, Tokat and Şebinkarahisar, had 75,324 Greek Orthodox, and Kastamonu, with Sinop, 20,958.

title: Turkish scholarship on the crypto-Christian declarations: foreign instigation and the search for privileges
summary: Turkish state-institution scholarship (Kuş 2018, in Belleten, the journal of the Turkish Historical Society; the study 'Trabzon vilayetinde iki din taşıyanlar') presents the Kromlides and Stavriotes who declared themselves Christian after 1856 as people encouraged by foreign powers, above all Russia, and moved by the wish to escape conscription and to gain privileges.
disputed: The Ottoman documents these works print are valuable; their interpretation is the Turkish reading.
counter_evidence: Partly supported by Bryer (1983, British, from the British consular archives), who agrees that worldly motives and Russian backing played a part: by declaring themselves Christian, 'Kurumlis could not only evade military service, but seek Russian protection to avoid any other kind of obligation to the Ottoman state'. Palgrave in 1867 blamed Russian influence; Bryer traces their status to the Chaldian miners' exemptions after the mines failed about 1829; and the recognition of 1910 came through Russian and French pressure. The British acting consul Stevens says that he himself advised them to petition. Neither Bryer nor Tzedopoulos calls the declarations insincere: Bryer says that the concealment of faith was real ('there is no doubt that this was done') and their sufferings 'undoubted', while denying that they were long-enduring martyrs. Tzedopoulos reads the declarations as a modern political act by people of several negotiated identities, and Deringil's verdict is that 'what was at issue was not religion at all, but sovereignty'.
sources_primary: Ottoman documents as printed by Kuş 2018
sources_modern: Kuş 2018, Belleten 82/294 | 'Trabzon vilayetinde iki din taşıyanlar'

title: The Ottoman report on the Trebizond events of October 1895
summary: A report of the officials and notables of Trebizond, forwarded by the Ottoman minister in Washington, Mavroyeni Bey, on 27 December 1895, blames the violence of 8 October on Armenian gunfire, names no Armenian death toll, and says that 'the Greeks … had joined the brawl'.
disputed: An official report written to answer Western accusations; the American diplomatic papers (Foreign Relations of the United States) print it in full.
counter_evidence: Contemporary non-Ottoman reports describe a massacre of Armenians: 'four hundred' (a period narrative) to 'nine hundred … said to have been massacred' (press cable, Manawatu Herald, 31 Oct 1895); the French consul Cillière also reported it, and the vilayet toll is estimated at 1,000-2,000. Western accounts say the Greeks were not attacked; no non-Ottoman source known to us says that Greeks took part. The wounding of Bahri Pasha and Hamdi Pasha by two Armenians on 2 October is told in the chapter (H5-047).
sources_primary: Ottoman report of the officials and notables of Trebizond, via Mavroyeni Bey to Olney, 27 Dec 1895 (FRUS 1895 II, doc. 701)

title: Expulsion of Greeks from Eastern Thrace and the Aegean coast (context)
summary: Special Organization bands, coordinated with the CUP, drive Greeks out of Eastern Thrace and the Aegean coast; at Phocaea the attack begins on 12 June 1914. 150,000–300,000 Ottoman Greeks are expelled to Greece or moved inland. Talat ends the campaign on 2 November 1914. Pontus was barely touched in this phase, but the methods were a precedent.
disputed: The totals differ: Bjørnlund gives 150,000–200,000, Akçam about 300,000, and Meichanetsidis higher partial figures. Akçam (2012, pp. 88–89) lists the contemporary counts: by the Greek government's figures, 60,926 people (15,572 families) expelled from eastern Thrace in the first half of 1914 and about 150,000 leaving western Anatolia during the year; 150,000–200,000 before the war by a 1930 report of the US ambassador at Athens, which Akçam thinks conservative. Talat blamed the excesses on local men such as Rahmi Bey. One cable bears on Pontus: on 15 April 1914 the ministry's immigrant office asked Trebizond how many of the Greek emigrants bound for Salonica had been let on board without the 10-kuruş fare, and whether there were enough for another ship (BOA DH.ŞFR 40/13; Akçam 2012, p. 77).

title: Cemal Azmi becomes vali of Trebizond
summary: Cemal Azmi, a CUP man and co-founder of the Special Organization, takes over the vilayet of Trebizond. He will direct the destruction of the Armenians of the vilayet in 1915 and hand the city to Metropolitan Chrysanthos before fleeing the Russians in April 1916.
sources_modern: Kévorkian, The Armenian Genocide: A Complete History (2011)

title: Chrysanthos' account: Greek loyalty guaranteed; Russian subjects and labour battalions spared
summary: Chrysanthos writes that in August 1914 he 'ὑπὸ προσωπικὴν αὐτοῦ εὐθύνην ἠγγυήθη … περὶ τῆς νομιμοφροσύνης τῶν Ἑλλήνων τῆς ὅλης … βιλαετίου' (guaranteed on his personal responsibility the loyalty of the Greeks of the whole vilayet) to the vali Cemal Azmi, and set up a network with the centres of Trebizond, Rhodopolis and Chaldia. Through the vali he had cancelled the mid-winter exile to Harput of 'τριακόσιοι' (300) Russian-subject Greeks. Because the vali ran army supply and the labour battalions, most Greek conscripts were given light work in Trebizond's army workshops, and church officers and teachers were exempted; in April 1916, ordered to follow the retreating army, the battalions were freed 'at the last hour'. A gendarmerie post was obtained to protect Santa from çetes.
disputed: All of this rests on Chrysanthos. Other sources confirm Cemal Azmi's governorship and the labour battalions, but not these exemptions.

title: The Interior Ministry has the Greek property of Trebizond, Ordu and Giresun listed
summary: On 5 September 1914 the Interior Ministry's Security Directorate asked the provinces of Aydın and Trebizond and the district of Canik (Samsun), all with large Greek communities, for a report on all the property and buildings of the Greek community, with their value and owners. Ten days later nearly every province was asked for the farms and estates owned by Greeks, and on 6 October Trebizond and Canik were ordered again. On 24 December 1914 the governor of Trebizond (then Cemal Azmi, H6-006) sent three notebooks giving the number, kind, value and owners of the Greek community's properties and buildings in the towns of Trebizond, Ordu and Giresun. Akçam, who found the cables in the Ottoman archive, notes that the lists were made while a commission was studying a Turkish-Greek exchange of populations, and thinks it likely that they were drawn up for it (Akçam 2012, pp. 37-39).
disputed: Akçam quotes the cables and the governor's covering reply; as far as we know the notebooks themselves have not been published. That they were made for a possible exchange of populations is Akçam's inference; the commission and its instructions for lists for an exchange are documented (BOA DH.EUM 3. Şube 2/26-A, cited by Akçam, p. 39).

title: War with Russia; Trebizond shelled; Sarıkamış
summary: The Ottoman fleet's raid on the Russian Black Sea coast (29 October) brings war with Russia. The Russian Black Sea Fleet shells Trebizond in mid-November 1914; a Capuchin missionary's diary entry dated Trebizond, 16 November 1914, describes the bombardment, with women and children crowding into the Catholic church and garden and civilians killed or wounded. Enver's winter offensive at Sarıkamış (22 Dec 1914 – 17 Jan 1915) destroys most of the Third Army and exposes the eastern provinces.
disputed: The accounts give only 'mid-November' for the bombardment; the earliest dated witness is the missionary's diary entry of 16 November 1914.

title: The first guerrilla bands (andartes)
summary: Deserters from the labour battalions form armed bands in the mountains. Santa organises its own defence in 1916 under Efkleidis Kourtidis. In the hills of Erbaa and Taşova a band led by Kapetan Iakof (killed near Endik Pınar, 1916) passes to the 20-year-old Anastasios Papadopoulos, 'Kotsa Nastas'. Bands are also active in the Çarşamba and Bafra hills; the Bafra-area leader Antonis Hacılefteryu, known as Anton Pasha, on whom the authorities had put a price of 5,000 lira, is murdered by a fellow Greek in August 1917, and his wife Pelagia leads the band until 1923 (Agtzidis 2005). Morris & Ze'evi accept that during the war these bands, 'composed chiefly of youngsters avoiding the draft', 'occasionally attacked Turkish villagers and gendarmes'. A Greek historian, Agtzidis (1992, p. 167), writes that the bands began as village self-defence, that calls for a 'general revolution' were made from 1916, and that their arms came from battles, from Russian Greek networks and from 'Russian aid'.
disputed: Greek sources call the bands self-defence by men escaping death in the labour battalions. Morris & Ze'evi (p. 383) accept that wartime bands 'occasionally attacked Turkish villagers and gendarmes' and report that 'the Turks charged' that Russia armed and reinforced them; their note cites only Shaw, a historian close to the Turkish view who relied on Ottoman sources, so the Russian arming remains a Turkish charge. A Greek primary source points the same way: the Metropolitan of Amaseia wrote on 27 February 1917 that the pretext for the persecution was 'about 300 deserters' who had gone to Trebizond for arms brought by a Russian torpedo boat, and that the government had the right to punish them, but not the women, children and villages (Patriarchate 1919, p. 121). The detailed Turkish accounts of raids on Muslims in 1916–18 (Duman 2012; Aydın & Duman 2012), with road blocks and raids on convoys and grain stores around Çarşamba, are given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-013, H7-004). The size of the bands in 1916–18 is unknown.

title: First deportations of Greek notables; violence in Santa
summary: Leading Greeks of Eastern Thrace, Pontus and Constantinople are sent inland: on 8 March 1915 the Constantinople police deported some 200 Greek community leaders, intellectuals, clergy and businessmen (Morris & Ze'evi), while the Greek Legation reported up to 10,000 sent from the capital (2 March 1915). In April 1915 an Ottoman band hunting deserters burns and loots Greek houses in Santa and takes 50 men to the labour battalions, almost all of whom die.
disputed: The Santa episode rests on a refugee's memoir, known to us through later Greek works. For Constantinople, about 200 notables (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 387) against up to 10,000 (Greek Legation note); the two figures may count different groups.

title: The Armenian genocide in the Trebizond vilayet
summary: Armenian leaders are arrested in late June; the deportation order is posted and convoys leave from 1 July. Men are killed in the valleys behind the city; women and children are loaded onto boats 'for Samsun' and drowned at sea, as the US consul Heizer, the Italian consul Gorrini, an Ottoman deputy and a Turkish officer later testified. Topal Osman's band took part. About 30,000 Armenians lived in and around Trebizond before the war; about 500 survivors returned under the Russians in 1916. Chrysanthos, an eyewitness, translates the ten-article deportation proclamation dated 13 June 1331 (26 June 1915 N.S.), says Bahaeddin Şakir came from Erzurum in early June and with the vali gave secret orders for a general massacre, and describes about 300 young Armenians killed at sea off Platana, corpses in the Değirmendere, and Greek villagers (above all at Sana in Gemura) feeding Armenians hidden in the forests until April 1916.
disputed: The dates: Morris & Ze'evi (pp. 181–184), after Kévorkian (2011, p. 469), give the vali's word to his staff on 24 June, the round-up of the notables on 25 June, the public announcement on 26 June and the first convoys on 1 July 1915, and date an earlier proclamation of the vali to 16 June; Chrysanthos' proclamation of 13 June 1331 (26 June 1915) agrees. The numbers: the Ottoman count of 1914 gives 37,549 Armenians in the vilayet (Karpat, as reprinted by Akçam 2012, p. 262), the Armenian Patriarchate's count more; about 30,000 lived in the city and its district. Talat's register records 34,500 removed (Akçam, p. 259). Chrysanthos' figure of 300 killed at sea is approximate.

date_text: June – July 1915 (Samsun and Merzifon); reports to December 1915
title: The Armenians of Samsun and Merzifon in 1915, and Armenians hidden in Greek villages
summary: Talat's own register of the deportations, published by Murat Bardakçı, gives 26,374 Armenians removed from the district of Samsun (Canik), against 27,058 Armenians in the Ottoman count of 1914. At Samsun the American consul William Peter reported in June 1915 that about 150 families had become Muslims and the rest had been sent inland; the German consul Kuckhoff wrote on 25 June that all the Armenian villages in and around Samsun had been Islamised under threat. Armenians at Ordu and Fatsa, and local imams and muftis, petitioned that converts be spared; an Armenian party report of August 1915 counted 160 of 250 families converted at Ordu and 200 of 400 at Giresun. On 9 July the district governor of Canik, Necmi Bey, reported that the last convoy had left Samsun four days earlier with its clergy and the last group from Alaçam had been sent by Kavak and Havza, and that converts were being settled in scattered places; Talat soon ordered that converts be deported all the same. At Merzifon, according to the missionary J. K. Marden, over 11,500 of 13,000 Armenians were deported and about 1,500 accepted Islam. Another missionary at Merzifon reported in December 1915 that 'thousands' of Armenians were hidden in the Greek mountain villages of her district alone, and the Patriarchate's compilation records that at Nicopolis (Şebinkarahisar) the Greek houses were set on fire to find Armenians hiding in them (p. 98; Akçam, p. 123, has Tokat). At the Trebizond court-martial a Justice Ministry inspector, Kenan Bey, said that he had seen the deportations at Samsun and that the kaymakam of Bafra had been killed (Akçam 2012, pp. 123, 196, 259, 263, 292-296).
disputed: Talat's register counts those removed, not the dead. The Ordu and Giresun conversion figures come from an Armenian party report forwarded by the US ambassador Morgenthau. Akçam quotes Kenan Bey from the trial reports without the kaymakam's name or the date of the killing, in a passage on officials removed for resisting the killings. The missionary's 'thousands' is one estimate for her district. The Nicopolis report is the Patriarchate's (p. 98); Akçam (p. 123) places it at Tokat, but Tokat appears on that page only as where deportees arrived. Greek villagers in the Trebizond hills also fed hidden Armenians (Chrysanthos; H6-011).

title: Deportations of Greek villages behind the Ottoman lines in the Trebizond vilayet
summary: As the Ottomans fall back before the Russian offensive, the regional commander Kâmil Pasha orders the deportation of Greek villagers immediately behind his lines; they are driven out in midwinter and some freeze on the roads ('We must suffer, so must you'). In spring and summer the inhabitants of dozens of villages of the Trebizond vilayet are deported. A Greek Legation report says that on 15 April 1916 the people of sixteen villages of the Vazelon district were ordered to march to Argyroupolis; fearing the fate of the Armenians on that road, about 6,000 fled to the forests: 650 sheltered in the Vazelon monastery, where they found 130 refugees from Trebizond, and 1,200 hid in a cave near Kounaka until hunger forced them out, after which 26 young women and girls threw themselves into the river near Gephyra. Other Greek reports say women were taken to Vazelon and killed there. An Ottoman cable to Trebizond of 15 May 1916 set the rule for the coast: since a 'benign and tolerant policy' was being followed toward Greece, the coastal Greeks were not all to be moved inland, only those in places judged unsafe for military reasons, and those moved were to be sent to Kastamonu and to districts of Sivas without Muslim refugees (Akçam 2012, pp. 106-107). An eyewitness who reached the monastery after the Russian advance found it wrecked, with ten unburied bodies, among them the priest Constantine of Thersa and a young woman of the same village (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 45-46).
disputed: Kâmil Pasha's order rests on the letter of an American missionary in Erzurum (Morris & Ze'evi), which does not name Rize or Trebizond. The Vazelon, Kounaka and Gephyra details rest on Greek reports only. The Legation report (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 45) has 130 refugees from Trebizond at Vazelon and 1,200 people in the cave at Kounaka (probably Kunaka, today Bağışlı in Maçka; Nişanyan). The Patriarchate's account of Rodopolis (p. 109) has 200 people in the cave at 'Kaneka', and the 26 women drowning themselves 'while passing over a bridge'; since γέφυρα is Greek for bridge, 'Gephyra' may not be a village. It dates the emptying of Vazelon (its monks, 780 refugees and 29 Armenians) to 22 April 1916 and the pillage of Soumela to 19 April (p. 110), and, on the word of Metropolitan Cyril (12 November 1918), gives 487 people hiding in the mountains and caves of Rodopolis massacred (p. 111). The Ottoman cable of 15 May 1916 agrees with what Talat told the German ambassador Radowitz in October 1916, that a removal of all the coastal Greeks had been planned and stopped (H7-054).

title: The Russian coastal offensive: Arhavi to the İyidere
summary: General Lyakhov's coastal detachment, supported by the Black Sea Fleet, attacks the Ottoman line at Arhavi on 5 February 1916, and the Ottomans order a withdrawal on 6 February. The Russians reach the Viçe (Vitze, Fındıklı) line on 7 February; the line there breaks on 15-16 February. They land behind the Ottoman positions at Atina (Pazar) on 4 March and Mapavri (Çayeli) on 5 March. Rize is taken on 6 March (Ottoman documents; 8 March in Russian-based accounts), and the front reaches the İyidere (Kalopotamos), the Trebizond-Lazistan boundary, on 9 March.
disputed: Rize fell on 6 March by the Ottoman military archives (Bilgin; the Ottoman reports are dated 7 March) or on 8 March (Fevzi Çakmak); Bilgin (n. 68) takes the difference for a calendar slip. Enver's telegram puts the landing at Atina on 5 March, not 4 March. Mapavri fell on 5 March by the Ottoman documents, on 6 or 7 March in other accounts.

title: Russians take Erzurum
summary: Yudenich's Caucasus Army storms the Erzurum forts. The fall of Erzurum makes Trebizond indefensible from the landward side, and the vali Cemal Azmi begins to plan the evacuation of the city.

title: Muslim flight from the Russian-occupied zone
summary: Tens of thousands of Muslims of Lazistan, Trebizond and Gümüşhane flee west ahead of the Russian army, by sea and over the mountains, to Giresun, Ordu, Samsun, Sinop and further inland (Merzifon, Çorum, Ankara, Konya, Niğde). Chrysanthos, who stayed in Trebizond, confirms that much of the city's Muslim population left (H6-018).

We have not found an independent count of the deaths.

date_text: 15–18 April 1916 (the Russians enter on the evening of 18 April)
title: Trebizond handed to Chrysanthos; the Russians enter
summary: The Ottoman troops withdraw from Trebizond (night of 15/16 April, after Walton). On the night of Palm Sunday, 3/16 April, the vali Cemal Azmi hands the city by a written order to a provisional government under Metropolitan Chrysanthos, who receives it at the vali's villa at Kryoneri, and leaves around midnight; much of the Muslim population flees west by sea and land. Russian troops enter on the evening of 18 April 1916 (5 April Old Style); Chrysanthos receives them, and the Russians keep him as the head of the civil administration of the city.
disputed: By Walton's account the troops left on the night of 15/16 April (1984, pp. 1306–13, known to us only as cited on Wikipedia); Chrysanthos has the vali hand over and leave on the night of Palm Sunday, 3/16 April. Both may be right if the troops left a night before the vali. The Russians entered on 18 April New Style, 5 April Old Style (Çakıcı; Allen & Muratoff). Hofmann's '16 April' is the evacuation, not the entry.

title: The Russian occupation and Chrysanthos' administration
summary: Under the Russian military government Chrysanthos runs the civil affairs of Trebizond. Greek accounts say he helped Muslims who stayed or returned to recover their property and institutions, and organised relief across communities; about 500 Armenian survivors and the monks of Kaymaklı return. Greek schools and the press revive. A Catholic missionary wrote in March 1917 that the Catholics enjoyed liberty and gentle treatment under the occupation. In a letter in Greek, signed by him and dated 31 January 1918 by Greek sources, the Ottoman commander Vehip Pasha thanked Chrysanthos for his 'wholly paternal and willing care and protection' of 'the Ottoman element' since the Russian entry (Chrysanthos prints it in facsimile). Chrysanthos's own account (pp. 764-766): he protected Turks against Armenian volunteers 'thirsting for revenge', resettled 'tens of thousands' of Muslim refugees in their villages of Rize, Of, Sourmena, Gemura, Matsouka and Platana and fed 'other tens of thousands' for two years, and set up mixed Greek-Muslim courts and a local guard.
disputed: Vehip Pasha's letter, which Chrysanthos prints in facsimile (fig. 116), carries no visible date; '31 January 1918' comes from Chrysanthos' memorandum to the Peace Conference (1919) and Le Martyre du Pont-Euxin (1922, p. 9), whose 'noble... protection' of 'the Turkish element' loosens the Greek 'wholly paternal and willing care and protection' of 'the Ottoman element'. The Catholic letter of 1917 confirms the good conditions for Catholics, not Chrysanthos' role. The 'tens of thousands' are Chrysanthos' phrases, not counts. Turkish historians' accounts of Greek and Armenian bands burning Turkish houses in the occupied countryside are given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T01); we found no non-Turkish source for them.

title: Sazonov–Paléologue agreement: Trebizond promised to Russia

title: The front settles on the Harşit; Gümüşhane, Bayburt and Erzincan fall
summary: In July 1916 the Russians take Gümüşhane, Bayburt and Erzincan (25 July), and the coastal force reaches the Harşit river at Tirebolu. The Ottoman Third Army holds the west bank of the Harşit, its last defensive line, until the Russian army dissolves. Tirebolu and its villages sit in the front zone, which shaped the deportations there.

title: Topal Osman's arrests in Giresun
summary: According to Sigalas, Topal Osman, the Giresun band leader of the Armenian deportations, arrested Orthodox merchants in Giresun as 'spies'; one, Ioannis Deligiorgis, died in custody. Unusually, after the vali Cemal Azmi and the mutasarrıf of Giresun complained that he was interfering in government affairs, Osman was summoned before the court-martial at Sivas and held under guard for a time (Ottoman army records). A Greek metropolitan's letter of 15 December 1916 describes a raid by 'Osman Aga', an agent of the vali Cemal Azmi, on the village of Prossori 'about a month' before the letter, so about November 1916: his men plundered the houses, raped the women, 'murdered four young Greeks, and beat the parish priest to death', then forced the peasants to sign a document certifying that the murderers were Armenians. The same letter, by the Metropolitan of Chaldia, writing from Kerasous, says that the merchant Iordanni Sourmeli was seized at night by members of the CUP, and that the rich merchant Ioanni Deliyorghi was taken by a band of about 150, accused on anonymous letters of signalling to Russian ships, and died in custody at the court-martial of Tirebolu; the kaymakam Rechid Bey protested and was replaced by Nihad Bey (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 103-104).
disputed: The Prossori raid and the arrests of the merchants rest on the Metropolitan of Chaldia's letter, printed by the Patriarchate (1919, pp. 102–107) and also in the Greek government's collection (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 17–18, 'a report of 1917 from Kerasounda'), so the two are one witness; Morris & Ze'evi (p. 390) repeat it. The letter does not say that Osman arrested the merchants; it names him afterwards as the vali's agent in the villages (pp. 104–105). Prossori is probably the Prassari of the book's list of villages (p. 107). That Osman was behind the Giresun arrests is Sigalas' account, known to us only as cited on Wikipedia. The court-martial is confirmed by Ottoman army records (ATASE folder 1888, doc. 362, files 41 and 43), cited by Balcıoğlu (2001, p. 178) and quoted by the Turkish writers Çetinoğlu & Cibran (2007); they give the reason as his interference in government affairs, not the arrests of Greeks, and print the date as '25 August 1936', evidently a misprint, perhaps for 25 August 1332 (7 September 1916).

title: Chrysanthos' account: Grand Duke Nicholas asks him to sound out the Turks on peace
summary: Chrysanthos writes that Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, visiting Trebizond on 17/30 July 1916, confided his fear of revolution and his worry about an ally's gains in Mesopotamia, and asked him to sound the Turkish government confidentially on peace talks; he did so, without result.

title: Deportation of the Greeks of Tripolis (Tirebolu) and Elevi
summary: With the front on the Harşit, the Greeks of the Tirebolu and Elevi (Görele) districts are marched inland in winter. The route ran south over the Pontic range to Şebinkarahisar (Nikopolis), Koyulhisar and Suşehri; survivors were scattered between Karahisar and Tokat (Reşadiye, Niksar, Erbaa, Amasya) and held there until August 1918. The Greek Legation's table of January 1917 lists 3,000 deported from Tripoli itself and 29 villages of its sub-district (from 157 to 1,650 people each), 800 from Elevi and 580 from Satou-Maden (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 67); the figure for each village is given in the Villages section. Metropolitan Chrysanthos wrote on 12 October 1918 that the Christians left in Elevi and Tripoli were driven to Sivas in midwinter over snow-covered mountains: of 1,250 people of Elevi 150 survived, of 2,300 of Tripoli about 200, and of 30,000 Christians of the Tripoli district 1,500 to 2,000 (Patriarchate 1919, p. 113). The Patriarchate's account of Chaldia gives 35,000 expelled from the Tripoli and Kerasous regions by the end of 1916, with 2,000 Tripoli refugees at the Aksu refused bread by the acting governor Nihad Bey (p. 107).
disputed: The figures conflict. Valavanis gives 15,195 Greeks before and about 12,000 after, a loss of a fifth; Hofmann (2011, p. 62) gives 16,750, of whom only 550 survived, without a footnote; Kelly (2023, p. 239, after Fotiadis 2019, pp. 182–183) has 13,000 Greeks of Tripolis set out for Birk, 'a village in Armenia whose residents had been slaughtered', and 800 left three months later. Chrysanthos' letter of 1918 implies a loss of more than nine-tenths, as Travis reckons it (2017, p. 3, n. 24); it was printed in a compilation prepared for the peace settlement. Tamzara is located (Nişanyan); Birk was not found. The Patriarchate's book prints the writer of the letter as 'Chryssostomos', an error for Chrysanthos.

title: The Patriarchate's record: villages of the diocese of Kolonia expelled at a few hours' notice
summary: The Patriarchate's compilation records that in November 1916, on the order of a governor it calls Assaf, the Greeks of Valdjana and Troupsi were expelled at three hours' notice and driven to Tokat, where the men were separated and dispersed among Turkish villages; a widow was killed in front of her six children and a man who protested was cut to pieces. The villages of the Alucra region were emptied at the same time, their people fleeing to Sivas, Çankırı and Kastamonu. In July 1917 Kadıköy and six other villages of the Refahiye region were given two days to leave and dispersed in the Sivas villages, and four villages of the Abeş region were expelled; eleven more were partly emptied. Villages around Suşehri and Mesudiye were not evacuated but were terrorised by bands raised by the troop commander Feizi Bey. Allowed home in 1917, the Valdjana and Troupsi people were attacked by brigands and fled again (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 97-99). Each village's fate is given in the Villages section.
disputed: This rests on one Greek compilation, in which some dates are misprinted (the arrival at Tokat is dated '26th December, 1918'). We found no other source on these villages.

title: The Patriarchate's record: Chaldia in 1916, the villages of Torul and Argyroupolis plundered, Cheriana and Kelkit deported
summary: After the fall of Erzurum, Muslim refugees from Argyroupolis and Ardasa, joined by others from Trebizond, Yomra and Platana, gathered at the Turkish village of Monastir near Ardasa and plundered the Christian villages around it. The Patriarchate's compilation names more than thirty villages of the Torul and Argyroupolis region whose people fled to the mountains while their houses and churches were plundered and burnt, with killings in many (sixty at Simikli, twenty at Desmena, fifteen each at Sarandar and Gargaena). Before Ardasa fell to the Russians on 8 July 1916, the Christian houses and shops there were burnt, and the remaining people of Kurtakous were deported to Sivas and Tokat; the rest of the region came under Russian protection. In the Cheriana and Kelkit region, all but 200 of the people of sixteen villages were deported to Sivas during the Russian advance, and their houses, churches and schools plundered and burnt (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 100-101). Each village's fate is given in the Villages section.
disputed: This rests on one Greek compilation; the Black Book (1922) prints the same village lists, so it is not an independent witness.

title: The Stavriote priests' report: the Stavriotes of Akdağmadeni registered as Muslims during the war
summary: A report of the Stavriote priests of Akdağmadeni, dated 8 November 1918, says that during the war the Stavriotes whose Christian registration had not been recognised were conscripted as Muslims, and that about 200 families let themselves be registered as Muslims to receive relief; even a priest, Joanni, was entered as a Muslim (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 117-118). It continues the story of the crypto-Christians' registration under Christian names in 1909-10 (H5-051).

title: The Patriarchate's record: the villages of Ordu and Fatsa deported, 1916–17
summary: The Patriarchate's compilation records that the Greek villages around Ordu were deported between October 1916 and September 1917, 'without any military reason' in its words, and names 24 of them; the town's Greeks had averted expulsion for a time by hauling 200 tons of supplies a month to Mesudiye for the vali Cemal Azmi, but were expelled from September 1917 to the Sivas and Kastamonu provinces. A letter of Metropolitan Polycarpos of 29 January 1917 says that the priests of Vona, Andouz and Elez-keuy died after beatings or prison. At Fatsa the Greeks were exiled from November 1916 to February 1917 to Samsun, Tokat and Zile, their houses demolished and seven villages emptied (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 125-127). Each village's fate is given in the Villages section.

title: Enver orders Greeks removed from the coastal strip
summary: War Minister Enver orders the deportation of Greeks living within about 50 km of the Black Sea coast, 'for purely military reasons' in the order's words; German diplomats were told it would be carried out more mildly than the Armenians' deportation. Notables of Samsun, Bafra, Ordu, Tirebolu, Amasya and Çarşamba are deported, and about 200 Greeks are reported hanged for 'desertion'. Despite promises, the Greeks of Kerasous (Giresun) were not allowed to stay at Kulakkaya, 50 km inland, but were driven over the mountains towards Sivas in midwinter.
disputed: The Ottoman security case is given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T03). Vehip Pasha's telegram of 20 November 1916 called the measure 'purely a military measure' (Çilingir, p. 54). Talat told the German ambassador Radowitz in October 1916 that a deportation of all the Greeks of the coast had been planned earlier that year and stopped by Enver so as not to provoke Greece (Hofmann 2011, p. 59). Akçam (2012, p. 109) dates the change of policy to the autumn of 1916 and gives three causes: the Entente's occupation of Lesbos, Chios and Samos, the Russian advance, and an expected Greek entry into the war; on 11 September 1916 Talat told provinces of the west to prepare, in secret, to move the Greeks of border regions inland at an order from Istanbul (pp. 109–110). Akçam quotes no December order of Enver; the Ottoman documents he gives for this phase are Talat's cables of January 1917 (H7-011). Most non-Turkish historians read the removals as demographic homogenisation with security as the pretext (Minasidis 2024), and Pallavicini wrote in January 1918 that the deportations were not dictated by military reasons (quoted by Agtzidis 2005, p. 155). Morris & Ze'evi (p. 385) write that the CUP leadership 'never adopted a policy of genocide or even of comprehensive ethnic cleansing' toward the Ottoman Greeks, but that there was 'real persecution … orchestrated by Constantinople'. Minasidis notes that Vehip Pasha protected some communities near Giresun; German reports say that the Giresun Greeks were driven inland despite a promise to let them stay at Kulakkaya. The 200 hanged rest on 'Greek witnesses' and a British intelligence profile of Refet (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 390: 'apparently hanged'); the Patriarchate's compilation, which Morris & Ze'evi also cite, has no Greeks hanged anywhere in its Pontus part. In that book's English edition 'Amassia' (pp. 120–122) is Samsun (Amisos), so 'Amasya' in the list of towns is probably Samsun counted twice.

title: Deportations from the Kerasous and Ordu hinterland
summary: Villages of the Kerasous (Giresun) hinterland, such as Panagia at Kuşkaya, are marched south over the mountains in winter towards Şebinkarahisar, Zara and Tokat, escorted by paramilitaries who had taken part in the Armenian deportations. By 13 January 1917 the American relief treasurer in Constantinople reported that the Greeks had been expelled from Kerasous. In July 1917, an order of the army headquarters at Suşehri, reported by the American missionary Lyndon Crawford, read: 'By 12 July let no Greek man over 16 and under 50 be found in Ordou. Send all such on into the interior. As for the families, we will send further orders later'; a month later the women and children were being told to 'move on' to places without food. One Kerasous survivor's column of 660 is said to have ended with 10–15 survivors. Chrysanthos (p. 765) describes the winter deportation of the Greeks of Turkish-held Pontus over snow-covered mountains towards Sivas, 'so that they would die on the road of cold, hardship and hunger', without places or figures. Greek Legation reports give the scale. On 7 February 1917: 38 villages of the coast emptied within 24 hours, 23,000 people, driven off under escort without food, clothes or baggage, despite the assurances of the Third Army's commander (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 47). The Legation's table to January 1917 lists 22,356 deported from the Kerasous district, village by village (p. 67). A report of 21 April 1917 gives 88 villages evacuated and burned from December 1916 to February 1917, 'on account of three hundred deserters', and about 30,000 people taken to the Ankara district, a quarter of whom died on the road (p. 13).
disputed: The Kerasous deportation of the winter of 1916–17 and the Ordu men's deportation of July 1917 are attested by American missionary letters (Peet; Crawford) and by German reports (in Hofmann), which confirm the forced march towards Sivas but give no numbers. The three Greek figures for the Kerasous district, 23,000 (38 coastal villages, 7 February 1917), 22,356 (table to January 1917) and about 30,000 (88 villages, 21 April 1917), are counts at different dates from Greek consular reports, published in wartime to rouse opinion; they are the reporters' estimates. The survivor's figures (a column of 660 reduced to 10–15) come from one memoir. The Patriarchate's compilation says that the expulsion of the Kerasous town families (60, then 50 more, posted on 1 January 1917) was averted after the Metropolitan appealed to Suşehri, while Bulancak was emptied in two hours (p. 108); Peet has the Greeks 'expelled from Kerasous'. For Ordu it gives the villages deported between October 1916 and September 1917 (24 named) and the town's expulsion from September 1917, after a Russian shelling on '19th August' when about 2,500 left by sea for Trebizond (pp. 125–126); Chrysanthos has 11 August and about 3,000 (C3-043).

title: Burning and deportation in the Samsun and Bafra districts
summary: On 11 December five Greek villages of the Samsun district are looted, burned and their people deported. The Austro-Hungarian ambassador Pallavicini forwarded reports that 'entire villages including schools and the churches are set on fire' (entry for 14 December), that 'in the district of Samsun they burnt eleven villages' (17 December), and that by 31 December about 18 villages had been burnt completely and 15 partly, with 'around 60 women' raped; 28 villages had been burned by 15 January. The village of Kadıköy is marched south on 28 December. Mass expulsions from Samsun town follow on 10-13 January 1917 and from Bafra on 17-18 January. Deportees go by Kavak and Havza to the provinces of Ankara and Sivas: about 20,000 (Greek Legation) or 30,000 (Karavangelis). An Ottoman report gives 13,406 Greeks sent inland from Samsun (H7-053). The Greek Legation's reports from Samsun (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 48-55) add: 28 more villages burnt in the week from 15 January; eight Bafra villages that grew the best tobacco burnt and twenty more later; Turkish refugees settled in the houses of eight Samsun villages and promised title deeds; the tobacco of villages emptied but not burnt (Aylaskoy, Andreanta, Tekkeköy, Kadıköy) auctioned by the government; all the men of Bafra sent to Boyabat; the richest men of Bafra to Kastamonu, and the merchants of Samsun and Çarşamba to villages around Çorum, Sungurlu, Mecitözü and İskilip. An Interior Ministry official called 'Vehaedin' drew up the lists of those to be deported, which Rafet carried out; he is most likely Bahaeddin Şakir, whom Akçam places in the region from December 1916 (H7-011). The Legation's list of the villages of the Samsun district emptied by February 1917, all those of the coast as far as Alaçam, (Brown & Ion, pp. 68–69), is given in the Villages section.
disputed: The numbers: about 20,000 deported by the Greek Legation's rough estimate (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 52), and 30,000 from the Samsun district by February 1917, a quarter of whom were said to have died already (pp. 55, 68); 30,000 by Karavangelis (cited by Akçam); and 13,406 sent inland from Samsun by the Ottoman report of Refet, which is a floor. The Austrian report puts the people of Aylaskoy and Kadıköy alone at 3,000–4,000 (Hofmann 2011, p. 60). Akçam (2012, p. 112) gives the same counts for the end of December 1916 as Pallavicini (18 villages wholly and 15 partly), but as evacuated where Pallavicini has burnt; Talat's own cable of 26 February 1917 asked Canik which villages had so far been burnt and destroyed 'in bandit raids', so the burning was known in Istanbul. The '28 villages burnt by 15 January' may come from the Legation report's '28 other villages burnt within a week from January 15th' (p. 51). The Patriarchate's letters from Samsun are the same reports as the Greek Legation's, so the two are one witness; its letter of 15 March 1917 says that two-thirds of those expelled had died in the Turkish villages of the Ankara province from want and neglect (p. 122), which Akçam renders as 'massacred'. Its 'February 1916' and 'February 1915' for the Bafra and Samsun burnings (p. 122) are the events of early 1917. The book names Refet's partner as 'Behaeddine Effendi', a special delegate of the Interior Minister from Constantinople (p. 121), which supports reading the Legation's 'Vehaedin' as Bahaeddin Şakir; neither gives his full name. A US consul's post-war inquiry suggested that about 5,000 Greeks and as many Armenians had been 'eliminated' from Samsun by massacre, expulsion and flight, and noted that Samsun's Turks had also suffered heavy losses in the war, in combat and from disease (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 391). Metropolitan Germanos told US officers that 'the greatest cause' of the Bafra deportations was 'religion' (p. 391). Karavangelis' claim that only a tenth to a twentieth of 160,000 Pontic deportees survived is an advocacy figure.

title: German and Austrian protests
summary: The Ottoman Empire's allies, Germany and Austria-Hungary, protest the Pontic deportations. In early February 1917 German diplomats, informed by Austrian reports, concluded that the 'ban' on the Greeks of Samsun, carried out on the pretext of pursuing Greek bands, was a 'large scale' persecution; ambassador Kühlmann (16 February 1917) expected the new grand vizier Talat to end 'the locally committed persecution of Greeks'. Pallavicini raised the matter with the Porte. A text dated 31 January 1917, quoted by Midlarsky as Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg's and by Greek and Turkish writers as an Austrian Foreign Ministry document sent to Berlin, says the Turks 'plan to eliminate the Greek element as enemies of the state, as they did earlier with the Armenians'. The deportations slow in 1917 but those deported are not returned until after the armistice.
disputed: The German protests and assessments are documented by Hofmann (2011, pp. 59–61) from the German Foreign Office archive, as published by Fotiadis. The sentence dated 31 January 1917 has been given to different authors: Midlarsky quotes it as Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg's, and Hofmann's web essay and Kelly (2023, p. 239) cite only Midlarsky; Çetinoğlu (after Frangos 2012, p. 118) and Çilingir (pp. 56–57) quote it as a document of the Austrian Foreign Ministry sent to Berlin. Since German diplomats were using Austrian information in early February 1917 (Hofmann 2011, p. 60), it is probably an Austrian text forwarded to Berlin and later attributed to the chancellor; we have not found the original. It should not be confused with Talat's remark to an Austrian agent in January 1916 (H7-054).

title: 1917: the soldiers' soviet, the Youth Union and the evacuation of the Ordu Greeks
summary: After the February revolution, Chrysanthos writes, the Russian army deposed its officers, and he accepted a seat on the Trebizond soldiers' soviet 'ἵνα διαφωτίζῃ' (to enlighten it). A 'Ἐθνικὴ Ἕνωσις τῶν Νέων' (National Union of Youth) was founded in Trebizond and Rize. On 11 August 1917 the Bolshevik fleet bombarded Turkish-held Ordu; the Greek population rushed into the sea towards the ships, and the Russians took '3.000 περίπου ψυχὰς' (about 3,000 souls) to Trebizond, where they were housed within three hours.
disputed: The Patriarchate's compilation dates the shelling of Ordu to '19th August' and gives about 2,500 taken to Trebizond (p. 125).

title: Chrysanthos' account: the çete campaign against the Greek villages, self-defence, and the flight of half the Greeks to Russia
summary: Chrysanthos writes that from December 1917 Turkish leaders 'ἐξαπέλυσαν στίφη «τσετέδων»' (let loose bands of çetes) on the unguarded countryside 'ἵνα τρομοκρατηθῇ ὁ χριστιανικὸς κόσμος καὶ μεταναστεύσῃ εἰς Ῥωσίαν' (to terrorise the Christians into emigrating to Russia). The Youth Union armed villagers with weapons left by the Bolshevik authorities, about 80 young men held Boz Tepe, and a district defence (Trebizond, Sourmena, Matsouka, Santa, Mesochaldion) repelled 'thousands' of çetes led by Turkish officers 'for whole months'. The village of Uz was destroyed and its people came to Trebizond naked. In the end 'κατωρθώθη νὰ περισωθῇ τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ Ἑλληνικοῦ πληθυσμοῦ τῆς Τραπεζουσίας χώρας, τοῦ ἑτέρου ἡμίσεος μεταναστεύσαντος εἰς Ῥωσίαν' (half the Greek population of the Trebizond region was saved, the other half having emigrated to Russia).

title: Erzincan armistice; the Russian army dissolves
summary: After the revolutions of 1917 the Russian Caucasus Army falls apart. The armistice of Erzincan ends fighting on 18 December 1917 (5 December Old Style), and Russian soldiers begin leaving Trebizond in late December. On 11/24 December the French military representative in Tiflis, Colonel Chardigny, with the approval of his British and American colleagues, asked Chrysanthos to help the Russian General Kolosowski raise a Greek volunteer regiment at Trebizond, part of a Greek division under General Ananias, for order in the city and defence against the Turks; Chrysanthos was cautious, fearing to inflame the Muslims. Turkish armed bands grow bolder (US consul, late January 1918). Chrysanthos appeals to Vehip Pasha about attacks on Christians and distributes arms to Greek villages for self-defence; Santa is among the districts saved.
disputed: The armistice is dated 5 December 1917 in the Russian (Old Style) calendar, the date some English works give, and 18 December in the New Style used in this chapter. The Allied plan for a Greek regiment is documented by a French officer's letter printed in a Greek advocacy pamphlet; that the regiment was not formed rests on Georganopoulos, after Chrysanthos' reply. The arming of the villages for self-defence rests on Greek sources.

title: Armenian irregulars' killings of Muslims during the Russian withdrawal (context)
summary: As the Russian army melts away, Armenian irregular units left holding the front kill Muslim villagers around Erzincan and Erzurum. Ottoman commanders publicised these killings and they were used to justify the Ottoman advance. This is outside the core region but shaped Muslim fears in Pontus.

title: Pontic Greeks leave with the Russian army for the Caucasus and Russia
summary: Fearing reprisals, Greeks of eastern Pontus follow the retreating Russians to Batum, Sukhumi, Novorossiysk, the Kuban, Rostov and the Azov towns, adding to the older Pontic communities there. The Greeks of Kars and Ardahan follow in 1918–20.

Chrysanthos says that half the Greeks of the Trebizond region left for Russia in 1918 (C3-045); against his count of 1913–14 that would be about 23,000–25,000, a reckoning of ours, not his figure.

title: The Ottoman return to Pontus
summary: Vehip Pasha's Third Army advances into the vacuum: Kelkit (7 Feb), Erzincan (13 Feb), Bayburt (19 Feb), Tercan (22 Feb) and Trebizond (23 Feb 1918, by Kâzım Bey's letter and Chrysanthos; 24 Feb in Erickson), with troops also landed by sea; Erzurum follows on 12 March. An ammunition depot explodes at Trebizond with about 600 killed. The head of the Capuchin mission recorded that the city's commander announced orders from Constantinople to deport all the Greeks, men, women, old people and children, inland, and that Chrysanthos protested; Turkish irregular bands burned and killed in the villages around the city, and many Greeks left for Batum. Greek sources say Chrysanthos' negotiations and his record towards Muslims spared the Greeks of the city from reprisals. The divisional commander Kâzım Bey's letter of 22 February (Rumi 22/2/1334), printed in facsimile by Chrysanthos, announced that the troops would occupy the city by daylight on 23/2/1334 ('10 Şubat 1918' in the Julian style); Chrysanthos drove to Kâzım's headquarters at Kryoneri and brought him into the city, where Russian troops rendered honours (Chrysanthos, a participant).
disputed: That the Greeks of Trebizond were spared because of Chrysanthos rests on Greek accounts (Chrysanthos 1933, pp. 767–772; Vehip's letter, as printed in 1919–22). The Capuchin diary shows that a deportation of all the Greeks was ordered after the Ottoman return, but not how far it was carried out. Morris & Ze'evi (p. 390), after a Greek metropolitan's letter of October 1918, say that the Ottomans 'continued expelling Greeks systematically' in the reconquered vilayet; the letter is printed in the Patriarchate's compilation under 'Chryssostomos, the Metropolitan of Trebizonde' (p. 112), an error for Chrysanthos. The entry into Trebizond is dated 23 February 1918 by Kâzım's letter and Chrysanthos' narrative, 24 February by Erickson (2001, p. 183).

title: Brest-Litovsk, the Trebizond conference, Batum and Kars
summary: By the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (3 March) Russia cedes Kars, Ardahan and Batum. Ottoman and Transcaucasian delegates meet at Trebizond from 14 March; talks fail and Ottoman troops take Batum (14 April) and Kars (25 April). The Treaty of Batum (4 June) closes the Ottoman–Transcaucasian war. In March 1918 Hüseyin Rauf Bey, Ali Rıza Bey, the vali and staff officers, in Trebizond for the talks with the Georgian prime minister, met at Chrysanthos's villa to discuss post-war cooperation of the peoples of the East; the metropolis's committee meanwhile fed and clothed returning Muslim refugees (Chrysanthos, pp. 771-772).

title: Topal Osman returns to power in Giresun; first nationalist killings
summary: In the first months after the armistice, Unionist networks arm Muslim villagers and bands. A US officer at Samsun reported in January 1919 that the authorities had armed the Turkish villagers of the Tsinik district in 'a carefully laid down plan … to eliminate the Greek and Armenian elements'. The French commissioner at Trebizond reported returning Greek refugees murdered as alleged revolutionaries (January), 600 returnees prevented from landing (late May), and organised persecution of Greeks at Kerasous, Merzifon and Bulancak (4 June); in September British officers reported that 'public security all along the Black Sea Coast was very bad'. Giresun's Defence of Rights committee mandates Topal Osman to act against what it called the Greek guerrilla groups; by mid-1919 he is mayor of Giresun, which the Ottoman investigating judge at Trebizond cited as proof that the government would not punish the massacrers of 1915. A Catholic missionary reported that his roughly 600 Laz were responsible for many murders in Giresun, and on 19 December 1919 the head of the Capuchin mission wrote that the Giresun nationalists had decided in council to 'get rid of the Christians' but had postponed it, keeping them as hostages until the Paris decisions were known. Returning Greek refugees near Merzifon formed bands to defend themselves and recover their property. In September 1919 an armed band attacks Santa women returning from Trebizond, and the guerrillas of Santa dig in for the winter.
disputed: The Armenian Patriarchate's report dates Topal Osman's appointment as mayor to August 1919 (Kévorkian), but the Ottoman investigating judge at Trebizond, Karagueuzian, already wrote in June 1919 that he had been 'officially named mayor'. The reports of 1919 come from French, American and Catholic observers, from the Armenian Patriarchate and from Greek sources. The figure of 12,000 Pontic Greeks killed in 1919 is often quoted; we found no source for it.
