title: The Greek memorandum on Pontus, and the Turkish response in Trebizond
summary: A Greek memorandum to the Peace Conference (Oeconomos) asks for self-determination for Pontus and puts its pre-war Greek population at 700,000. In Trebizond, Muslims found the Trabzon Society for the Defence of National Rights in February 1919 to oppose any Pontic or Armenian claim; an Armenian Patriarchate report of 17 February 1919 describes Turkish notables implicated in the wartime massacres forming a 'pan-Turk committee' with branches in the other towns of the vilayet.
disputed: The 700,000 was a figure made for the case; the Greek census of 1910–12 counted 400,586 in the six metropolises. Other claims ran higher: over 800,000 Greeks in Pontus plus 250,000 refugees in Russia (Le Martyre du Pont-Euxin, 1922, p. 6), and some two million between Rize and Sinop (Pontic spokesmen). Western diplomats thought about 450,000 more likely (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 382, citing a Foreign Office minute by Toynbee of December 1918). The 850,000 of 1920 included about 250,000 in Russia and the Caucasus; we have not consulted the memorandum of 1919 and do not know whether its 700,000 did the same.

title: The Trabzon court-martial
summary: An Ottoman court-martial in Constantinople tries the officials of the Trebizond vilayet for the Armenian deportations. Witnesses include the Giresun governor Arif Bey, who said Azmi ordered deportations 'towards Mosul by way of the Black Sea', meaning drowning. Cemal Azmi and the CUP secretary Nail Bey are sentenced to death in absentia. Azmi is shot in Berlin by an Armenian avenger on 17 April 1922.
disputed: Most accounts date the verdict to 22 May 1919; the published verdict carries the date 8 July 1919. The trial opened about 26 March.

title: Chrysanthos at the Peace Conference
summary: Chrysanthos arrives in Paris on 29 April with an 18-page memorandum for an independent Pontic republic. On 16 May, with Venizelos' consent, he meets President Wilson and raises an American or Greek mandate for Pontus. The proposed state was to cover the sancaks of Trebizond, Samsun (Canik), Sinop and Amasya, later extended to Karahisar.
disputed: Wilson's reported promise to vote for independence comes from Greek accounts. Chrysanthos' position is reported differently: the French commissioner Lépissier (March 1919) counted him among the leaders of a movement for autonomy and then union with Greece (Georganopoulos, p. 77), whereas the American Chesbrough, who toured Pontus in the summer of 1919, reported that many influential Greeks of Trebizond 'view this policy [of separatism] with disfavor' and that 'the local Greek Archbishop … was also opposed' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 383). Chrysanthos' own account of 1933 (pp. 772–775) presents his line in Paris as a Greek-Muslim administration of Pontus 'on equal terms' ('ἐν ἰσοπολιτείᾳ'), with a possible federation with Armenia, cites his memorandum La question du Pont-Euxin of 2 May 1919, and is silent on an independent republic and on Wilson. It was written fourteen years later and should be weighed against the documents of 1919.

title: The Greek landing at Smyrna (context)
summary: Greek troops land at Smyrna under Allied mandate, with killings of Turkish civilians on the first day. The landing begins the Greco-Turkish war of 1919–22 and turns Turkish opinion; from now on Pontic Greeks were treated as a fifth column of an enemy state.
sources_primary: Inter-Allied Commission of Inquiry report (1919)

date_text: 19 May 1919 (Havza 28 May; Amasya 22 June; Erzurum 23 July – 7 Aug; Sivas 4–11 Sept)
title: Mustafa Kemal lands at Samsun
summary: Mustafa Kemal arrives at Samsun aboard the Bandırma as inspector of the Ninth Army, officially to restore order. From Havza (circular of 28 May) and Amasya (circular of 22 June) he organises resistance, then the congresses of Erzurum and Sivas. In Turkey 19 May is the start of the National Struggle; in Greece it is the day of remembrance of the Pontic genocide.

The Turkish foreign ministry's objection to the Greek day of remembrance is given there too (H7-T09).

title: Repatriation of Caucasus Greeks to Greece
summary: In summer 1919 the Greek Ministry of Relief, under Nikos Kazantzakis, sends a mission to the Caucasus to bring Greeks to Macedonia. Between May 1920 and February 1921, by Topalidis' account, about 53,000 Pontic Greeks sail from Batum to Greece, three-quarters of them from Kars and Ardahan, which fell to the Turkish army in the war with Armenia (Kars, 30 Oct 1920).
disputed: The Kazantzakis mission at Batum is attested by a Greek Foreign Ministry document of 1 August 1919 (Georganopoulos, n. 71). Agtzidis (2001, p. 165) names its members (Kazantzakis, Polemarchakis, Zervos), quotes Kazantzakis' estimate that about 100,000 Greeks of Transcaucasia wished to move to Greece, and says that the relief service fed more than 70,000 refugees. In July 1919 the Greek government, under British pressure, for a time stopped the return of refugees from southern Russia to Pontus (Georganopoulos, p. 81). The 53,000 who sailed in 1920–21 is Topalidis' figure; we have not found it in another source.

title: Negotiations in Constantinople: ten terms for an autonomous Pontus under mandate
summary: Chrysanthos writes that in Constantinople in September 1919 he negotiated with the former vali Süleyman Necmi Bey, the Trebizond deputy Hafız Mehmed Bey, the former grand vizier İzzet Pasha and Kara Vasıf Bey (Kemal's representatives) 'περὶ τῆς ἐν ἰσοπολιτείᾳ Ἑλλήνων καὶ Μουσουλμάνων αὐτονομίας τοῦ Πόντου ὑπὸ ἐντολὴν (mandat) τῆς κοινωνίας τῶν ἐθνῶν' (on the autonomy of Pontus, with Greeks and Muslims equal, under a League of Nations mandate). He prints ten terms written in Turkish in Hafız Mehmed's hand (fig. 120): a mandate; free community institutions and courts; courts, councils, police and gendarmerie half Muslim and half Greek; Greek deputies, ministers and battalions; and Greek as an official language.

title: The Pontic–Armenian confederation plan
summary: Chrysanthos and the Greek consul Stavridakis negotiate in Tiflis and Yerevan; letters between Chrysanthos and the Armenian prime minister Khatisian (10–16 January 1920) agree in principle on a confederation, with an autonomous Pontus sharing foreign policy, customs and currency with Armenia. A military pact foresaw a Greek landing at Trebizond as the Armenians advanced on Erzurum. The Entente (February) and the San Remo conference (April 1920) refuse to give Trebizond to Armenia. Chrysanthos (pp. 775–776) also records a joint telegram of 16 January to the Greek and Armenian delegations in Paris, and British refusals (December 1919 - January 1920) of Pontic battalions at Batum and of a Greek landing at Trebizond.

title: The Ankara assembly and the Treaty of Sèvres
summary: The Grand National Assembly opens in Ankara on 23 April 1920. The Treaty of Sèvres (10 August) leaves the Turkish–Armenian frontier in the vilayets of Erzurum, Trebizond, Van and Bitlis to arbitration (article 89); it says nothing about Pontus. In May Venizelos told the Greek parliament that an independent Pontus could not be realised.
sources_primary: Treaty of Sèvres, art. 89
sources_modern: Yerasimos 1989

title: Escalation in 1920: Giresun, Samsun, Ordu
summary: In Giresun, Topal Osman, now mayor, had Greek houses destroyed and shops looted (February 1920, according to an Armenian Patriarchate report); from the night of 13 August 1920 he imprisoned all the Christian men and had five or six shot each evening until the community paid 300,000 lira, while women were raped. Greek men are deported inland from Giresun and Samsun. A British officer at Samsun reports Kemalist officers preaching the extermination of Christians, and placards at Ünye and Fatsa blaming the Christians for the occupation (spring 1920); Bishop Polykarpos of Ordu is arrested on his return from Kastamonu and taken to Ankara (early June 1920); in June, a French consular report says, the Kemalists kill Greeks mainly around Bafra. In November 1920 a Kemalist militia burns eight Greek villages near Vezirköprü with some 600 dead (Armenian Patriarchate report). In October Osman is given authority over the coast from İnebolu to Hopa. In December 1920, according to an Armenian Patriarchate report, Greek men of 18–34 are mobilised into labour battalions, and the arrests of Greek notables across Pontus begin, the prelude to the Amasya trials.
disputed: The Giresun ransom rests on the minutes of the Armenian-Greek Section of the British High Commission, which record what the Patriarchate's representatives told the British (Hofmann 2011, p. 67), and on Armenian Patriarchate reports. Kévorkian gives about sixty executed and dates the destruction of Greek houses to February 1920; Morris & Ze'evi date the imprisonment to 13 August 1920.

title: Venizelos' last Pontic plan, and his fall
summary: Venizelos proposes to Lloyd George an advance on Ankara and a landing at Trebizond to set up a Pontic republic; the British Cabinet defers the idea on 12 October. Venizelos loses the Greek election of 14 November 1920, which ends the Pontic project.
sources_primary: British Cabinet minutes, 12 Oct 1920

title: The Sivas and Kastamonu independence tribunals in Pontus
summary: Independence tribunals, created by the Ankara assembly on 18 September 1920 against desertion and given jurisdiction over treason and espionage on 26 September, sit in the Pontus before the Samsun tribunal. The Sivas tribunal, mostly sitting at Amasya, heard 160 cases (besides desertion), passed 122 death sentences, of which 12 were carried out, and between 20 October 1920 and 15 March 1921 punished 454 Greeks for espionage, ignoring summonses, aiding bandits, desertion, joining Greek bands, 'Ponticism' (Pontusçuluk), banditry and 'suspicious behaviour'. The Kastamonu tribunal, covering Sinop and the western coast, passed 420 sentences between 16 October 1920 and 2 March 1921 and executed 11; the records do not say how many were Greek. All but the Ankara tribunal were abolished on 17 February 1921 and re-established in July.
disputed: The figures come from the tribunals' own dockets, as read in the parliamentary archive by the Turkish historian Aybars and reported by Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, Turkish journalists who call the events a genocide. They are counts of persons sentenced, not of the guilty, and the charges are the tribunals' own.

title: Wilson's arbitral award on the Turkish–Armenian frontier
summary: Wilson's 'Decision … respecting the Frontier between Turkey and Armenia' (Washington, 22 November 1920) awards Armenia the city and harbour of Trebizond and the 'Karshut' (Harşit) valley 'ending at the town of Tireboli'. The line runs from the Kelkit Chai north to Borgha Paya (about 38 km south-west of Gümüşhane), then along the Pontic crest to the sea 'approximately 9 kilometers eastward from the city of Kerasun', about 1 km west of Keşap. Kerasun and Ordu 'and hinterland' stay Turkish. Wilson notes that the Pontic request concerned 'the region stretching from Riza to a point west of Sinope' and that his jurisdiction 'does not include the possibility of decision or recommendation by me' on it; that the majority in the vilayet was Muslim; and that 'the Armenian element was undeniably inferior numerically to the Greek portion of the Christian minority'. The award was never applied: Armenia had already been defeated, and signed the Treaty of Alexandropol on 2-3 December 1920.
disputed: Some works date the Treaty of Alexandropol to 2 November; the usual date is the night of 2–3 December 1920.
sources_primary: Wilson's arbitral decision, Washington, 22 Nov 1920, with Colby's despatch No. 671, in FRUS 1920 vol. III, doc. 949 (history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1920v03/d949)

title: The Central Army (Merkez Ordusu) under Nureddin Pasha
summary: On 9 December 1920 Ankara forms the Central Army, about 15,000 men under Nureddin Pasha with headquarters at Amasya, to deal with the 'Pontic question' and the Kurdish Alevi rising of Koçgiri; it suppresses Koçgiri and carries out the operations and deportations in Pontus, working with irregulars such as Topal Osman's men. Martial law is declared in Canik, Tokat, Amasya and Çorum on 5 March 1921. Nureddin, who called the Greeks 'a snake' whose 'poison' was their women, is removed by the Assembly on 3 November 1921 on charges that included using irregular forces, taking a bribe from a Pontic Greek, ordering public plunder during the relocation of the Greeks and 'harming the Muslims by setting the stage for the Pontians to take to the mountains'; at Mustafa Kemal's insistence the Assembly dropped his trial in January 1922, and the army was abolished on 8 February 1922.
disputed: Who was responsible for the excesses of 1921 is disputed: Turkish deputies blamed Nureddin personally; others stress that Kemal protected him and that the deportation policy was Ankara's. According to the closed sessions of 16–17 January 1922, Nureddin had also ordered Topal Osman to kill the Koçgiri leaders who had agreed to negotiate, and had barred 56 Samsun notables who objected to the deportation of Greek women and children from travelling (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 14, n. 16). Morris & Ze'evi write that 'Kemal knew how to get the worst out of his subordinates' (p. 404), that Nureddin was charged with 'the mal-execution of his orders', as US diplomats were told (p. 406), and quote Yusuf Kemal on 'local officials' exaggerated zeal' (p. 415); Korucu & Dağlıoğlu (p. 27) call Nureddin 'one of the primary perpetrators'; Hofmann (2011, p. 76) notes that no action was taken against Osman after Merzifon. The Sivas tribunal's record (160 cases besides desertion, 122 death sentences, of which 12 were carried out) is not broken down by community in the summary we have read. Ankara's own description of the army's mission, against a 'Pontus' rising, is given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T04).

title: Turkish state counts of Greeks killed in the Pontus operations, 1921–1923
summary: Turkish military and parliamentary records count the Greeks killed in the Pontus operations: 1,275 killed (of 4,444 'neutralised') between 29 December 1921 and 20 March 1922, and 3,777 'armed Greeks' killed between 20 March and 15 May 1922 (Interior Minister Fethi in closed session, 10 June 1922); about 15,000 killed or captured in the two months after 18 February 1922 (the 10th Division's commander); and, when the operations ended in February 1923, 11,198 Greeks killed and 10,886 surrendered. title: Merzifon, Samsun and Zile: the searches and the first arrests for Amasya
summary: At the end of January 1921 the Central Army arrests 75 Greeks of Samsun for the Sivas Independence Tribunal, and in February Mustafa Kemal orders such arrests continued. In February a Muslim teacher of Anatolia College at Merzifon (named in Turkish accounts as Zeki Bey) is murdered by an unknown assailant. On 16 February the Central Army searches the college, the American hospital and the Samsun metropolis; no arms are found, but the searchers seize papers they deem 'subversive'. Four teachers and two students, all members of the college's Greek literary society, called 'Pontos', are arrested; the college is closed and 29 of its 32 missionaries expelled. According to an Armenian Patriarchate report, Bishop Euthymios of Zela and about 100 notables of Zile were deported on 15 February 1921, and the protosynkellos Platon is sent to the tribunal; on 21 July 1921 the same source reported that Euthymios had died in Amasya prison of ill-treatment.
disputed: How many of the arrested were executed: two teachers and one student (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 412) or all six (Kyriakidis, p. 57). Biber dates the sending of Euthymios and Platon to the tribunal to 9 February 1921; the Armenian Patriarchate's report from Zile has Euthymios deported on 15 February. No source we have read says who killed the teacher. Ankara's use of the seized papers as proof of a Pontic conspiracy is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T05).

title: The Koçgiri rebellion and its suppression (context)
summary: Alevi Kurds of the Koçgiri region (Zara, İmranlı) rise for autonomy. The Central Army crushes the revolt, using Topal Osman's Giresun men as the 47th Regiment; deputies later accused Nureddin of excesses in Sivas. The same units then turned to Pontus.

title: Labour-battalion call-up and village burnings in western Pontus
summary: In February 1921 Interior Minister Fethi, after visiting the region, urges Kemal to authorise 'more expeditious and larger scale' deportations. On 2 March the Assembly orders labour battalions for non-Muslims re-formed, and in March about 1,500 non-Muslim men of Havza, Merzifon, Tokat, Çorum, Sivas and Samsun are sent to them; on 18 April the battalions at Samsun, Havza, Merzifon, Sivas and Tokat held 597, 339, 204, 285 and 201 men, and in May they were sent east of the Trabzon–Erzincan line to stop desertions (Çilingir, pp. 112–114). On 16 April, according to an Armenian Patriarchate report, the men of Gümüşhane aged 15–50 are called up. On 26 March Greece declared a naval blockade of the Turkish Black Sea coast. From spring the Central Army and çetes attack Greek villages around Alaçam, Bafra, Çarşamba, Havza and Vezirköprü. For the operation in the Nebyan mountains the army's orders were to 'chasten the Greeks so they never again attempt banditry' and to 'destroy villages which serve as bandit shelters', and the deputy governor of Samsun proposed that the people of all the Greek villages of the area be expelled inland, so that they would nowhere be a majority, and Turks settled in their place (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, pp. 24–25, after Balcıoğlu). In May all Christian males over 12 at Alaçam are held and massacred. US officers at Samsun quoted an American missionary that about 100 Greek villages south of Bafra had been destroyed in a few days from 17 May, the villagers murdered and 'the priests … crucified', and judged the campaign 'directed by high authority—probably Angora'.
disputed: The 'about 100 villages' south of Bafra is a missionary's figure, relayed by the US destroyers Fox and Overton. The Alaçam massacre reached the British through the Patriarchate's representatives, in the minutes of the Armenian-Greek Section of the British High Commission. The orders' language of 'banditry', and the claim that the villages sheltered bands, are the army's own framing (H7-T04, H7-T08). The deputy governor's proposal is reported, not quoted.

title: Topal Osman in Samsun, Merzifon, Giresun and Tirebolu
summary: In Samsun, nightly murders in spring 1921 are followed by the first deportation of 200 men on 28 May. Topal Osman's men enter the town; a Constantinople press dispatch quoted by the British diplomat Rendel says he killed ten Greeks on arrival, arrested about 800 Greek clerks of the American Tobacco Company and 1,500 other Greeks, and deported them inland. Seventy Turkish notables telegraphed Kemal that it was against their religion to massacre women and children, and the town's mufti issued a fatwa to the same effect; Kemal replied that exile was 'a merciful act', and Osman was recalled. At Merzifon, from 23–24 July, Osman's band and then local men, gendarmes and troops spend more than a week killing, raping and looting; men and boys sheltering in the French school, which is burned, are taken out and shot. Of 2,000–2,500 Christians almost all the men are killed, and the remaining Greeks deported. Osman then moves to Tirebolu and Giresun, where many Greeks are killed or deported; he is welcomed in Ankara and given command of 6,000 men.
disputed: The Merzifon toll is given as 'upwards of 700' (Hosford, quoted by Rendel; Hofmann 2011, p. 77); 950 (the Armenian-Greek Section, and the British government in the Commons, 7 November 1921); about 1,000 in one week, 24–31 July (Anthony, cited by Kyriakidis, p. 51); about 1,200 (Bristol and Anthony, cited by Morris & Ze'evi, n. 223); 'more than a thousand' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 411); and 300 Armenians and Greeks (the Ottoman officer Mehmed Rauf, cited by Kévorkian). The damage: about 400 Armenian houses burned and the Greek quarter left untouched (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 413), or the Greek quarter burned (Rauf's deposition; the Black Book). The 800 tobacco clerks come from a press dispatch quoted by Rendel. The nationalists' denials are under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T06).

title: İnebolu shelled; Ankara orders Greek men off the coast
summary: On 29 May 1921 the idea of moving Greek men of certain ages from the Black Sea coast inland is raised in Ankara. A Greek naval squadron arrives in the Black Sea in summer 1921, stops Turkish ships and takes passengers prisoner, and on 9 June lightly shells İnebolu, without casualties according to an Italian witness. On 12 June the Ankara government orders the removal inland of all Greeks aged 15 to 50 living on the coast, applied from 16 June through the Central Army; in July the whole Black Sea coast is declared a war zone as from 12 June.
disputed: The age band is 15–50 in the Turkish order and in the US naval notes on the Samsun round-up of 16 June (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 410), 15–55 in a British cabinet paper (CAB 24/131, cited by Biber). Morris & Ze'evi (p. 407) record the Italian Count Schmeccia's view that the İnebolu bombardment 'produced no casualties' and was 'merely a Turkish "excuse for the massacres"', and note that the campaign had begun weeks before. The studies of the Turkish documents differ slightly on the sequence: Biber (from BCA 941/95-12) has the war zone declared on 12 June and the decree on 16 June; Korucu & Dağlıoğlu (pp. 12–13) have the order issued on 12 June and applied on 16 June, and the war zone declared in July with effect from 12 June. Ankara's stated reasons are under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T06). The Greek navy's documented shelling of Samsun came a year later, on 7 June 1922 (H6-061).

title: The 1921 deportations of Pontic men, then women and children
summary: Convoys of men leave Samsun (from 16 June), Bafra and Alaçam; Greek men of 15–50 are rounded up at Samsun from 16 June and, according to an Armenian Patriarchate report, at Ordu, Fatsa, Ünye and Çarşamba on 27 June. On the road the escorts kill many: a deportee of the third Samsun convoy wrote that 660 were killed by the gendarmes as the column descended a mountain; Cosmos Lilidas said that of his convoy of about 1,000, which left Samsun around 20 June, 292 remained after the guards opened fire near 'Djinbush'; Stanley Hopkins of Near East Relief reported 550 Greeks executed at Kavak on 26 June and 1,300 on 15 August; and Lazistan deputies told the Assembly that the first convoy from Samsun was attacked six hours outside the town. From mid-July the remaining women and children are ordered to go too: Admiral Bristol asked Kemal on 18 July to stop it, and the Apostolic Delegate Dolci asked him on 18 August to cancel an order to exile 5,000 women and children from near Samsun; Samsun's Muslim notables protested, and the deportations there were paused in July. The route ran Samsun-Kavak-Havza-Amasya-Tokat-Sivas-Harput, then on to Diyarbakır, Bitlis and Van. At Mezre-Harput Mark Ward registered 20,526 deportees between May 1921 and February 1922, about 18,000 of them Greeks. According to Central Army records, 63,844 Greeks had been moved by November 1921, or, district by district, 58,974 (Samsun 27,995; Amasya 14,000; Giresun 8,500; Ordu 4,910; Sivas 1,448; Tokat 1,000; Çorum 571; Sinop 550) to Sivas, Tokat, Yozgat, Çorum, Şebinkarahisar and further.
disputed: Other figures: 216 killed near Kavak, 258 at 'Djib-is-han' and 700 of 850 at 'Tsakali on the Mamour-dagh', that is Çakallı on the Samsun–Kavak road (the Patriarchate, 13/26 November 1921, in Le Martyre du Pont-Euxin, p. 44); 660 and 530 in two groups (US destroyer logs, cited by Kyriakidis, p. 51); 3,000 killed around Kavak (one testimony, p. 52). The Armenian Patriarchate's Information Bureau reported 30,000 Greeks massacred between Ünye and Samsun by August and 6,500 of 7,000 conscripts killed on the Samsun–Kavak road on 2 August (Kévorkian, n. 100); these are far above any other source and are not confirmed. Ward's total is 20,526 in Morris & Ze'evi (p. 426); his pamphlet gives 20,378. The two Central Army counts (63,844 and 58,974) come from the same records through different works of Balcıoğlu; Çilingir's 'about 59,000' matches the second. Overall estimates: 'well over 35,000' deported from Pontus in 1921 (Rendel), and 'at least 75,000', of whom 20,000 survived (missionaries, reported by the US consul at Aleppo in March 1922; Morris & Ze'evi, p. 415). Of 30,000 who passed Sivas, 5,000 died before Harput and 5,000 escaped (Yowell and Ward; Morris & Ze'evi, p. 425).

title: Trebizond men marched inland; Santa occupied and deported
summary: In early April 1921 elders of the Greek community of Trebizond, among them the publisher Nikos Kapetanidis and Matthaios Kofidis, are imprisoned on charges of planning a Pontic state; US naval reports have the men of Trebizond deported in groups of fifty twice a week in May and about 300 Greeks on their way to Erzurum by the end of July. In August over 500 Greek men who reported for paid 'fortification work' are imprisoned, deported in groups of fifty and many of them shot at night in groups of ten, according to two refugee witnesses. In early September the army orders the men of Santa aged 20-45 to enlist; on 6 September it occupies three of the Santa villages, and on 10-12 September the people of six villages and then Pistofantoi are deported by way of Erzurum, where typhus broke out. About 370 reached their place of exile in October 1921 and fewer than 200 came back in January 1923. Kourtidis' guerrillas and 300-400 women and children stay in the mountains and fight on until 1923.
disputed: The 'fortification work' episode of August 1921 rests on two Greek refugees' statements recorded by the British (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 423). The deportation of Trebizond's men in groups of fifty is dated May 1921 in the US naval reports cited by Kyriakidis, and May 1922 by Rumbold and by Morris & Ze'evi (p. 419; H6-060); it may have happened in both years. The place 'Hunuz' (Χουνούς) on the Santa route has not been identified.

title: The Samsun Independence Tribunal at Amasya
summary: The Samsun Independence Tribunal (İstiklâl Mahkemesi), which began work on 17 August 1921 with jurisdiction over Tokat, Amasya, Samsun, Ordu, Giresun and Sivas but sitting at Amasya, tries Greek notables arrested since December 1920 on charges of working for a Pontic state. Those hanged include the former deputy Matthaios Kofidis, the journalist Nikos Kapetanidis, the Ottoman Bank director at Samsun Pavlos Papadopoulos, teachers of Anatolia College and the archimandrite Platon Aivazidis, about seventy years old; Bishop Euthymios of Zela had died in prison at Amasya. Chrysanthos, Germanos of Amaseia, Polykarpos of Neocaesarea and Laurentios of Chaldia were condemned in absentia. By its own records the tribunal had executed 177 people (three of them Muslims) and sentenced 74 to death in absentia by 10 October 1921, and by December it had passed 1,163 sentences, 622 of them death sentences (137 in absentia). Chrysanthos (pp. 775-782) writes that Greek clergy and notables were hanged 'by the hundreds', naming Kofidis as the representative of the metropolis of Trebizond; these are round words, not a count, and he does not name the tribunal.
disputed: The court was the Samsun Independence Tribunal sitting at Amasya; a separate Amasya tribunal, created on 27 July 1922, never sat and was abolished on 27 November 1922 (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 18). There is no single confirmed figure for the hangings. By the tribunal's records 177 had been executed and 74 sentenced in absentia by 10 October 1921, of 622 death sentences in all (Aybars, cited by Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, pp. 17–18); Tsirkinidis gives 177 hanged and 44 in absentia; the 622 include those in absentia and cover the whole region and period, not only Amasya. Hosford gave about 250 hanged at Amasya in September, the Armenian-Greek Section 168 (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 416–417); the Patriarch's telegram counted 168 Greeks and 3 Armenians named in the Samsun papers of 18, 19 and 25 September (Hofmann, p. 75); Tepeyran, and Shaw as cited by Morris & Ze'evi (n. 255), give 485 death sentences. The Ehali lists of the executed, reprinted in the Black Book, name about 60 (list of 12/25 September) and about 92 executed at Amasya 'on 8 September 1921', three of them Armenians; Vergeti counts the names as 155, Çilingir as 132. Kyriakidis (p. 79, after Fotiadis) has 72 hanged in the square of Amasya on 8/21 September 1921, one day in the Old and New Styles, which is probably what Hofmann gives as '8 and 21 September'. The teachers of Anatolia College executed are given as two teachers and one student (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 412) or four teachers and two students (Kyriakidis 2023, p. 57); the Patriarchate names Prof. Georges Papamarkou, D. Theocharidis and the missionary Paul Bacon. Platon is a protosynkellos or archimandrite in some accounts and 'Metropolitan of Samsun' or 'Metropolitan Vicar of Samsun' in others; Morris & Ze'evi repeat the confusion (p. 417). Scholars call the sentences 'arbitrary' (Hofmann 2011, p. 74), the trials a 'parody' (Agtzidis 2005, p. 212) and the courts 'sham' ones whose archives are still closed (Çetinoğlu). Turkish historiography's view of the trials, as the lawful suppression of a conspiracy, is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T04, H7-T07).

title: Fethi's 1922 sweep of the Pontic mountains
summary: After the Central Army is dissolved, Interior Minister Fethi publishes a proclamation (14 February 1922) and launches a new operation on 18 February under the 10th Division. Its commander reported about 15,000 Greeks killed or captured in some two months; Fethi told a closed session that 3,777 'armed Greeks' had been killed between 20 March and 15 May (H6-078). In February the hinterland of Bafra was swept; a telegram from 21 Greek and Circassian refugees from Bafra says rewards were offered for heads and 'five sacks full of heads' were brought in, and that Bafra Circassians hid about 140 Greek neighbours. Metropolitan Kyrillos of Rhodopolis was arrested at Trebizond, about April 1922, accused of supplying the 'rebellious Greeks' with arms and food; a friendly judge saved him by transferring the case to the civil court, and he was freed in 1923.

title: The last deportations
summary: About 1,324 Greeks, mostly women and children, are deported from Samsun on 10–11 April and 1,462 women and children, many just down from the mountains, on 15 April; the wife of a Turkish officer later said they were marched into the hills near Kavak and murdered. From late April the whole Greek male population of the Trebizond region from the age of 15 is deported in groups of fifty every few days, and boys of 11 to 14 are rounded up for a camp near Cevizlik, though Trebizond's mayor and vali opposed the persecution. In May the head of the Capuchin mission wrote that in Trebizond only women and children remained of the Greeks, that in Samsun there were no men but a few old ones, that no Greek villages were left inland, and that Topal Osman's band was killing in the Giresun countryside, supported by the government and honoured by the Muslim population. By June 1922 American missionaries reported the Pontic villages empty; in May the British High Commissioner Rumbold and the Commons (15 May) took up the reports.

title: Violence by Pontic bands against Muslims: the Turkish claims
summary: Ottoman and Turkish sources record attacks by Greek bands on Muslims: road blocks, attacks on supply convoys, raids on Muslim villages and the looting of grain stores around Çarşamba and Bafra in 1916-18, with logistic help from the Russian command at Trebizond (Ottoman archives, via Duman 2012 and Aydın & Duman 2012). For 1921–22 the claims are quantified: Interior Minister Ali Fethi told the Assembly on 29 December 1921 that armed Greek bands had killed 1,303 Muslims, wounded 147 and damaged 3,303 dwellings, and that the Central Army had largely destroyed 50–60 bands of 180–200 men around Nebyan; in closed session on 10 June 1922 he added 69 killed in October–December 1921 and 82 in January–May 1922. Deputies claimed on 29 October 1921 that 60 Muslim villages had been burned in the Trebizond area and 30 in Samsun. The Ankara government's Pontus Meselesi (1922) counted 1,641 Muslims killed, 323 wounded, 3,723 dwellings burned and 1,800 robberies, and said that over 10,000 rifles had been distributed to the Greeks by Tsarist Russia and later Britain, of which only about 2,000 were surrendered. Two Lazistan deputies, attacking Nureddin in October 1921, said that Greeks fleeing his deportations had joined the bands and begun attacking Muslim villages. Turkish-language writers also describe the Bafra band leader Anton Pasha storming the Bafra gendarmerie post and holding soldiers hostage to free his wife (Çilingir 2014).
disputed: The Pontus Meselesi of 1922 is the Ankara government's own case, published by its press directorate. The village and death figures were stated in the Assembly in the weeks when Nureddin's conduct was under attack there; we found no document behind them. Çilingir writes sympathetically about Anton Pasha, so his account is not a nationalist one, but it is still a Turkish source alone.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated, and those parts are given in the chapter's events: a US destroyer's war diary records a Greek band of nearly a hundred attacking a Turkish village about eight miles from Samsun in early September 1921, killing villagers and burning houses, and a similar raid in October (Shenk 2017, p. 201); and Morris & Ze'evi accept that wartime bands of draft evaders 'occasionally attacked Turkish villagers and gendarmes' (p. 383). A French officer's letter of 11/24 December 1917 shows that the Allies, with Russian officers, wanted a Greek volunteer regiment raised at Trebizond (Le Martyre du Pont-Euxin, 1922, pp. 12–13; H6-030), but Chrysanthos was cautious and no regiment is known to have been formed; Greek memoirs say the departing French commissioner let the Greek Red Cross pass its weapons to the Santa guerrillas in August 1920 (Georganopoulos 2023, p. 86 n. 118). A British observer put the armed Greeks in the mountains at 20,000–30,000 in May 1922 (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 415). Against the totals: no non-Turkish source confirms the casualty figures, which were stated in the Assembly while Nureddin's conduct was under attack; Morris & Ze'evi write that the agitation of 1919 produced 'almost no acts of overt rebellion' and very little anti-Turk terrorism (p. 383) and that Western observers 'uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine "rebellion"' (p. 406); and the Lazistan deputies themselves blamed the bands' growth on Nureddin's deportations (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 13). The figures here (1,303 and 1,641 Muslims killed; 3,303 and 3,723 dwellings; 60 and 30 villages; over 10,000 rifles from Russia and Britain) are found only in Turkish sources.

title: Muslim deaths in the flight of 1916: the Turkish figures
summary: Turkish works put the losses of the Muslim flight from the Russian-occupied zone very high: about 220,000 dead in the displacement (Kaya 2002) and a population decline of 204,130 (McCarthy 1998, as cited by Çakıcı). Many refugees are said to have died of hunger and epidemics on the way and in the reception areas (Öksüz & Usta 2008), and Trebizond city to have fallen from about 45,000 people to about half that by the end of the occupation.
disputed: The figures include deaths from all causes in a wider region than the occupied Pontus.
counter_evidence: The flight itself is confirmed by Chrysanthos and is told in the chapter (H6-017, H6-018). We have found no independent count of the deaths. A US consul's post-war inquiry noted that Samsun's Turks had 'endured heavy losses during the war, in combat and from disease' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 391), which supports heavy Muslim losses in the region in general but not these figures. McCarthy is an American scholar, not a Turkish source, but we know his figure only as cited by Çakıcı, and it is a fall in population from all causes, not a count of deaths.

title: The Ottoman security case for the deportations of 1916-17
summary: Ottoman orders and later Turkish historiography justify the removal of Greeks from the coast in 1916-17 as a military necessity: fear of Russian landings on an exposed coast, of Greek help to the Russian army, and of deserters' bands in the mountains. Enver's order of December 1916 speaks of 'purely military reasons'.
disputed: The orders themselves are told in the chapter (H6-026, H7-011); this entry gives their justification.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: the Russians did land on the Lazistan coast in March 1916 (H6-015); many Greek men had deserted the labour battalions and some formed bands (H6-009); and Morris & Ze'evi, writing of the removals of 1915 from the Straits, grant that 'military concerns, without doubt, played a part', while adding that 'hovering in the background were nationalism and religion' (p. 388). Against the rest: the German consular telegram from Samsun of July 1916 called desertion and espionage 'a pretext to annihilate the entire people' and blamed the vali's fanaticism (Hofmann 2011, p. 57); Talat told the German ambassador in October 1916 that a deportation of all the Greeks of the coast had been planned earlier that year and stopped by Enver so as not to provoke Greece (p. 59); German diplomats learned from Austrian sources in February 1917 that the 'ban' on the Greeks of Samsun, carried out under the pretext of pursuing Greek bands, was 'in reality' a 'large scale' persecution (p. 60); Rafet Bey told the Austrian consul in November 1916 that they must do with the Greeks 'as we did with the Armenians' (H7-008); Pallavicini reported burned villages, and women, children and the old deported in winter (January 1917), and wrote in January 1918 that the deportations were not dictated by military reasons (quoted by Agtzidis 2005, p. 155); Talat had told an Austrian agent in January 1916 of 'the increased necessity for Turkey to get rid of Greeks' (H7-054); Metropolitan Germanos told US officers that 'the greatest cause' of the Bafra deportations was 'religion' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 391); and the Russian-held zone, where collaboration was most possible, was the one area not deported. Morris & Ze'evi see 'real persecution … orchestrated by Constantinople', though no CUP policy of genocide towards the Ottoman Greeks (p. 385; p. 490: 'centrally orchestrated efforts'), and Minasidis (2024), with most non-Turkish historians, reads security as the pretext for demographic homogenisation.

title: The Turkish-speaking Orthodox of Anatolia as ethnic Turks (Baykurt, İzzet Ulvi, Papa Eftim)
summary: Cami Baykurt (articles of 1918–19; Osmanlı Ülkesinde Hıristiyan Türkler, 2nd ed. 1932) and İzzet Ulvi (in Hâkimiyet-i Milliye) held that the Turkish-speaking Orthodox of Anatolia were Turks by descent who had become Christians, and Papa Eftim's Turkish Orthodox movement of 1921–23 took the same line. Applied to the Pontus, the thesis concerns the Turcophone Orthodox of the metropolis of Amaseia (Bafra, the Samsun–Çarşamba plain, Amasya) and the Urum of Erzurum and Kars. We know it only through Vryonis (1971, pp. 453–457) and have not consulted these texts.
disputed: A thesis found only in Turkish writers.
counter_evidence: Vryonis 1971, pp. 453–457, sets out the thesis and argues for a gradual language shift among Anatolian Greeks; he dates the Turkish-origin thesis to the politics of 1918–23 (p. 455). For the Pontus: Ioannidis 1870 (pp. 180, 185–186) has the Turcophone Orthodox of Bafra and Çarşamba keeping Greek schools 'to recover their ancestral language' and Merzifon's Greeks coming from Cappadocia; the 1911 consular census (Kitromilides & Alexandris 1984, Table VI) counts them in the Patriarchate's dioceses; they were exchanged as Orthodox in 1923.

title: The 'Pontus question': a separatist rising that made deportation necessary
summary: Turkish historiography (Biber in the TÜBA volumes; Duman; the Ankara government's Pontus Meselesi of 1922) treats the Pontic movement of 1919-23 as a Greek-backed separatist rising. Mustafa Kemal reported in late May 1919 that 'forty guerrilla' bands were killing Turks 'in an organized program' to 'establish a Pontus state', and in later reports that the real problem was the armed Greek groups, the Muslim bands being self-defence; on 24 April 1920 he told the Assembly that a Pontus government directed by committees in Athens and Istanbul aimed to rule the coast north of Amasya and Tokat, and on 13 August 1923 he announced that 'the Pontus Government … has been defeated along with its supporters'. Replying to Pope Benedict XV in March 1921, he said the Christians under the Assembly's government were 'altogether calm' and accused Greeks and Armenians of crimes. The bands are said to have been organised from Greece and supported by Pontic societies; the Central Army was formed in December 1920 against this movement as well as against Koçgiri; the deportations of 1921 were a necessary wartime measure; and the Amasya tribunal tried a real conspiracy.
disputed: The core of the Turkish national narrative on the Pontus.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: Pontic leaders abroad did seek a Pontic state (Chrysanthos' memorandum at Paris, May 1919; the Pontic-Armenian confederation plan, January 1920; Venizelos' proposal of a landing at Trebizond, October 1920: H6-040, H6-044, H6-047); the French commissioner at Trebizond reported in March 1919 that Chrysanthos, Germanos, Lavrentios and Konstantinidis led a movement for autonomy and then union with Greece (Georganopoulos 2023, p. 77); the British official Rendel wrote that the Greek ecclesiastical authorities 'had fostered a Greek national movement' in Pontus (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 383); and armed Greek bands existed (20,000–30,000 men in May 1922 according to a British observer; Morris & Ze'evi, p. 415). Against the rest: Morris & Ze'evi write that 'all this separatist hubbub had resulted, after the war, in "almost no acts of overt rebellion" and very little anti-Turk terrorism', that 'most Ottoman Greeks, in the Pontus as elsewhere in Anatolia, remained unmoved by ethnic-nationalist appeals' (p. 383), and that 'Western observers uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine "rebellion," either underway or in preparation' (p. 406); even Justin McCarthy, whom they call sympathetic to the Turkish narrative, judged that 'the "Pontus Republic" revolutionaries were never a potent political or military force and would have been better dealt with by police than by deportation' (p. 382); an American observer in Trebizond reported in 1919 that many influential Greeks, and Chrysanthos himself, opposed separatism (p. 383); Venizelos told the Greek parliament in May 1920 that an independent Pontus could not be realised; Wilson declined to rule on the Pontic request; and the Amasya hangings, which included teachers, journalists and men already dead, drew Greek and British protests and a speech in the US Senate (H6-058).

title: The Merzifon search of February 1921 as proof of a Pontic conspiracy
summary: Turkish accounts (the Ankara government's Pontus Meselesi, 1922; Biber, TÜBA; bianet) present the killing of Zeki Bey, a Muslim teacher at Anatolia College, on 12 February 1921 and the papers seized in the searches that followed (a map labelled 'Pontus', a Greek flag, photographs of the football team and theatre club of the Greek students, papers of their 'Pontos' society, documents on Pontic autonomy) as evidence that the college and the Samsun metropolis were centres of a Pontic separatist organisation, which justified the arrests and the trials at Amasya.
disputed: The killing itself is confirmed by American sources and is told in the chapter (H6-050); this entry gives the reading of it as proof of a conspiracy.
counter_evidence: The killing is corroborated by American sources: a Muslim teacher of the college was murdered 'by an unknown assailant', and the searches of the college and hospital found no arms (Bristol's draft letter of 28 July 1921, via Morris & Ze'evi, p. 412). Bristol, no friend of the Greeks, thought the Turks 'over-zealous and unreasonable' and the college president White called them 'sedition-mad' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 412); White had asked the governor whether the 'Pontus' literary society should be suppressed and was told it could go on (Kyriakidis 2023, p. 57). The seized papers are held in over 160 dossiers in the closed TBMM archive (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 19). No source we have read says who killed the teacher.

title: Operations against 'bands': Ankara's account of the killings of 1921-23
summary: Turkish accounts present the killings of Greek men in 1921–23 as the result of fighting with Greek bands. Yusuf Kemal told the Allied high commissioners on 15 September 1921 that the roughly 1,300 men killed in the Kavak gorge on 15–16 August had died in battle after an attack by 'Greek bands' on Turks (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 408). Topal Osman's biographers describe his 47th Regiment as ambushed by Pontic bands at Havza and Merzifon and fighting Greek bands at Erbaa, Çakallı and Bafra (Alpaslan 2007, pp. 525-536; Doğan 2014). The Turkish records that count 1,275 Greeks killed in December 1921 – March 1922, 3,777 in March–May 1922, and 11,198 in all by February 1923 describe them as 'bandits' or 'armed Greeks' killed in operations (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu 2019, pp. 15, 25).
counter_evidence: The numbers are given in the chapter as the state's own counts, without the framing (H6-078). Greek bands did fight in these hills (H6-009, H6-079), so some deaths in combat are likely, but no source separates combatants from civilians.

title: Ankara's reasons for the deportation order of June 1921
summary: Ankara's stated reasons for declaring the coast a war zone and moving Greek men inland were the fear of a Greek landing at Samsun, the Greek bands, and Greeks signalling to Greek warships. Biber (TÜBA) presents the deportation as a security necessity. In a circular to the foreign representatives, forwarded to Rome by the Apostolic Delegate on 25 July 1921, Foreign Minister Yusuf Kemal said that bands of the 'Pontus' organisation were slaughtering the people of Muslim villages and that this was the reason for deporting the whole Greek population of the region; on 21 July he told Admiral Bristol that there was no order to deport civilians, only those who had supported the 'Pontus' movement or the rebels.
disputed: The order itself is told in the chapter (H6-055); this entry gives its justification.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: Greece declared a naval blockade of the Black Sea coast on 26 March 1921, and in summer 1921 a Greek squadron stopped Turkish ships, took passengers prisoner and lightly shelled İnebolu (HMS Sportive report, via Morris & Ze'evi, p. 407). Against the rest: the İnebolu shelling caused no casualties and was, in an Italian witness's words, 'merely a Turkish "excuse for the massacres"', the campaign having begun weeks earlier (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 407); the relocation of Greek men had been proposed in Ankara on 29 May, before the shelling (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 12); no Greek landing on the Pontic coast was attempted; and women and children were deported from the summer of 1921, which the stated reasons do not cover; the Interior Ministry's own order of 25 June did not recommend it (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 25), and Nureddin admitted it (B1-022).

title: Ottoman mobilisation: Christian men drafted into labour battalions
summary: With the general mobilisation of August 1914, non-Muslim men, Pontic Greeks among them, were drafted largely into unarmed labour battalions (amele taburları) that built and maintained roads, railways and tunnels and carried supplies to the fronts. Rations, clothing and shelter were poor and mortality was high: a postwar Greek report gives 23 survivors of some 3,000 labour conscripts from Ayvalık, another report an 80 percent death toll among labourers at İslahiye, and Col. Rawlinson, a British officer held hostage in the eastern vilayets, estimated that 'the life of a Greek in a labor gang is generally about two months' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 387). By early 1916 most adult Greek men of the coast were in the battalions or in hiding, so the deportations of 1916-17 fell mainly on women, children and the old. At Samsun, a Greek report of 19 May 1916 says that deserters who surrendered were held by the hundred for six weeks without bread, fed only by the community, and then sent in handcuffs to Sivas, fifteen days' march (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 12-13). A decision of the recruiting office of 21 October 1915 ordered the families of deserters who did not surrender sent to the interior (p. 10).
disputed: That the battalions existed and were deadly is not in dispute. Basso's death rates 'sometimes over 90%' (2016, p. 22) are the highest for particular battalions, not an overall rate, and no total of labour-battalion deaths for the Pontus has been established. The age bands given for the call-up vary (18–48, 20–45).

title: Greeks of the Ünye district expelled
summary: Morris and Ze'evi (p. 389), in a paragraph on the deportations of 1915, write that the villagers of the Ünye (Ounia) area were deported 'in December', and that according to the Greek Patriarchate Turkish troops murdered batches of Greek men and raped women. Their source is a memorandum by Jesse B. Jackson, the former US consul at Aleppo, dated 4 March 1918. The Patriarchate's compilation dates the evacuation of seven villages of the Ünye region (Tzaguere, Touz-messe, Tchoktze, Tzillar, Kiretch-tepe, Liman-dere, Tere-Bashi) to December 1915, and the deportation of the town's community to July 1917 and after, to Kastamonu, Zile and elsewhere; a letter from Ünye of 10 March 1917 describes the men taken off in small groups and killed by Kurds under a Circassian, Ismail Bey (Patriarchate 1919, p. 126).
disputed: Morris & Ze'evi (p. 389) place the Ünye deportation among those of 1915; their source is a Greek Patriarchate report forwarded in a US memorandum of 1918, so the killings rest on a Greek source. The date, December 1915, is given both by that memorandum and by the Patriarchate's compilation. Burnings in Ünye villages in October 1916, given in the Villages section, would be a second wave.

title: Greek armed bands in the Pontic mountains: what non-Turkish sources say
summary: Non-Turkish sources confirm that Greek armed bands existed and at times attacked Muslims, but give no casualty totals. Morris & Ze'evi write that in 1914-18 bands of draft evaders 'occasionally attacked Turkish villagers and gendarmes' (p. 383; no source cited). In early September 1921 the USS McFarland's war diary recorded a Greek band of nearly a hundred attacking a Turkish village eight miles from Samsun, killing some villagers and burning houses, and a similar raid seems to have followed in early October (Shenk 2017, p. 201; H6-079). In May 1922 Col. Rawlinson told the Foreign Office that 20,000-30,000 armed Greeks were banded together in the mountains (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 415). Greek and American sources describe the bands of Mount Nebyan as the refuge of those fleeing the burned villages (B1-007), and a Turkish deputy said in the Assembly that Nureddin's methods had driven Greeks to the mountains (H7-031). Western observers in 1921 'uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine rebellion, either underway or in preparation' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 406). Agtzidis (1992, p. 167), a Greek historian, puts the bands at more than 18,000 armed men at the peak, about 1920 (beside Rawlinson's 20,000–30,000), and names 'Russian aid' among their sources of arms: this partly corroborates the Turkish claim of Russian arms for the bands. Agtzidis (2005, pp. 165, 184) writes of an 'uprising' after the armistice and of Muslim–Christian clashes with 'hundreds of victims', and says that Germanos and Chrysanthos 'encouraged the insurgents'.
disputed: Rawlinson's 20,000–30,000 is one officer's estimate, and Agtzidis' 18,000 is set beside it, not averaged with it. A Greek primary source also speaks of armed deserters: the Metropolitan of Amaseia wrote on 27 February 1917 that the pretext for the persecution was 'about 300 deserters' who had gone to Trebizond for arms brought by a Russian torpedo boat, and that the government had the right to punish them, but not the women, children and villages (Patriarchate 1919, p. 121). The Turkish accounts of particular raids, and the Muslim casualty figures, which no non-Turkish source confirms, are given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-004, H6-013, H7-T08, H7-T10).

title: Talat on the Greeks, as reported by the Central Powers' diplomats (1916)
summary: On 31 January 1916, according to an Austrian report cited by Fotiadis, the interior minister Talat told an Austrian agent that 'he sees the increased necessity for Turkey to get rid of Greeks, as she did before with Armenians' (Kyriakidis 2026, p. 50). In October 1916 Talat confirmed to the German ambassador Radowitz that a wholesale deportation of all Greeks from the Ottoman coasts had been planned earlier in the year, but that Enver had stopped it so as not to provoke Greece, then still neutral; on 3 October Radowitz reported that the 'cleansing' had been partly accomplished by expelling 'the Greeks from certain districts of Asia Minor and Rumelia' (Hofmann 2011, p. 59).
disputed: Both are diplomats' reports of conversations, reaching us through Greek-edited compilations (Fotiadis). The Austrian agent is not named.

title: Deportation of the Greeks of İnebolu, Sinope and the Kastamonu coast; Kuckhoff's telegram
summary: The Greek population of İnebolu and its villages (Cide, Patheri, Atsidono, Karaca, Askordassi) was deported in June 1916 (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 389-390, after the Patriarchate). In mid-July 1916 the German vice-consul at Samsun, Kuckhoff, telegraphed that, 'according to trustworthy sources', the whole Greek population of Sinope and of the coast of the Kastamonu province had been deported; that 'in Turkish the terms deportation and destruction have the same meaning, for in most cases those who are not killed fall victim to diseases or starvation'; and that the vali of Kastamonu was using 'the flight of Greek conscripts over the sea and the prevention of espionage as a pretext to annihilate the entire people' (Hofmann 2011, p. 57). Hofmann's German (aga-online) reads 'Ausweisung und Ausrottung sind türkisch gleiche Begriffe'. Hofmann adds that the Greeks of Sinope were given four hours' notice, and quotes a New York Times cable of 21 August 1916 on caravans sent to 'concentration camps in the interior'. The Patriarchate's compilation adds that at the end of July 1916 Sinope, Gerze and its villages as far as Alaçam, Ayancık and Ayandon were evacuated; after eight days' march the people reached Kastamonu, where the vali Atif Bey sent them on to Taşköprü, Boyabat and Safranbolu; and that a fire at Sinope destroyed 400 Greek houses and shops (Patriarchate 1919, p. 119). For Cide and İnebolu it confirms June 1916 (p. 127).
disputed: The date and the sender: the published texts give 16 July and Kuckhoff (Hofmann 2011, text; Shirinian; Kyriakidis, p. 62; Kévorkian & Astourian), but Hofmann's footnote, after Fotiadis, reads 'Telegramm Nr. 129, 15 July 1916 by Heinrich Bergfeld, Consulate Samsun' (n. 55), and so does his web essay; elsewhere Hofmann calls Kuckhoff the German consul at Samsun in February 1916 (p. 97) and Bergfeld the consul at Trebizond in August 1915 (p. 56). The addressee is given as the embassy, as 'Berlin' (Shirinian, who also calls the sender 'the German ambassador at Amisos', an error), or as 'the German Ministry of the Interior' (Kyriakidis, an error). The English versions differ: 'deportation and destruction have the same meaning' (Hofmann 2011), 'Exile and annihilation have the same meaning' (Shirinian 2017) and 'Deportation and extermination mean the same' (Kyriakidis 2026); the German is given above. Travis (2017, p. 2, n. 18) gives only 'summer 1916', after Thea Halo (2000, p. 127).

title: Talat orders Greeks of Görele, Vakfıkebir and Şarlı sent to Sivas
summary: A cipher telegram from the interior minister Talat to the vali of Sivas, Muammer Bey, dated 20 Haziran 1332 (3 July 1916), states that, since some Greeks of the Görele and Vakfıkebir kazas and the Şarlı nahiye of Trabzon vilayet had been found to engage in espionage, the army had asked for these Greeks, men and women, to be sent by way of Giresun and Samsun to Sivas vilayet, and that they were to be settled there in scattered places. The document comes from Sait Çetinoğlu's collection and is transcribed by Çilingir (2016, p. 51). A later instruction of Talat (22 May 1917) to Ankara, Sivas, Kastamonu and Samsun ordered that deportees suspected of harmful activity be split into small groups under surveillance (BOA DH.ŞFR 60/144, 73/72, 76/243; ibid.).
disputed: The number of deportees is unclear in the transcription ('zükür ve inas üç-dört bir raddesinde'). Görele and Vakfıkebir lay close to the front of July 1916; whether these Greeks were refugees from the Russian-held zone is not stated. Akçam (2012, p. 107) quotes a cable of Talat to Sivas of 29 June 1916 (BOA DH.ŞFR 65/126) saying that Greeks reported earlier had been sent to Sivas for military reasons, without naming their places of origin; it may belong to the same affair, but the dates differ (3 July in Çilingir's document). The May 1916 rule for the coast sent those moved from the Trebizond vilayet to Kastamonu and to Sivas (H6-014).

title: Kwiatkowski reports Rafet Bey's words: 'do with the Greeks as we did with the Armenians'
summary: Ernst von Kwiatkowski, the Austro-Hungarian consul for Trebizond, who had moved to Samsun after the Russian capture of Trebizond, reported to Foreign Minister Burián at the end of November 1916 what the local commander Rafet (Refet) Bey had told him. In the English of greek-genocide.net, which cites the file (report of 30 November): on 26 November, 'We must at last do with the Greeks as we did with the Armenians…'; on 28 November, 'We must now finish with the Greeks. I sent today battalions to the outskirts to kill every Greek they pass on the road.' Kyriakidis (2026, p. 50), after Enepekidis (1996, p. 139), dates the 'top secret report' from Samsun to 29 November 1916 and renders the words: 'We must at last do away with the Greeks. Today I sent patrols of gendarmes to the outskirts ordering them to kill any Greek they would come across.'
disputed: A reported conversation, not an order. The report is dated 30 November 1916 by greek-genocide.net, which gives the Vienna archive reference, and 29 November by Kyriakidis (p. 50), after Enepekidis (1996). Fotiadis, as cited by Kyriakidis (n. 47), dates a remark of Refet's to Kwiatkowski 'in the same sense' to 26 November 1915, probably a slip for 1916. Bjørnlund's chapter on the Danish sources in Hofmann et al. (2011), sometimes cited for the episode, does not give it; it notes that there were no Danish observers in Pontus in 1916 (p. 176).

title: Talat's cable to Samsun: the coastal Greeks to be taken 30-50 km inland
summary: On 11 January 1917 the interior minister, Talat, sent a coded telegram to the district (sancak) of Samsun (Canik). He had spoken with Enver, who said that the Third Army had made the arrangements; the aim was to take the Greeks along the coast "some thirty to fifty kilometers inland", and no person or property was to be attacked during the deportations. On 21 January the Security Directorate told the provinces of Sivas, Kastamonu and Ankara and the district of Bolu that the Third Army command judged it urgent to remove the Greeks of the Samsun basin further inland, and that they were to be placed in villages in those provinces. Akçam, who quotes both cables from the Ottoman archive, adds that the order was not carried out as written: some villages had a few hours' notice, men were taken into labour battalions, women and children could take nothing with them, Muslim neighbours looted the villages, and villagers were made to sign statements that their attackers had been Armenians (Akçam 2012, pp. 111-112). Kieser writes that 'Talaat ordered the deportation of the Pontus Greeks of the Black Sea coast' (2018, pp. 257-258). The removals in the Samsun district had begun in December 1916 (H6-028).
disputed: Scope: the cable went to the Samsun district, but its words speak of 'the Greeks along the coast'; the circular of 21 January speaks of the Samsun basin. As Akçam quotes them, neither names the Trebizond vilayet; Kieser's 'Black Sea coast' is wider. Distance: the cable gives 30-50 km, but the circular ten days later sends the Samsun Greeks to villages in Sivas, Kastamonu, Ankara and Bolu, far beyond that band, and the deportees went by Kavak and Havza to Çorum, Amasya and beyond (H6-028). Companion orders: Enver's 50-km evacuation order of December 1916 (Hofmann 2011, pp. 59-60) and the 50-km notice of November 1916 relayed to the Metropolitan of Kerasous, repeated by Vehip Pasha on 20 November 1916 (Emmanouilidis' memoir, via Çilingir, p. 54). The instructions of 3 February 1917 left the choice of places to the army and extended the removals to townspeople (AK-003). The Ottoman security rationale is given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T03).

title: Mass expulsion of the Greeks of Samsun town
summary: In Samsun, deportation of notables was followed by mass removal on 10, 11 and 13 January 1917; the columns were mostly women and children (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 391). A postwar investigation by the American Ralph Chesbrough (8 August 1919) suggested that about 5,000 Greeks and a similar number of Armenians were 'eliminated' from Samsun 'by massacre, expulsion, and flight to the hills'; Morris & Ze'evi add that Samsun's Turks also suffered heavy wartime losses in combat and from disease. In all, they write, 'tens of thousands of Greeks were marched inland from the Pontus coastline' in late 1916 and early 1917 (p. 391, after Germanos's letter of 20 December 1916 to the American missionary Mary Graffam at Sivas). The Metropolitan of Amaseia, Germanos Karavangelis, reported about 30,000 deportees from his diocese sent towards Ankara, most of whom died. Çetinoğlu, after Germanos's letters, writes that on 9 January 80 Samsun notables were arrested and sent to Havza, and that the general deportation began the same day from the Greek suburb of Kadıköy, 4,000 people being sent to Havza and then Çorum. The first of the Legation's reports (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 48-50) dates the arrest of eighty of the richest Greeks of Samsun to 27 December 1916; the same day the army surrounded the town, the people of Upper Samsun (Kadıköy) were called to the square to hear the governor and seized, and the same was done at Aylaskoy. They were marched through the night over the snow, by Mount Tsoumbouz and Kavak to Havza, four days without food, then on to Çorum. More arrests followed on 10, 11 and 13 January and on 17 and 18 January 1917.
disputed: The 30,000 is the Metropolitan's. An Ottoman report gives 13,406 Greeks sent inland from Samsun (H7-053). Chesbrough's 5,000 covers massacre, expulsion and flight together. Akçam (2012, p. 112) gives the same 80 notables and 4,000 deportees as Çetinoğlu, and adds that they were settled in the houses of deported Armenians; both rest on Germanos' letters, Akçam through Yerasimos (1994). The Legation report dates the arrest of the 80 notables to 27 December 1916 (Brown & Ion 1918, p. 48); Çetinoğlu has 9 January and Akçam 'the first month of 1917'. The report names the stop before Çorum 'Kaphzan, in the Province of Sebastia, 80 kilometres from Samsoun', which by the route and the distance is Havza.

title: Pallavicini: 'Death awaits them all'
summary: Ambassador Pallavicini reported: 'The situation of the deported is for despair. Death awaits them all.' The same letter says he had warned the Grand Vizier that the persecution could take 'the form and dimensions of the Armenian persecutions'. Austria-Hungary was then the Ottoman Empire's ally.
disputed: The letter is known only from the English translation on greek-genocide.net ('The Samsun Deportations', n. 5), which gives the Vienna archive reference. Çetinoğlu's Turkish version cites the same file and is not an independent witness. Enepekides published the Austrian documents on the Pontic Greeks, but neither his edition nor the original in Vienna was consulted for this atlas.

title: Rules for the emptied Greek villages, 1917: Muslim refugees settled, Greek property kept
summary: On 16 January 1917 the Interior Ministry's directorate for tribes and immigrants told Trebizond and Canik that Muslim immigrants were being settled in the areas the Greeks had left, above all on the coast, and that the Greeks' movable goods were to be kept in churches and depots. On 30 January its inspectors reported that the immigrants and refugees at Bafra had been badly settled, without proper homes, land or seed. On 3 February a list of instructions to Canik laid down that the army would decide which Greek townships and people were to be removed, and extended the removals on the coast to people from the towns. On 8 February the directorate complained to Samsun that no committees had been formed to keep the evacuees' goods and livestock, that the depots had not been sealed and that houses had been wrecked. Instructions of 13 and 24 February, and of 20 March to the Canik commission for abandoned property, ruled that, unlike Armenian property, the Greeks' property was not to be liquidated: it was to be kept, or left with relatives and partners, and only perishable goods were to go to the immigrants and the army against receipt. Akçam, who quotes these cables, concludes that the government did not mean the deportees to return, since Muslims were settled in their villages at once, and notes that the Greek property was handled by the commissions set up for Armenian property (Akçam 2012, pp. 112-113, 118-119, 354).
disputed: The cables state the rules; the cable of 8 February itself reports unguarded goods and wrecked houses, and the Austrian and Greek reports describe looting and burning (H6-028). Akçam also cites a cable to Trebizond of 30 July 1917 (BOA DH.ŞFR 78/154) for coastal populations in some areas largely left in place (p. 113). Whether the kept property was returned after 1918 is not covered by these documents. A Greek Legation report from Samsun of February 1917 says that the tobacco of villages emptied but not burnt (Aylaskoy, Andreanta, Tekkeköy, Kadıköy) was put up for auction by the government, which kept the proceeds, and that Turkish refugees settled in eight Samsun villages were promised title deeds to the houses and land (Brown & Ion 1918, pp. 18, 53-54).

title: An Ottoman count: 13,406 Greeks sent inland from Samsun
summary: A report by Refet (Rafet) Bey, the commander at Samsun, gives 13,406 Greeks (Rum) sent inland from Samsun in the deportations of winter 1916-17. It is a lower limit from the Ottoman side, to set beside the Greek figures of about 20,000 (Greek Legation) and 30,000 (Karavangelis).
disputed: A count of those moved, not of the dead, which may not cover the whole Samsun district or every convoy. It is an admission by the state, and so is given here although it reaches us through a Turkish historian. Other Ottoman-side figures: Talat estimated in late 1917 that more than 93,000 Greeks had been deported to the interior and 164,000 to Greece during the war, for all the Ottoman Greeks (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 392, after Suny). A table 'according to official sources' of Greeks deported in 1914–17 gives Canik 62,000 and Trabzon 29, out of 213,483 in all (Çilingir 2016, p. 53, without a source); if genuine, its figure for the whole Canik sancak is far above Refet's for Samsun. Its provincial figures add up to 201,312, not the printed 213,483.

title: The Patriarchate's record: Samsun and Bafra after the winter deportations (burnings, Turkish villagers armed, the Metropolitan removed)
summary: The Patriarchate's compilation continues the Samsun record after January 1917. In March and April 1917 Turkish villagers burnt Ayak-lalan, Hizirlou and Arandjak, and the army burnt Karaman, Dikedjik and Karadja-klisse and drove out their people; women were raped at Tzartak-Gueriz, Touzeren and other villages, and at Tangarlou fourteen people were killed. Kadıköy and Aylaskoy were turned into settlements for Muslim refugees. In October 1917 the Bafra authorities armed the Turkish villagers, and killings followed at several villages. On 15 October 1917 Metropolitan Germanos was sent under escort to Constantinople for not handing over Greek deserters who had attacked the Turkish village of Tcharson; he returned after the armistice. On 16 December 1917 an order at Bafra gave the Greeks ten days before deportation in midwinter (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 123-125).
disputed: This rests on one Greek compilation. The deserters' attack on Tcharson is the Ottoman ground for the Metropolitan's removal, as the book reports it. How far the order of December 1917 was carried out is not stated.
sources_primary: [Patriarchate compilation] Persecution of the Greeks in Turkey 1914-1918 (Constantinople 1919), pp. 123-125
sources_modern: Greek Patriarchate, Persecution of the Greeks in Turkey 1914-1918 (Constantinople, 1919), English edition, Part III (Pontus) [Patriarchate compilation, Greek, 1919, for the peace settlement]

date_text: After the Russian withdrawal from Trebizond (February 1918)
title: Trebizond after the Russian withdrawal: orders to deport all Greeks, and irregulars in the villages (Catholic witness)
summary: The Capuchin superior at Trebizond, Father Lorenzo da Montemarciano, recorded in his diary that after the Russian withdrawal the city's commander issued orders, said to have come from Constantinople, that all Greek men and women, the old and the children, were to be deported inland ('deportation inland means slow death', he noted); when Metropolitan Chrysanthos asked what the government feared from women and children, the governor answered that he had to follow orders, which also mentioned forced labour. Bands of Turkish irregulars gathered in the villages around Trebizond, 'burning, killing, destroying', and many Greeks left for Batum (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 62-63).
disputed: Kyriakidis does not date the diary entries precisely. Chrysanthos's letter of 12 October 1918 (printed under 'Chryssostomos') says that Ahmed Bey, president of the Muslim committee, went to Rize and launched the attack: the Greek villages from Rize to Platana were destroyed, Rize in a day, with four of its 2,000 Greeks left; Sourmena paid 70,000 roubles to stay; Tsita, Kapıköy, Livera, Hamsiköy and Santa defended themselves; 'scarcely 2,300 Christians remained' in his diocese (Patriarchate 1919, pp. 113-116). That last figure conflicts with Chrysanthos's later account that about half were saved (C3-045), and may be a misprint for 23,000.

title: The French commissioner at Trebizond, Paul Lépissier, reports renewed persecution of the Greeks (1919-1920)
summary: Paul Lépissier, the French High Commission's delegate (vice-consul) at Trebizond from November 1918, placed gendarmerie inspectors in the coastal towns and inland, and reported in detail. According to Georganopoulos, who read his reports, he recorded that the Ottoman authorities and local Muslims, who were armed, obstructed the return of Greek refugees from Russia and killed returnees as alleged revolutionaries; that in May 1919 600 Pontians on the ship Pinios were prevented from landing; that by early June 1919 only 5,000-6,000 Greeks and 300 Armenians had returned to the Trebizond area; and that on 4 June 1919 organised persecutions of Greeks had begun around Kerasous, Merzifon and Bulancak. The French gendarmerie officer Ancery and Colonel Chardigny reported in the same sense. In 1919 the religious leaders of Trebizond (the Metropolitan's representative Matthaios Kofidis, the Protestant pastor Stapleton, Mgr Arzeruni and the Capuchin fathers Lorenzo and Cirillo) jointly protested to Lépissier about raids on Christian villages (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 63-64). Lépissier was forced out of Trebizond on Ankara's orders in 1920.
disputed: The 'commission' was the French commissioner's post with a few gendarmerie officers, not an investigative commission. The French envoy Damien de Martel, briefed by Lépissier in 1920, thought he 'greatly dramatized the events' (Georganopoulos p. 84). Georganopoulos also notes French policy in 1919-20 was not favourable to Greek claims.

date_text: Motion dated 2 November 1918, read on 4 November 1918
title: Ottoman Chamber: a motion by Greek deputies speaks of 550,000 Greeks 'killed and annihilated'
summary: After the armistice of Mudros, the Greek deputy for Aydın, Emmanouil Emmanouilidis, with Tokinidis (Çatalca) and Vangel (İzmir), put a question to the new government. As transcribed by Çilingir from the minutes, it listed among the acts of the previous five years: one million Armenians killed; 250,000 Greeks expelled beyond the Ottoman borders and their property confiscated; 'after the war [began], 550,000 more Greeks killed and annihilated (katl ve imha edilmiş) on the coasts and in the hinterland of the Black Sea, the Dardanelles, the Marmara and the islands and elsewhere', their property seized; and 250,000 men of the labour battalions dead of hunger and privation. The figure covers all coastal Greeks in 1914-18, not the Pontus alone.
disputed: The motion, as transcribed, says 'killed and annihilated', not 'deported'. It is a claim by Greek deputies, not a count. Morris & Ze'evi treat 550,000 as the number of Greeks uprooted during the war, citing Rendel. Whom the Turkish deputies' 500,000-600,000 covered is not clear in Hofmann's summary.

title: The Patriarchate's Black Book: 257,019 Pontic Greeks deported in 1914-18
summary: The Ecumenical Patriarchate's Μαύρη Βίβλος διωγμών και μαρτυρίων του εν Τουρκία Ελληνισμού (1914-1918) gives the number deported during the war by metropolis: Amaseia 89,370; Chaldia 64,582; Trebizond 38,434; Neocaesarea 27,216; Kolonia 19,938; Rhodopolis 17,479; total 257,019. These are deportees, not deaths. The same book gives 774,235 deported for all Ottoman Greeks, 1913-18.
disputed: The figures were compiled for the peace conference. They are counts of the deported, sometimes misquoted as deaths. For all Ottoman Greeks Hofmann (2011, p. 102) gives the Patriarchate's total of wartime deportees as 490,063 and Puaux's (from Patriarchate statistics) as 773,915. Agtzidis 2005, p. 156, gives Puaux's 257,019 as 'victims' (θύματα) of the Asia Minor Pontus, an example of the deportation counts being read as deaths. The 1919 English edition (Persecution of the Greeks in Turkey 1914-1918) has no deportation table; each diocese heading gives only communities and inhabitants (e.g. Amaseia 340 communities, 131,181 inhabitants; Chaldia 145, 77,845; Trebizond 73, 58,734; Neocaesarea 195, 67,424; Kolonia 91, 52,855; Rodopolis 47, 20,657).

title: Rıza Nur's instruction to Topal Osman: 'leave no stone on stone in the Greek villages' (memoir)
summary: Rıza Nur, health minister in the Ankara government, wrote in his memoirs that when Topal Osman was reproached for robbing the people he defended him, told him 'Ağa, clean the Pontus well', and, when Osman said he was sparing churches and good buildings in case they were needed, told him to destroy them too and scatter their stones 'so that they cannot say there was a church here'; Osman agreed (Rıza Nur, Hayat ve Hatıratım, vol. 3, pp. 163-164, as quoted by Çetinoğlu and by Ayşe Hür).
disputed: A memoir written years later by a minister who fell out with Kemal; it is an admission by a member of the Ankara government, but its date and accuracy are uncertain.

title: Giresun: Topal Osman holds the Christian men for ransom
summary: Osman Ağa ('Topal Osman'), mayor of Giresun and leader of an irregular force later made the 47th regiment, imprisoned the Christian men of Giresun on the night of 13 August 1920; thereafter 'every evening five or six Christians' were shot until the community paid a ransom of 300,000 Turkish lira, and Greek men were deported inland from Giresun and Samsun 'at the order of Mustafa Kemal' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 401, after British records). A Capuchin missionary's report of the period blames Topal Osman's 'approximately six hundred Laz' for many assassinations at Giresun (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 66-67). In October 1920 Osman met Kemal at Ankara and was made governor general of the coast from İnebolu to Hopa (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 404).
sources_primary: [British] Minutes of the 45th and 46th meetings of the A.G.S. and Armenian and Greek Representatives, 1 and 15 Sept 1920, FO 371/5214; A.G.S. memorandum, 20 Oct 1920, FO 371/5057 (via Morris & Ze'evi n. 129) | [Catholic missionary] Fra Cirillo Giovanni Zohrabian, A servizio dei fratelli, pp. 344-346 (via Kyriakidis 2026)
sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP, 2019), pp. 401, 404 | Kyriakidis (trans. Nikoloudis), The Genocide of Orthodox Greeks and the Persecution of Christians in the Pontus Region according to Vatican Archives (Gorgias Press, 2026), pp. 66-67

title: Nureddin's circular No. 2082 (12 January 1921): deportation of Christian men aged 16-50 and new labour conscription
summary: On 12 January 1921 Nureddin issued circular No. 2082. The Turkish writer Çilingir (2016, p. 117), from Turkish military documents, gives it as announcing that Christian men aged 16 to 50 able to bear arms in Samsun, Ordu, Amasya, Tokat and Şarkikarahisar would be deported, and that those born in 1901 would be conscripted into labour battalions; Çetinoğlu quotes it as ordering labour-battalion recruits from the Ordu sancak to be gathered at Şarkikarahisar and those from Samsun at Amasya, with punishment for slack officials and 'distant exile' for any Christian who fled and for those who hid them. Güzel (2006, p. 151, as cited on Wikipedia) reads it as a proposal to deport Greek men to Amasya, Tokat and Şebinkarahisar. Early in 1921 Greek men were again conscripted; to take younger boys the authorities forged orphans' birth certificates to make them 'one to four years older than their real age' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 404, after a relief worker's report from Sivas).
disputed: The readings of order No. 2082 differ: places of origin (Çilingir: Samsun, Ordu, Amasya, Tokat, Şarkikarahisar) or collecting and destination points (Güzel: to Amasya, Tokat and Şebinkarahisar; Çetinoğlu: recruits gathered at Şarkikarahisar and Amasya). Nureddin's stated reason (a feared Greek landing at Samsun) is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T04).
