title: Trebizond 1921: notables arrested, men deported; Greeks shelter in the Catholic monastery
summary: Early in April 1921 the persecution of the Greeks of Trebizond began openly: notables, among them the journalist Nikos Kapetanidis and the Metropolitan's representative Matthaios Kofidis, were imprisoned on charges of working for an independent Pontus and later condemned to death, and the men over sixteen were deported, many dying of hunger and exhaustion; frightened Greeks repeatedly took refuge in the Catholic monastery (Kyriakidis 2026, p. 75, citing Father Cirillo's memoir and Fotiadis). An undated note sent to the Apostolic Delegation reports that at Zonguldak the Kemalist authorities began deporting the Orthodox Greek men in early November 1921 (H7-062).
disputed: Kyriakidis (p. 75) covers the paragraph with one note (n. 120), citing Father Cirillo's memoir (pp. 371–373) and, for comparison, Fotiadis (p. 370); only the shelter in the Catholic monastery is clearly Cirillo's, and the arrests, the death sentences and the deportation of the men over sixteen have no separate reference. The arrests of early 1921 in Bafra, Amasya, Merzifon, Erbaa, Samsun and Alaçam are from Fotiadis (p. 365; n. 119).

title: Spring 1921: the villages around Bafra and Alaçam are destroyed and the men of Alaçam arrested
summary: The Central Army began its first operations in the Bafra district on 5 April 1921 (Çetinoğlu). US naval officers at Samsun quoted an American missionary that about 100 Greek villages south of Bafra had been destroyed in a few days from 17 May, the villagers murdered and 'the priests... crucified', and reported that the campaign was 'under strict control of the military' and 'directed by high authority—probably Angora'. A British compilation records that the whole male Christian population of Alaçam above the age of 12 was imprisoned in May 1921 and then massacred; a Greek paper of 13 May 1921 described the prison of Bafra as full of Greeks arrested without cause.
disputed: The 'about 100 villages' figure is a missionary's, relayed by the US officers. The Alaçam statement reached the British through the Greek Patriarchate. The 5 April date for the first operations rests on Çetinoğlu; Çilingir puts it in April.

title: Harput, Malatya, Arapgir and Diyarbakır: what the Near East Relief recorded
summary: Mark Ward, NER director at Harput, recorded 20,526 deportees passing through Mezre-Harput between May 1921 and February 1922 (his pamphlet gives 20,378 to January 1922), about 18,000 of them Greeks. Yowell and Ward reported that of 30,000 deportees who passed Sivas in early summer 1921, 5,000 died before Harput and 5,000 escaped; of the 20,000 who reached Harput, 2,000 died there and 3,000 were scattered in the vilayet; of 15,000 sent on to Diyarbakır, 3,000 died on the way and 1,000 in the town, 2,000 stayed and 9,000 were sent towards Bitlis. Ward's pamphlet puts 4,000 deportees at Malatya in autumn and winter, of whom about 2,000 died of hunger or typhus. Stanley Hopkins met 12,000 Greeks being driven south between Harput and Malatya on 1 September 1921 and about 10,000 around 1 October, one group of about 2,000 women alone. At Arapgir the missionaries saw a convoy of about 1,000 old people, women and children in late autumn 1921 and took in about 20 children left by the road.
disputed: Ward's total is 20,526 in Morris & Ze'evi (p. 426) and 20,378 in his pamphlet, for slightly different periods. Bafra is not named in his table; the Bafra women's convoys reached Malatya and Hekimhan in late November and early December (B1-017, B1-019), which fits his Malatya figures. 'Osmaniye' in his table (23 Oct, 6 Nov, 8 Dec 1921) has not been identified.

title: The death marches from Samsun to Harput, Diyarbakır and Bitlis
summary: Deportees from the coast were marched via Amasya and Sivas to Harput and on to Diyarbakır, Bitlis and Van. An estimated 70,000 Pontus deportees passed through Sivas, where the relief worker Theda Phelps saw 1,000-2,000 Christians arrive each week (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 421). The Near East Relief officers at Harput, Major Forrest D. Yowell and Dr Mark Ward, reported that of 30,000 deportees who passed Sivas in early summer 1921, 5,000 died before Harput and 5,000 escaped; of the 20,000 who reached Harput, 2,000 died there and 3,000 were scattered in the vilayet; of 15,000 sent on to Diyarbakır, 3,000 died on the way and 1,000 in the town, 2,000 stayed and 9,000 were sent towards Bitlis (p. 425). Ward recorded 20,526 deportees through Mezre-Harput between May 1921 and February 1922, about 18,000 of them Greeks (p. 426; his pamphlet gives 20,378 for a shorter period). The relief worker Ethel Thompson wrote that 'The Turks had given them no food on the 500 mile trip from Samsun'; those who survived were those who could pay the guards for food (p. 422). There were local exceptions: the vali of Diyarbakır let the Near East Relief shelter and feed Greek deportees and, in October-December 1921, allowed some to settle and work, and a missionary wrote that 'the Turkish Government helped us by every means in their power' (p. 424 n. 286).
disputed: The waypoints between Samsun and Sivas and between Harput and Bitlis are the usual road route, not confirmed for every convoy. The Yowell-Ward figures are on p. 425; '70,000 through Sivas' is an estimate (p. 421).

title: Dilmitzoglou: the second convoy burned in the church of Selamelik
summary: According to the Bafra notable Ioannis Dilmitzoglou, the second convoy of about 500 Bafra men, among them the merchants George Kouzloo (killed on the way, his head taken to the under-governor) and Kyriako Solomonoglou, was shut in the church of the village of Selamelik and burned alive; a few escaped and told of it. A semi-official Athens statement of 8 September 1921 said that 'at Bafra the male population were strangled in the church and schools'.
disputed: One Greek witness, repeated by Morris & Ze'evi; we found no American or other foreign report of this burning. Ankara attributed the Bafra dead to fighting with bands; that account is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T05).

title: Dilmitzoglou: the third convoy (680) taken to the church of Kocasu, the fourth sent to Elbistan
summary: When the under-governor divided the remaining men into those liable to military service and those to be exiled, over 500 young men aged 15–35 reported to the recruiting office. The third convoy, of 400 recruits and 280 exiles (680 in all), among them the banker Demosthenes Dilmitzoglou, was taken to the church of the village the witness calls Kodje-sou (Morris & Ze'evi: Kavdje-son); 'as none escaped we know neither details nor the manner of their destruction'. A fourth convoy of 35 was sent safely to 'a town near Marash called Elvistan' (Elbistan), from where its members telegraphed friends.
disputed: Some accounts give 680–780; the witness gives 680 (400 + 280) and does not know how they died. Morris & Ze'evi's 'murdered' goes beyond the witness. Kocasu has not been located.

title: Dilmitzoglou: villages of the Bafra plain burned with their people (Muğamlı, Sürmeli and others)
summary: The witness says that at Muğamlı ('Mooamli'), three hours from Bafra, all 250 inhabitants were shut in the house of Dzigaloglou and burned alive, and that Sürmeli, Akgüney ('Ak konney'), Kızılgöl and Ada 'suffered the same fate'. Morris & Ze'evi report that at Sürmeli 300 were herded into houses 'and burnt alive', and that around Bafra the deportations inland 'were regularly accompanied by mass murder'. A Black Book note adds that at Bafra the men were made to pay 50–2,000 pounds each, then deported, and 200 were killed near the town within a week.
disputed: No exact dates. Turkish accounts say the villages destroyed had supplied the bands (B1-T05). Kızılgöl and Ada have not been located.

title: The Patriarch's report: seven priests of Alaçam and Bafra crucified at Gözköy
summary: According to the Ecumenical Patriarch, seven priests from Alaçam, Bafra and their environs were arrested, tortured in public and crucified in the marketplace of Gözköy ('Guioz-Keuy').
disputed: May be another version of the seven priests axed at Elezli (B1-010); place and manner differ.

title: Escapes: to Mount Nebyan, and by sailing ship to Midye in Thrace
summary: Dilmitzoglou writes that four wounded men fled by night to Mount Nebyan ('Nepien'), 'the centre of the Greek refugees'; that men escaping from Bafra through the military cordon joined their companions there; and that about 500 women and children were saved with the help of men from Nebyan. He himself was rescued with about 100 others by a sailing ship and taken to Midye (Medea, today Kıyıköy) on the Black Sea coast of Eastern Thrace, then held by Greece.
disputed: The 500 saved are a Greek figure. Turkish accounts treat Nebyan as a rebel base (B1-T05). Nebiyan Dağı rises to 1,285 m, the second-highest peak of the Bafra district (PeakVisor).

title: Totals for Bafra: 14,010 deported, at least 9,140 dead (Gavriilidis)
summary: Sam Topalidis, citing the Bafra tobacco merchant and deportee Antonios Gavriilidis (1924, via Hionides 1996), gives 14,010 men, women and children deported from Bafra between mid-June and the end of September 1921, of whom at least 9,140 were killed directly or died of hunger or disease.
disputed: Topalidis writes 'at least 9,140 (at least 83%)', but 9,140 of 14,010 is 65%; one number is wrong. Compare the US reports' 6,000 + 2,500 women and children (B1-015, B1-018) and Yerasimos's three men's convoys of 500–600 (B1-009).

title: The Kavak road: convoys of deported men shot (June-August 1921; 1,300 on 15-16 August)
summary: Convoys of men deported from Samsun and Bafra were fired on by their escorts on the road to Kavak. A western report, Rendel's Foreign Office memorandum, claimed that 1,300 Greeks were murdered in the gorge on 15 or 16 August 1921; the Greek representative to the League of Nations put the dead of at least two convoys shot near Kavak at 'at least 900' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 408). The missionary Gertrude Anthony reported that many from the first and third groups of Samsun men had been massacred near Kavak (Shenk 2017, p. 203). On 2 June 1921 the mutasarrıf of Canik and the commander of the 10th Division reported to the Central Army that a convoy of 766 Greeks sent from Samsun to Kavak had been attacked in the Canik mountains and that many Greeks had been killed and wounded (Çilingir, p. 117); in the Grand National Assembly the Lazistan deputy Ziya Hurşit said that the first convoy from Samsun was attacked six hours out of the town (ibid., p. 118). Further counts: 330 and 660 of two convoys (Black Book), and 550 executed on 26 June and 1,300 on 15 August (Stanley Hopkins of the NER).
disputed: The counts overlap and should not be added. The Ottoman report of 2 June 1921 attributes the attack to 'brigands' and Ankara later said the Kavak dead fell in battle; both claims are under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T05).

title: Greek navy bombards İnebolu
summary: Greek warships shelled İnebolu, the port through which supplies reached Ankara, on 9 June 1921. Morris & Ze'evi (p. 407) call it a light shelling that 'produced no casualties'; Count Schmeccia of Lloyd Triestino at Samsun, formerly a representative of the Italian High Commission, called it merely a Turkish 'excuse for the massacres'. They add that the shelling 'may indeed have hastened the deportation process, but it wasn't the cause of the campaign, which was launched weeks before'.
disputed: The date is confirmed by the Turkish documents (Biber; Korucu & Dağlıoğlu; H6-055). Ankara's use of the danger of a Greek landing as a reason for the deportations is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T04).

title: Ankara decrees the deportation of Greek men of military age from the Pontic coast
summary: On 3 June 1921 the defence minister Fevzi (Çakmak) told the Central Army that the government had decided to move armed Greeks of the coast inland; the Council of Ministers' order of 12 June relocated Greeks aged 15 to 50 from the coast and was put into effect on 16 June (decree No. 941 is dated 16 June); the coast had been declared a war zone from 12 June, and in July the area of relocation was widened (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, pp. 12-13; Çilingir, pp. 117-118). US sources give 16-50, British 15-55. On 16 June police began to round up Samsun's Greek males aged 15-50, and on the 19th about 2,000 were marched inland (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 410). Nureddin's order No. 2245 of 19 June sent armed Greek men to the Ergani Madeni, Malatya and Maraş sancaks and, from Sivas, to Gürün and Darende. An Interior Ministry order of 25 June did not recommend sending women and children inland, but on Nureddin's orders they were sent too (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 25). In Samsun seventy Turkish notables telegraphed Kemal that it was 'against their religion to massacre' women and children, the mufti issued a fatwa against it, and Kemal replied that exiling Samsun's Greeks was 'a merciful act' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 410); in July relocation was suspended at Samsun after Muslim notables complained of massacres. The memoirist Tepeyran puts the number deported from Samsun at nearly 21,000. By November 1921 the Central Army's records counted 63,844 Greeks moved inland (Biber, after Balcıoğlu); another breakdown from the same records gives 27,995 from Samsun, 14,000 from Amasya, 8,500 from Giresun, 4,910 from Ordu, 1,448 from Sivas, 1,000 from Tokat, 571 from Çorum and 550 from Sinop, 58,974 in all, relocated to Sivas, Tokat, Yozgat, Çorum and Şebinkarahisar (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 25).
disputed: The two Central Army figures differ (63,844 by November 1921; 58,974 in the breakdown) and may cover different dates. Turkish historiography's description of the measure as a lawful wartime relocation is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T04). Critics point to the inclusion of women and children and the mortality on the marches; the Interior Ministry's own order of 25 June did not cover women and children.

title: The first convoys of men leave Samsun, Bafra and Alaçam
summary: On 16 June 1921 police began to round up the Greek men of Samsun aged 15–50; on the 19th, US officers reported, about 2,000 were marched inland. Stefanos Yerasimos gives the convoy dates: Samsun on 16 and 17 June (the second, of about 700, reached Amasya) and 25 June; Bafra on 17, 21 and 24 June, each of about 500–600 men; Alaçam on 18, 21 and 22 June (one of about 1,000). Kévorkian dates the call-up of the Bafra men to 28 June. From September old people, women and children were sent too.
disputed: Biber gives the third Alaçam convoy as 22 June in one place and 20 June in another. A Bafra convoy on 17 June comes a day before the round-up of Saturday 18 June (B1-010); Kévorkian's 28 June is later still.

title: Bafra district, June-September 1921: the men seized and killed, villages burned, women and children deported
summary: On the morning of Saturday 5/18 June 1921 (Julian/Gregorian; the 'June 5' of Morris & Ze'evi, p. 408, is the Julian date) troops, gendarmes and armed local Turks surrounded Bafra and seized the Greek men, who were marched off in convoys. The killing of the convoys in churches rests on a single Greek eyewitness, the Bafra notable Ioannis Dilmitzoglou, whose account (signed Athens, 13 October 1921) is printed in the 1922 Black Book: about 535 men taken to the church at Suludere near Elezli (Morris & Ze'evi's 'Blezli'), the seven priests killed with an axe at the door; about 500 burned in the church of Selamelik; and a third convoy of 680 (400 recruits and 280 exiles) taken to the church of 'Kodje-sou' (Morris & Ze'evi's 'Kavdje-son'), whose fate the witness did not know. Morris & Ze'evi's figures (p. 408) cite this same text from the Toynbee Papers. Villages were burned with their people: 300 at Sürmeli (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 409) and 250 at Muğamlı (the same witness). On 8 July 1921 the US destroyer Brooks reported that in the Bafra area 'as many as 90 percent of deported Greeks have been killed' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 409, n. 200); dated before any women were deported, it concerns the men's convoys of June. On 3 August the mutasarrıf of Bafra told a US officer that the deportation 'of all remaining Greeks, including women and children, had been ordered by Angora' (p. 407). US destroyers then reported about 6,000 women and children deported from Bafra around 31 August and 2,500 more on 19 September (p. 408; Shenk 2017, pp. 200-201). These convoys and those described by Fotiadis (16 September, 4,120 people; 24 September, 1,900) may be the same convoys dated differently, so the figures must not be added up.
disputed: Ankara's version is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T05, H6-T08). The witness writes '5th/18th of June 1921, Saturday morning'; 5 June, the date in Morris & Ze'evi, is the Julian date. The church burnings rest on one Greek witness, whose text Morris & Ze'evi's figures also cite (p. 408). He gives 680 for the Kocasu convoy, not the '680–780' sometimes quoted, and does not say how they died. The '90 percent' is the report of the USS Brooks of 8 July 1921, not of Yowell or Ward, and concerns the men. The US and Fotiadis convoys may overlap. 'Soulou Dere' may be the Suludere rural district of Bafra (Nişanyan); Elezli and Kocasu are not in Nişanyan.

title: Bafra surrounded and the men seized; Dilmitzoglou's account of the killings at Elezli (Suludere)
summary: On the morning of Saturday 5/18 June 1921 troops and armed local Turks surrounded Bafra and demanded the surrender of the men. According to the account of the Bafra notable Ioannis Dilmitzoglou, written in Turkish in Greek characters and printed in translation in the Black Book, about 535 men were tied back to back and taken to the church at Suludere near the village of Elezli; the seven priests were killed with an axe at the church door, the rest shot, bayoneted or axed, and Nicolas Jordanoglou paid his last 300 Turkish lira to be shot. Four wounded men escaped to Mount Nebyan. The Patriarchate reported that the Greek notables had first been invited to a dinner at the house of one Efrem Aga and murdered there.
disputed: The witness writes '5th/18th of June 1921, Saturday morning', and 18 June 1921 (New Style) was a Saturday; Morris & Ze'evi's 'June 5', after a British enclosure, is the Julian date. The same text opens with attacks on the villages 'on the 5th of July', a slip. Morris & Ze'evi's figures for 'Blezli', Selamelik and Kavdje-son (p. 408, n. 186) come from this same text, so the numbers rest on one Greek witness. Kyriakidis (p. 61, after Shenk) describes Bafra deportees of October 1921 shot, burned and knifed in three groups, which looks like a misdated echo of the same account. 'Soulou Dere' may be the Suludere rural district of Bafra (Nişanyan); Elezli is not in Nişanyan.

title: The Samsun–Bafra convoys shot on the road near Kavak
summary: The Black Book's notes list men's convoys from the Samsun–Bafra district of about 2,000, 1,901, 2,000, 500 and 620; on a descent near Kavak the escort fired on them, killing 330 of the first convoy and 660 of the third, and the survivors were sent on stripped 'to Malatia, Harpout, Mamouret-oul-Aziz, and Alpistan'. A deportee of the third Samsun convoy wrote that '660 were killed' as the column descended a mountain; Cosmos Lilidas said his convoy, which left Samsun around 20 June, was fired on near 'Djinbush', '292 remaining out of the thousand'. Stanley Hopkins of the NER reported 550 Greeks executed at Kavak on 26 June and 1,300 on 15 August; Rendel's Foreign Office memorandum has 1,300 shot near Kavak on 15 or 16 August 'in about two and a half hours'. The League of Nations circulated a Greek figure of at least 900.
disputed: 330 and 660 make 990, consistent with 'at least 900'; Hopkins' 550 (26 June) and 1,300 (15 August) are separate killings; Kyriakidis also cites naval logbooks with 660 and 530 killed in two convoys. Kévorkian's 6,500 of 7,000 conscripts killed on the Samsun–Kavak road on 2 August, with the last 500 sent to Malatya, come from an Armenian Patriarchate Information Bureau report of August 1921 (Kévorkian, part III, ch. 3, n. 100); we found no second source for them. Kévorkian also gives the Samsun–Bafra convoys from another Patriarchate report (nn. 103–104), with 3,000 in the fourth convoy and 660 dead from the second. Ankara said the Kavak dead fell in battle (H6-T08).

title: Orders extend the deportations to all adult Christian men, then to all Ottoman Greeks
summary: An Armenian report of 18 July 1921 refers to a 2 July order from Ankara for the deportation of all 'adult male' Christians 'throughout the interior of Anatolia'; another report indicates that two weeks later Ankara ordered the 'immediate deportation of all Ottoman Greeks'. Ankara denied that orders had been issued to deport women and children. A British cabinet paper (CAB 24/131) said that Greeks aged 15–55 were being moved to areas near Syria, Mesopotamia and Diyarbakır.
disputed: No text of the 2 July order has been found.

title: Near East Relief workers meet the first convoys between Samsun, Amasya and Sivas
summary: Wilford W. Fuller of the Near East Relief, leaving Sivas on 4 July 1921, met five convoys of Greek men deported from Samsun; of the first two, of 900, only 200 reached Sivas, naked and robbed, saying the others had been killed at Kavak. On 26 July he met about 3,000 women and children driven inland by gendarmes on the road between Amasya and Merzifon. On 8 July the US destroyer Brooks reported that in the Bafra area 'as many as 90 percent of deported Greeks have been killed'.
disputed: The '90 percent' report is dated 8 July 1921, so it concerns the men's convoys of June, not the women and children deported from late August. It is not by Yowell or Ward (NER at Harput). The officer could not leave Samsun freely; the figure may count the missing as dead.

title: Western protests to Ankara over the Pontic deportations and executions
summary: On 18 July 1921 the US High Commissioner Bristol telegraphed Mustafa Kemal asking him to prevent the expulsion of women, children and the old from Samsun; Yusuf Kemal replied on 21 July. On 22 September the French, British and Italian representatives (Fourcade, Rumbold and Garroni) telegraphed the Ankara government their concern about the relocation; these texts, with Yusuf Kemal's note of 15 September to the Entente representatives, are reproduced in Ankara's own book Pontus Meselesi (1922) (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 21). In October Rumbold and the other Allied High Commissioners sent Ankara a protest telegram on the forced migration and the executions in the eastern Black Sea region (Rumbold to Curzon, 15 October 1921, via Çetinoğlu).
disputed: Rumbold also told the Patriarchal vicar (6 Oct 1921) that both sides were sending massacre allegations and that only peace would end them (Çetinoğlu, after Bilgiç).

title: Merzifon: Topal Osman's men and local Turks kill Christians over a week
summary: From 23-24 July 1921 Topal Osman's irregulars spent four days pillaging and killing in Merzifon, followed by four or five days of violence by locals assisted by gendarmes and troops. Men and boys sheltering in the French school were taken out and shot and girls abducted, and the school was torched; about 400 Armenian houses were burned, while the Greek quarter was left untouched (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 411-413). Before the massacre the town had 2,000-2,500 Christians; 'almost all the men were killed', and the remaining Greeks were deported (p. 413). Estimates of the dead: 'more than a thousand' (p. 411); 950 (the Armenian-Greek Section of the British High Commission) and about 1,200 (Bristol and the missionary Gertrude Anthony) (p. 413, n. 223); 'maybe 1,000 or 1,500', though 'no one could say for sure' (Anthony, via Shenk 2017, p. 203). In May 1922 only 14 Armenian and Greek men were left in the town (Theda Phelps, ibid.).
disputed: The toll is an estimate, 950–1,500 according to the source; no count exists. Ankara's denial ('legend', p. 413) is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T06).

title: Two refugees' account: Trabzon's Greek men summoned for 'fortification work', then deported and shot
summary: Two refugees from the Pontus told the British that in August 1921 the Trabzon authorities ordered all adult Greek men to report for paid labour on fortifications; 500 or more who did were imprisoned and their homes pillaged, then deported in groups of fifty, marched for seven days 'without as much as a morsel of bread', and one night taken away in groups of ten and shot (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 423).
disputed: Two witnesses, recorded by the British; no other source for this episode was found.

title: The mutasarrıf of Bafra: all remaining Greeks, women and children included, to be deported
summary: On 3 August 1921 the commander of USS Overton recorded that the mutasarrıf of Bafra had told him that the deportation 'of all remaining Greeks, including women and children, had been ordered by Angora', reinforced by Nureddin Pasha's instruction to proceed 'with all dispatch' or cease to be mutasarrıf; the officer judged it 'part of an official plan which contemplates extermination of the Greeks'. On 8 August the women and girls of Bafra were collected, 'stripped and violated', many forced to convert; those who refused were led off 'to different unknown places'. Dilmitzoglou describes groups of 1,000–1,500 women and children held for days without food in the yard of the Bafra church and then driven towards Kastamonu. Only the sick who paid bribes were allowed to stay (USS Williamson).
disputed: Ankara told Bristol (2 Aug 1921) and Bristol's aide that it had not ordered the deportation of women (Morris & Ze'evi pp. 407, 415); its later admissions are in B1-022. The Kastamonu direction is in the Greek account only and may be a separate early drive west.

title: Pope Benedict XV asks Kemal to cancel the exile of 5,000 women and children near Samsun
summary: After appeals from the president of the Pontian Association, Dr Thoidis, the Pope had the Apostolic Delegate, Mgr Angelo Dolci, telegraph Mustafa Kemal on 18 August 1921 asking for the cancellation of the order to exile 5,000 women and children from the areas near Samsun. In March 1921 the Pope had already asked Kemal, through Cardinal Gasparri, to protect the lives and property of Christians; Kemal replied that Christians under the Grand National Assembly were calm and accused Greeks and Armenians of crimes (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 76-79). On 24 July 1921 Dolci wrote that the Delegation was receiving reports of massacres from all the Christian communities and that 'Christians kept being murdered' (p. 78).
disputed: The papal telegram is a neutral document; the number 5,000 came from the Pontic appeals.

title: About 6,000 women and children deported from Bafra
summary: Some 6,000 Greek women and children were deported from Bafra around 31 August 1921 (USS McFarland, 1 Sept). The McFarland's war diaries of 31 August – 8 September record 1,500 women and children of nearby villages, who had been living in Samsun, being deported, and say that, according to the American tobacco men, the deportation of 'some six thousand women and children from the Bafra district was well underway'.
disputed: The McFarland's Bafra figure was hearsay from the tobacco company men at Samsun. Route not given.

title: Fotiadis: the convoy of 16 September, 4,120 deported, 1,270 reach Malatya
summary: According to Fotiadis, 4,120 people, among them 150 orphans from the American orphanage, were deported from Bafra on 16 September 1921 and walked for 70 days by way of Hacıhamza, Osmancık, Çorum, Mecitözü, Turhal, Tokat, Sivas, Tecer Han, Deliktaş, Kangal and Hekimhan to Malatya. 130 of the orphans and 2,700 women, children and old people died of cold, hunger and exhaustion; at Sivas the Americans took the 20 surviving orphans; 1,270 reached Malatya, where most died in a typhus epidemic (4,120 − 2,700 − 130 − 20 = 1,270). American sources confirm a convoy of this size on this road: a party of Americans met a column of 4,000 Bafra women and children near Sivas, with about seventy old men, 'little clothing, many... without shoes and apparently... no food' (USS McFarland, October 1921); a traveller reported to the British a convoy of about 4,000 Greeks deported from Samsun to Tokat (9 Nov 1921); and Theda Phelps at Sivas met a Bafra woman who had made her two children walk the snowy mountain paths because 'the children who were being carried were all freezing to death'.
disputed: The numbers 4,120, 1,270, 2,700 and 1,900 are not in Dilmitzoglou's account as printed in the Black Book, which was signed on 13 October 1921, before the convoy could have reached Malatya, so Fotiadis took them from a source he does not name; Antonios Gavriilidis, a Bafra deportee to Malatya who wrote in 1924, may be that source. The US reports have about 6,000 deported on 31 August and 2,500 on 19 September; Fotiadis' 16 and 24 September may be other convoys, or the same ones dated differently (in the Julian calendar they would be 29 September and 7 October). The McFarland's '4,000 near Sivas' fits the 4,120 best. The convoys should not be added up. Some stages of the route have not been located: 'Turtmen Tayi' and 'Batman Tayi' (mountains), 'Kaynarhan', 'Cenkel' and 'Tuzla' (south of Sivas).

title: 2,500 more deported from Bafra; local Muslim dissent
summary: A further 2,500 Greek women and children were deported from Bafra on 19 September 1921 (USS Sturtevant, 20 Sept). The Sturtevant's commander, Lt Cdr E. G. A Turkish notable told an American businessman that 'what had happened made him ashamed to be a Turk'.
disputed: May be the same convoy as Fotiadis's 4,120 of 16 September, counted differently.

title: Fotiadis: the 'eighth convoy', 1,900 deported, 800 reach Hekimhan
summary: Fotiadis writes that the eighth convoy, of 1,900 people, left Bafra on 24 September 1921. Between Deliktaş and Kangal 310 froze to death and 790 died of disease and exhaustion; after a 70-day march 800 reached Hekimhan. About 400, the most exhausted, were left there, where almost all died; the rest were sent on to Malatya and Harput, where almost all of them died too.
disputed: We found no independent report of this convoy, and Fotiadis does not name his source (see B1-017).

title: The Black Book: the last 1,600 women and children of Alaçam driven inland via Boyabat towards Osmancık
summary: The Black Book's supplementary notes (Athens, 25 September 1921) say the remaining 1,600 women and children of Alaçam were deported inland; they had reached Boyabat ('Boivat'), 127 km from Alaçam, most having died on the way of illness and ill-treatment, and their destination was Osmancık. The same notes report 17 orphans of the Bafra orphanage dead of starvation and left unburied for days.
disputed: Greek source only. The Black Book's '120 km from Angora' for Osmancık is wrong (about 200 km).

title: The Grand National Assembly debates Nureddin's conduct; he is removed
summary: Deputies in the Grand National Assembly at Ankara attacked Nureddin's conduct in Koçgiri and the Pontus. On 5 October 1921 the Lazistan deputies Ziya Hurşit and Osman Bey brought an interpellation on 'banditry in Samsun', and on 29 October, in secret session, they accused Nureddin of having ordered the deportation of Greek women and children beyond the scope of the relocation order, of killings in the middle of Samsun in front of Americans and other foreigners, of attacks on the first convoy six hours out of Samsun, and of putting under town arrest the 56 notables of Samsun, among them its mayor and mufti, who had appealed to Kemal against the deportation of women and children; they said that his use of irregular bands had driven Greeks to the mountains. The Trabzon deputy Hafız Mehmet said he had seen a battalion of the Giresun regiment loot and burn villages under the pretext of collecting arms. Nureddin was relieved of command on 3 November 1921 on charges including the use of irregular forces in Koçgiri and Samsun, accepting a bribe from a Pontic Greek, ordering public pillage during the relocation, and harming Muslims by driving the Pontic Greeks to the mountains; Mustafa Kemal blocked his trial, and he later commanded the First Army in 1922.
disputed: The debate concerned both Koçgiri (where Ziya Hurşit said many Muslim villages had been burned) and the Pontus; the Samsun deportations, the women and children and the 56 notables were central to it (Çilingir's extracts; Korucu & Dağlıoğlu). The deputies also blamed Nureddin for driving Greeks to the mountains and some claimed Muslim villages had been burned: those claims are under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T08). Morris & Ze'evi write that 'Kemal knew how to get the worst out of his subordinates' (p. 404), that Nureddin was charged with 'the mal-execution of his orders', as US diplomats were told (p. 406), and quote Yusuf Kemal on 'local officials' exaggerated zeal' (p. 415); Korucu & Dağlıoğlu (p. 27) call Nureddin 'one of the primary perpetrators'; Hofmann (2011, p. 76) notes that no action was taken against Osman after Merzifon.

title: The Bafra witness writes in Turkish: the Turkish-speaking Orthodox of Bafra
summary: The fullest account of the Bafra killings, by the notable Ioannis Dilmitzoglou, was written 'in the Turkish text written in Greek characters' (Karamanlidika) and translated for the Black Book (signed Athens, 13 October 1921). The Orthodox of Bafra town were Turkish-speaking: the 1911 Greek consular census marks them so, and the village list of the Centre for Asia Minor Studies says that 'the native Greeks and the Cappadocian Greeks only spoke Turkish', while settlers from elsewhere in the Pontus spoke Pontic. No source we have found treats them differently from Pontic-speakers in 1921: their men were killed and their women and children deported like the rest.
disputed: The census entry is Kitromilides & Alexandris 1984–85, Table VI, p. 41, row 243, 'Bafra' (2,822 inhabitants), where the language column carries a ditto mark of the 'Turcophone' printed at row 237. Some deportees were forced to convert (B1-014), but no source shows that speaking Turkish spared anyone.

title: The British High Commission's Armenian-Greek Section: 420 of 720 Greek villages of the Pontus destroyed (October 1921)
summary: A report of the Armenian-Greek Section of the British High Commission at Constantinople, 'Deportations and Massacre on Black Sea Littoral, and Massacre at Marsovan' (covering note from Rumbold to Curzon, 22 October 1921), stated that of the 720 majority-Greek villages in the Pontus, 420 had been 'burnt or destroyed, the men killed or deported, and the women removed', and the other 300 partially destroyed, with the men deported (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 416, n. 247). Earlier, in May 1921, US officers at Samsun had relayed a missionary's report that about 100 Greek villages south of Bafra were destroyed within a few days from 17 May (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 405, 408; B1-001).
disputed: The 'about 100 villages' is a missionary's estimate for the Bafra area in May 1921, not a count for the Samsun district in October.

title: Zonguldak: the Greek Orthodox men deported (Catholic missionary note)
summary: A note from the Catholic mission at Zonguldak, sent to the Apostolic Delegation, reports that from early November 1921 the Kemalist authorities deported the male Greek Orthodox population to distant provinces: about 750 men and youths, boys of 14 among them, leaving about 2,500 old men, women and small children without support; the missionaries asked that their authorship be kept secret (Kyriakidis 2026, Text 4, pp. 159-160).
disputed: Zonguldak lies west of the Pontus proper. Kyriakidis's narrative (p. 83) says the note concerns 'the whole Orthodox Greek male population' without naming Zonguldak; the note itself is about Zonguldak.

title: Nureddin and Yusuf Kemal admit the deportation of women and children; Bafra Turks armed
summary: In his defence against the Assembly's charges, Nureddin Pasha said that the women 'had helped their men in thought, body and property', that 'the Greeks in our country are a snake; the poison of these snakes is the women', and that 'therefore we did the same to them as to the men; we did not separate them from their children either'. He also said that local Turks had been organised in security units, with 600 armed men from Kavak and 1,000 from Bafra. In February 1922 the foreign minister Yusuf Kemal, who had earlier told the Americans that Ankara had not ordered the deportation of women, told a journalist that 'the military command... has judged it necessary to deport them'. These are admissions; the justifications are given under 'What the Turkish sources say' (B1-T03, H7-T14, B1-T08).
disputed: The date of Nureddin's statement is not given (after his removal on 3 November 1921).

title: Where the deportees were sent: the Central Army's list and the Greek testimonies
summary: The Central Army's records count 63,844 Greeks moved inland by November 1921, to Sivas, Tokat, Yozgat, Çorum, Şebinkarahisar, Elazığ, Ergani, Malatya and Maraş. Testimonies in the Exodus volumes of the Centre for Asia Minor Studies, listed by Karas & Tsilfidis, place deportees from Bafra, Samsun and Havza in Sivas in 1922 and deportees from Alaçam in Malatya (May 1921), and record two villages of the Havza–Vezirköprü area ('Hodjas', perhaps Koçaş, June 1921; 'Karatzoren', summer 1921) as deported 'to Aleppo'. Kévorkian notes that the destinations named by the Arapgir missionaries were all to the south, perhaps with a view to a final expulsion into the French or British mandates.
disputed: 'To Aleppo' in a 1921 testimony may mean the southern road rather than arrival in French-mandate Syria. Kévorkian's reading of intent is an interpretation.

title: Central Council of Pontus, Black Book: an 'Exterminated Population' of 303,238 by the end of 1921
summary: The bilingual (English and French) Black Book of the Central Council of Pontus (Athens, 1922) gives, in a table headed 'General description of the victims of Pontus according to ecclesiastical provinces and Greek communities', a column 'Exterminated Population' ('Population détruite'): Amaseia 134,078; Chaldia 64,582; Trebizond 38,434; Neocaesarea 27,216; Kolonia 21,448; Rhodopolis 17,479. The printed total, in the table and in the text ('a Population of 303238 men has been exterminated by the fire and the steel'), is 303,238; the rows add to 303,237. The communities (815) and schools (960) add up; the church column is printed 1,134 but its rows (603 + 135 + 127 + 182 + 53 + 74) add to 1,174. Each district list is headed 'Exterminated by the confiscation of their fortunes, exile, violations, cold, hunger, assassination and massacre' ('dépouillés de leurs biens confisqués, morts en exil, par la faim et le froid, violés, pillés, assassinés, tués et massacrés'), so the column counts the dispossessed and exiled as well as the dead. Four of the six figures are identical to the Patriarchate's 1919 count of those deported in 1914-18; only Amaseia (+44,708) and Kolonia (+1,510) differ. The text names as proof the massacres near Kavak, Djimbouch Han, Selamelik and Kiz Alan, the 'holocausts' at Ada, Karapertchine, Tekke Keuy and the French school at Merzifon, and the hangings at Amasya.
disputed: The identity with the 1919 deportation figures, and the book's own definition of 'exterminated' (confiscation, exile, violation, cold, hunger, murder and massacre), show that 303,238 is not a count of deaths.

title: Bafra emptied: 321 Greeks brought from Samsun for a possible Allied visit
summary: According to the war diary of USS Sands, after the deportations and massacres no Greeks were left in the Bafra district, and the Turks sent 321 Greeks there from Samsun in case an Allied commission came to check the charges.
disputed: Date of the diary entry not given.

title: Winter 1922: the women in the mountains deported; the Bafra hinterland swept
summary: In January 1922, after an amnesty, about a thousand women who had sheltered in the mountains returned to Samsun, many wounded and starving; officials promised them safety, but soon 'the whole band was deported to the interior'. In February 1922 Turkish forces directed by Fethi swept the hinterland of Bafra and captured those hiding in the mountains; according to a telegram from 21 Greek and Circassian refugees from Bafra, the interior minister offered rewards for heads and 'five sacks full of heads were brought to him at Baffra'. The same telegram says Circassians of Bafra saved about 140 Greek neighbours by hiding them in cellars.
disputed: The 'sacks of heads' is the refugees' allegation. Morris & Ze'evi's 'Fethi' is presumably the interior minister Fethi (Okyar).

title: A survivor's account: women and children burned in houses in the villages above Ordu (February 1922)
summary: On 15 February 1922 two to three hundred irregulars led by Osman Ağa rode into 'Ordu' (the report concerns the villages above the town), largely emptied of men. According to a survivor, they torched all but two houses, into which about 170 women and children and a handful of men were herded and burned; about fifteen young girls were taken aside, abused and killed the next day, though five or six were rumoured spared 'for the harem of the Pasha'. Nine neighbouring villages received the same treatment (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 416).
disputed: One survivor's account, forwarded by an American missionary; the villages are not named, and we found no other report of this raid. The Armenian Patriarchate also reported an army attack on Greek villages of the Ordu kaza, including Yanakandon, dated '22 March 1922' in Kévorkian's text, which may be a slip for 1919 (Kévorkian 2023, part III, ch. 3, n. 51, a report of March 1919).

title: Yowell and Ward expelled from Harput; their reports reach the press
summary: Expelled from Harput in March 1922, Yowell and Ward reported to the US consul at Aleppo (5 April 1922) that the Turkish authorities 'were frank in their statements that it was the intention to have all the Greeks die' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 425). In May they published their findings in the New York Times and the Times of London; the British High Commission called the reports evidence of 'the deliberate attempt of the Angora Government to exterminate the Greek population of Anatolia' (p. 425). Rumbold, citing Ward, wrote that 'the Turks appear to be working on a deliberate plan to get rid of minorities', and that Turkish officials had told Ward that 'in 1915 Turks had not made a clean job of massacres' (p. 419). Admiral Bristol, the US High Commissioner, called the publication a British 'intrigue' and acted to discredit the reports (p. 427), though he had protested to Ankara about the deportations in July 1921. Harold Jaquith of the NER, touring eastern Anatolia that summer, saw 'thousands of shallow mounds' along the roads and found deportees removed from towns before his visits (pp. 427-428).

title: The reports leave by the south: Harput relief workers reach Aleppo and Beirut
summary: Expelled from Harput in March 1922 (Ward left on 15 March), Yowell and Ward reported to the US consul at Aleppo, Jesse B. Jackson, on 5 April 1922. In late March Jackson reported that American missionaries arriving in Aleppo from Harput said that 'at least 75,000 Greeks' had been deported from the Pontus in the previous months, of whom only '20,000' had survived; the British consul at Beirut forwarded the account of a Harput missionary (3 April 1922).
disputed: 75,000 deported and 20,000 survivors is a second-hand estimate; compare 63,844 moved (Central Army) and Rendel's 'well over 35,000' for 1921 (Morris & Ze'evi p. 415).

title: The Rendel memorandum (Foreign Office)
summary: George W. Rendel of the Foreign Office compiled a 'Memorandum on Turkish Massacres and Persecutions of Minorities since the Armistice' (20 March 1922). Its sentence that 'over 500,000 Greeks were deported, of whom comparatively few survived' concerns the World War I period and all Ottoman Greeks (Hofmann 2011, p. 103, quoting p. 1 of the memorandum); Morris & Ze'evi (p. 385) cite a similar phrase from Rendel's memorandum of 28 December 1921 for the 'as many as 550,000' Greeks uprooted during the war. For the Pontus in 1921 Rendel estimated that 'well over 35,000 Greeks' had been deported, the balance being 'massacred... in circumstances of utmost barbarity' (28 December 1921; Morris & Ze'evi, p. 415), and his memorandum of 20 March 1922 recorded 1,300 men shot near Kavak on 15 or 16 August 1921 (p. 408).
disputed: The 500,000 is not a Pontic figure: it covers all Ottoman Greeks deported in 1914-18.

title: Samsun: further deportations of women, children and the old
summary: On 10 or 11 April 1922 a reported 1,324 Greeks, 'mostly women and children... [with] a few old men', were deported from Samsun; some 'were said to be so weak they could not walk out to the truck for their bread'. Another 1,462 women and children, many recently down from the mountains, were deported inland on 15 April (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 417-418, after the diary of USS Fox). The wife of a Turkish officer later reported that Greeks had been 'marched into the hills near Kavak and murdered' (pp. 418-419). By September 1922 virtually no Greeks remained in Samsun.
disputed: 1,324 (Morris & Ze'evi) or about 1,300 (Shenk).

title: Trabzon: all Greek men from 15 upwards deported
summary: In early May 1922 Rumbold reported that at Trabzon 'the whole Greek male population from the age of 15 upwards' was 'being deported', in groups of fifty every few days (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 419). The American Herbert Adams Gibbons, of Robert College and the Christian Science Monitor, wrote on 20 May 1922 that Trabzon was left with 'half a dozen priests and ten other men and boys', not one doctor or teacher, and that the Turks were now seizing boys of 11 to 14; he also named the mayor, Hussein Effendi, and the vali as opponents of the persecution (p. 420). The Capuchin superior Father Lorenzo wrote from Trabzon on 14 May 1922 that every week groups of men were deported inland by way of Erzurum and that most died of hunger or disease (Kyriakidis 2026, p. 82).

title: Catholic reports from Trebizond, May 1922: no Greek men left on the coast
summary: The Capuchin superior at Trebizond, Father Lorenzo, wrote on 8 May 1922 that there were hardly any Armenians left in the city and only women and children among the Greeks; that in Samsun there were no men but a few elderly; that inland no Greek villages remained, their people killed and the villages looted; and that at Giresun Topal Osman, with about a hundred men, killed and looted unpunished, 'supported by the Turkish government and honoured by the Muslim population'. On 14 May he added that at İnebolu, Samsun and Giresun only the old, women and children remained, and that every week groups of men were deported from Trebizond via Erzurum, most dying of hunger or disease; on 30 May he asked that his letter not be mentioned, since 'it could cost me my life' (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 82-84).

title: Interior minister Fethi in secret session: 5,051 Greeks dead in four months; 'starving them is the most effective measure'
summary: Answering an interpellation by the Trabzon deputy Ali Şükrü, the interior minister Ali Fethi (Okyar) told a secret session of the Grand National Assembly on 10 June 1922 that he had taken the most effective measures 'to cleanse (tathir etmek, temizlemek) these Greeks who have been a calamity to the country for eight years'. He reported that up to 15 May 1922 the operations had disposed of 13,175 people: 3,388 surrendered, 5,051 dead, 1,592 captured alive and 3,144 wounded; that the food depots had been destroyed, 'leaving them hungry; starving them is the most effective measure'; and that, according to the Samsun mutasarrıflık, the Greeks remaining in that zone would not reach even five percent of the Muslim population (Çilingir, p. 121, from the published minutes). Korucu & Dağlıoğlu give the same session's figures by period: 1,275 killed of 4,444 'neutralised' between 29 December 1921 and 20 March 1922, and 3,777 killed and 1,150 taken into custody between 20 March and 15 May 1922 (p. 15). In May 1922 Fethi also reported that two months of operations under Cemil Cahit had led to the death or capture of 15,000 Greeks (p. 25).
disputed: The two transmitters agree on the totals (3,388 surrendered; 5,051/5,052 killed) but date the start of the period differently (29 January 1922 in Çilingir, 29 December 1921 in Korucu & Dağlıoğlu).

title: Near East Relief takes the surviving Greek children from Malatya and Harput to Syria
summary: In June 1921 the NER at Malatya ran two orphanages with about 800 children and fed 1,700 people. In autumn 1922, as Ankara closed the interior, it moved its children south. Lester J. Wright, director at Malatya, wrote from Aleppo on 10 October 1922 that he had taken 214 children over the mountains from Malatya in seven days to the railhead at Jarabulus, in French territory, and that 'we have permission to move out Greek children... About 700 of them at Malatia and 100 at Harpoot. We had many more at Malatia last fall but thousands died during the winter... they were all refugees that were driven from their homes a year ago or more'; eleven men had been hired all winter just to bury the dead. On 27 October 1922 Wright was killed by Turkish irregulars in French territory while escorting 200 children, half Greek and half Armenian, from Harput to Aleppo; he was buried in Beirut. The NER described the whole movement as '5,000 children' trekking 500 miles from Harput into Syria, 'to be distributed among the orphanages there or to be sent on further to Constantinople or Greece'. In 1923 Greece agreed to take more than 16,000 NER orphans, many of them housed on Syros.
disputed: How many of the Malatya Greek children were from Bafra is not known; Wright's description fits the Bafra and Samsun women's convoys that reached Malatya in late 1921. We have not found the ships and dates of the voyage from Beirut to Greece.

title: A Bafra deportee escapes from Malatya to Aleppo, Beirut and Athens
summary: Antonios Gavriilidis, a tobacco merchant of Bafra deported to Malatya, agreed on 26 August 1922 with two Armenian friends (Hosrob Derohanesian and Serkiz Kalaytzian) and the brothers Ioannis and Aristidis Lazaridis (not related to the author of this atlas) to escape. Disguised and under Turkish names, with two muleteers (the Turk Hadji Ali and the Kurd Pakash, paid 125 gold lira) and 45 loaded donkeys, they travelled by night, bribed a Kurdish chief who detained them, and reached Aleppo, where the Greek community helped them. They went on by train to Beirut, by French ship to Constantinople, and reached Athens on 1 November 1922.
disputed: The route between Malatya and Aleppo is not given; the NER orphan caravans of the same weeks went from Malatya over the mountains to Jarabulus on the Euphrates (B1-027).
sources_primary: Gavriilidis, Η μαύρη εθνική συμφορά του Πόντου 1914-1922 (Athens 1924), excerpted in translation on greek-genocide.net
sources_modern: greek-genocide.net, 'Antonios Gavriilidis' (testimonies)

title: Greek refugees at Aleppo: 12,000 in January 1923, most shipped to Greece by August
summary: After Ankara ordered the remaining Christians out in October 1922, most went to the ports, but a few Greeks travelled by land southward toward Aleppo, sometimes offered the option of staying if they converted; 'practically all' those heading for Mersin, Alexandretta and Aleppo were robbed on the way. In January 1923 a US destroyer reported 50,000 Armenian refugees in Aleppo 'along with 12,000 Greeks', the figure on the Library of Congress photograph captioned 'Where 12,000 Greek refugees were fed by Americans'. In early April Bristol counted 60,000 refugees in Aleppo, 50,000 of them Armenians. By August 1923 most of the Greeks had been shipped to Greece, though 'the poorest and weakest in health, mostly women and children' remained, begging (NER, Beirut, 28 Aug 1923).
disputed: None says how many were Pontic; most were probably from Cilicia and central Anatolia.

title: Expulsion to the ports: Samsun and Mersin
summary: In early October 1922 Ankara instructed the provinces to let the remaining Christians go, 'really an order for them all to get out'; on the Black Sea coast they were told they had thirty days to leave or be marched inland. In November 1922, according to Fotiadis, 10,460 Christians of the Samsun area, including Bafra, were shipped out. In March 1923 the NER fed 9,000 refugees at Samsun one hot meal a day while 4,000 had no aid; 10,000 awaited passage at Samsun, 3,000 at Trabzon, 1,500 at Ordu, 500 at Ünye and 300 at Fatsa, and 8,000 at Alexandretta and 3,500 at Mersin. In mid-March a proclamation at Samsun threatened to send home those who did not leave within days; in April embarkations stalled over fares and Greece's refusal to take more until the exchange began. Bristol reported on 29 March that the refugees at Mersin had been allowed to stay until ships came.
disputed: The 10,460 of November 1922 rests on Fotiadis via Topalidis.
sources_primary: USS Overton, Samsun diary, Oct–Nov 1922; CO USS McFarland, Simpson, Litchfield, Overton diaries, March 1923 (via Morris & Ze'evi) | Bristol to SecState, 28 and 29 Mar 1923, FRUS 1923, vol. II, docs 222-223
sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP 2019), pp. 456-457, 462-464 | Fotiadis 2019 (via Topalidis, S., 'A History of Bafra, Pontos', pontosworld.com (no. 792)) for the 10,460

title: A Turkish count: 11,198 Greeks killed and 10,886 surrendered in the Pontus operations (to February 1923)
summary: According to Turkish military records summarised by Balcıoğlu, the operations in the Pontus, from early 1921 until they ended in February 1923, killed 11,198 Greeks, and 10,886 surrendered (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 25). The General Staff's history of the War of Independence gives 11,188 killed (İstiklal Harbi Tarihi, vol. IV, p. 294, via Çetinoğlu). The records describe the dead as bandits killed in operations.
disputed: A lower limit for those killed in operations, from the state's own count, and so an admission; its description of the dead as bandits is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T10). It does not include deaths on the deportation marches. Korucu & Dağlıoğlu (and bianet, 2018) give 11,198 killed; Çetinoğlu, twice, after the General Staff's history, and Çilingir (2016) give 11,188, so one reading is probably a slip; all give 10,886 surrendered.

title: Refet Pasha to the Apostolic Delegate: Greeks and Armenians 'will have to pay the price for their sins'
summary: After the Allied evacuation of Constantinople, the new Apostolic Delegate, Mgr Filippi, asked Refet Pasha to prevent reprisals against Christians. Refet replied that 'Latin Catholics have nothing to fear... As for Greeks and Armenians, they will have to pay the price for their sins' (a following phrase, 'I mean the guilty ones', is crossed out in Filippi's report). Filippi also reported that high Turkish officials such as Nureddin Pasha had publicly roused Muslim feeling against Christians (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 100-101). In December 1923 the Capuchin Father Michele counted 2,000-2,500 Greek refugees still waiting to leave Samsun (p. 100).
sources_primary: [Vatican] Filippi to Cardinal Gasparri, 20 Sept 1923, Segreteria di Stato, AA.EE.SS., Turchia 1923-1924, Pos. 23, fasc. 43, pp. 50r-51v; F. Michele, Samsun, 22 Dec 1923, ASV, Arch. Deleg. Turchia, 119, fasc. 674, p. 11r (via Kyriakidis 2026)
sources_modern: Kyriakidis (trans. Nikoloudis), The Genocide of Orthodox Greeks and the Persecution of Christians in the Pontus Region according to Vatican Archives (Gorgias Press, 2026), pp. 100-101

title: The last Pontic bands leave for Poti
summary: Kapsis records that the band leader Pantelis Anastasiadis, with 25 armed men and 300 civilians, reached Poti in Georgia on two schooners in late December 1923.
sources_modern: Kapsis, 1922: Η μαύρη βίβλος (1992), p. 313 (as cited on Wikipedia)

title: Exiles at Diyarbakır leave for Greece through Aleppo and Beirut (route example)
summary: Georgios Kopasis, a Greek of Sille near Konya deported in December 1921 through Niğde, Kayseri, Sivas, Malatya and Elazığ to Diyarbakır, tells how in summer 1924 the exiles there were certified as 'exchangeable', walked about twenty days to Aleppo, stayed four months, then four to five months in Beirut, helped by the Patriarchate of Antioch, and sailed for Greece in 1925 on a ship he believed was the 'Archangelos'. He was not from the Pontus, but he was held on the same road and in the same place as Pontic deportees.
disputed: One testimony; it shows that the Syrian route was used by exchangees from the south-east, not how many took it.
sources_primary: Testimony of Georgios Kopasis, excerpts in Ta Nea, 27 Sept 2003

title: The figure of 353,000 Pontic Greek dead, 1914–1924, and how it was reached
summary: The figure most often given for the Pontic Greek dead is 353,000. It is in G. K. Valavanis, Σύγχρονος γενική ιστορία του Πόντου (Athens 1925), p. 24, and is repeated by Fotiadis, by Tsirkinidis (quoted in Hofmann 2011, p. 104), by Bartrop (2017, p. 140: 'an estimated 353,000 died'), by Shirinian (2017, p. 56: 'about 350,000'), by Çilingir, and in the Rhode Island Senate resolutions of 2010 and 2025. How it was reached: the Central Council of Pontus (Black Book, 1922) counted 303,238 victims up to 1922, including the deportees of four metropolises, and Pontic refugee writers added 50,000 'new martyrs' for 1922 to March 1924 (Agtzidis 2005, p. 201). We have not consulted Valavanis' book; the figure and page are known to us through Shirinian (2017, p. 73, n. 187, after Fotiadis).
disputed: Other estimates: greek-genocide.net calls 353,000 too high and suggests about 250,000; Jones (2010) gives 300,000–360,000 and Peterson (2004) 360,000 for 1914–23. The ranges by phase and source are in the chapter's figures table.

title: Greece: Law 2193/1994 makes 19 May the day of remembrance of the genocide of the Pontic Greeks
summary: Law 2193/1994 (ΦΕΚ Α΄ 32/11.3.1994), article 1: 19 May is the Day of Remembrance of the Genocide of the Greeks in Pontus. Article 2 leaves the ceremonies to a presidential decree (PD 99/1994, ΦΕΚ Α΄ 78/20.5.1994). The law does not name the perpetrator; a bill tabled on 20 May 2025 by a group of MPs proposed amending it to do so. Kritikakos (2026, p. 124) writes that the Hellenic Parliament declared 19 May after lobbying by Fotiadis and Charalambidis, with PASOK support.

title: Greece: Law 2645/1998 makes 14 September the day of remembrance of the genocide of the Greeks of Asia Minor
summary: Law 2645/1998 established 14 September as a day of national remembrance of the 'Genocide of the Greeks of Asia Minor by the Turkish State'. With the 1994 law it underpins the wider 'Greek genocide' framing. The designation was unanimous (Kritikakos 2026, p. 125); the presidential decree implementing the law was withdrawn in 2001 and re-signed without the word 'genocide' (Agtzidis 2010, p. 274).
disputed: The Turkish foreign ministry's condemnation of the law is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H7-T09).
sources_primary: Law 2645/1998, ΦΕΚ Α΄ of 13 Oct 1998
sources_modern: Kritikakos 2026, p. 125 (the designation unanimous) | Agtzidis 2010, p. 274 (the presidential decree implementing Law 2645/1998 withdrawn in 2001 and re-signed without the word 'genocide') [Greek]

title: International Association of Genocide Scholars resolution
summary: The IAGS resolved, with 83 percent of voting members in favour, that 'the Ottoman campaign against Christian minorities of the Empire between 1914 and 1923 constituted a genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Pontian and Anatolian Greeks', and called on Turkey to acknowledge it, apologise and make restitution.
sources_primary: IAGS resolution and press release, Dec 2007 (copy at aga-online.org/wp-content/uploads/IAGS_Resolution.pdf)
sources_modern: Charny, in Hofmann, Bjørnlund & Meichanetsidis (eds) 2011, pp. 33–37 (text of the resolution; opposition inside the IAGS) [international scholar] | Kritikakos 2026, p. 43 (83%; the Weitz, Feinstein and Akçam letter, 'too general and without nuance'; Balakian's memo; after Sjöberg 2016, pp. 194–196)

title: South Australia: the Parliament passes a motion condemning the genocide of the Armenians, Pontian Greeks and Syrian Orthodox
summary: On 30 April 2009 the Parliament of South Australia (House of Assembly, per the Hansard reference) passed a motion moved by Michael Atkinson which condemns 'the genocide of the Armenians, Pontian Greeks, Syrian Orthodox and other Christian minorities', describes 'the genocide by the Ottoman state between 1915-1923 of Armenians, Hellenes, Syrian and other minorities in Asia Minor' as one of the greatest crimes against humanity, and calls on the Commonwealth Parliament to condemn it. The Turkish Embassy called it 'the work of an ethnic lobby' (19 June 2009) (Kritikakos, pp. 190-191).
disputed: A state-parliament motion, not a law; it names the Pontian Greeks explicitly. The chamber is inferred from the Hansard reference ('lh', the lower house) and the House of Assembly travel report cited with it; Kritikakos says 'the Parliament of South Australia'.

title: Sweden: the Riksdag calls for recognition of the 1915 genocide including the Pontic Greeks
summary: On 11 March 2010 the Riksdag passed, by 131 votes to 130 and against the advice of its Foreign Affairs Committee, motion 2008/09:U332, which recognises as genocide the killing in 1915 of 'the Armenian, Assyrian/Syriac/Chaldean and Pontic Greek populations'. It is a statement to the government (tillkännagivande), not a law; the government did not adopt it.
disputed: The Swedish historian Ingmar Karlsson called the inclusion of the Pontic Greeks 'inaccurate historiography' and spoke of ethnic cleansing (Kritikakos p. 44).

title: Rhode Island Senate commemorates the 'Pontian Genocide of 1914-1922'
summary: Senate resolution 10-R196 (2010-S 2815) of 28 April 2010 proclaimed 19 May 2010 'Greek Pontian Genocide Remembrance Day', for the 'Pontian Genocide of 1914-1922', with 353,000 'Pontian and Anatolian Greeks'. Similar resolutions followed (e.g. 14-R222, 1 May 2014), and R 299 (2025-S 1080) of 15 May 2025 named a 'Greek and Pontic Genocide Remembrance Day' for 1913-1923, again with 353,000.
disputed: One-chamber commemorative resolutions, not laws.
