title: Armenia: the National Assembly condemns the genocide of the Greeks and Assyrians
summary: The National Assembly of Armenia adopted unanimously (117-0-0) a statement condemning 'the genocide of the Greeks and Assyrians, committed by the Ottoman Turkey in 1915-1923'.
sources_primary: Armenpress, 24 March 2015

title: Austria: the parliamentary groups' declaration on the Armenian genocide names the Pontic Greeks among the victims
summary: The joint declaration of the leaders of the six parliamentary groups (Schieder, Lopatka, Strache, Glawischnig, Dietrich, Strolz), titled on the genocide 'an den Armeniern', names among the victims of 'Gewalt, Mord und Vertreibung' tens of thousands of members of other Christian groups of the Ottoman Empire, the Aramaeans, Assyrians, Chaldeans and 'Pontos-Griechen'. The next sentence speaks of the duty 'die schrecklichen Geschehnisse als Genozid anzuerkennen und zu verurteilen'. The genocide it names explicitly is that of the Armenians; 'die Geschehnisse' can be read to cover all the victims, and Wikipedia and the Armenian National Committee of America count it as a recognition. We describe it as having named the Pontic Greeks among the victims, not as an explicit recognition.
disputed: An ambiguous text.
sources_primary: 'Gemeinsame Erklärung der KOs der 6 Parlamentsparteien zum Genozid an den Armeniern' (copy at erinnern.at) | salzburg24.at, 22 Apr 2015

title: Tasmania: the House of Assembly recognises the Armenian, Greek and Assyrian genocides
summary: On 11 May 2023 the Parliament of Tasmania (House of Assembly) passed a motion, proposed by Premier Jeremy Rockliff with support from Labor, Liberal and the Greens, that 'condemns the genocide of the Armenians, Assyrians and Greeks' and honours 'over 1 million Assyrians and Greeks' among the victims; Tasmania became the third Australian state to do so (Kritikakos, pp. 209-210).
disputed: Names the Greeks generally, not the Pontic Greeks in particular.
sources_primary: Parliament of Tasmania, House of Assembly, Hansard, 11 May 2023, as cited by Kritikakos, Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian Genocide Recognition in Twenty-First Century Australia (Palgrave Macmillan, 2026), n. 120
sources_modern: Kritikakos, Armenian, Greek, and Assyrian Genocide Recognition in Twenty-First Century Australia (Palgrave Macmillan, 2026), pp. 209-210

title: Cyprus: the House of Representatives designates 19 May and recognises the genocide
summary: The Cypriot House of Representatives unanimously designated 19 May the 'Official Day of Remembrance and Honor for the Greeks of Pontus'. The Cyprus News Agency reported this as 'formally recognizing the genocide committed … by the Young Turks and Kemalists between 1914 and 1923'.
disputed: The news report does not give the date of the plenary session or the form of the act. Syriac Press (27 May 2026) reports a memorial and measures for schools; we have not consulted the text.
sources_primary: Cyprus News Agency, 19 June 2025 (cna.org.cy/en/article/8634681)

title: Greek bands raid Muslim villages around Çarşamba, 1916-18 (Turkish scholarship)
summary: Turkish historians Aydın and Duman describe Greek armed bands in the Çarşamba-Samsun area in 1916-18 that set road blocks, raided Muslim villages, attacked supply convoys and looted grain stores, with logistic support from the Russian command at Trebizond. One band leader of the Bafra area, known as Anton Pasha, was killed in 1917. The journalist-historian Ayşe Hür, in an article reprinted by Çilingir (pp. 226-227), writes from Turkish memoirs that the Russians armed Greeks of Bafra, that the band leader Vasil Usta (Vasilis Anthopoulos), landed at Samsun by a Russian torpedo boat, raided Turkish villages after the Russian withdrawal, and that Greek bands looted Turkish villages around Merzifon in November 1918.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated, in general terms only: Morris & Ze'evi (p. 383) write that during the war bands of draft evaders 'occasionally attacked Turkish villagers and gendarmes', and that the Turks charged that they were armed from Russia (H7-063). The specifics here (road blocks, raids on convoys and grain stores, logistic support from the Russian command at Trebizond, Vasil Usta's raids) have no non-Turkish source. Greek sources describe the bands as self-defence.
sources_primary: Ottoman archival documents as used by Aydın & Duman (not consulted)
sources_modern: Aydın & Duman, 'I. Dünya Savaşı Yıllarında Çarşamba/Samsun ve Çevresinde Rum Çete Faaliyetleri', History Studies 4.2 (2012), pp. 39-51 | Ayşe Hür, 'Pontus'un gayri resmi tarihi' (Taraf), reprinted in Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], pp. 226-227 [Turkish writer relaying Turkish memoirs] | Agtzidis 1992, p. 167 (corroborating, in general terms: 'Russian aid') [Greek]

title: Pontic bands attack Muslim villages: a rebellion organised from Greece
summary: Turkish accounts say that the Greek bands active in the mountains behind Bafra, Kavak and Çarşamba in 1919-23 attacked Muslim villages and were a rebellion organised from Greece (with the Mavri Mira and Pontus societies distributing arms). In the Grand National Assembly in 1921 deputies said that more than sixty Muslim villages had been burned in three months (Hafız Mehmet, 29 October 1921) and ministers gave figures for Muslims killed (H7-T10). Turkish official sources put the bands at 6,000-7,000 armed men at first and 25,000 later (Cibran & Çetinoğlu, after Turkish official history).
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated (H7-063): a Greek band of nearly a hundred attacked a Turkish village near Samsun in early September 1921 (USS McFarland), with a similar raid in October; Col. Rawlinson put the armed Greeks in the mountains at 20,000-30,000 in May 1922. Against the rest: we found no non-Turkish count of Muslim victims; 'Western observers uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine rebellion' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 406); Hafız Mehmet himself said he had seen a battalion of the Giresun regiment burn villages under the pretext of collecting arms, and the Lazistan deputies blamed Nureddin for driving Greeks to the mountains (H7-031), so some burned villages may have been burned by Turkish forces; Greek sources honour the bands as defenders of villages and refugees (H7-042; B1-007).
sources_primary: TBMM secret session, 29 Oct 1921 (Hafız Mehmet), via Çilingir p. 119 | Kemal's reports of May-June 1919 (H.T.V.D. no. 4, via Balcıoğlu and Cibran & Çetinoğlu)
sources_modern: Aydın & Duman 2012; Biber (TÜBA); Pontus Meselesi (1922) | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], p. 119 | Cibran & Çetinoğlu, The Pontos Question (English summary, January 2007) [Turkish writers]

title: Kemal's report of 'forty guerrilla bands'
summary: Mustafa Kemal reported to Constantinople in late May 1919 that since the armistice 'forty guerrilla' bands, 'in an organized program', were killing Turks to 'establish a Pontus state' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 384). His report of 22 May 1919, as summarised by Cibran & Çetinoğlu after Balcıoğlu, counted about forty Greek bands, thirty-three of them in Samsun, and about thirteen Turkish bands, six of them in Samsun.
counter_evidence: Morris & Ze'evi, who report the claim (p. 384, after Shaw), write that 'the reality was different' (p. 383): the separatist agitation had resulted in 'almost no acts of overt rebellion' and very little anti-Turk terrorism, and they add that 'it is possible that many Turks believed these allegations' (p. 384). Kemal's own report counted Turkish bands as well (thirteen).
sources_primary: Kemal's reports to Constantinople, May 1919 (Shaw, From Empire to Republic, vol. 2, pp. 592-593, via Morris & Ze'evi n. 17); report of 22 May 1919, H.T.V.D. no. 4 (June 1953), doc. 69, via Balcıoğlu, Bir Paşa, p. 82, via Cibran & Çetinoğlu, The Pontos Question (English summary, January 2007) [Turkish writers]
sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP, 2019), p. 384 | Cibran & Çetinoğlu, The Pontos Question (English summary, January 2007) [Turkish writers]

title: Yusuf Kemal: Greek bands burned Koçhisar and the Sakızcı quarter of Bafra
summary: The Ankara foreign minister Yusuf Kemal (Tengirşenk) said that Greek bands had burned Koçhisar in Bafra and the Sakızcı quarter, and that Muslims who could not flee were 'burned alive in their houses' (no place given for the latter).
counter_evidence: No non-Turkish source for these particular burnings was found. The Greek deputy Theotokas told the British in July 1921 that all the villages around Bafra had been burned by the government side (cited by Biber, p. 436), and US officers reported about 100 Greek villages south of Bafra destroyed from 17 May 1921 (B1-001).
sources_primary: Statement of Yusuf Kemal (via Biber, nn. 98-99, from Echos d'Orient)
sources_modern: Biber, ch. 13 in the TÜBA history series, p. 441

title: An old Greek signalled a Greek warship near Bafra
summary: Nureddin Pasha justified deporting the old by the case of a 65-year-old Greek at 'Gümenez', left behind for his age, who waved a flag to a Greek torpedo boat; its men came ashore in boats, a group from Bafra arrived with their forces, 'old Bald Nikola' was hanged and the enemy fleet driven off. Yusuf Kemal cited the same case.
counter_evidence: Partly in context: Greece blockaded the coast from 26 March 1921 and its warships were offshore. But one incident does not explain the deportation of women, children and orphans (B1-015, B1-017 to B1-019); and the hanging of the old man is itself an admission.
sources_primary: Nureddin Pasha's statement of defence (Balcıoğlu 2000, p. 275) | Statement of Yusuf Kemal (via Biber, n. 99)
sources_modern: Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Turkish-language work), p. 130 | Biber, ch. 13 in the TÜBA history series, p. 441

title: Ankara's case for the deportations of 1921-22
summary: Ankara justified the deportation of Greek men from the coast by the danger of a Greek landing at Samsun (Nureddin's circular of 12 January 1921; the Council of Ministers' order of 12 June 1921 cites a Greek landing at Samsun), by the Greek bands, and by the Greek navy's shelling of İnebolu (June 1921) and later of Samsun (June 1922), which it cited as proof of Greek designs on the Pontus. The Turks also claimed that Pontic Greeks had joined the Greek army and that the deportations were meant to force the bands to give up their arms (Morris & Ze'evi, pp. 406-407). An Interior Ministry letter of 25 June 1921 described the measure as a security measure, not a deportation (tehcir) (Cibran & Çetinoğlu). Turkish historiography calls it a lawful wartime relocation (sevk/tehcir) of men of military age from a coast exposed to Greek attack; the Central Army's orders spoke of 'chastening' the bands and destroying the villages that sheltered them (H6-052).
disputed: The orders themselves are told in the chapter (H7-022, H7-026); this entry gives their justification.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: Greece blockaded the coast from 26 March 1921, and Greek warships shelled İnebolu on 9 June 1921 and Samsun on 7 June 1922 (H7-023, H6-061). Against the rest: the İnebolu shelling 'produced no casualties' and an Italian at Samsun called it 'an excuse for the massacres'; it 'may indeed have hastened the deportation process, but it wasn't the cause of the campaign, which was launched weeks before' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 407); a convoy from Samsun was already on the road to Kavak by 2 June (H7-029); no Greek landing on the Pontic coast was attempted; 'Western observers uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine rebellion' (p. 406); the Interior Ministry's own order of 25 June 1921 did not cover women and children, yet they were deported on Nureddin's orders (H7-026); the deputy governor of Samsun proposed expelling all Greek villages so that Greeks would nowhere be a majority (H6-052), and in June 1922 the interior minister reported that the remaining Greeks would not reach five percent of the Muslims (H7-065); the Near East Relief officers reported that officials 'were frank in their statements that it was the intention to have all the Greeks die' (H7-038); and deputies in Ankara attacked Nureddin's conduct (H7-031).
sources_primary: Order No. 2082 (12 Jan 1921), via Güzel 2006, Çilingir and Çetinoğlu | Council of Ministers' order of 12 June 1921 (via Çilingir p. 117) | Decree of 16 June 1921 (its justification), via Biber | 'Answers by Mustapha Kemal Pasha (written by Yussuf Bey)', memorandum to Lt R. S. Dunn, 3 July 1921, LC, Bristol Papers 35 (via Morris & Ze'evi n. 169); Allen Dulles to SecState, 28 June 1921 (n. 173)
sources_modern: Güzel, Dünden Bugüne Yunanistan'ın Pontus Hedefi (2006) | Biber (TÜBA) ch. 13 | Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP, 2019), pp. 406-407 | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], p. 117 | Cibran & Çetinoğlu, The Pontos Question (English summary, January 2007) [Turkish writers]

title: Mount Nebyan as a rebel base; the villages destroyed had supplied the bands
summary: Biber writes that the Greeks of Samsun planned to gather on Nebyan Dağı above Bafra; that Ankara postponed a disarmament measure on 12 January 1921; that Greeks who fled to Nebyan clashed with the Central Army, some later surrendering their arms; that men who refused conscription joined the bands; and that the villages destroyed were those that supplied the bands, their people, women and children included, fleeing to the mountains or being sent inland.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: the Greek witness calls Nebyan 'the centre of the Greek refugees' (B1-007), and a US naval diary records a Greek band raid on a Turkish village (H6-079). The admission that villages were destroyed and women and children sent inland is told in the chapter (B1-005, B1-015). Against the rest: the women's and orphans' convoys were not band supporters in any ordinary sense, and Morris & Ze'evi write that 'Western observers uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine “rebellion,” either underway or in preparation' (p. 406).
sources_primary: Ottoman and Turkish archival documents (via Biber, nn. 57, 60)
sources_modern: Biber, ch. 13 in the TÜBA history series, p. 434

title: Mustafa Kemal's reply to Pope Benedict XV: the Christians are calm; the Greeks and Armenians commit crimes
summary: Replying in March 1921 to the Pope's appeal, sent through Cardinal Gasparri, to protect the lives and property of Christians, Mustafa Kemal telegraphed that he considered it his duty to safeguard the life of all, irrespective of nation or religion, that Christians in the areas under the Grand National Assembly were altogether calm, and that Greeks and Armenians were committing crimes (Kyriakidis 2026, p. 76, after Carolla).
counter_evidence: Within months Dolci reported that Christians 'kept being murdered' and the Pope asked Kemal to cancel the exile of 5,000 women and children near Samsun (H7-061). Dolci himself thought the papal intervention useful and rejected the view that it had only let Kemal reassure public opinion (Kyriakidis p. 77).
sources_primary: Kemal to the Pope, March 1921 (Carolla, La Santa Sede e la Questione Armena (2006), pp. 62, 220-221, doc. 99, via Kyriakidis 2026)
sources_modern: Kyriakidis (trans. Nikoloudis), The Genocide of Orthodox Greeks and the Persecution of Christians in the Pontus Region according to Vatican Archives (Gorgias Press, 2026), p. 76

title: Ankara: the Kavak dead fell in battle with Greek bands, and the Bafra dead in fighting with bands
summary: On 15 September 1921 the Ankara foreign minister Yusuf Kemal told the Allied High Commissioners that the men killed at Kavak had been killed justifiably in battle after Greek bands attacked Turks first (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 408). As early as 2 June 1921 the mutasarrıf of Canik and the 10th Division reported that a convoy of 766 Greeks sent from Samsun to Kavak had been attacked by 'brigands' in the Canik mountains (Çilingir, p. 117); Turkish sources say the convoy was fired on by Greek bands (Cibran & Çetinoğlu). For Bafra, Ankara and Turkish historiography say the dead fell in fighting with bands based on Mount Nebyan, that Greek bands burned Koçhisar and the Sakızcı quarter of Bafra, and that the destroyed villages had supplied the bands (B1-T01, B1-T05).
counter_evidence: The Kavak victims were deportees under escort: survivors and relief workers say the escort fired on the columns (Fuller saw only 200 of the first 900 reach Sivas; a deportee of the third Samsun convoy wrote that '660 were killed' as it descended a mountain; Hopkins reported 550 executed on 26 June and 1,300 on 15 August; Rendel recorded 1,300 shot in the gorge; H7-029, B1-011, B1-013). In the Grand National Assembly the Lazistan deputy Ziya Hurşit said the first convoy was attacked six hours out of Samsun and blamed Nureddin's use of irregular bands (H7-031); Turkish documents summarised by Korucu & Dağlıoğlu (p. 25) say the relocated Greeks were killed by militias, notably those of Topal Osman and Şaki Ali. At Bafra the Greek witness describes men tied together and killed in churches (B1-010, B1-003, B1-004), and US officers reported deportations 'regularly accompanied by mass murder' around Bafra (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 409). The convoy figures from different sources may overlap and should not be added. Greek bands did fight in these hills (H7-063, B1-007), so some deaths in combat are possible, but no non-Turkish source describes the Kavak or Bafra dead as combatants.

sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP, 2019), p. 408 | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], p. 117 | Cibran & Çetinoğlu, The Pontos Question (English summary, January 2007) [Turkish writers] | See also B1-T01, B1-T05 | Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP 2019), p. 408 | Alpaslan 2007; Doğan 2014 (via H6-T08)

title: Yusuf Kemal: the Merzifon massacre a 'legend'
summary: The Ankara foreign minister, Yusuf Kemal, announced that 'it is not exact that the population of Merzifoun has been massacred and dispersed': it was a 'legend'. Later the Nationalists said that 'the troops simply got from under control', or that brigands, not the army, were to blame, and that the offenders had been sent into battle 'and most... were killed' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 413).
counter_evidence: The American missionaries at Merzifon (Hosford, Anthony) and the staff of Anatolia College described the massacre in detail; the Armenian-Greek Section of the British High Commission estimated 950 killed, Bristol and Anthony about 1,200 (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 413, n. 223; H7-027). Ankara's own later explanations (troops out of control; brigands) concede that killings took place.
sources_primary: Youssouf Kemal to the High Commissioner, 15 Sept 1921, RG 84 vol. 438 (via Morris & Ze'evi n. 224); Gillespie to Bristol, 10 Jan 1922, quoting Yusuf Kemal (n. 225) | Youssouf Kemal to the High Commissioner, 15 Sept 1921, USNA RG 84 vol. 438; Gillespie (US trade commissioner, Ankara) to Bristol, 10 Jan 1922 (via Morris & Ze'evi, nn. 224–225)
sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP, 2019), p. 413 | Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP 2019), p. 413

title: Yusuf Kemal's circular to the foreign representatives: a Greek plot, band massacres and Greek mobilisation
summary: In a circular of 16 July 1921 to the High Commissioners of France, Britain, Italy, Japan and the United States, the ministers of Spain, the Netherlands, Sweden and Denmark and the Apostolic Delegate, the Ankara foreign minister Yusuf Kemal wrote that the Greek army was laying waste the regions it occupied; that Greek secret societies, 'among others the famous society PONTOS', had provoked armed risings in the province of Samsun a few weeks earlier to draw Turkish forces from the front; that their bands, supplied from arms depots set up after the 1918 armistice, were massacring all Muslim villagers they found; that the Greek official gazette of 1 July had called up Greeks of the 1920 and 1921 classes, including Ottoman Greeks of Anatolia; and that the British were arming Greek and Armenian bands around Constantinople. The Ankara government declared that responsibility for any reprisals by the Turkish people would fall entirely on the Greeks (Kyriakidis 2026, pp. 75-76 and Text 1, pp. 149-151).
counter_evidence: Western observers 'uniformly asserted that there was no Pontine rebellion' (Morris & Ze'evi, p. 406). The circular's warning that reprisals would be the Greeks' fault came as the deportations of men and then of women and children were under way (H7-024, H7-026).
sources_primary: Circular of the Ankara Minister of Foreign Affairs, 16 July 1921, transcribed in Dolci to Van Rossum, 25 July 1921, Propaganda Fide, Nuova Serie vol. 692, p. 433rv (printed as Text 1 in Kyriakidis 2026)
sources_modern: Kyriakidis (trans. Nikoloudis), The Genocide of Orthodox Greeks and the Persecution of Christians in the Pontus Region according to Vatican Archives (Gorgias Press, 2026), pp. 75-76, 149-151

title: The Amasya trials as the suppression of a separatist conspiracy
summary: Turkish historiography treats the Independence Tribunals of 1921 at Amasya as the lawful suppression of a separatist conspiracy for an independent Pontus. Ankara's agent in Constantinople, Hamid Bey, told Rumbold in October 1921 that those sentenced to death had engaged in separatist activities and collaborated with Greek forces; the Ankara government's book Pontus Meselesi (1922) presents the tribunal's reasoning in several cases, without naming the defendants, and says that officials who abused the population during weapons searches were punished by the tribunals.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: Pontic leaders abroad did campaign for a Pontic state, and the tribunal condemned three of them (Chrysanthos, Germanos, Laurentios) in absentia (H6-058); the US High Commissioner Bristol, no friend of the Pontic cause, judged that the condemned had played a part in propaganda for a Greek state fostered by Venizelos, as the Turkish historian Bilgiç reports him (quoted by Çetinoğlu). Against the rest: Bristol allowed that innocents may have been punished with them; the tribunal passed 622 death sentences (137 in absentia) in four months (H6-058); those hanged included teachers and students of Anatolia College, doctors, pharmacists and bankers; the tribunal's archives are still closed and its procedure is known mainly from memoirs and the Turkish government's own publication (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, p. 18; Çetinoğlu); and the hangings drew Greek, British and Allied protests and a speech in the US Senate (H6-058, H7-060).
sources_primary: Tribunal verdicts (as presented in Pontus Meselesi (1922), pp. 381-390) | Rumbold to Curzon, 15 Oct 1921 (Hamid Bey), DBFP, via Çetinoğlu, 'Pontos'taki Düzmece İstiklal Mahkemeleri ve Yargılamaları' (posted 7 Jan 2020; reprinted in Çilingir 2016, pp. 229ff.) [Turkish writer], pp. 9-10
sources_modern: Turkish historiography of the Pontus question (see H6-T04) | Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, 'Mapping Out the Turkish Documents on the Unweaving of Greeks from the Black Sea (The Pontic Genocide, 1919-1923)', in Shirinian (ed.), The Greek Genocide, 1913-1923: New Perspectives (Asia Minor and Pontos Hellenic Research Center, 2019), pp. 20-21 | Çetinoğlu, 'Pontos'taki Düzmece İstiklal Mahkemeleri ve Yargılamaları' (posted 7 Jan 2020; reprinted in Çilingir 2016, pp. 229ff.) [Turkish writer]

title: Ankara: the deportations were orderly and lawful
summary: Yusuf Kemal said that the deportation had gone without serious incident on the roads, with only 'one or two cases of theft' reaching the military courts (Biber). At a secret session on 18 May 1922 the interior minister Fethi told the Assembly that 'no Christians, Greek or Armenian, had been illegally punished' and that any deported 'provisionally from the sea coast' had been moved 'solely in the interests of safeguarding [Turkish] independence'; Mustafa Kemal denounced the 'lying Yowell' and his 'calumnious statement'.
counter_evidence: Contradicted by the Near East Relief officers (Ward and Yowell: 5,000 dead between Sivas and Harput, 3,000 between Harput and Diyarbakır; B1-002), by US naval reports (90 percent of the Bafra men killed, USS Brooks, 8 July 1921; B1-013), by the sighting of 4,000 Bafra women and children near Sivas without food or shoes (B1-017), by Nureddin's own admission that women and children were deported with the men (B1-022), and by the deputies in Ankara who attacked Nureddin.
sources_primary: Statement of Yusuf Kemal (via Biber) | Grand National Assembly secret session, 18 May 1922 (via Morris & Ze'evi nn. 299-300)
sources_modern: Biber, ch. 13 in the TÜBA history series, p. 442 | Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP 2019), p. 426

title: Ankara's figures for Muslim victims of the Greek bands, and for the bands' arms
summary: Ankara's ministers and publications gave figures for Muslim victims. The interior minister Ali Fethi told the Assembly on 29 December 1921 that, in reply to the Central Army's operations against 50-60 bands of 180-200 men in the Nebiyan region and the raids on metropolises and schools, armed Greek groups had killed 1,303 Muslims, wounded 147 and damaged 3,303 dwellings; on 10 June 1922 he reported 69 killed, 51 wounded and 415 structures damaged between 15 October and December 1921, and 82 dead, 26 wounded, 5 kidnapped and 151 dwellings pillaged between January and May 1922 (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, pp. 14-15). The government's book Pontus Meselesi (1922) gave 1,641 Muslims killed and 323 wounded, 3,723 dwellings burned and 1,800 robberies, and said that over 10,000 weapons had been distributed to the Greeks by Tsarist Russia and later Britain, of which only about 2,000 were handed in (ibid., pp. 20-21). The General Staff put the Turks killed by Greek bands in 1916-23 at 1,817 (Ayşe Hür, in Çilingir p. 228).
counter_evidence: We found no non-Turkish count of Muslim victims. The figures conflict among themselves (1,303 killed to December 1921; 1,641 in the 1922 book; 1,817 for 1916-23). One band raid with deaths is documented by the US Navy (H7-063). The same ministers' statements admit far larger Greek losses: 5,051 'dead' in four months of 1922 (H7-065) and 11,198 killed by February 1923 (H7-067); by the Turkish figures themselves, Greek deaths in operations exceeded Muslim deaths several times over.
sources_primary: TBMM Zabıt Ceridesi, Term I, vol. XV, 29 Dec 1921, pp. 240-241; TBMM Gizli Zabıt Ceridesi, Term I, vol. III, 10 June 1922, p. 373 (via Korucu & Dağlıoğlu) | Pontus Meselesi (TBMM Hükümeti Matbuat Müdüriyet-i Umumisi, 1922; facsimile 1995), ch. 2 and 4 (via Korucu & Dağlıoğlu) | General Staff figure (via Ayşe Hür, reprinted in Çilingir p. 228)
sources_modern: Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, 'Mapping Out the Turkish Documents on the Unweaving of Greeks from the Black Sea (The Pontic Genocide, 1919-1923)', in Shirinian (ed.), The Greek Genocide, 1913-1923: New Perspectives (Asia Minor and Pontos Hellenic Research Center, 2019), pp. 14-15, 20-21 | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], p. 228

title: Nureddin Pasha's defence: the Greeks a 'snake' whose 'poison' is the women
summary: In the two defences he sent to Ankara after his dismissal (30 December 1921 and 3 January 1922), read in the Assembly on 17 January 1922, Nureddin Pasha justified the deportation of women and children: 'All Greeks have the ideal of a state... the Greeks in our country are a snake; the poison of these snakes is the women'; the women had helped their men 'in thought, body and property', so 'we did the same to them as to the men; we did not separate them from their children either'. He cited an old Greek hanged near Bafra for signalling a Greek warship (Balcıoğlu, via Çilingir pp. 126, 130; Korucu & Dağlıoğlu p. 23).
counter_evidence: His admissions (women and children deported with the men; armed local Turks enrolled at Bafra and Kavak) are told in the chapter (B1-022, H7-026). No non-Turkish source describes the women of Bafra as combatants or informers; US officers called their treatment 'an unpardonable sin against civilization' (B1-018), and the Assembly in Ankara itself attacked Nureddin's conduct and removed him (H7-031).

sources_modern: Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], pp. 126, 130 | Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, 'Mapping Out the Turkish Documents on the Unweaving of Greeks from the Black Sea (The Pontic Genocide, 1919-1923)', in Shirinian (ed.), The Greek Genocide, 1913-1923: New Perspectives (Asia Minor and Pontos Hellenic Research Center, 2019), p. 23 | See also B1-T03 | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Turkish-language work), p. 130

title: The Ankara government's case: the book Pontus Meselesi (1922)
summary: For the Lausanne talks the Ankara government's press directorate published Pontus Meselesi ('The Pontus Question', 1922; French 1923; modern Turkish facsimile by the Grand National Assembly, 1995). It argues that Anatolia was a Turkish homeland before 1071 and that the Turks had been tolerant; that churches, the Patriarchate, Greek societies and the Pontus organisation (founded at the American College of Merzifon) incited the Christians; it prints documents seized at the metropolises and the college, lists murders and robberies by Greek bands in Bafra, Nebyan, Samsun, Ladik, Gümüşhacıköy, Havza, Çarşamba, Terme, Merzifon, Amasya, Köprü and Tokat, with Muslim casualty figures (H7-T10); and it presents the disarmament call, the 1921 relocation as carried out 'fastidiously', the trial of the 'very small number' of officials who abused it, the tribunals' sentences, Nureddin's orders, and Ankara's replies to American and Allied protests (Korucu & Dağlıoğlu, pp. 19-21). Çetinoğlu and Ayşe Hür note that the Turkish official thesis from Kemal's 1927 speech to the present largely repeats this book.
counter_evidence: The book's own appendices admit the relocation of women and children (Bristol's protest of 18 July 1921 is printed in it) and the tribunals' death sentences. US, British and relief reports describe the marches as lethal (H7-025, H7-038); Ankara's own deputies accused Nureddin of massacre and pillage (H7-031); its claim that the relocation was orderly is contradicted by the interior minister's figures of Greeks killed (H7-065) and by the Interior Ministry's order of 25 June 1921, which did not cover women and children (H7-026).

[Turkish writer], p. 1 | Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], p. 121

title: Yusuf Kemal: women and children deported because of spies and military operations
summary: Asked by a journalist in February 1922 what the women and children were guilty of, Yusuf Kemal replied that the military command had judged it necessary to deport them 'so that they do not interfere with military operations', and that 'there are many spies among the Christians, and this is the main cause of the deportations'.
counter_evidence: He had told Bristol's aide that Ankara had not ordered the deportation of women (Morris & Ze'evi p. 415). The '15 to 50' decree of June 1921 named men only (H7-026). US and NER observers saw women, children and orphans deported in winter without food (B1-017, B1-002, B1-027).
sources_primary: Yusuf Kemal to a journalist, Feb 1922 (via Morris & Ze'evi n. 243)
sources_modern: Morris & Ze'evi, The Thirty-Year Genocide (Harvard UP 2019), p. 415

title: The Turkish state's position on the term 'genocide'
summary: Turkey does not recognise a Pontic or Greek genocide. Its foreign ministry issues a statement each 19 May (e.g. No. 167 of 19 May 2022; No. 95 of 19 May 2026). These call the 'Pontus' allegations baseless; say that Greece promotes them through the 1994 law and school circulars, to cover its defeat in the 'Megali Idea' campaign and its own army's atrocities; and cite the Allied commission reports, Article 59 of the Treaty of Lausanne and Tripolitsa (1821). The ministry objects to Greece's choice of 19 May, a Turkish national day (Kemal's landing at Samsun), and condemned the 1998 law on Asia Minor as 'without any historical basis'. The Turkish Embassy in Australia called the South Australian motion 'the work of an ethnic lobby' (19 June 2009; Kritikakos 2026, p. 191); Morris & Ze'evi (p. 382) trace the official narrative to Kemal's Nutuk (1927).
disputed: The statements are the official position; what they establish is the position itself, not the facts they assert.
counter_evidence: Partly corroborated: the Greek army's atrocities in western Anatolia, which the statements cite, were documented by the Inter-Allied commission (Yalova, 1921), but they were not in the Pontus. Against the rest: the deportation orders of 1916-17 and 1921 are Ottoman and Ankara documents (H6-026, H7-011, H7-026, H7-055); the Ottoman Empire's own allies reported the burnings and deaths of 1916-17 (Kwiatkowski, Pallavicini, the German consulate at Samsun); US naval and Near East Relief officers reported the marches of 1921-22; Turkish deputies in Ankara attacked Nureddin in 1921 (H7-031) and the interior minister reported thousands of Greeks killed in 1922 (H7-065); the term genocide is used by the IAGS (2007), Greece (1994), Armenia (2015), Cyprus (2025), the Swedish Riksdag (2010), South Australia (2009), Tasmania (2023) and others. The Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the New South Wales Legislative Council's motion of May 2013 (press release No. 133, 7 May 2013; Kritikakos p. 273 n. 79).

title: Sait Çetinoğlu's theses
summary: Sait Çetinoğlu, a Turkish writer who argues for recognition, uses Ottoman, Turkish and Greek documents. His main theses in the texts read: the Pontic genocide continued from the Unionists to the Kemalists, with the same methods and some of the same men (Topal Osman; the Special Organization) ('TC'nin soykırımlar geleneği', pp. 14-16); the 1916 decision to clear a 50-km strip behind the front was part of a German-Unionist plan to homogenise Anatolia and seize Christian wealth (The Pontos Question, 2007); the Independence Tribunals of the Pontus were 'sham' execution bodies whose archives are still closed, and the official Turkish thesis repeats what he calls 'the 1922 propaganda book', Pontus Meselesi ('Düzmece İstiklal Mahkemeleri', pp. 1-10); the resistance in the western Pontus consisted of self-defence groups (ibid., p. 4); and official documents record 11,188 Greeks killed (ibid., p. 10). Entries that use him as a source include H7-012, H7-022, H7-026, H7-029, H7-057, H7-060 and H7-067.

title: Tamer Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği (2016): a Turkish writer's theses
summary: Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 ('The Pontus Truth', Belge, 2016) argues for recognition of a Pontic Greek genocide. Its main claims: (1) the persecution of the Pontic Greeks by the Unionists (1908-18) and the Kemalists (1919-23) was one continuous, planned genocide, which official Turkish history splits in two in order to exonerate the founders of the Republic (pp. 6-7); (2) 353,000 Pontic Greeks were killed, the figure he repeats throughout (pp. 7, 19, 66); (3) the 1916 deportations were a Turkish-German plan disguised as a military measure (pp. 54-57); (4) the Central Army organised the deportations, used irregular bands and labour battalions, and plundered Greek property (pp. 112-126); (5) Ankara's own record, the secret sessions, the 1922 book Pontus Meselesi and Nureddin's defence, documents the genocide (pp. 117-130); (6) the descendants of Islamised Pontic Greeks today make up much of the Black Sea population, and Turkish nationalism on the coast is a reaction to that lost identity (pp. 6, 17-18, 174 ff.). He relies heavily on Turkish archival documents (ATASE, BOA, TBMM minutes), which is why this chapter cites him for those documents. The Turkish official claims he reproduces are given under their authors (H7-T05, H7-T08, H7-T10, H7-T14).
counter_evidence: His 353,000 is Valavanis's figure (H7-043), itself built on the 1922 Black Book's recycled deportation counts (H7-034), and he treats it as established; his population arithmetic (e.g. 'at least 90,000 Greeks of Canik destroyed', p. 121) is his own reckoning, not a source.
sources_modern: Çilingir, Pontos Gerçeği 1914-1923 (Istanbul: Belge, 2016) [Turkish writer], pp. 1-7, 50-57, 112-130, 226-229

title: Turkish historiography: the Bafra and Kavak figures are Greek propaganda
summary: Biber treats the Black Book's convoy figures for Samsun and Bafra (2,000; 1,901; 2,000; 500; 620; 330 and 660 killed at Kavak) as exaggerated and unreliable propaganda, and notes that Turkish archival detail on the convoys has not been found.
counter_evidence: Partly fair: the Black Book is an advocacy work and its Bafra narrative rests on one witness (B1-010). But its Kavak figures are matched by a deportee's letter (660 in the third convoy), by Fuller (700 of 900 missing), by Hopkins (550 on 26 June, 1,300 on 15 August) and by Rendel (1,300) (B1-013, B1-011); US naval records confirm the deportation of thousands of Bafra women and children (B1-015, B1-018); and the Central Army's own count of 63,844 moved (B1-023) is of the same order as the Greek figures for those deported.
sources_modern: Biber, ch. 13 in the TÜBA history series, pp. 437, 440, 443

title: Pontic refugees settle in Macedonia: villages named after the old ones
summary: Pontic refugees, mostly farmers and herders from the highlands, are settled above all in Macedonia (Kozani, Kilkis, Pieria, Pella, Imathia, Drama, Thessaloniki) and in western Thrace, often in hill villages. Many villages took the names of the homes they had lost: Nea Trapezounta and Neokaisareia in Pieria, Kromni in Pella, Nea Santa in Kilkis, Imera in Kozani, Nea Kerasounta and Nea Sinopi in Preveza, and the Sourmena quarter in Attica. The icon of Panagia Soumela, buried in 1923, was recovered in late 1931 and kept in the Byzantine Museum in Athens; it was taken to Kastania on Mt Vermio in 1951 and enthroned in the new church there on 15 August 1952.
disputed: We could not confirm a village called Matsouka in Greece; the name survives in the names of associations. The Soumela dates: the mission left for Turkey on 22 October 1931, and the icon was kept in Athens for twenty years, moved to Kastania in 1951 and enthroned on 15 August 1952 (Bouzikos, on pontosworld). Bouzikos places the icon in the Benaki Museum; other Greek accounts, such as skai.gr's history of the icon, place it in the Byzantine Museum.

title: The exchange: about 52,000 Christians leave the Samsun region
summary: Under the Lausanne convention of 30 January 1923 nearly 52,000 Christians left the Samsun region (Aydan 2016; Çomu 2012, via Topalidis). Çilingir mentions a refugee village 'Yeni Bafra' (Nea Pafra) near Serres in Greek Macedonia, where people of Bafra settled.

title: Trebizond cleared before the treaty
summary: On 11 December 1922 the vali of Trebizond, Kâzım Bey, regarded by the Catholic missionaries as friendly to Christians, is removed and Greeks are dismissed from the civil service. His successor orders the Greeks and Armenians to leave within fifteen days (a notice in the Trebizond paper İstiklal gave the Greeks of the vilayet and of Bayburt a fortnight); from mid-January 1923 they are forced out, often without their belongings, while their houses are plundered; the whole Orthodox clergy leaves on 17 January, and the Capuchin Fr Cirillo takes the church plate into safe keeping. Turkish government ships carry them to Constantinople twice a week, and they pay their own fares (7.5 Turkish pounds a head from Trebizond). In February 700 families in Trebizond and its suburbs are turned out of their houses. At the Selimiye barracks in Scutari 9,884 refugees are crowded together and 297 die in a week of typhus and smallpox; Greece, having received over 60,000, asks Turkey to stop sending them. Chrysanthos writes that in the exodus of 1923 the metropolis and its archives were plundered, and that the Phrontisterion teacher Filippos Cheimonidis died in Constantinople in 1923 of typhus caught nursing refugees from Trebizond.
disputed: Turkey's statement at Lausanne that the departures were voluntary is under 'What the Turkish sources say' (H6-T10); the Manchester Guardian's correspondent and the Catholic missionaries contradicted it. The notice given is a fortnight (İstiklal), fifteen days (Fr Cirillo), or five days for the last Christians (Mgr Naslian, February 1923). In late December 1922 Fr Cirillo counted about 5,000 people gone and three times as many still in the region (Kyriakidis, p. 91).

title: The Lausanne convention on the exchange of populations
summary: Greece and Turkey agree a compulsory exchange of 'Turkish nationals of the Greek Orthodox religion' in Turkey and 'Greek nationals of the Moslem religion' in Greece: religion, not language, is the criterion. The Greeks of Constantinople, Imbros and Tenedos and the Muslims of Western Thrace are exempt. The convention is retroactive to 18 October 1912, so those who had already fled cannot return, and a Mixed Commission is to oversee departures and property. It takes effect on 1 May 1923.

title: The exchange from the Pontic ports
summary: Under the Mixed Commission the last Orthodox of Pontus, survivors of the deportations and those who came down from the mountains, leave from Samsun, Trebizond, Kerasous and Ordu, mostly by way of Constantinople, for Thessaloniki, Kavala and Piraeus, with quarantine on arrival. The Mixed Commission counted 189,916 Greeks transferred after the convention from all of Turkey (Eddy: 192,356). By the end of 1924 no Orthodox Christians remained in Pontus apart from those who had become Muslims.
disputed: We have not found the names of the ships or the numbers leaving each port in 1923–24. A count of those waiting at the ports in March 1923 survives: about 10,000 at Samsun, 3,000 at Trabzon, 1,500 at Ordu, 500 at Ünye and 300 at Fatsa (US naval diaries, cited by Morris & Ze'evi, p. 463).

title: Muslims from Greece settled in the Pontus
summary: The exchange ran both ways. About 400,000 Muslims came from Greece to Turkey, and the Pontic provinces (Samsun, Ordu, Giresun, Trabzon, Gümüşhane, Amasya, Tokat, Çorum and Sinop) formed one of the zones set aside for them. Çapa's figures, as Kaya and Yılmaz give them, are 18,410 settled in and around Samsun, most of them from Drama and Thessaloniki, 6,800 in Tokat, 5,440 in Amasya, 1,679 in Ordu, 1,594 in Sinop, 1,328 in Trabzon, 748 in Giresun and 543 in Gümüşhane. Few sound houses were left on the Black Sea coast for them; where the Greek houses still stood, as at Karacaköy near Sinop, the newcomers moved into them. Nişanyan's index records immigrants from Greece after 1923 in 130 places of the region covered by this atlas, 107 of which had been Greek Orthodox before 1923: 14 in the Bafra district, 12 in Havza, 11 at Akdağmadeni, 9 in Canik (Samsun), 8 in Niksar and 7 in Tekkeköy.
disputed: The provincial figures are Çapa's, quoted without a date; for Sinop, Kaya and Yılmaz also give 225 families and 920 people settled by the end of the exchange (p. 282). Nişanyan's records count places, not people.

title: The Treaty of Lausanne
summary: The peace treaty between Turkey and the Allies replaces Sèvres. It contains no provision on Pontus or Armenia; the exchange convention is annexed to the settlement.

title: The Refugee Settlement Commission
summary: Set up under a League of Nations protocol and financed by the refugee loan of 1924 (£12,300,000 nominal, issued at 88%, 7% nominal interest), the autonomous commission settles refugee farmers on land left by departing Muslims and on large estates, mostly in Macedonia, and builds urban quarters.

title: The Greek census of 1928
summary: The census counts 1,221,849 refugees, about a fifth of Greece's population; 45% of the population of Macedonia were refugees. 182,169 refugees give Pontus as their origin, another 47,091 the Caucasus (most of whom were also Pontic Greeks) and 11,435 Russia: 240,695 together. The census volume on place of birth, religion and language (vol. IV, 1935) counts 159,945 inhabitants born in Pontus (77,766 men, 82,179 women), 33,690 born in the Caucasus and 12,643 in Russia, a different category from 'refugees from Pontus' (Table 6, Introduction, p. κ΄). It counts 191,254 people of Turkish mother tongue, 103,642 of them Orthodox and 86,506 Muslim, and comments that the Orthodox Turkish-speakers are Greeks by national consciousness, expelled from Turkey for that reason (Table 12, p. κη΄). It does not cross the language of refugees with their place of origin, so it does not say how many of the Pontic refugees were Turkish-speaking.
disputed: The split of the 182,169 into 17,528 who arrived before 1922 and 164,641 after is Mavrogordatos's table (1983), reproduced by the Foundation of the Hellenic World, which calls it based on his estimates; most Caucasus refugees (32,421 of 47,091) had come before 1922. Vergeti considers the Pontic figure an undercount and suggests over 230,000; about 75,000 refugees of all origins had died in Greece by 1928, and some had moved abroad.

title: The NKVD's 'Greek operation'
summary: NKVD directive 50215 (11 December 1937) orders the arrest of Greeks across the USSR as suspected spies and nationalists. Greek schools, theatres, newspapers and the Greek national districts are closed, and men over 16 are arrested to fill quotas in the Black Sea regions, Krasnodar and Georgia. About 20,000 Soviet Greeks leave for Greece in 1938.
disputed: Deaths: about 15,000 shot and 20,000 sent to the Gulag (Dzhukha); about 50,000 dead (Agtzidis). Gkikas gives much lower figures.

title: Wartime deportations of Soviet Greeks
summary: On 29 May 1942, 1,402 Greeks of Krasnodar krai are sent east. A State Defence Committee decree of 2 June 1944 deports 15,040 Greeks from the Crimea, 8,300 from Krasnodar and Rostov, and 16,375 from Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan to Kazakhstan and the Urals.

title: The 1949 deportation ('Volna') and release in 1956
summary: A Council of Ministers decree of 29 May 1949 removes 'unreliable elements' from the Black Sea and Transcaucasian border zones; in June 1949 Greeks, many of them Pontic refugees of 1918–22 holding Greek or Turkish papers, are deported from Abkhazia, Georgia, Krasnodar and elsewhere to Kazakhstan and Central Asia. The Greek population of Abkhazia falls from 34,621 (1939) to 9,101 (1959). Restrictions are lifted in 1956. A Russian decree of 21 April 2014 rehabilitated the Greeks deported from the Crimea, with the Armenians, Bulgarians, Crimean Tatars and Germans. About 100,000 Soviet Greeks emigrated to Greece after 1990.
disputed: Greeks deported in 1949: 27,000 (de Waal), 31,386 (Kaiser), 36,000 (Kaya). Across 1942–49, 70,000–80,000 uprooted; at least 15,000 dead (Gkikas 2007).

title: Those who stayed: the Romeyka-speaking Muslims
summary: Because the exchange went by religion, the Greek-speaking Muslims of the Of and Sürmene valleys and of Tonya, whose ancestors converted in the Ottoman centuries, stayed in Turkey. Their Pontic dialect, Romeyka, is still spoken, mostly by older people, around Çaykara and Tonya; it keeps features lost in the Christian Pontic of Greece.

title: The liturgy at Soumela
summary: With the permission of the Turkish government, Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew celebrates the Dormition liturgy at the Soumela monastery, the first there since 1923, before Pontic Greeks from Greece, Russia and Georgia and local visitors. It was repeated in later years, with interruptions during restoration.

title: Turkey at Lausanne: the Trebizond departures were voluntary
summary: Turkey told the Lausanne conference that the departures of Greeks from Trebizond in January-February 1923 were voluntary.
counter_evidence: The Manchester Guardian's Constantinople correspondent (24 Feb 1923) disputed it: a notice in the Trebizond paper İstiklal ordered the Greeks to leave within a fortnight, and they were forced out, often without their belongings. Catholic witnesses in Trebizond say the same: the new vali ordered the Greeks and Armenians to leave within fifteen days, their houses were plundered as they left (Fr Cirillo, via Kyriakides & Nikoloudis 2026, p. 85), and the last Christians were turned out of their homes and given five days to board a Turkish ship (Mgr Naslian, 15 Feb 1923, p. 98).
sources_primary: Turkish statement at Lausanne, as reported by the Manchester Guardian, 24 Feb 1923
